Together they form:

A real distributed system
N+1 PROBLEM (DATABASE + ORM PERFORMANCE BUG)
🧱 1. CORE IDEA (VERY SIMPLE FIRST)

❌ What is N+1 problem?

It happens when:

You execute 1 query, then inside a loop you execute N more queries

So total:

1 + N queries

📌 Example

You want:

All users and their posts

❌ BAD WAY (N+1)

SELECT*FROM users;

Then for each user:

SELECT*FROM postsWHERE user_id=1;
SELECT*FROM postsWHERE user_id=2;
SELECT*FROM postsWHERE user_id=3;
...

🔥 Result:

If you have:

  • 1 query for users
  • 100 users → 100 queries

👉 Total = 101 queries

🧠 2. WHY THIS IS EXTREMELY BAD

Because now you already know DB internals:

Each query causes:

  • parser
  • planner
  • executor
  • buffer manager access
  • possible disk I/O
  • network round trip

🚨 Real cost model:

1 query ≠ small cost
1 query = full database pipeline

So N+1 becomes:

N × full DB execution overhead
🧱 3. ROOT CAUSE (IMPORTANT)

N+1 is NOT a database problem.

It is caused by:

👉 ORM behavior

Example in Django / Hibernate / Sequelize:

users=User.findAll()

foruserinusers:
posts=user.posts# triggers query

🧠 Why ORM does this:

Because:

  • it loads relations lazily (Lazy Loading)
  • tries to save memory
  • but ignores query cost
🧱 4. CONNECTION TO YOUR DB KNOWLEDGE

Now map it to your mental model:

Each loop query triggers:

Parser → Planner → Executor → Buffer Manager → Disk

So instead of:

  • 1 execution pipeline

You get:

  • N full pipelines

💥 That’s why it explodes performance

Even if each query is fast:

1ms × 100 = 100ms
BUT real world:
disk + network + locks → 500ms+ or seconds
🧱 5. HOW DATABASE SEES IT

Database does NOT know it is “N+1 problem”.

It just sees:

many independent queries

No optimization across queries.

🧱 6. SOLUTION (CRITICAL)

✅ 1. JOIN (BEST CASE)

SELECT users.*, posts.*
FROM users
LEFTJOIN postsON posts.user_id= users.id;

👉 single query

✅ 2. EAGER LOADING (ORM FIX)

User.findAll({
include:Posts
})

✅ 3. BATCH QUERY (SECOND BEST)

SELECT*FROM postsWHERE user_idIN (1,2,3,4,...)
🧠 7. WHY IN CLAUSE IS FAST

Because now DB:

  • uses index lookup once
  • avoids repeated planner execution
  • reduces network round trips
🧱 8. DEEP INTERNAL VIEW (IMPORTANT)

Compare:

❌ N+1

100 queries →
100 planners →
100 executor runs →
100 buffer manager lookups →
100 network round trips

✅ JOIN

1 query →
1 planner →
1 execution pipeline →
streamed results
🧱 9. WHY THIS HAPPENS EVEN WITH INDEXES

Even if posts.user_id is indexed:

👉 still slow because:

  • query overhead dominates
  • not index problem
  • execution repetition problem
🧠 10. SENIOR INSIGHT (IMPORTANT)

N+1 is NOT about:

  • SQL skill
  • index optimization

It is about:

❌ “execution repetition explosion”
🔥 FINAL MENTAL MODEL

Bad design:

loop → query → loop → query

Good design:

1 query → batch → stream result

🚀 CONNECTION TO EVERYTHING

Now you can connect:

  • Planner → runs repeatedly in N+1
  • Executor → repeated full pipeline
  • Buffer manager → repeated page fetch
  • WAL → repeated unnecessary writes
  • Network → biggest hidden cost
🧠 FINAL SUMMARY

N+1 problem =

“Application-level query explosion caused by lazy loading, resulting in repeated full database execution pipelines”
🧱 DATABASE MIGRATIONS — DEEP DIVE
🧠 1. WHAT IS A MIGRATION?

Simple definition:

A migration is a version-controlled change to the database structure

Not data queries.

It changes:

  • tables
  • columns
  • indexes
  • constraints
  • relationships

🧩 Think of it like Git, but for schema:

v1 → v2 → v3 → v4

Each version = a migration file.

🧱 2. WHY MIGRATIONS EXIST (REAL PROBLEM)

Without migrations:

  • everyone edits DB manually ❌
  • no history ❌
  • no rollback ❌
  • team conflicts ❌

🧠 Problem scenario:

Developer A:

ALTERTABLE usersADD ageINT;

Developer B:

ALTERTABLE usersADD birthdateDATE;

👉 Now environments diverge

🧱 3. MIGRATION SYSTEM CORE IDEA

Every migration has:

UP → apply change
DOWN → rollback change

Example:

UP migration:

ALTERTABLE usersADDCOLUMN ageINT;

DOWN migration:

ALTERTABLE usersDROPCOLUMN age;
🧱 4. HOW MIGRATIONS RUN IN REAL SYSTEMS

Migration system keeps a table:

schema_migrations

Example:

versionapplied_at
00110:00
00210:05

🧠 Meaning:

DB tracks which migrations already ran

So it never runs same migration twice.

🧱 5. REAL EXECUTION FLOW

When you run:

migrate up

System does:

1. Read migration files
2. Check schema_migrations table
3. Find missing migrations
4. Execute SQL in order
5. Record version in table
🧱 6. IMPORTANT REALITY: MIGRATIONS ARE NOT ATOMIC BY DEFAULT

⚠️ Big problem:

If migration fails halfway:

ALTERTABLE usersADDCOLUMN ageINT;
ALTERTABLE usersDROPCOLUMN name;-- fails here

👉 DB is now in partial state

🧠 Solution:

Use:

  • transactions (if supported)
  • or safe migration design
🧱 7. MIGRATION + TRANSACTION LINK (IMPORTANT)

Many systems wrap migration in:

BEGIN;
-- migration
COMMIT;

But NOT ALL operations are safe inside transactions:

  • index creation (sometimes)
  • large table rewrites
  • locking operations
🧱 8. TYPES OF MIGRATIONS (VERY IMPORTANT IN REAL SYSTEMS)

🟢 1. ADDITIVE MIGRATION (SAFE)

  • add column
  • add table
  • add index

👉 backward compatible

🔴 2. DESTRUCTIVE MIGRATION (DANGEROUS)

  • drop column
  • rename column
  • change type

👉 breaks old code

🟡 3. DATA MIGRATION

Example:

UPDATE usersSET age= birth_year-2026;

👉 slow + dangerous on large DBs

🧱 9. THE BIGGEST REAL-WORLD PROBLEM: ZERO-DOWNTIME MIGRATIONS

In production:

👉 you cannot stop database

So migrations must be:

  • backward compatible
  • incremental
  • safe under old + new code

Example bad migration:

DROPCOLUMN name;

👉 breaks old app instantly

Correct approach:

Step 1:

ADDCOLUMN new_name TEXT;

Step 2:

Deploy app using both

Step 3:

Backfill data

Step 4:

Remove old column later

🧠 10. WHY MIGRATIONS ARE HARD (REAL ENGINEERING VIEW)

Because they touch:

  • live data
  • locks
  • indexes
  • replication
  • backups
  • WAL logs

⚠️ A bad migration can:

  • lock entire table
  • block production traffic
  • trigger replication lag
  • cause downtime
🧱 11. MIGRATIONS VS SQL SCRIPTS
SQL ScriptMigration
manualautomated
no historyversioned
riskycontrolled
ad-hocrepeatable
🧱 12. HOW MIGRATIONS CONNECT TO DB INTERNALS (IMPORTANT)

Now connect to your deep DB model:

When migration runs:

1. Planner involved

  • checks schema

2. Executor runs DDL

  • modifies catalog tables

3. WAL logs everything

  • schema changes are logged

4. Buffer manager updates pages

  • system catalogs are cached

🧠 Key insight:

Schema is also data inside database

(Postgres stores schema in system tables)

🧱 13. SYSTEM CATALOG (HIDDEN LAYER)

Example:

pg_table
pg_index
pg_attribute

👉 migrations actually modify THESE tables

🔥 FINAL MENTAL MODEL
Migration system
   ↓
Schema change SQL
   ↓
System catalog update
   ↓
WAL log recorded
   ↓
Buffer manager updates pages
   ↓
Indexes rebuilt if needed

🧠 FINAL SUMMARY

Migration =

“Controlled, versioned evolution of database schema with safety, rollback, and consistency guarantees”

Now you can connect:

  • N+1 → query inefficiency
  • Indexing → performance layer
  • WAL → safety layer
  • MVCC → concurrency layer
  • Migration → schema evolution layer

GENERAL

HASHING — COMPLETE INTERVIEW GUIDE (Backend + JS)

▶️ What is Hashing?

  • Hashing is the process of converting input data of any size into a fixed-size value called a hash using a hash function.
  • Example:
    hash("apple") → 928374
  • Key properties:
    • Deterministic (same input → same output)
    • Fast (O(1) average)
    • Fixed-size output
    • Non-reversible (for good hash functions)
  • Core idea:
    “Hashing maps data to a fixed index for fast access.”

▶️ Why do we need Hashing?

  • Fast data access (O(1) lookup)
  • Efficient storage and retrieval
  • Used in:
    • Databases (indexing)
    • Caching (Redis)
    • Password storage
    • Data deduplication
    • Compilers & interpreters
  • Without hashing:
    • Search → O(n)
  • With hashing:
    • Search → O(1) average

▶️ How do we implement Hashing?

Step-by-step:

  1. Take input (key)
  1. Apply hash function
  1. Convert hash → array index
  1. Store value in that index

Example:

function hash(key, size) {
  let total = 0;
  for (let char of key) {
    total += char.charCodeAt(0);
  }
  return total % size;
}

▶️ In how many ways is Hashing implemented in JavaScript?

JavaScript uses hashing internally in:

  1. *Object **{}
  1. Map
  1. Set

👉 Important:

  • You cannot directly control hashing
  • It is handled internally by engines like V8

▶️ How does Hashing work in Set? Which algorithm?

How it works:

  • Set stores unique values only
  • Internally:
    • Value → hash → index
    • If already exists → ignored
const set = new Set();
set.add("apple");
set.add("apple"); // ignored

Algorithm:

  • Uses hash table internally
  • Uses SameValueZero comparison
    • NaN === NaN (true in Set)
    • +0 === -0

▶️ How does Hashing work in Map? Which algorithm?

How it works:

  • Key → hashed → index → value stored
const map = new Map();
map.set("name", "Ali");

Important details:

  • Keys can be ANY type
  • Objects are compared by reference
map.set({a:1}, "x"); // unique reference

Algorithm:

  • Internally uses hash table
  • Optimized with:
    • dynamic resizing
    • collision handling

▶️ What is a Hash Table?

  • A hash table is a data structure that:
    • Stores key-value pairs
    • Uses hashing to compute index

👉 Structure:

Index → Bucket → Data

▶️ How is a Hash Table stored?

  • Internally:
    • An array
    • Each index = bucket

Example:

[
  0: null,
  1: ["apple", 10],
  2: ["banana", 20],
]

▶️ How does a Hash Table look like?

  • Conceptually:
Key → Hash Function → Index → Value
  • With collisions:
Index 1 → [ ["apple", 10], ["grape", 15] ]

▶️ Real-life implementation examples

  • Password hashing (bcrypt)
  • URL shorteners
  • Caching systems
  • Database indexing
  • Blockchain (hash linking)

▶️ What are Hash Collisions?

  • When:
    hash("apple") = 5
hash("grape") = 5

👉 Two keys → same index

▶️ Why do collisions happen?

  • Limited array size
  • Infinite possible inputs
  • Poor hash function

▶️ How to solve collisions?

1. Chaining

  • Store multiple values in same bucket
[ ["apple", 10], ["grape", 20] ]

2. Open Addressing

  • Find next empty slot

Types:

  • Linear probing
  • Quadratic probing
  • Double hashing

▶️ How are Linked Lists related to Hashing?

  • Used in chaining

Example:

Index 1 → apple → grape → mango

👉 Each bucket = linked list

▶️ Alternatives to Hashing

  • Trees (Binary Search Tree, AVL)
  • Trie
  • Arrays (for small datasets)
  • Skip Lists

👉 Comparison:

  • Hashing → O(1) average
  • Trees → O(log n)

▶️ At least 5 Hashing Algorithms

  1. MD5
  1. SHA-1
  1. SHA-256
  1. SHA-3
  1. MurmurHash
  1. DJB2
  1. Fowler–Noll–Vo (FNV)

▶️ Advanced Insights (Interview GOLD)

  • Worst case complexity → O(n)
  • Good hashing minimizes collisions
  • Load factor affects performance:
    load factor = elements / size
  • Rehashing happens when load factor increases

▶️ One-line Summary (for interview)

“Hashing is a technique that maps data to fixed-size values using a hash function, enabling fast O(1) average access through hash tables while handling collisions using strategies like chaining or probing.”
Q&A
what are currently used hashing algorithms

🔥 HASHING ALGORITHMS (WITH SAMPLES)

▶️ 1. SHA-256 (Cryptographic — Security)

👉 Used in:

  • Password hashing
  • Blockchain
  • HTTPS

Sample (Node.js)

constcrypto=require("crypto");

consthash=crypto
.createHash("sha256")
.update("hello")
.digest("hex");

console.log(hash);

👉 Output:

2cf24dba5fb0a... (fixed length)

👉 Key point:

  • Very secure
  • Slow (on purpose)

▶️ 2. MD5 (OUTDATED but still asked)

👉 Used in:

  • Checksums (NOT security)
constcrypto=require("crypto");

consthash=crypto
.createHash("md5")
.update("hello")
.digest("hex");

console.log(hash);

👉 Interview line:

“MD5 is fast but broken due to collisions.”

▶️ 3. MurmurHash (VERY IMPORTANT for backend)

👉 Used in:

  • Hash tables
  • Databases
  • Caching systems

Simplified JS version:

functionmurmurHash(str) {
leth=0;
for (leti=0;i<str.length;i++) {
h=Math.imul(31,h)+str.charCodeAt(i)|0;
  }
returnh;
}

console.log(murmurHash("hello"));

👉 Why important:

  • Fast
  • Good distribution

▶️ 4. FNV Hash

👉 Used in:

  • Compilers
  • Lightweight hashing
functionfnv1a(str) {
lethash=2166136261;

for (leti=0;i<str.length;i++) {
hash^=str.charCodeAt(i);
hash*=16777619;
  }

returnhash>>>0;
}

console.log(fnv1a("hello"));

👉 Features:

  • Very fast
  • Simple

▶️ 5. DJB2 (Classic Simple Hash)

👉 Used in:

  • Teaching
  • Small systems
functiondjb2(str) {
lethash=5381;

for (leti=0;i<str.length;i++) {
hash= ((hash<<5)+hash)+str.charCodeAt(i);
  }

returnhash;
}

console.log(djb2("hello"));

👉 Insight:

  • Easy to implement
  • Not very strong

▶️ 6. JavaScript Internal Hashing (IMPORTANT)

In engines like V8:

👉 There is NO single exposed algorithm.

Instead:

  • Strings → hashed using optimized internal algorithms
  • Objects → hashed by reference (memory identity)

Example:

constmap=newMap();

constobj1= {a:1};
constobj2= {a:1};

map.set(obj1,"first");
map.set(obj2,"second");

console.log(map.size);// 2 (different references)

👉 Key idea:

  • JS does NOT deep-hash objects

⚡ Real-Life Example (IMPORTANT)

Password Storage

constpassword="mypassword";

consthash=crypto
.createHash("sha256")
.update(password)
.digest("hex");

👉 Store hash, NOT password

Caching (Hash key)

constcacheKey=fnv1a("user_123_profile");

Hash Table Indexing

constindex=djb2("apple")%100;

💣 Interview Killer Explanation

“Different hashing algorithms are used depending on requirements. Cryptographic hashes like SHA-256 are used for security because they are collision-resistant and irreversible, while non-cryptographic hashes like MurmurHash or FNV are optimized for speed and are used in hash tables, databases, and JavaScript engines.”
cryptographic vs non-cryptographic hashing

🔐 What does “cryptographic” mean?

👉 Cryptographic = designed for security

A cryptographic hash function is a hash function that is:

  • Secure
  • Hard to break
  • Safe for sensitive data (passwords, payments, authentication)

⚡ Simple way to understand

  • Normal hashing → fast lookup
  • Cryptographic hashing → protect data

👉 Example:

  • Map/Set → NOT cryptographic
  • Password hashing → MUST be cryptographic

🔥 Properties of Cryptographic Hash Functions

These are the real interview points:

1. Pre-image resistance

Given a hash → you CANNOT find the original input

Example:

hash("password123") → a8f5f...

You cannot reverse it.

2. Collision resistance

Hard to find two inputs with same hash
hash("A") ≠ hash("B")

3. Avalanche effect

Small change → completely different hash
"hello"  → abc123...
"hello1" → f9x82k...

4. Deterministic

Same input → same output (always)

🔥 Which algorithms are cryptographic?

✅ Secure (USED TODAY)

  • SHA-256
  • SHA-512
  • SHA-3

👉 Used in:

  • HTTPS (TLS)
  • Blockchain
  • Password hashing (with salting)

⚠️ Weak / Deprecated

  • MD5
  • SHA-1

👉 Why?

  • Collisions found → not safe

👉 Interview line:

“MD5 and SHA-1 are cryptographic by design but no longer secure.”

❌ NOT Cryptographic (Important contrast)

These are fast but NOT secure:

  • MurmurHash
  • FNV
  • DJB2

👉 Used in:

  • Hash tables
  • Databases
  • JavaScript internals

⚡ Real-world comparison

Use CaseAlgorithm Type
Password storageCryptographic (SHA-256, bcrypt)
Map / SetNon-cryptographic
Caching keysNon-cryptographic
BlockchainCryptographic

💣 Interview-ready answer

“Cryptographic hashing refers to hash functions designed for security. They provide properties like pre-image resistance, collision resistance, and the avalanche effect, making them suitable for sensitive data like passwords and encryption systems. Examples include SHA-256 and SHA-3. In contrast, non-cryptographic hashes like MurmurHash are optimized for speed and used in data structures like hash tables.”

🧠 One sentence memory trick

👉 “Cryptographic = cannot be reversed, cannot be predicted, cannot be collided easily.”

hashing in MAP AND SET

Good — this is the core of hashing interviews. Let’s make it crystal clear.

🔥 How are hashes generated in hash tables?

⚡ Simple answer first:

👉 A hash is generated by applying a hash function to a key, which converts it into a numeric value, then compresses it into an index of an array.

🧠 Step-by-step (how it REALLY works)

▶️ Step 1: Take the input (key)

Example:

"apple"

▶️ Step 2: Convert key into numeric form

Usually:

  • ASCII / Unicode values
  • Bit operations

Example:

'a' → 97
'p' → 112
'p' → 112
'l' → 108
'e' → 101

▶️ Step 3: Apply hash function (mixing)

Simple example hash function:

functionhash(key,size) {
lethash=0;

for (leti=0;i<key.length;i++) {
hash= (hash*31+key.charCodeAt(i))%size;
  }

returnhash;
}

What is happening here?

  • hash * 31 → spreads values (reduces collisions)
  • + charCode → adds character info
  • % size → compresses into array index

▶️ Step 4: Output index

Example:

hash("apple") → 17

Now stored at:

table[17] = "apple"

⚡ Why multiplication (like 31, 33, 37)?

👉 Because:

  • It spreads values better
  • Reduces collisions
  • Works well with primes

This is called:

Polynomial rolling hash idea

💥 Real-world hash generation is more advanced

In real systems (like V8 engine / databases):

They use:

  • Bitwise operations (<<, >>, XOR)
  • Large prime multipliers
  • Randomization seeds
  • MurmurHash-style mixing

🧠 Example: better hash (conceptual)

functionbetterHash(str) {
lethash=5381;

for (leti=0;i<str.length;i++) {
hash= ((hash<<5)+hash)+str.charCodeAt(i);
  }

returnhash;
}

👉 This is DJB2 hash (very famous)

⚡ What happens AFTER hash is generated?

▶️ Step 1: Modulo operation

index = hash % tableSize

▶️ Step 2: Store in bucket

table[index] = value

💣 But what about collisions?

Even with good hashing:

hash("apple") = 5
hash("grape") = 5

So we handle it using:

  • Chaining (linked list)
  • Open addressing

🔥 Final interview answer (say this)

“Hashes in hash tables are generated by applying a hash function to the input key. The key is converted into numeric form (like ASCII values for strings), then processed using operations like multiplication, addition, and bit shifting to distribute values evenly. Finally, the result is compressed using modulo operation to fit into the array size. In real systems, more advanced techniques like bitwise operations and algorithms such as MurmurHash or DJB2 are used to minimize collisions.”
What is Load Factor (VERY IMPORTANT)
Load Factor (VERY IMPORTANT)

What it is:

load factor = number of elements / table size

Why it matters:

  • If load factor increases → collisions increase
  • Performance degrades from O(1) → O(n)

What systems do:

👉 They resize (rehash) the table

What is rehashing

When table gets full:

What happens:

  1. Create bigger array (usually 2x)
  1. Recompute all hashes
  1. Insert again

👉 This is expensive → O(n)

👉 Modern JS engines (like V8)
  • Hybrid structures:
    • hash table (large size)
    • ordered array (small size optimization)
  • Transition between structures depending on size

👉 This is a BIG senior-level detail

“Why is Map faster than Object sometimes?”
  • Better hash handling
No prototype chain lookup

What is “prototype chain lookup”?

In JavaScript, when you access a property, JS looks for it in this order:

  1. Object itself
  1. If not found → its prototype
  1. Then prototype’s prototype
  1. … until null

This is called the prototype chain lookup.

  • Optimized insertion order
  • Engine-level optimizations
are hash tables fixed in size

▶️ 1. Conceptually (theoretical model)

👉 Yes — a basic hash table is usually described as:

  • A fixed-size array
  • Hash function maps keys → array index
table[0..N]

So in theory:

“Hash table = fixed-size array + hash function”

▶️ 2. In real-world systems ❌ NOT fixed

Modern hash tables are dynamic (resizable).

They:

  • Grow when full
  • Shrink when underused
  • Rehash elements when needed

⚡ What actually happens in practice

▶️ Step 1: Start with initial size

Example:

size = 16

▶️ Step 2: Insert elements

As elements increase:

load factor = elements / size

▶️ Step 3: Resize trigger

When load factor gets too high (example > 0.7):

👉 Table is resized

▶️ Step 4: Rehashing happens

  1. Create bigger array (e.g. 32, 64…)
  1. Recompute all hashes
  1. Insert again into new table

💣 Important concept: Rehashing

old table → new bigger table → recompute all keys

👉 This is expensive: O(n) operation

⚡ What about JavaScript?

In JavaScript (Map / Set):

  • Internally dynamic hash tables
  • Managed by engine like V8

👉 You don’t see resizing, but it happens automatically.

🧠 So final answer (interview-ready)

“Hash tables are conceptually defined as fixed-size arrays, but in real-world implementations they are dynamic. When the number of elements grows and the load factor exceeds a threshold, the table is resized and all elements are rehashed into a larger array. This ensures performance stays close to O(1) on average.”

COMPLEXITY
DEFINITION

🚀 1. Complexity Concept (Big-O)

▶️ What is time complexity?

👉 Time complexity = how execution time grows as input grows

We describe it using Big-O notation:

🔥 O(n) vs O(log n)

▶️ 1. O(n) — Linear Time

💡 Meaning:

👉 The operation grows directly with input size

If data doubles → time doubles

⚡ Example

for (leti=0;i<n;i++) {
console.log(i);
}

👉 Steps:

  • n = 10 → 10 operations
  • n = 1000 → 1000 operations

🧠 Real-world examples:

functionbinarySearch(arr,target) {
letleft=0;
letright=arr.length-1;

while (left<=right) {
letmid=Math.floor((left+right)/2);

if (arr[mid]===target)returnmid;
if (arr[mid]<target)left=mid+1;
elseright=mid-1;
  }

return-1;
}
  • Array .find()
  • Linear search in DB (no index)
  • Scanning all users in memory

💣 Key idea:

“Worst case: you check everything”

🔥 2. O(log n) — Logarithmic Time

💡 Meaning:

👉 Each step reduces the problem size by half

If data doubles → time increases very slowly

⚡ Example (Binary Search)

🧠 What is happening?

Each step:

  • cuts search space in half

Example:

1000 → 500 → 250 → 125 → 62 → 31 → 15 → 7 → 3 → 1

Only ~10 steps instead of 1000

⚡ 3. Real-world examples of O(log n)

  • Binary search in sorted array
  • SQL index lookup (B-tree)
  • Database indexing
  • Searching in balanced trees (AVL, Red-Black Tree)

💣 4. Key difference (VERY IMPORTANT)

FeatureO(n)O(log n)
GrowthLinearVery slow
SpeedSlower for large dataVery fast
StrategyScan everythingDivide & conquer
ExampleArray searchBinary search

→ cut in half
→ cut in half

💣 6. Interview-ready answer

“O(n) means linear time complexity where the operation grows proportionally with input size, such as scanning an array. O(log n) means logarithmic time complexity where the input size is reduced by half at each step, like binary search or B-tree lookups in databases. Therefore, O(log n) scales much better for large datasets compared to O(n).”

💣 9. Interview killer explanation

“SQL databases are optimized for structured data and complex relationships using indexing and joins, typically achieving O(log n) performance for filtered queries. NoSQL databases prioritize flexibility and horizontal scaling, often using denormalized data models that allow faster access, sometimes O(1), but may degrade to O(n) without proper indexing. SQL is better for relational integrity and complex queries, while NoSQL is better for high-speed, large-scale, schema-flexible systems.”

💣 What are “complex filters” in databases?

👉 A complex filter is NOT just:

WHERE age=25

It is when filtering involves:

  • multiple conditions
  • nested logic
  • relationships (joins / references)
  • full-text / array / JSON queries
  • range + aggregation + sorting together

🔥 1. Multi-condition filters (AND / OR logic)

SQL example:

SELECT*FROM users
WHERE age>18AND city='Tashkent'ORrole='admin';

👉 Complexity increases because:

  • multiple conditions must be evaluated
  • optimizer decides execution plan

🔥 2. Range queries (VERY COMMON)

SELECT*FROM orders
WHERE priceBETWEEN100AND500;

👉 Harder than equality:

  • cannot always use hash indexing
  • usually uses B-tree (O(log n))

🔥 3. LIKE / pattern matching (expensive)

SELECT*FROM users
WHERE nameLIKE'%ali%';

👉 Why complex:

  • % at start disables index
  • forces full scan → O(n)

🔥 4. JOIN-based filters (VERY IMPORTANT)

SELECT users.name, orders.amount
FROM users
JOIN ordersON users.id= orders.user_id
WHERE orders.amount>100;

👉 Complexity:

  • multiple table scans
  • join algorithm (nested loop / hash join / merge join)

👉 Can become:

  • O(n log n)
  • or even O(n²) worst case

🔥 5. Aggregation filters (GROUP BY / HAVING)

SELECT user_id,COUNT(*)
FROM orders
GROUPBY user_id
HAVINGCOUNT(*)>5;

👉 Why complex:

  • must scan entire dataset
  • then group + compute aggregation

👉 Complexity:

  • O(n) or O(n log n)

🔥 6. Sorting + filtering together

SELECT*FROM products
WHERE price>100
ORDERBY created_atDESC;

👉 This is heavy because:

  • filtering first
  • then sorting (O(n log n))

🔥 7. JSON / nested queries (NoSQL + modern SQL)

MongoDB example:

db.users.find({
"address.city":"Tashkent",
"orders.amount": { $gt:100 }
})

👉 Complexity:

  • nested document traversal
  • index may or may not help

🔥 8. Full-text search (advanced filtering)

SELECT*FROM articles
WHEREMATCH(content) AGAINST('database indexing');

👉 Why complex:

  • tokenization
  • ranking (TF-IDF or similar)
  • inverted index usage

JOINmultiple tablesO(n log n) or worse

⚡ Key interview insight

👉 “Filtering becomes complex when it involves:

  • scanning large datasets
  • combining multiple datasets (JOINs)
  • or doing computation (GROUP BY, ORDER BY, LIKE, full-text search)”

“Complex filters in databases include operations beyond simple equality, such as range queries, pattern matching, joins, aggregations, sorting, and full-text search. These operations often require scanning large portions of data or combining multiple datasets, which increases complexity from O(1)/O(log n) to O(n) or O(n log n), depending on indexing and query structure.”

⚡ 7. Real-world architecture insight

👉 Modern systems often use BOTH:

  • SQL → core relational data
  • NoSQL → JSON-heavy dynamic data

Example:

  • User preferences → JSON in SQL or NoSQL
  • Messages → NoSQL
💣 8. Interview killer answer

“SQL databases support JSON storage using JSON or JSONB types, allowing semi-structured data to coexist with relational models. They provide strong consistency and support indexing on JSON fields, but performance can degrade with complex queries. NoSQL databases store JSON natively as documents, making them more efficient for flexible and nested data access, but they sacrifice strict schema and relational integrity. The choice depends on whether the system prioritizes structure and consistency (SQL) or flexibility and scalability (NoSQL).”

COMPLEXITY
NOSQL

🚀 Why NoSQL can be O(1) or O(log n)

▶️ 1. Hash-based lookup (O(1) average)

Some NoSQL systems (like key-value stores e.g. Redis):

key → hash → direct bucket → value

👉 Steps:

  • compute hash
  • jump directly to memory location

Complexity:

  • Average: O(1)
  • Worst: O(n) (collisions)

▶️ 2. Tree-based NoSQL (O(log n))

MongoDB uses B-Trees for indexes

So:

search → tree traversal → O(log n)

💡 So NoSQL is not always O(1)

It depends on engine:

  • Redis → O(1)
  • MongoDB indexed → O(log n)
  • MongoDB unindexed → O(n)
SQL

🧠 Why SQL is usually O(log n)

SQL databases like PostgreSQL / MySQL use:

👉 B-Tree / B+ Tree indexes

▶️ How it works:

Instead of scanning all rows:

root → internal nodes → leaf → value

Each step:

👉 cuts search space significantly

Complexity:

  • Search = O(log n)

💣 Why SQL is NOT O(1)

Because:

  • Data is NOT directly addressed by hash
  • It must preserve:
    • ordering
    • range queries
    • sorting
    • joins

👉 Hash tables cannot efficiently support:

  • BETWEEN queries
  • ORDER BY
  • range scans

So SQL prefers trees over hashing

⚡ Key reasoning difference

🟨 NoSQL (fast path)

👉 Designed for:

  • direct key lookup
  • document retrieval
  • horizontal scaling

So:

key → hash → direct access

✔ can be O(1)

🟦 SQL (structured path)

👉 Designed for:

  • relationships
  • range queries
  • ordered data

So:

tree traversal → structured navigation → O(log n)

💣 1-line intuition (VERY IMPORTANT)

👉 NoSQL optimizes direct access → hashing → O(1)

👉 SQL optimizes structure + range queries → trees → O(log n)

⚡ Real-world truth (what seniors say)

ClaimReality
NoSQL = O(1)Only for key-value stores
SQL = O(log n)Only when indexed
Both = O(n)when no index exists

💣 Interview-ready answer

“NoSQL databases can achieve O(1) average complexity when using hash-based key-value lookups, such as in Redis, because the key is directly mapped to memory using hashing. Some NoSQL systems like MongoDB use B-tree indexes, resulting in O(log n) operations. SQL databases typically rely on B-tree or B+ tree indexes to maintain ordered data and support range queries, which leads to O(log n) complexity. SQL does not use hashing for indexing because it needs to support sorting and range-based queries efficiently, which hash tables cannot handle.”

GIT CHERRY PICK
DEFINITION
git cherry-pick is a powerful command that enables arbitrary Git commits to be picked by reference and appended to the current working HEAD. Cherry picking is the act of picking a commit from a branch and applying it to another. git cherry-pick can be useful for undoing changes. For example, say a commit is accidently made to the wrong branch. You can switch to the correct branch and cherry-pick the commit to where it should belong.
PRACTICE
WILL it create new commit

Yes — cherry-pick creates a new commit.

Why?

Because Git does not copy the original commit, it:

  • takes the changes (diff)
  • applies them again on your branch
  • creates a new commit with a new hash

Example:

Original branch:

A --- B --- C

You cherry-pick C into another branch:

feature: A --- B --- C'

Key point:

  • C = original commit
  • C' = new commit (same code, different hash)
commands
  • git cherry-pick <commit-hash>
  • git cherry-pick --continue
  • git cherry-pick --abort

  • duplicated data

OSI layers-(Open System Interconnection)
Q&A

🔁 Git / Version Control

What is the size of the TCP header without options?

Minimum TCP header = 20 bytes (UDP header = 8 bytes).

  1. Can rebase cause duplicate commits?
    👉 Yes, if the same changes are introduced via different commit paths.
  1. When does rebase cause duplicates?
    👉 When rebased commits and original commits are both merged/applied again.
  1. Does cherry-pick create a new commit?
    👉 Yes, it creates a new commit with a new hash.

🌐 Networking / Signals

  1. How is binary converted to signals?
    👉 By modulating a carrier wave (changing amplitude, frequency, or phase).
  1. How does modulation work?
    👉 It encodes 0/1 by modifying properties of a signal wave.
  1. How are multiple signals separated?
    👉 By using different frequency, time slots, or codes.
  1. Is frequency mainly used?
    👉 No, modern systems use frequency + time + coding together.
  1. How do we know how many bits are in a signal?
    👉 By dividing signal using fixed time intervals (bit duration).
  1. How is bit interval decided?
    👉 It is defined by the data rate (bits per second).
  1. Data rate table?
    👉 Bit interval = 1 / data rate (faster speed = smaller interval).

📡 OSI / Layers

  1. Does Data Link control duplex mode?
    👉 No, duplex is determined by hardware/network design, not per connection.
  1. Simplex, half, full duplex?
    👉 One-way, two-way alternately, and two-way simultaneously.
  1. Is Data Link node-to-node delivery?
    👉 Yes, it handles delivery between directly connected devices.
  1. Does data skip Physical layer in same network?
    👉 No, all data always passes through Physical layer.
  1. Does Data Link add MAC address?
    👉 Yes, it adds source and destination MAC in frames.
  1. How is source MAC known?
    👉 It is taken directly from the device’s NIC hardware.
  1. How do we find another device’s MAC?
    👉 Using ARP (broadcast request and reply).
  1. ARP flow?
    👉 Broadcast request → reply → store MAC → send frame.
  1. Is IP also used?
    👉 Yes, IP identifies destination, MAC is used for local delivery.
  1. How do we get IP?
    👉 Usually from DHCP server or manual configuration.
  1. 7 OSI layers?
    👉 Application → Physical (top to bottom stack).
  1. Is Physical layer only in routers?
    👉 No, it exists in every network device.
  1. Does Data Link “transfer” data from Physical?
    👉 No, Physical sends bits; Data Link frames/unframes them.

🌐 TCP / WebSocket

  1. Does Data Link decide direction after TCP?
    👉 No, TCP already provides full-duplex communication.
  1. Is WebSocket full duplex?
    👉 Yes, both sides can send data simultaneously.

📡 Signals / Modem

  1. How does modem convert 0/1?
    👉 By encoding bits onto a carrier wave.
  1. How are bits separated from signal?
    👉 By using clock timing and encoding rules.
  1. What is carrier wave?
    👉 A base wave whose properties are modified to carry data.

🧠 IP / MAC / Flow

  1. How do we know MAC of another laptop?
    👉 Using ARP request in the local network.
  1. How do we know IP of a device?
    👉 Through DHCP, configuration, or DNS resolution.
  1. Full flow IP → MAC → send data?
    👉 IP identifies target, ARP finds MAC, frame is sent via Physical layer.

🔌 Data Link concept

  1. What is node-to-node delivery?
    👉 Communication between directly connected devices using MAC addresses.

🌐 OSI basics

  1. Are there 7 OSI layers?
    👉 Yes, from Application (top) to Physical (bottom).
1. Physical Layer
DEFINITION
  • Responsible for transfering raw data bits between the nodes of endpoints
  • Handles physical and electrical data transmission
  • Includes cables, connectors, plugs, and receivers
  • Transfers raw bits between devices
  • Defines hardware standards and signal types
FUNCTIONALITY
encoding
converts data into signals that can travel through wires, fiber optics, or wireless channels (encoding)
decoding
turns these signals back into data at the receiver (decoding).
modem
definition

 Short for MOdulator-DEModulator. It is the single most common device that handles both tasks to connect your home to the internet.

modulation / modulator
converting the 010101 to signal
demodulation/demodulator

converting the singals into 010101001

carrier_vawe

6

  • Change height of the wave

Example:

  • 1 → high amplitude
  • 0 → low amplitude

👉 So bits are encoded as strong vs weak signal

how does it seperate signals like signal one signal two?
  • 📡 Cable / DSL / Radio → often frequency (FDM)
  • 🌐 Modern networks (WiFi, 4G/5G) → combination
    • frequency + time + encoding (codes)
If the signal is continuous, how do we know where one bit ends and the next begins?

👉 “Bits are determined by time intervals, not signal length — a long signal is split into multiple bits based on the data rate.”

how we will decide the interval

👉 You don’t “decide” the interval dynamically

👉 It is predefined by the data rate (bit rate)

👉 Then:

  • 1 bit = 1 / 1,000,000 sec = 1 microsecond

Layer 1 protocols
  • Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) : Widely used for wired networks.
  • Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) : For wireless communication.
  • Bluetooth (IEEE 802.15.1) : Short-range wireless communication.
  • USB (Universal Serial Bus) : For connecting devices over short distances.
Need of Physical Layer in Security
  • Cable Tapping: Hackers can intercept data by directly connecting to network cables.
  • Physical Access: If someone gets into server rooms or hardware areas without permission, they can steal or damage equipment.
  • Wireless Signal Interception: Attackers can capture Wi-Fi signals from outside using special tools.
  • Hardware Manipulation: Someone might tamper with physical devices like routers or USB ports to secretly install harmful software.
Q&A

🌐 Networking / Signals

  1. How is binary converted to signals?
    👉 By modulating a carrier wave (changing amplitude, frequency, or phase).
  1. How does modulation work?
    👉 It encodes 0/1 by modifying properties of a signal wave.
  1. How are multiple signals separated?
    👉 By using different frequency, time slots, or codes.
  1. Is frequency mainly used?
    👉 No, modern systems use frequency + time + coding together.
  1. How do we know how many bits are in a signal?
    👉 By dividing signal using fixed time intervals (bit duration).
  1. How is bit interval decided?
    👉 It is defined by the data rate (bits per second).
  1. Data rate table?
    👉 Bit interval = 1 / data rate (faster speed = smaller interval).
2. Data Link layer
RESPONSIBILITY
  • Responsible for the node-to-node delivery of data within the same local network.
  • Major role is to ensure error-free transmission of information.
  • Also responsible for encoding, decoding, and organizing the outgoing and incoming data.
  • Considered as the most complex layer of the OSI model as it hides all the underlying complexities of the hardware from the other above layers.
Logical Link Control (LLC)
RESPONSIBILITY
This sublayer of the data link layer deals with multiplexing, the flow of data among applications and other services, and LLC is responsible for providing error messages and acknowledgments as well.
Media Access Control (MAC):
Responsibility
MAC sublayer manages the device's interaction, responsible for addressing frames, and also controls physical media access. The data link layer receives the information in the form of packets from the Network layer, it divides packets into frames and sends those frames bit-by-bit to the underlying physical layer.
acquiring MAC address in IN LANs

🧠 STEP 1: You only know IP

  • You want to send data to:
    • IP = 192.168.1.20
  • MAC is unknown

📢 STEP 2: ARP Request (Broadcast)

Your laptop asks everyone:

👉 “Who has 192.168.1.20?”

  • Sent to:
    • MAC = FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF (everyone in LAN)

🙋 STEP 3: ARP Reply (Unicast)

Target laptop responds:

👉 “I have that IP”

👉 “My MAC = AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF”

💾 STEP 4: Store in ARP Table

Your laptop saves:

192.168.1.20 → AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF

📦 STEP 5: Create Data Frame

Now Data Link layer builds frame:

  • Source MAC = your laptop MAC
  • Destination MAC = target laptop MAC

⚡ STEP 6: Physical Transmission

  • Frame becomes electrical / radio signals
  • Sent through switch/router/cable

📥 STEP 7: Receiver gets it

  • Checks MAC address
  • If match → accepts frame
  • Passes data up to IP → TCP → App

🧠 FINAL FLOW (1 line memory)

👉 IP used to identify destination → ARP finds MAC → frame created → Physical layer sends signals → receiver accepts by MAC

💣 Interview version:

👉 “To send data in a local network, the device uses ARP to resolve the destination IP into a MAC address, stores it in the ARP cache, then encapsulates the data into an Ethernet frame and sends it via the Physical layer.”

Devices
1 - Switch
  • A switch is a key device in the Data Link Layer.
  • It uses MAC addresses to forward data frames to the correct device within a network.
  • Works in local area networks (LANs) to connect multiple devices.
2. Bridge
  • A bridge connects two or more LANs, creating a single, unified network.
  • Operates at the Data Link Layer by forwarding frames based on MAC addresses.
  • Used to reduce network traffic and segment a network.
3. Network Interface Card (NIC)
  • A NIC is a hardware component in devices like computers and printers.
  • Responsible for adding the MAC address to frames and ensuring proper communication with the network.
  • Operates at the Data Link Layer by prep
4. Wireless Access Point (WAP)
  • A WAP allows wireless devices to connect to a wired network.
  • Operates at the Data Link Layer by managing wireless MAC addresses.
  • Uses protocols like Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) to communicate with devices.
5. Layer 2 Switches
  • These are specialized switches that only operate at Layer 2, unlike multi-layer switches.
  • Responsible for frame forwarding using MAC address tables.
Note: The Data Link Layer can be targeted by attacks like MAC spoofing or ARP poisoning. Understanding how devices and frames operate at this layer helps detect and mitigate such threats.
Limitations of Data Link Layer
  • Limited Scope: It operates only within a local network and cannot handle end-to-end communication across different networks.
  • Increased Overhead: Adding headers, trailers, and redundant data (for error correction) increases the size of transmitted data.
  • Error Handling Dependency: While it can detect and correct some errors, it relies on upper layers for handling more complex issues.
  • No Routing Capability: The Data Link Layer cannot make routing decisions. It only ensures delivery within the same network segment.
  • Resource Usage: Flow control and error correction mechanisms may consume extra processing power and memory
Applications of Data Link Layer
  • Local Area Networks (LANs): Enables reliable communication between devices within a local network using protocols like Ethernet (IEEE 802.3).
  • Wireless Networks (Wi-Fi): Manages communication between devices in wireless networks via protocols like IEEE 802.11 hence, handling media access and error control.
  • Switches and MAC Addressing: Facilitates the operation of switches by using MAC addresses to forward data frames to the correct device within the network.
  • Point-to-Point Connections: Used in protocols like PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) to establish and manage direct communication between two nodes.

3. Network Layer (Layer 3)
OVERAL
  • Handles logical (IP) addressing of devices
  • Determines optimal routing paths between networks
  • Enables host-to-host communication across multiple networks
  • Takes segments from transport layer
  • Adds IP header (source + destination IP)
  • Wraps them into packets
RESPONSIBILITIES
  • Logical Addressing: Assigns unique IP addresses to devices, ensuring accurate identification and communication across networks.
  • Packetization: Encapsulates transport layer segments into packets for efficient transmission.
  • Host-to-Host Delivery: Ensures reliable delivery of packets from the sender to the intended receiver across diverse networks.
  • Forwarding: Moves packets from the input interface of a router to the appropriate output interface based on the destination IP.
  • Routing: Determines the optimal path for packets to travel across multiple networks using routing algorithms and protocols.
  • Fragmentation and Reassembly: Splits large packets into smaller fragments to match the maximum transmission unit (MTU) of a network, and reassembles them at the destination.
  • Subnetting: Divides larger networks into smaller subnetworks for efficient addressing and traffic management.
  • Network Address Translation (NAT): Maps private IPs to public IPs for internet communication, conserving address space and adding security.
(MTU) maximum transmission unit
  • amount of data one packet can have
  • it is 1500 bytes which is 1500*8
IMAGES
DEVICES


👉 Network layer = routing between different networks using IP addresses

1. Router (MOST IMPORTANT)

2. Layer 3 Switch (Multilayer switch)

3. Gateway (concept device)

Protocols
IP (Internet Protocol - IPv4/IPv6):
ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol):

Sends error reports and diagnostic messages (e.g., destination unreachable, ping).

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol): 

Maps IP addresses to MAC addresses within a local network.

RARP (Reverse Address Resolution Protocol)

Retrieves a device’s IP address using its MAC address (largely obsolete).

NAT (Network Address Translation):

Converts private IP addresses to public IPs, conserving addresses and improving security.

IPSec (Internet Protocol Security):

Secures IP communication through encryption and authentication.

MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching):

Uses labels to forward packets efficiently and manage traffic.

Routers shares and stores routing tables

Each router stores:

  • destination network
  • next hop
  • hop count

Every 30 seconds:

  • each router sends its entire routing table to neighbors
Routing Protocols
  • RIP (Routing Information Protocol): Distance-vector protocol using hop count to select routes.
  • OSPF (Open Shortest Path First): Link-state protocol that computes the shortest path using network topology.
  • BGP (Border Gateway Protocol): Path-vector protocol that routes data between autonomous systems on the internet.
Advantages of the Network Layer
  • Enables end-to-end communication across multiple networks.
  • Supports scalability by allowing subnetting and hierarchical addressing.
  • Efficiently routes packets using shortest-path and dynamic routing algorithms.
  • Provides inter-networking by connecting heterogeneous networks.
Limitations of the Network Layer
  • No flow control mechanism; congestion may occur if too many datagrams are in transit.
  • Limited error control; mainly relies on upper layers for reliability.
  • Routers may drop packets under heavy load, leading to possible data loss.
  • Fragmentation increases processing overhead and may affect performance.

💻 What it looks like (simple idea)

5

Destination        Next Hop

Will All network devices work together

👉 Network devices do NOT all act at once

👉 They are used based on destination and network boundaries

🌐 What happens in a LAN vs outside LAN

4

🔹 1. If destination is in SAME LAN

Example:

  • PC A → PC B (same WiFi)

👉 What happens:

  • Uses Switch (Layer 2)
  • Uses MAC address
  • NO router involved

✔ Flow:

PC A → Switch → PC B

🔹 2. If destination is OUTSIDE LAN (Internet)

Example:

  • PC → google.com

👉 What happens:

  • Uses Router (Gateway)
  • Uses IP address
  • Switch is still used inside LAN, but router is needed next

PC → Switch → Router (Gateway) → Internet

🔹 3. What is Gateway?

  • It is the exit point of your network
  • Used when destination is NOT in local subnet
what it does and does not

1. 📍 Logical addressing

  • Uses IP address
  • Identifies source and destination host

2. 🧭 Routing (YES — next hop only)

  • Chooses next router
  • Uses routing table

3. 🔁 Packet forwarding (hop-by-hop)

  • Sends packet from router to router

4. ⏳ TTL (Time To Live)

  • Prevents infinite loops
  • Decreases at each hop

5. ✂️ Fragmentation (sometimes)

  • Splits packets if MTU is too small

❌ What Network layer does NOT do

  • No retransmission
  • No reliability guarantee
  • No ordering of packets
  • No connection management
4.Transport layer
DEFINITION
The Transport Layer is the OSI Layer 4 responsible for providing reliable, efficient, and ordered end-to-end communication between applications on different hosts.
OVERAL
  • Operates at Layer 4 (Transport Layer) of the OSI model
  • Enables process-to-process communication using port numbers
  • Ensures reliability through error control, sequencing, and retransmission
  • Supports flow control to prevent receiver overload
  • Uses protocols like TCP, UDP, and SCTP for different application needs
RESPONSIBILITY
  • Operates at Layer 4 (Transport Layer) of the OSI model
  • Enables process-to-process communication using port numbers
  • Ensures reliability through error control, sequencing, and retransmission
  • Supports flow control to prevent receiver overload
  • Uses protocols like TCP, UDP, and SCTP for different application needs
USAGE
  • Implemented only in end systems, not in intermediate routers.
  • Uses port numbers to identify sending and receiving applications.
  • Supports process-to-process delivery, enabling multiple applications to share a single network connection.
  • Performs multiplexing and demultiplexing using port numbers to direct data to the correct process.
  • Divides data from upper layers into segments (TCP) or datagrams (UDP) and adds necessary headers.
  • Handles error detection, retransmission, and sequencing to maintain reliable communication.
  • Coordinates flow control to ensure the receiver is not overloaded.
  • Communicates with the Network Layer, which handles addressing and routing, to send data across networks.
  • At the receiving end, it remove

VISUAL
3-Way Handshake

The 3-Way Handshake ensures both client and server are ready before data transmission begins:

Step 1: SYN (Client -> Server)

  • Client sends a TCP segment with SYN=1, including its ISN (Initial Sequence Number).
  • Marks the request to initiate a connection

Step 2: SYN‑ACK (Server -> Client)

  • Server replies with SYN=1 & ACK=1, containing its own ISN and ACK = client_ISN + 1.
  • Confirms receipt of client’s SYN and initiates its own sync

Step 3: ACK (Client -> Server)

  • Client sends an ACK=1 segment with ACK = server_ISN + 1.
  • Completes synchronization; connection enters ESTABLISHED state
What is QUIC?
KEY IDEA


QUIC = one connection with many streams

DETAILS

👉 QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections) is a modern transport protocol built on top of UDP, designed to replace TCP + TLS for web communication.

🔹 Simple idea

👉 QUIC =

TCP + TLS + HTTP/2 features, but built over UDP

🔥 Why QUIC was created

TCP has problems:

  • Slow handshake (TCP + TLS = 2 separate handshakes)
  • Head-of-line blocking
  • Hard to improve (kernel-level protocol)

👉 QUIC fixes these at the user space level

🔹 Key features of QUIC

✔ 1. Faster connection setup

  • Combines transport + encryption handshake
  • Usually 1 RTT or 0-RTT connection setup

✔ 2. Built-in encryption

  • TLS 1.3 is integrated
  • Every QUIC connection is encrypted by default

✔ 3. No head-of-line blocking

  • Multiple independent streams
  • If one stream loses packet → others continue

✔ 4. Runs on UDP

  • UDP gives flexibility
  • QUIC handles reliability itself

✔ 5. Connection migration

👉 You can change network (WiFi → mobile data) without dropping connection

🔥 Simple comparison

FeatureTCPQUIC
BaseTCPUDP
EncryptionSeparate (TLS)Built-in
StreamsSingle streamMultiple streams
Head-of-line blockingYesNo
Connection speedSlowerFaster

🔹 Where QUIC is used?

👉 Mainly in modern web:

  • 🌐 HTTP/3 (runs on QUIC)
  • YouTube
  • Google Search
  • Chrome / Chromium browsers
  • Cloud services (Google, Cloudflare)
A stream = a logical sequence of data that can be sent and received independently within one connection.


Protocols
1. Transmission Control Protocol(TCP)
  • TCP is connection-oriented Protocol.
  • TCP is reliable protocol.
  • As TCP is connection-oriented protocol, so first the connection is established between two ends and then data is transferred and then the connection is terminated after all data being sent.
2. User Datagram Protocol (UDP)
  • UDP is not reliable protocol
  • The protocol UDP is connectionless.
  • When speed and size are more important than security and dependability, this kind of protocol is employed.
  • The data from the higher layer is supplemented with transport-level addresses, checksum error control, and length information by UDP, an end-to-end transport level protocol.
  • A user datagram is the packet that the UDP protocol generates.
Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)
DEFINITION
👉 SCTP is a transport-layer protocol like TCP and UDP, but more advanced and specialized.
🔹 When is SCTP used?

👉 SCTP is used in specialized high-reliability systems, like:

📡 Telecom systems

  • 4G / LTE / 5G core networks
  • SS7 signaling replacement

🏦 Financial systems

  • High-reliability trading systems

🏭 Industrial / control systems

  • Systems needing failover + redundancy
comparison
ProtocolTypeKey idea
TCPbyte streamreliable, single stream
UDPdatagramfast, no guarantee
SCTPmessage-basedmulti-stream + multi-path
👉 In SCTP, one connection can carry multiple independent streams of data at the same time.

Connection → Stream 1 (data A)
→ Stream 2 (data B)
→ Stream 3 (data C)

FINISHING
  • FIN: The client sends a FIN (finish) packet to the server to terminate the connection.
  • ACK: The server acknowledges the FIN packet with an ACK.
  • FIN: The server sends a FIN packet to the client to terminate its side of the connection.
  • ACK: The client acknowledges the server's FIN packet with an ACK.
Q&A
what is a socket

👉 Socket = door + receptionist + mailbox

  • Door → entry/exit point
  • Receptionist → decides where data goes (demultiplexing)
  • Mailbox → buffers data
source port vs destination port
  • Source port: the port number of the sender’s application.
  • Destination port: the port number of the receiving service on the server.
source ip vs destination ip
  • Source IP: the IP address of the device sending the data.
  • Destination IP: the IP address of the device receiving the data.
how does the servers or nodes now which is the first segment in sequence if the connection is new?

It knows through the TCP 3-way handshake, where the Initial Sequence Number (ISN) is established before any data is exchanged, marking the start of the byte stream.

Is ISN the starting point of packets being sent?

ISN is not for packets; it is the starting sequence number for the TCP byte stream, and packets carry ranges of those byte numbers.

Application vs Process:

An application is a program stored on disk, and when it is executed in memory (RAM), it becomes a process managed by the OS, and it may spawn multiple processes or threads while running.

1. Is one TCP request one process?

👉 No — one process can handle many TCP connections.

2. Does TCP use multiplexing/demultiplexing?

👉 Yes — to combine multiple app data streams and route them correctly.

3. Can TCP handle only one instance at a time?

👉 No — TCP handles many simultaneous connections.

4. How does transport layer know which socket gets data?

👉 It uses the 4-tuple (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port).

5. Do segments store socket IDs?

👉 No — they store IP/port info, not socket IDs.

6. What are sequence number and ACK number?

👉 They ensure ordering and reliability, not routing.

7. What is a socket?

👉 A socket is an OS endpoint for network communication.

8. What does a socket contain?

👉 Buffers, connection state, and IP/port metadata.

9. Is a socket like a tube into an application?

👉 Not exactly — it’s a smart endpoint, not a simple pipe.

10. Do TCP segments store the 4-tuple?

👉 Not directly — IP + TCP headers together form the 4-tuple.

11. How does demultiplexing work when ports are same?

👉 Source IP/port differences make connections unique.

12. What if same device sends multiple requests?

👉 OS assigns different source ports or reuses one connection.

13. What if everything is identical (IP, ports, seq)?

👉 That’s impossible — TCP/OS prevents duplicate connections.

IMAGES
5.Session Layer
OVERAL
  • Operates at Layer 5 (Session Layer) of the OSI model
  • Manages session setup, maintenance, and termination
  • Controls dialogue (who sends/receives and when)
  • Provides synchronization and recovery mechanisms
  • Many of its functions are integrated into Transport or Application layers in modern TCP/IP networks
Key functions
  • Session Establishment: Initiates and negotiates communication parameters (e.g., authentication, duplex mode).
  • Communication Synchronization: Keeps data streams in order using checkpoints.
  • Activity & Dialog Management: Controls turns, prevents collisions, and avoids duplication.
  • Resynchronization & Recovery: Recovers from failures using synchronization points.
  • Session Termination: Gracefully ends communication after all data is exchanged.
FLOW
  • Establishes and negotiates session parameters (e.g., authentication, duplex mode).
  • Manages token-based dialogue control to avoid collisions.
  • Inserts synchronization checkpoints for recovery from failures.
  • Ensures data integrity by reducing duplication or message loss.
  • Gracefully terminates sessions after confirming all data has been exchanged.
Protocols
AppleTalk Data Stream Protocol (ADSP): Developed by Apple for LAN communication with self-configuration support.

communication over LAN.

It provides a reliable, ordered byte-stream connection between devices on an AppleTalk network.

•
It uses connection-oriented communication similar to TCP.

It handles error detection, retransmission, and flow control automatically.

It supports self-configuring network communication within Apple’s AppleTalk suite.

It was mainly used for Mac-to-Mac or printer/file sharing in old Apple LANs.

It is not used on the modern internet or non-Apple systems.

Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP): Provides QoS feedback for RTP-based multimedia sessions.
🔥 How RTCP is implemented

🔹 1. Transport layer implementation

  • RTP → carries audio/video data
  • RTCP → carries control/feedback data
  • Both run over UDP ports

👉 Usually:

RTP → even UDP port
RTCP → next odd UDP port

Example:

RTP: 5004
RTCP: 5005

RTCP (Real-time Transport Control Protocol) → a control protocol used alongside RTP for real-time media (audio/video) streaming.

  • It works with RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) to transmit media data like voice and video.
  • It provides feedback about network quality (packet loss, delay, jitter).
  • It helps adjust Quality of Service (QoS) during streaming.
  • It does not carry media itself — only control and monitoring data.
  • It is commonly used in VoIP, video calls, and live streaming systems.
  • Point-to-Point Tunnelling Protocol (PPTP): Enables Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) over TCP/IP.
  • Password Authentication Protocol (PAP): Provides password-based user authentication in PPP connections.
  • Remote Procedure Call Protocol (RPCP): Allows a program to execute procedures in another address space (client-server interaction).
  • Sockets Direct Protocol (SDP): Supports socket communication over RDMA-enabled networks.
Devices
  • Firewalls: Monitor and control sessions for security.
  • Proxy Servers: Act as intermediaries, managing sessions between clients and servers.
  • Session Border Controllers (SBCs): Secure and manage VoIP sessions.
  • Application Servers: Create and maintain user sessions for applications.
6.Presentation Layer

🧠 Presentation Layer (OSI Model - Layer 6)

📌 Overview

The Presentation Layer is the 6th layer of the OSI model responsible for ensuring that data is properly formatted, translated, encrypted, and compressed so that different systems can understand each other.

👉 It acts as a translator between the Application Layer and the lower layers of the network stack.

📍 Key Responsibilities

  • Ensures data compatibility between different systems
  • Handles data formatting and structure (syntax + semantics)
  • Provides encryption and decryption
  • Applies data compression
  • Acts as a data translation layer

⚙️ Role in OSI Model

  • 📤 Sender Side:
    • Converts application data into a standard transferable format
    • Encrypts and compresses data
    • Passes data to Session Layer
  • 📥 Receiver Side:
    • Decrypts data
    • Decompresses data
    • Converts it back into application-readable format

🛠️ Functions of Presentation Layer

1. Data Translation

Converts data formats between systems

(e.g., ASCII ↔ Unicode, JSON ↔ XML)

2. Data Compression

Reduces data size to:

  • Save bandwidth
  • Improve transmission speed

3. Encryption & Decryption

  • Encrypts data for security before transmission
  • Decrypts data after reception

4. Syntax & Semantics Management

Ensures:

  • Data structure (syntax) is correct
  • Meaning (semantics) is preserved

5. Transfer Syntax Negotiation

Agrees on:

  • Encoding type
  • Compression method
  • Data representation format

6. Interoperability

Enables communication between:

  • Different operating systems
  • Different architectures
  • Different data formats

🔌 Services Provided

  • 🔒 Encryption / Decryption
  • 📦 Compression
  • 🔄 Format Translation
  • 🌐 Cross-platform compatibility

🔄 Working of Presentation Layer

📤 Sender Side

Application Layer → Presentation Layer:

  • Format data
  • Compress data
  • Encrypt data
  • Pass to Session Layer

📥 Receiver Side

Session Layer → Presentation Layer:

  • Decrypt data
  • Decompress data
  • Convert to readable format
  • Pass to Application Layer

📡 Protocols in Presentation Layer

  • SSL (Secure Socket Layer) – legacy secure communication
  • TLS (Transport Layer Security) – modern secure protocol
  • XDR (External Data Representation) – data encoding standard
  • NDR (Network Data Representation) – data representation format
  • AFP (Apple Filing Protocol) – file services for macOS
  • NCP (NetWare Core Protocol) – file/print services (Novell systems)
  • LPP (Lightweight Presentation Protocol) – ISO presentation services over TCP/IP

⚠️ Presentation Layer Attacks

🔴 Man-in-the-Middle (MITM)

Intercepts communication to steal or modify data

🔴 SSL/TLS Downgrade Attack

Forces weaker encryption protocols to break security

🔴 Certificate Spoofing

Uses fake certificates to impersonate trusted servers

🔴 Code Injection

Exploits parsing/formatting vulnerabilities in data handling

🧠 Key Idea (Interview Insight)

👉 The Presentation Layer ensures:

“Data is in a format both sender and receiver can understand securely and efficiently.”

🎯 One-line summary

👉 The Presentation Layer is responsible for translating, encrypting, and compressing data so that different systems can communicate correctly and securely.

7.Application Layer

🌐 Application Layer (OSI Model – Layer 7)

📌 Overview

The Application Layer is the topmost layer (Layer 7) of the OSI model that directly interacts with the end-user applications.

👉 It provides network services to software applications like browsers, email clients, file transfer tools, and remote login systems.

📍 Key Role

  • Acts as the interface between user applications and the network
  • Provides network services to applications
  • Enables communication between software and remote systems
  • Handles user-level network interactions

🧠 Important Clarification (Common confusion)

👉 Application Layer ≠ Applications themselves

It provides services for applications, not the apps themselves.3

Example:

  • Chrome = Application
  • HTTP = Application Layer protocol used by Chrome

⚙️ Core Functions

1. Data Representation

  • Converts user data into network format
  • Converts received data into readable format

Example:

  • HTML, JSON, XML formatting

2. Network Service Access

  • Provides direct access to network services

Example:

  • Email (Gmail, Outlook)
  • File downloads (FTP, HTTP)

3. Application Protocol Handling

Defines rules for communication between applications

Example:

  • HTTP → Web browsing
  • SMTP → Email sending
  • DNS → Name resolution

4. Session Management (logical concept here)

  • Maintains communication sessions
  • Starts and ends application-level interactions

Example:

  • Login session in a website
  • SSH connection session

5. Resource Sharing

  • Enables sharing of:
    • files
    • printers
    • services

🔄 How it works (step-by-step)

📤 Sender side:

  1. User requests action (e.g., open website)
  1. Application Layer formats request
  1. Sends it to lower layers (Presentation → Transport)

📥 Receiver side:

  1. Data arrives from network
  1. Application Layer processes it
  1. Converts it into readable output for user

📡 Services Provided

  • File transfer
  • Email communication
  • Web browsing
  • Remote login
  • Name resolution
  • Network resource sharing

🔌 Key Application Layer Protocols

🌐 Web & Communication

  • HTTP / HTTPS → Web browsing
  • WebSocket → Real-time communication

REST vs Restful API diff
DIfference
  • REST is an architectural style (set of rules/constraints for designing APIs and web services).
  • RESTful API is an actual API that is built following REST principles.
  • In short: REST = concept/rules, RESTful API = implementation of those rules in real systems.
sample usages

👉 A real working API built using REST rules

Example: GitHub API

GET https://api.github.com/users
GET https://api.github.com/users/octocat

Example: E-commerce API

GET    /products
POST   /products
PUT    /products/10
DELETE /products/10

🔥 Simple takeaway

  • REST = rules/design style
  • RESTful API = real API built using those rules
  • REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing networked applications where resources are accessed using standard HTTP methods.
  • A RESTful API is an API that follows REST principles like stateless communication, resource-based URLs, and standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE).
  • It is widely used in web services because it is simple, scalable, and works over HTTP.
API DESIGN
API TYPES
  1. REST (Representational State Transfer) - REST uses standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to manipulate resources identified by URLs. For standard CRUD operations in web and mobile applications, REST maps naturally to your database operations and HTTP semantics, making it the go-to protocol for most web services. This should be your default choice.
  1. GraphQL - Unlike REST's fixed endpoints, GraphQL uses a single endpoint with a query language that lets clients specify exactly what data they need. Think about a mobile app that needs only basic user information versus a web dashboard that displays comprehensive analytics - with REST, you'd either create multiple endpoints or force clients to fetch more data than they need, but GraphQL lets each client request exactly what it needs in a single query. If your interviewer mentions "flexible data fetching" or talks about avoiding over-fetching and under-fetching, they're signaling you to consider GraphQL.
  1. RPC (Remote Procedure Call) - RPC protocols like gRPC use binary serialization and HTTP/2 for efficient communication between services. While REST treats everything as resources, RPC lets you think in terms of actions and procedures - when your user service needs to quickly validate permissions with your auth service, an RPC call like checkPermission(userId, resource) is more natural than trying to model this as a REST resource. If the interviewer specifically mentions microservices or internal APIs, consider RPC for those high-performance connections. Use RPC when performance is critical (see Networking Essentials for deeper protocol details).
USAGE
GRAPHQL
OVERAL

GraphQL

GraphQL emerged from Facebook in 2012 to solve a specific problem: their mobile app needed different data than their web app, but they were stuck with REST endpoints that returned fixed data structures. The mobile team kept asking for new endpoints or modifications to existing ones and this was slowing down development on both sides.

With REST, you typically have two unpleasant choices when different clients need different data. You can create multiple endpoints for different use cases, leading to endpoint proliferation and maintenance headaches. Or you can make your endpoints return everything any client might need, leading to over-fetching where mobile clients download megabytes of data they don't use.

GraphQL consolidates resource endpoints into a single endpoint that accepts queries describing exactly what data you want. The client specifies the shape of the response, and the server returns data in that exact format.

HOW WORKS

query {
event(id: "123") {
name
date
venue {
name
address
}
tickets {
section
price
available
}
}
}

The server returns exactly what you asked for, nothing more, nothing less. If the mobile app only needs event names and dates, it can request just those fields. If the web dashboard needs comprehensive event details with venue information and ticket availability, it can request all of that in a single query.

Schema desing

type Event {
id: ID!
name: String!
date: DateTime!
venue: Venue!
tickets: [Ticket!]!
}

type Venue {
id: ID!
name: String!
address: String!
}

type Query {
event(id: ID!): Event
events(limit: Int, after: String): [Event!]!
}

N+1 problem

But this flexibility creates the N+1 problem, the biggest GraphQL gotcha. When a client queries events with their venues, you might execute one query for events, then N separate queries for each venue. With 100 events, that's 101 database queries instead of 2. The solution is batching/dataloader patterns that group related queries together, but it adds complexity you don't have with REST.

Is graph ql implemented on both sides(FRONT AND BACK)

Yes — GraphQL is implemented on both frontend and backend, but with different roles 👇

🔹 Backend side (GraphQL Server)

👉 Backend is where GraphQL is actually implemented

It defines:

  • Schema (types, queries, mutations)
  • Resolvers (logic to fetch data)
  • Data sources (DB, APIs)

👉 Example:

type Query {
  user(id: ID!): User
}

✔ Backend handles:

  • data fetching
  • business logic
  • response building

🔹 Frontend side (GraphQL Client)

👉 Frontend only uses GraphQL

It sends:

  • queries (what data it needs)
  • mutations (change data)

👉 Example:

query {
  user(id: 1) {
    name
    email
  }
}

✔ Frontend handles:

  • requesting data
  • selecting fields
  • rendering UI

🔥 Simple flow

Frontend (query)
     ↓
GraphQL Server (schema + resolvers)
     ↓
Database / Services
     ↓
Response back to frontend

🎯 Final answer

👉 GraphQL is implemented on the backend (server), while the frontend only consumes it by sending queries and receiving structured data.

does graphql use different API endpoints

🔥 Does GraphQL use different API endpoints?

👉 No — GraphQL usually uses only ONE API endpoint.

🔹 Key idea

Instead of many endpoints like REST:

GET /users
GET /users/1
GET /users/1/posts

👉 GraphQL uses:

POST /graphql

🔥 What changes then?

👉 Not the endpoint

👉 But the query inside the request

Example:

query {
  user(id: 1) {
    name
    posts {
      title
    }
  }
}

🔹 Why only one endpoint?

Because GraphQL:

  • uses a schema
  • dynamically decides what data to return
  • routes everything through a single resolver system

🔥 REST vs GraphQL (endpoint view)

FeatureRESTGraphQL
EndpointsMany (/users, /posts)One (/graphql)
Data controlServer decidesClient decides
FlexibilityLowHigh
how does graph ql know which data to send where the schema comes

🔥 How does GraphQL know what data to send?

👉 GraphQL knows what to return using a Schema + Resolvers

🔹 1. Where does the schema come from?

👉 The backend developer writes the schema manually

It is not automatic.

Example:

type User {
  id: ID
  name: String
  email: String
}
type Query {
  user(id: ID!): User
}

👉 This schema defines:

  • what data exists
  • what can be requested
  • relationships between data

🔹 2. What are resolvers?

👉 Resolvers are functions written in backend code

They tell GraphQL:

“How to get the data”

Example (Node.js style):

constresolvers= {
  Query: {
    user: (parent,args,context) => {
returndb.users.findById(args.id);
    }
  }
}

🔥 3. What happens when a request comes?

Example query:

query {
  user(id: 1) {
    name
    email
  }
}

Step-by-step flow:

✔ Step 1: Schema validation

GraphQL checks:

  • Does user exist in schema?
  • Does name exist in User type?

✔ Step 2: Resolver execution

GraphQL calls:

resolvers.Query.user

✔ Step 3: Fetch data

  • Resolver gets data from DB/API

✔ Step 4: Field-level resolution

GraphQL builds final response:

{
  "data": {
    "user": {
      "name":"John",
      "email":"john@mail.com"
    }
  }
}

🔥 Key insight (VERY IMPORTANT)

👉 GraphQL does NOT automatically know data

👉 It only knows because of:

1. Schema → what is allowed

2. Resolvers → how to fetch it

🔹 Simple analogy

  • Schema = menu in restaurant 🍽️
  • Resolver = chef 👨‍🍳
  • Query = customer order 🧾

👉 Customer chooses

👉 Chef prepares data

👉 Server returns result

is single endpoint get or post which http

👉 GraphQL is usually sent as a POST request, even though it uses a single endpoint.

🔹 Default behavior

Most common setup:

POST /graphql

🔹 Why POST (not GET)?

Because GraphQL sends:

  • a query
  • variables
  • sometimes complex nested data

👉 This is usually placed in the request body, and POST supports that.

🔹 Can it use GET?

👉 Yes, sometimes (optional)

  • Query is sent in URL like:
GET /graphql?query={user{id,name}}

But:

  • limited URL length
  • not good for complex queries

🔥 Industry standard

MethodUsed in GraphQL
POST✔ Most common
GET⚠ Rare (simple queries)
what if some schema which is not defined in backend will come

🔥 What happens if a non-defined schema field is requested?

👉 If the client requests something not defined in the backend schema, GraphQL will:

❌ Reject the request immediately (error)

🔹 Example

Backend schema:

type User {
  id: ID
  name: String
}

Client query (invalid):

query {
  user(id: 1) {
    name
    email   # ❌ not defined in schema
  }
}

🔥 Result:

GraphQL response:

{
  "errors": [
    {
      "message":"Cannot query field 'email' on type 'User'"
    }
  ]
}

🔹 Why this happens

👉 GraphQL is strongly typed

So it:

  • checks schema before execution
  • ensures only allowed fields are requested
  • prevents unknown data access

🔥 Key idea

👉 Schema acts like a strict contract between frontend and backend

  • Frontend cannot “guess” fields
  • Backend controls everything

🔹 What if schema changes?

If backend adds:

email: String

👉 Then frontend can immediately use it

🎯 Final answer

👉 If a client requests a field not defined in the GraphQL schema, the request fails with a validation error because GraphQL strictly enforces the schema as the only allowed contract between client and server.

Does it support optional values?
👉 Yes. By default, fields are optional unless marked as required.
🔥 How does GraphQL check the schema

schema validation + query parsing + execution planning

✔ 1. Parse the query

GraphQL first converts your query into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)

Example:

query {
  user {
    name
  }
}

👉 becomes AST (structured object)

✔ 2. Validate against Schema

👉 This is the key step

GraphQL checks:

  • Does user exist in schema?
  • Does name exist inside User type?

👉 It uses the Schema Registry (in memory object)

🔥 Important point

👉 The schema is stored in backend memory as a GraphQLSchema object

Not in DB, not external — it is loaded at server startup.

✔ 3. Execution planning

If valid:

  • GraphQL builds an execution plan
  • maps each field to a resolver function

✔ 4. Resolver execution

Each field calls its resolver:

User.name→ resolverfunction

🔹 What method/library does this?

👉 In real implementations (like Apollo Server):

  • graphql() function (core engine)
  • validate() function (schema check)
  • execute() function (runs resolvers)

🔥 Core library (behind the scenes)

👉 From graphql-js (official library):

  • validate(schema, documentAST)
  • parse(query)
  • execute(schema, query)

🔥 Simple flow

Query → parse() → AST
            ↓
      validate(schema)
            ↓
      execute(resolvers)

🎯 Final answer

👉 GraphQL checks schema using an internal validation step where the query AST is validated against an in-memory schema object using functions like validate() in the GraphQL engine before execution begins.

Q&A

🔥 Top 30 GraphQL Interview Questions & Answers

1. What is GraphQL?

GraphQL is a query language for APIs and a runtime for executing those queries. It allows clients to request exactly the data they need.

2. GraphQL vs REST?

  • REST → multiple endpoints
  • GraphQL → single endpoint
  • REST → over-fetching / under-fetching
  • GraphQL → precise data fetching

3. What are the main components of GraphQL?

  • Schema
  • Query
  • Mutation
  • Resolver
  • Type system

4. What is a GraphQL Schema?

Defines:

  • Data structure
  • Available queries/mutations
  • Types and relationships

5. What is a Query?

Used to fetch data.

query {
  users {
    id
    name
  }
}

6. What is a Mutation?

Used to modify data (create/update/delete).

mutation {
  addUser(name: "Ali") {
    id
    name
  }
}

7. What is a Resolver?

A function that returns data for a field.

constresolvers= {
  Query: {
    users: () =>getUsersFromDB()
  }
}

8. What are Types in GraphQL?

GraphQL is strongly typed.

Example:

type User {
  id: ID!
  name: String!
}

9. What does ! mean?

It means non-nullable (required field).

10. What is ID type?

Special type used for unique identifiers.

11. What are Scalars?

Basic data types:

  • String
  • Int
  • Float
  • Boolean
  • ID

12. What are Custom Scalars?

User-defined types (e.g., Date).

13. What is a Fragment?

Reusable query parts.

fragment userFields on User {
  id
  name
}

14. What are Arguments in GraphQL?

Used to pass parameters.

user(id: 1) {
  name
}

15. What is Alias?

Rename fields in response.

u1: user(id: 1) {
  name
}

16. What is Subscription?

Used for real-time updates.

Example: chat apps

17. What is Apollo Client?

A popular client for GraphQL used in frontend apps.

18. What is Apollo Server?

A popular GraphQL server implementation for Node.js.

19. What is N+1 Problem?

Multiple DB calls for nested queries → performance issue.

20. How to solve N+1 problem?

Using DataLoader (batching + caching).

21. What is DataLoader?

A utility to batch and cache requests.

22. What is Schema Stitching?

Combining multiple GraphQL schemas.

23. What is Federation?

Modern way to split GraphQL into microservices (Apollo Federation).

24. What is Introspection?

Allows querying schema itself.

25. What are Directives?

Special instructions in queries.

Example:

@include(if: true)

26. What is Caching in GraphQL?

  • Client-side caching (Apollo)
  • Server-side caching

27. What is Error Handling?

GraphQL returns:

{
  "data":null,
  "errors": []
}

28. What is Pagination?

Used to limit data.

Types:

  • Offset-based
  • Cursor-based (better)

29. What is Context in GraphQL?

Shared object passed to all resolvers.

Used for:

  • Authentication
  • DB access

30. How authentication works in GraphQL?

Usually via:

  • JWT tokens
  • Passed in headers
  • Checked inside resolvers

👉 How you handled:

  • mutations from frontend
  • authentication
  • performance issues

👉 GraphQL is a query language + API runtime that lets clients request exactly the data they need from a server.

🔹 Simple idea

👉 Instead of:

  • REST → fixed endpoints (/users, /posts)
  • GraphQL → one endpoint + flexible queries

🔹 Example

REST:

GET /users/1
GET /users/1/posts

👉 Multiple requests

GraphQL:

query {
  user(id: 1) {
    name
    posts {
      title
    }
  }
}

👉 One request → only needed data

🔥 How GraphQL is handled (step-by-step)

🔹 1. Client sends a query

Client defines:

  • what data it needs
  • structure of response

🔹 2. Server has a schema

👉 Schema defines:

  • types (User, Post, etc.)
  • relationships
  • allowed queries

Example:

type User {
  id: ID
  name: String
  posts: [Post]
}

🔹 3. Resolvers execute logic

👉 Each field has a resolver function

  • Fetches data from:
    • database
    • API

🔹 4. Server builds response

👉 Combines all resolver results

👉 Returns exact structure requested

🔹 Internal flow

Client → GraphQL Query
        ↓
     Schema check
        ↓
     Resolvers run
        ↓
     Data fetched
        ↓
     Response returned

🔥 Key features

  • ✔ No over-fetching (only needed data)
  • ✔ No under-fetching (get nested data in one request)
  • ✔ Single endpoint (/graphql)
