🔥 What is gRPC?

👉 gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call) is a high-performance framework that lets services communicate by calling functions on another server as if they were local.

🔹 Simple idea

👉 Instead of sending HTTP requests like REST:

GET /users/1

👉 gRPC does:

getUser(1)

✔ Looks like calling a function

✔ But actually runs over the network

🔹 How gRPC works

1. Define service using Protocol Buffers (Proto file)

service UserService {
  rpc GetUser (UserRequest) returns (UserResponse);
}

2. Generate code

  • gRPC generates:
    • client code
    • server code

3. Client calls function

client.GetUser({ id:1 })

4. Server handles request

  • Executes logic
  • Sends response back

🔥 Key technologies used

  • HTTP/2 → fast, multiplexed communication
  • Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) → compact binary format

🔹 Features

  • ✔ Very fast (binary, not JSON)
  • ✔ Strongly typed
  • ✔ Supports streaming (send continuous data)
  • ✔ Bi-directional communication

🔹 REST vs gRPC

FeatureRESTgRPC
Data formatJSONBinary (Protobuf)
SpeedSlowerFaster
CommunicationRequest/ResponseFunction calls + streaming
ProtocolHTTP/1.1HTTP/2

🔥 When to use gRPC

  • Microservices communication
  • High-performance systems
  • Real-time streaming (chat, video)
  • Internal backend services

🎯 One-line answer

👉 gRPC is a fast RPC framework that lets applications communicate by calling remote functions using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers.

Docs

🚀 1. What is gRPC?

gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call) is a framework that allows one service to call a function in another service as if it were local, even though it's on another machine.

👉 Think:

Frontend → calls → Backend function
Service A → calls → Service B function

🧠 2. Core Idea (Very Important)

Instead of:

  • REST → you send HTTP requests (GET /users)

With gRPC:

  • You call functions directly
userService.getUser(id)

⚡ Feels like normal function call, but it's actually network communication

🧱 3. How gRPC Works (Step-by-Step)

Step 1: Define service in .proto file

syntax = "proto3";

service UserService {
  rpc GetUser (UserRequest) returns (UserResponse);
}

message UserRequest {
  int32 id = 1;
}

message UserResponse {
  string name = 1;
  int32 age = 2;
}

Step 2: Generate code

gRPC generates:

  • Client code
  • Server code

Step 3: Implement server

functionGetUser(call,callback) {
constuser= { name:"Ali", age:20 };
callback(null,user);
}

Step 4: Call from client

client.GetUser({ id:1 }, (err,response) => {
console.log(response);
});

📦 4. Key Components

1. Protocol Buffers (Protobuf)

  • Used to define data structure
  • Faster than JSON
  • Binary format

2. Service

Defines methods:

rpc MethodName (Request) returns (Response);

3. Messages

Like DTOs (data objects)

4. Client & Server

  • Client → calls function
  • Server → executes function

⚡ 5. gRPC vs REST (Important)

FeaturegRPCREST
ProtocolHTTP/2HTTP/1.1
Data formatBinary (Protobuf)JSON
SpeedVery fast ⚡Slower
StreamingBuilt-inHard
Human readable❌ No✅ Yes

🔄 6. Types of gRPC Calls (VERY IMPORTANT)

1. Unary (Normal request/response)

Like REST:

Client → Request → Server → Response

2. Server Streaming

Server sends multiple responses:

Client → Request → Server → stream of data

Example:

  • Live stock prices

3. Client Streaming

Client sends multiple requests:

Client → stream → Server → Response

4. Bidirectional Streaming 🔥

Both sides send streams:

Client ⇄ Server

Example:

  • Chat app

🧩 7. Why gRPC is Fast

  • Uses HTTP/2
  • Uses binary (Protobuf) instead of JSON
  • Supports multiplexing (multiple requests in one connection)

🔐 8. Authentication in gRPC

Usually done via:

  • Metadata (headers)
  • JWT tokens

🧠 9. When to Use gRPC

✅ Microservices communication

✅ Real-time systems

✅ High-performance systems

❌ Not ideal for:

  • Public APIs (hard to test in browser)
  • Simple CRUD apps

⚠️ 10. Common Problems

  • Hard to debug (binary)
  • Not browser-friendly
  • Requires .proto setup

💡 11. gRPC vs GraphQL (Important for YOU)

FeaturegRPCGraphQL
StyleFunction callsQuery language
FlexibilityFixed schemaFlexible queries
SpeedFasterSlightly slower
Use caseBackend servicesFrontend APIs

👉 Simple:

  • gRPC → backend-to-backend
  • GraphQL → frontend-to-backend

🧪 12. Real-Life Example

Imagine:

Without gRPC (REST)

GET /user/1

With gRPC

userService.GetUser({ id:1 });

🧠 Final Mental Model

👉 gRPC =

"Call remote functions like local functions using fast binary protocol"

🔥 Top 20 Tricky gRPC Interview Questions (FAANG-Level)

1. Why is gRPC faster than REST in practice, not just theory?

Because of:

  • HTTP/2 multiplexing → no repeated TCP connections
  • Binary Protobuf → smaller payload than JSON
  • Header compression → less overhead
  • Persistent connections

👉 In real systems, latency reduction is often 30–70%

2. If gRPC is so fast, why isn’t it used everywhere?

Because:

  • Not browser-friendly (needs gRPC-Web)
  • Harder debugging (binary format)
  • Requires schema management (.proto)

👉 Tradeoff: performance vs simplicity

3. How does gRPC handle backward compatibility?

Using Protobuf rules:

  • Never change field numbers
  • Only add new fields
  • Avoid removing fields (deprecate instead)

👉 Old clients simply ignore unknown fields

4. What happens if you reuse a field number in .proto?

💣 Critical bug

Old clients will:

  • Misinterpret data
  • Possibly crash or corrupt logic

👉 Field numbers are permanent identifiers

5. Explain how HTTP/2 multiplexing improves performance.

In REST (HTTP/1.1):

Request 1 → wait → Response 1 → Request 2

In gRPC (HTTP/2):

Request 1
Request 2
Request 3  → all in parallel → responses come independently

👉 No blocking → better throughput

6. What is head-of-line blocking and how does gRPC avoid it?

In HTTP/1.1:

  • One slow request blocks others

In HTTP/2:

  • Streams are independent

👉 gRPC avoids this via stream multiplexing

7. How would you debug a gRPC service?

Challenges:

  • Binary data

Solutions:

  • Use grpcurl
  • Enable logging interceptors
  • Use tools like Postman (gRPC support)

👉 Debugging is harder than REST

8. Explain the N+1 problem in gRPC (yes, it exists)

Example:

  • Client calls getUser
  • Then calls getOrders for each user

👉 Results in many RPC calls → latency increases

Solution:

  • Batch requests
  • Design smarter APIs

9. How does gRPC handle load balancing?

Options:

  • Client-side load balancing
  • DNS-based
  • Proxy (e.g., Envoy)

👉 Common in microservices: Envoy + gRPC

10. What is the role of interceptors?

Interceptors = middleware

Used for:

  • Logging
  • Authentication
  • Metrics
  • Retry logic

👉 Similar to Express middleware

11. What happens if a gRPC request exceeds deadline?

  • Request is cancelled
  • Server stops processing
  • Client gets error

👉 Prevents resource waste

12. Difference between timeout and deadline?

  • Timeout → "wait 5 seconds"
  • Deadline → "finish before 10:00:00"

👉 Deadline is absolute time

13. How does streaming improve performance?

Instead of:

Request → Response → Request → Response

Use stream:

Single connection → continuous data flow

👉 Reduces:

  • Latency
  • Network overhead

14. When would bidirectional streaming be a bad idea?

Bad when:

  • Simple CRUD app
  • Hard to manage state
  • Debugging complexity

👉 Use only when real-time needed (chat, live data)

15. How does gRPC ensure reliability in distributed systems?

  • Retries
  • Deadlines
  • Load balancing
  • Health checks

👉 But developer must design properly

16. What are common production issues with gRPC?

  • Connection leaks
  • Improper timeout settings
  • Large payloads
  • Version mismatch (.proto)

17. How do you version gRPC APIs?

Options:

  • Version in package:
package user.v1;
  • Or separate services

👉 Never break existing contracts

18. How would you design a scalable gRPC system?

  • Use microservices
  • Add load balancer (Envoy)
  • Use caching
  • Use batching

👉 Combine with message queues if needed

19. Compare gRPC vs GraphQL in real architecture

  • gRPC → service-to-service (fast, strict)
  • GraphQL → frontend-to-backend (flexible)

👉 Many companies use BOTH together

20. If you had to replace REST with gRPC, what challenges would you face?

  • Browser support
  • Team learning curve
  • Debugging tools
  • Migration complexity

👉 Real answer = gradual migration, not full replacement

🧠 FAANG Insight (Very Important)

In top interviews, they don’t care if you memorize definitions.

They test:

  • Can you design systems
  • Can you handle edge cases
  • Can you explain trade-offs
Custom QA

📘 1. Do microservices need to be in one big directory?

  • ❌ No, microservices do NOT need one shared directory
  • They are independent applications
  • They can be in a monorepo or separate repositories
  • Structure is just organization, not architecture rule
  • What matters is independent deployment and scaling

📘 2. Do microservices have separate .proto repositories?

  • 👉 In large systems, YES — often a separate proto/contract repo is used
  • It acts as a single source of truth for all service communication
  • Services depend on it to stay consistent
  • In small projects, proto files may be copied or kept in a monorepo
  • Goal is always consistency, not repo structure

📘 5. What is a .proto file?

  • Defines gRPC communication contract
  • Contains services (methods) and messages (data)
  • Ensures both services agree on structure
  • Not business logic, only rules
  • Used to generate client/server code

📘 6. Is .proto just listing microservice methods?

  • Partially yes (like GetUser, ProcessUser)
  • But more importantly it defines full communication format
  • Includes request + response structure
  • Ensures strict typing between services
  • It’s a contract, not just a list

📘 7. Is .proto a structure of communication?

  • Yes, exactly
  • It defines how services talk to each other
  • Includes methods, inputs, outputs, types
  • Ensures both sides follow same rules
  • Acts as a strict API contract

📘 8. What happens in gRPC callback?

  • Callback returns (error, response)
  • If error → reject/handle error
  • If success → resolve response
  • Used because gRPC is async network call
  • Wraps server response handling

📘 9. Can we use async/await in gRPC?

  • Yes, but only with Promise wrapper
  • gRPC uses callbacks by default
  • Wrap callback in Promise
  • Then use await getUser()
  • Makes code cleaner and modern

📘 10. What if services don’t match .proto?

  • Method missing → runtime error (UNIMPLEMENTED)
  • Wrong fields → silent bugs (default values)
  • Extra fields → ignored
  • Server still runs normally
  • Errors happen only during calls

📘 11. If method exists in proto but not in server?

  • Server still starts successfully
  • No startup error
  • Error happens only when method is called
  • gRPC returns UNIMPLEMENTED error
  • This is runtime validation

🧠 FINAL SUMMARY

👉 You learned:

  • Batch requests vs caching
  • Global state vs server data
  • gRPC architecture (proto, server, client)
  • Callbacks vs async/await
  • Contract mismatch behavior

🚀 Top 50 gRPC Interview Questions & Answers

🧠 BASICS (1–15)

1. What is gRPC?

gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework developed by Google that allows services to communicate by calling remote functions.

2. What does RPC mean?

Remote Procedure Call → calling a function on another machine like a local function.

3. What protocol does gRPC use?

gRPC uses HTTP/2.

4. What is Protobuf?

Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) is a binary serialization format used in gRPC.

5. Why Protobuf instead of JSON?

  • Smaller size
  • Faster parsing
  • Strong typing

6. What is a .proto file?

A file that defines:

  • Services
  • Methods
  • Request/response structure

7. What is a service in gRPC?

A collection of RPC methods.

8. What is an RPC method?

A function that can be called remotely.

9. What is a message in gRPC?

A structured data object (like a class or DTO).

10. What is code generation in gRPC?

gRPC generates client and server code from .proto.

11. What languages does gRPC support?

Many:

  • JavaScript / Node.js
  • Python
  • Java
  • Go
  • C++

12. Is gRPC synchronous or asynchronous?

Both — depends on implementation.

13. What is a stub?

Client-side generated code used to call the server.

14. What is a channel?

A connection between client and server.

15. What is a deadline in gRPC?

Time limit for a request.

⚙️ CORE CONCEPTS (16–30)

16. What are the 4 types of gRPC calls?

  1. Unary
  1. Server streaming
  1. Client streaming
  1. Bidirectional streaming

17. What is Unary RPC?

Single request → single response.

18. What is Server Streaming?

One request → multiple responses.

19. What is Client Streaming?

Multiple requests → one response.

20. What is Bidirectional Streaming?

Both client and server send streams.

21. What is HTTP/2 multiplexing?

Multiple requests over a single connection.

22. What is flow control in gRPC?

Controls data transmission rate.

23. What is metadata in gRPC?

Key-value pairs (like HTTP headers).

24. What is serialization?

Converting data into transferable format.

25. What is deserialization?

Converting received data back to object.

26. What is schema evolution?

Updating .proto without breaking clients.

27. How do you add new fields safely?

Add new field with a new number.

28. Can you remove fields?

Yes, but don’t reuse field numbers.

29. What is backward compatibility?

Old clients still work with new server.

30. What is forward compatibility?

New clients work with old server.

🔐 SECURITY & PERFORMANCE (31–40)

31. How is security handled in gRPC?

Using TLS (SSL).

32. What is TLS?

Encryption protocol for secure communication.

33. What is authentication in gRPC?

Usually via:

  • JWT
  • API keys

34. What is authorization?

Checking user permissions.

35. What is load balancing in gRPC?

Distributing requests across servers.

36. What is retry mechanism?

Retrying failed requests.

37. What is timeout vs deadline?

  • Timeout → duration
  • Deadline → exact time

38. Why is gRPC faster than REST?

  • Binary format
  • HTTP/2
  • Persistent connections

39. What is connection pooling?

Reusing connections instead of creating new ones.

40. What is compression in gRPC?

Reducing payload size (gzip, etc.)

🧩 ADVANCED & REAL-WORLD (41–50)

41. When should you use gRPC?

  • Microservices
  • High-performance systems

42. When NOT to use gRPC?

  • Public APIs
  • Browser-heavy apps

Not directly (needs gRPC-Web).

A version of gRPC for browsers.

45. What is service discovery?

Finding available services dynamically.

46. What is health checking?

Checking if service is alive.

47. What is interceptors in gRPC?

Middleware for requests/responses.

48. What is error handling in gRPC?

Uses status codes + messages.

49. What are gRPC status codes?

Examples:

50. gRPC vs REST vs GraphQL?

  • gRPC → fast, backend communication

🧠 Final Summary (Important)

👉 gRPC =

👉 GraphQL =

  • Simple and universal
Batching reques

🚀 What is a Batch Request?

A batch request means:

👉 Sending multiple operations in a single network call instead of making many separate requests.

🧠 Simple Idea

Instead of this ❌:

Request 1 → getUser(1)
Request 2 → getUser(2)
Request 3 → getUser(3)

You do this ✅:

Single Request → getUsers([1,2,3])

⚡ Why Batch Requests?

Because network calls are expensive.

Batching helps:

  • 🚀 Reduce latency
  • 📉 Reduce number of requests
  • ⚡ Improve performance

📦 Example in REST

Without batching:

GET /user/1
GET /user/2
GET /user/3

With batching:

POST /users
Body: [1, 2, 3]

🔥 Example in gRPC

.proto:

rpc GetUsers (UserIds) returns (UserList);

message UserIds {
  repeated int32 ids = 1;
}

message UserList {
  repeated User users = 1;
}

👉 repeated = array

Client call:

client.GetUsers({ ids: [1,2,3] },callback);

🧩 Batch vs Normal Requests

FeatureNormal RequestBatch Request
CallsManyOne
SpeedSlowerFaster
Network usageHighLow

🧠 Important: Batch vs Streaming (DON’T CONFUSE)

👉 Batching

  • Send many items once
  • One response

👉 Streaming

  • Continuous flow of data
  • Multiple responses over time

⚠️ When NOT to Use Batch

  • Real-time systems (use streaming instead)
  • Very large data (can overload server)

💡 Real-world Example

Imagine frontend needs:

  • User info
  • Orders
  • Notifications

❌ Without batching:

3 separate API calls

✅ With batching:

1 combined request → faster page load

🧠 Advanced Insight (Interview Level)

Batching is often used to solve:

👉 N+1 problem

Tools like:

  • DataLoader (in GraphQL)
  • Custom batching logic in gRPC

🔥 Final Mental Model

👉 Batch Request =

“Group multiple operations into one request to reduce network overhead”

SSE
OVERAL

👉 SSE is a way for the server to push real-time updates to the browser over a single HTTP connection.

So instead of:

Client keeps asking: "Any update? any update? any update?"

SSE does:

Server pushes updates automatically → Client just listens
Samples

⚡ Simple analogy

Think of it like:

  • 📺 TV broadcast
  • You (client) just watch
  • TV station (server) keeps sending updates
USAGE

🚀 What is Server-Sent Events (SSE)?

👉 SSE is a way for the server to push real-time updates to the browser over a single HTTP connection.

So instead of:

Client keeps asking: "Any update? any update? any update?"

SSE does:

Server pushes updates automatically → Client just listens

🧠 Core idea

👉 One-way real-time communication

  • Server → Client ✅
  • Client → Server ❌ (not via SSE)

⚡ Simple analogy

Think of it like:

  • 📺 TV broadcast
  • You (client) just watch
  • TV station (server) keeps sending updates

You don’t “request” each update.

🧩 How SSE works (step-by-step)

1. Client opens connection

consteventSource=newEventSource("/events");

2. Server keeps connection open

Instead of closing response, server keeps it alive.

3. Server sends events

data: Hello
data: New notification

4. Client listens

eventSource.onmessage= (event) => {
console.log(event.data);
};

🔥 Key feature

👉 SSE uses HTTP connection that stays open

Unlike REST:

request → response → close

SSE:

request → open forever → stream data

⚡ SSE vs WebSockets (VERY IMPORTANT)

FeatureSSEWebSockets
DirectionServer → ClientBidirectional
ComplexitySimpleComplex
ProtocolHTTPWebSocket protocol
Use caseNotifications, feedsChat, games

🧠 When to use SSE

✔ Live notifications

✔ Stock prices

✔ News feeds

✔ Progress updates (upload, build status)

❌ When NOT to use SSE

  • Chat apps (need 2-way communication)
  • Games
  • Collaborative editing

👉 Use WebSockets instead

Q&A

🚀 SSE + Backend + Microservices (30 Q&A)

🟦 SSE Basics

1. What is Server-Sent Events (SSE)?

👉 SSE is a browser feature where the server continuously sends updates to the client over a single HTTP connection.

2. How is SSE different from normal HTTP?

👉 Normal HTTP is request → response → close.

👉 SSE keeps the connection open and streams data continuously.

3. Is SSE one-way or two-way?

👉 SSE is one-way communication (server → client only).

4. Why does SSE keep connection open?

👉 To allow the server to continuously push real-time updates without re-requesting.

5. What header is required for SSE?

👉 Content-Type: text/event-stream

🟦 SSE Working

6. Who initiates SSE connection?

👉 The frontend (browser) initiates it using EventSource.

7. What happens when EventSource("/events") is called?

👉 Browser sends a GET request and keeps the connection open for streaming.

8. Why text/event-stream is used?

👉 It tells browser to treat response as continuous stream, not a normal response.

9. What does res.write() do in SSE?

👉 It sends partial data chunks to the client without closing the connection.

10. Why must SSE response not close?

👉 Because SSE is a persistent stream — closing breaks real-time updates.

🟦 Browser + CORS

11. Why do SSE requests get CORS errors?

👉 Because frontend and backend are on different origins (ports/domains).

12. What is Same-Origin Policy?

👉 A browser security rule that blocks cross-origin requests unless allowed.

13. Why did SSE fail on 5500 → 3000?

👉 Because 5500 (frontend) tried accessing 3000 (backend) without CORS permission.

14. What is EventSource?

👉 A browser API that opens and listens to SSE connections.

15. What happens if backend goes down?

👉 SSE connection breaks and client receives an error event.

🟦 SSE vs Other Tech

16. SSE vs WebSockets?

👉 SSE = server → client only

👉 WebSockets = two-way communication

17. When to use SSE?

👉 Notifications, live feeds, updates, progress tracking.

18. Can SSE send data client → server?

👉 No — SSE is only server → client.

19. SSE vs polling?

👉 SSE is better because it avoids repeated requests and reduces overhead.

20. SSE vs gRPC streaming?

👉 gRPC streaming is faster and binary-based; SSE is browser-friendly HTTP-based.

🟦 gRPC + Proto

21. What is a .proto file?

👉 A contract that defines communication between microservices.

22. Does proto define logic?

👉 No — only structure (methods, request, response).

23. What if method exists in proto but not server?

👉 Server starts fine, but runtime error occurs when method is called.

24. When does UNIMPLEMENTED error happen?

👉 When client calls a method not implemented on server.

25. Why use proto instead of REST only?

👉 Because it enforces strict contracts, faster communication, and type safety.

🟦 Microservices Architecture

26. One repo or multiple repos?

👉 Both are used: monorepo (small systems), multi-repo (large systems).

27. What is proto repository?

👉 A shared repo containing .proto files used by all services.

28. Why version proto files?

👉 To avoid breaking existing services when API changes.

29. What if services disagree on proto?

👉 It causes data mismatch, bugs, or runtime failures.

30. Why is CORS needed?

👉 Because browser blocks cross-origin requests for security unless backend allows it.

WebRTC: Peer-to-Peer Communication
Overall

👉 WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication) is a browser technology that enables direct peer-to-peer (P2P) communication between browsers — without needing a server for data transfer.

⚡ Core idea

Browser A ⇄ Browser B (direct connection)

Server is ONLY used for:

  • signaling (setup)
  • NOT for actual media/data transfer

🍽️ Simple analogy

  • HTTP = ordering food 🍔
  • SSE = radio 📻
  • WebSocket = phone call 📞
  • WebRTC = video call without middleman 📹

🧠 Key components

WebRTC has 3 main parts:

1. MediaStream

👉 camera + microphone access

2. RTCPeerConnection

👉 actual peer-to-peer connection

3. RTCDataChannel

👉 send text/data directly between browsers

🔥 Real-world usage
  • Video calls (Zoom-like apps)
  • Voice chat
  • Peer-to-peer file sharing
  • Live streaming
  • Online gaming communication
  • Remote desktop tools

🧠 Companies using WebRTC

  • Google (Meet, Chrome)
  • Discord (voice/video)
  • Zoom
Architecture

User A ────────┐
│
Signaling Server
│
User B ────────┘

Then:

User A ⇄⇄⇄⇄⇄⇄⇄ User B (direct P2P)

STUN vs TURN

🧠 0. Big Picture (why STUN/TURN exist)

WebRTC wants this:

Browser A ⇄ Browser B (direct P2P)

But reality is:

  • NAT (routers) hide devices
  • firewalls block connections
  • mobile networks are strict

👉 So direct connection is often NOT possible.

🧠 1. NAT problem (core reason STUN/TURN exist)

Your device is behind a router:

Device (192.168.1.5)
        ↓
     Router (NAT)
        ↓
   Public Internet

👉 External world does NOT see your private IP.

So Browser A cannot directly reach Browser B.

🧠 2. ICE = the system that solves this

ICE = tries multiple ways:

  1. Direct P2P (best)
  1. STUN-assisted P2P
  1. TURN relay (last resort)

🧠 3. STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT)

🧠 What STUN does

👉 It tells you:

“What is my public IP and port as seen from the internet?”

🔁 How STUN works

Client → STUN Server → returns public IP

Example:

  • Your local IP: 192.168.1.5
  • STUN returns: 203.0.113.10:54321

👉 Now other peers can try to connect to you.

🧠 Important point

👉 STUN does NOT relay data

👉 It only DISCOVERS address

⚡ STUN result types

  • Host candidate (local IP)
  • Server reflexive candidate (public IP)
  • Peer reflexive candidate (dynamic discovery)

🧠 When STUN works

✔ Symmetric NAT not too strict

✔ Firewall allows UDP hole punching

👉 Most home WiFi cases

🧠 4. TURN (Traversal Using Relays around NAT)

🧠 What TURN does

👉 TURN is a relay server

Instead of:

A ⇄ B (direct)

It becomes:

A → TURN → B

🧠 When TURN is used

TURN is used when:

  • NAT is too strict
  • firewall blocks UDP
  • corporate networks
  • mobile carrier restrictions

⚡ TURN is fallback

👉 ICE tries STUN first

👉 If fails → TURN

🧠 TURN behavior

TURN:

  • receives packets from A
  • forwards to B
  • returns responses back

👉 It is basically a proxy for WebRTC

⚠️ downside

  • higher latency
  • more cost (server bandwidth)
  • more infrastructure

🧠 5. STUN vs TURN comparison

FeatureSTUNTURN
PurposeDiscover public IPRelay traffic
Data transfer❌ No✅ Yes
SpeedFastSlower
CostFreeExpensive
UsagePreferredFallback

🧠 6. ICE candidate types (VERY IMPORTANT)

When WebRTC runs, it collects:

🟦 1. Host candidate

👉 Local network IP

192.168.x.x

🟦 2. Server reflexive (STUN)

👉 Public IP discovered via STUN

203.0.113.x

🟥 3. Relay candidate (TURN)

👉 TURN server address

turn.example.com:3478

🧠 7. Full connection decision flow

ICE gathers all candidates
        ↓
Try host → host (direct LAN)
        ↓
Try STUN → STUN (public IP)
        ↓
If fails → TURN relay

🧠 8. Real WebRTC flow (step-by-step)

Step 1: Candidate gathering

Browser collects all possible routes.

Step 2: Signaling exchange

Peers exchange candidates via server.

Step 3: Connectivity checks

WebRTC tests:

  • latency
  • packet loss
  • firewall rules

Step 4: Choose best path

👉 Usually STUN-based direct connection

Step 5: If all fail

👉 TURN becomes active relay

🧠 9. Why STUN works most of the time

Because most home routers support:

✔ UDP hole punching

✔ NAT mapping

✔ outbound connection reuse

🧠 10. Real-world analogy

STUN = GPS check

👉 “Where am I visible from outside?”

TURN = delivery service

👉 “If I can’t reach you directly, I will forward everything through a middleman”

🧠 11. One full mental model

WebRTC connection:

1. ICE gathers routes
2. STUN gives public identity
3. Try direct P2P
4. If blocked → TURN relay
5. Best route selected automatically

🧠 FINAL MEMORY (VERY IMPORTANT)

👉 STUN helps you discover your public address, TURN helps you communicate when direct connection is impossible. ICE chooses between them automatically.

Custom QA

🧠 1. Signaling server — what is it REALLY doing?

👉 Your understanding is almost correct, but let’s refine it:

❌ Wrong idea:

“Signaling server establishes the connection”

✅ Correct idea:

👉 Signaling server does NOT establish connection

It only helps peers exchange information needed to connect:

It exchanges:

  • Offer (SDP)
  • Answer (SDP)
  • ICE candidates

🧠 What actually happens:

Step 1: A → signaling server → B (offer)
Step 2: B → signaling server → A (answer)
Step 3: A ↔ B (ICE candidates exchange)
Step 4: DIRECT connection established (P2P)

⚡ After that:

👉 Signaling server is NO LONGER used

👉 WebRTC peers communicate directly

🧠 2. What are WebRTC channels?

There are 2 main “channels” concepts:

🟦 A) Media Channels (Audio/Video)

Used for:

  • camera stream
  • microphone stream

How they work:

Camera → encoder → RTP packets → peer

🟩 B) Data Channels (RTCDataChannel)

Used for:

  • text messages
  • file transfer
  • game data

How they work:

App data → WebRTC DataChannel → peer

🧠 Important concept:

👉 WebRTC does NOT go through modem like normal internet requests

Instead:

✔ uses UDP packets directly between peers

✔ NAT traversal decides route

✔ encryption wraps everything

🧠 How does router/modem know data belongs to WebRTC?

Because of:

  • port numbers
  • ICE candidates
  • DTLS encryption
  • SSRC (stream identifiers)

👉 OS + browser handle routing automatically

You don’t manually separate data — WebRTC stack does it.

🧠 3. Table of WebRTC “channels”

TypePurposeProtocolNotes
MediaStreamaudio/videoRTP/RTCPreal-time media
DataChanneltext/filesSCTP over DTLSflexible data
Signaling (not WebRTC core)setupHTTP/WebSocketexternal
ICE transportconnectivityUDP/TCPNAT traversal
TURN relayfallbackUDP/TCP relaywhen P2P fails

🧠 4. Deep dive: ICE (very important)

👉 What is ICE?

ICE = Interactive Connectivity Establishment

👉 It is a system that finds the best path between 2 devices

🧩 Why ICE exists?

Because devices are often behind:

  • routers (NAT)
  • firewalls
  • mobile networks

So direct connection is NOT guaranteed.

⚡ ICE process:

Step 1: Candidate gathering

Browser collects possible addresses:

  • local IP
  • public IP (via STUN)
  • relay IP (TURN)

Step 2: Exchange candidates

Peers send each other:

"I can be reached at this IP/port"

Step 3: Connectivity checks

ICE tests:

  • which route works fastest
  • which route is allowed

Step 4: Choose best path

👉 best working route becomes active connection

🧠 5. STUN vs TURN (deep explanation)

🟦 STUN

👉 “What is my public IP?”

Used for:

  • discovering external IP
  • enabling direct connection

Flow:

Client → STUN server → returns public IP

✔ lightweight

✔ fast

✔ no data relay

🟥 TURN

👉 “Relay everything if direct connection fails”

Used when:

  • strict NAT
  • corporate firewall
  • mobile restrictions

Flow:

Client A → TURN server → Client B

❌ slower

✔ always works

🧠 Simple rule:

ServerRole
STUNdiscovery
TURNbackup relay

🧠 6. WebRTC functions (important ones)

🟦 Connection setup

new RTCPeerConnection()

👉 creates peer connection

createOffer()

👉 creates connection request (SDP)

createAnswer()

👉 responds to offer

setLocalDescription()

👉 saves your own connection config

setRemoteDescription()

👉 stores other peer’s config

🟦 ICE functions

onicecandidate

👉 triggers when new network route found

addIceCandidate()

👉 adds peer’s network route

🟦 Media

getUserMedia()

👉 access camera/mic

addTrack()

👉 attach media to connection

ontrack

👉 receive remote media

🟦 Data

createDataChannel()

👉 create P2P data channel

onmessage

👉 receive data

🧠 7. Is handshake done via server?

YES — BUT ONLY INITIALLY

🧩 Step-by-step flow:

1. Signaling phase (via server)

A → server → B (offer)
B → server → A (answer)

2. ICE exchange (also via server)

A ↔ server ↔ B (candidates)

3. After that:

👉 SERVER IS NOT USED ANYMORE

🧠 Final connection:

A ⇄⇄⇄⇄⇄⇄⇄ B (direct P2P)

🚀 FINAL SUMMARY

1. Signaling server

👉 ONLY helps exchange setup info (not data)

2. WebRTC channels

  • Media = audio/video
  • DataChannel = text/files
  • Everything is encrypted + handled by browser

3. ICE

👉 Finds best possible network route

4. STUN/TURN

  • STUN = discover IP
  • TURN = relay if needed

5. Connection flow

Signaling → ICE → P2P connection → direct communication

🧠 One-line memory

👉 WebRTC uses a server only to introduce peers — after that, everything is peer-to-peer using ICE-selected network paths.

Q&A

🚀 WebRTC: 50 Questions + Answers

🟦 Basics (1–10)

1. What is WebRTC?

👉 WebRTC is a browser technology that enables real-time peer-to-peer communication (audio, video, data) without plugins.

2. Is WebRTC client-server or peer-to-peer?

👉 It is peer-to-peer (P2P).

3. What problem does WebRTC solve?

👉 It enables real-time communication between browsers without needing a media server for data transfer.

4. Does WebRTC need a server?

👉 Yes, but only for signaling (not for actual media transfer).

5. What is signaling in WebRTC?

👉 The process of exchanging connection setup information (offer, answer, ICE candidates).

6. Does WebRTC use HTTP for communication?

👉 No, after setup it uses direct P2P connection over UDP/TCP.

7. What is the main use of WebRTC?

👉 Video calls, voice calls, and real-time data sharing.

8. Is WebRTC secure?

👉 Yes, it uses encryption by default (DTLS + SRTP).

9. What browsers support WebRTC?

👉 All modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge).

10. What is the key advantage of WebRTC?

👉 Low latency real-time communication.

🟦 Core Concepts (11–20)

11. What is RTCPeerConnection?

👉 The API that establishes a connection between two peers.

12. What is MediaStream?

👉 It represents audio/video streams from camera or microphone.

13. What is RTCDataChannel?

👉 A channel used to send text or binary data directly between peers.

14. What is SDP?

👉 Session Description Protocol — describes connection details (media info, codecs, etc).

15. What is an ICE candidate?

👉 A possible network path used to connect peers.

16. Why do we need ICE candidates?

👉 To find the best possible route for peer-to-peer connection.

17. What is STUN server?

👉 Helps discover public IP address behind NAT.

18. What is TURN server?

👉 Relays traffic when direct P2P connection fails.

19. Why is TURN used?

👉 When NAT/firewall blocks direct peer connection.

20. What is NAT traversal?

👉 Technique to allow devices behind routers to connect directly.

🟦 Connection Process (21–30)

21. What is offer in WebRTC?

👉 The first connection request created by one peer.

22. What is answer in WebRTC?

👉 Response to the offer from the second peer.

23. What is handshake in WebRTC?

👉 Exchange of offer, answer, and ICE candidates.

24. What is setLocalDescription?

👉 Stores your own connection configuration.

25. What is setRemoteDescription?

👉 Stores the other peer’s configuration.

26. Why do we exchange ICE candidates?

👉 To find the best network path between peers.

27. What happens after connection is established?

👉 Direct peer-to-peer media/data flow begins.

28. What triggers connection failure?

👉 NAT issues, firewall blocking, or missing TURN server.

29. Can WebRTC reconnect automatically?

👉 No, you must implement reconnection logic.

30. What is signaling server role?

👉 Only exchanges metadata, not actual media.

🟦 Media & Streams (31–40)

31. What is getUserMedia()?

👉 API to access camera and microphone.

32. Can WebRTC stream only audio?

👉 Yes.

33. Can WebRTC stream only video?

👉 Yes.

34. What formats does WebRTC support?

👉 Audio/video codecs like VP8, H264, Opus.

35. Can WebRTC capture screen?

👉 Yes, using getDisplayMedia().

36. What is track in WebRTC?

👉 Individual media stream component (audio/video).

37. What is ontrack event?

👉 Event triggered when remote stream is received.

38. Can WebRTC handle multiple streams?

👉 Yes.

39. What is stream cloning?

👉 Reusing media stream for multiple connections.

40. Can WebRTC adjust quality?

👉 Yes, adaptive bitrate is supported.

🟦 Data Channels (41–45)

41. What is RTCDataChannel used for?

👉 Sending text/files between peers.

42. Is DataChannel reliable?

👉 It can be configured as reliable or unreliable.

43. Is DataChannel faster than WebSocket?

👉 Often yes (direct P2P, no server hop).

44. Can we send files using WebRTC?

👉 Yes, via DataChannel.

45. Is DataChannel ordered?

👉 It can be ordered or unordered depending on config.

🟦 Advanced (46–50)

46. What is STUN vs TURN difference?

👉 STUN finds public IP, TURN relays traffic.

47. What is SFU?

👉 Selective Forwarding Unit — server forwards streams to many users.

48. Can WebRTC scale to millions of users?

👉 Not directly — needs SFU/MCU architecture.

49. Is WebRTC connection always direct?

👉 No, TURN server may relay traffic.

50. What is biggest limitation of WebRTC?

👉 Complex setup and difficulty scaling.

🧠 FINAL MEMORY

👉 WebRTC = peer-to-peer real-time communication with signaling + ICE + STUN/TURN setup

//server.js
const express = require("express");
const http = require("http");
const { Server } = require("socket.io");

const app = express();
const server = http.createServer(app);
const io = new Server(server);

app.use(express.static("public"));

io.on("connection", (socket) => {
  console.log("User connected:", socket.id);

  socket.on("offer", (data) => {
    socket.broadcast.emit("offer", data);
  });

  socket.on("answer", (data) => {
    socket.broadcast.emit("answer", data);
  });

  socket.on("ice-candidate", (data) => {
    socket.broadcast.emit("ice-candidate", data);
  });
});

server.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Server running on http://localhost:3000");
});
//client.html in public
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
  <h2>WebRTC Camera + Mic Demo</h2>

  <video id="local" autoplay playsinline muted></video>
  <video id="remote" autoplay playsinline></video>

  <script src="/socket.io/socket.io.js"></script>

  <script>
    const socket = io();

    let localStream;
    let peerConnection;

    const config = {
      iceServers: [
        { urls: "stun:stun.l.google.com:19302" }
      ]
    };

    // 1. Get camera + mic
    navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ video: true, audio: true })
      .then(stream => {
        document.getElementById("local").srcObject = stream;
        localStream = stream;

        createPeer();
        createOffer();
      });

    // 2. Create peer connection
    function createPeer() {
      peerConnection = new RTCPeerConnection(config);

      // send tracks
      localStream.getTracks().forEach(track => {
        peerConnection.addTrack(track, localStream);
      });

      // receive remote stream
      peerConnection.ontrack = (event) => {
        document.getElementById("remote").srcObject = event.streams[0];
      };

      // ICE
      peerConnection.onicecandidate = (event) => {
        if (event.candidate) {
          socket.emit("ice-candidate", event.candidate);
        }
      };
    }

    // 3. Offer (A starts call)
    async function createOffer() {
      const offer = await peerConnection.createOffer();
      await peerConnection.setLocalDescription(offer);

      socket.emit("offer", offer);
    }

    // 4. Receive offer → create answer
    socket.on("offer", async (offer) => {
      if (!peerConnection) createPeer();

      await peerConnection.setRemoteDescription(offer);

      const answer = await peerConnection.createAnswer();
      await peerConnection.setLocalDescription(answer);

      socket.emit("answer", answer);
    });

    // 5. Receive answer
    socket.on("answer", async (answer) => {
      await peerConnection.setRemoteDescription(answer);
    });

    // 6. ICE candidates
    socket.on("ice-candidate", async (candidate) => {
      try {
        await peerConnection.addIceCandidate(candidate);
      } catch (e) {}
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>

Load_balancing
Overal

👉 Load balancing = distributing incoming traffic across multiple servers so no single server gets overloaded.

⚡ Simple idea

Users → Load Balancer → Server 1
                        → Server 2
                        → Server 3

🧠 Why it exists

Without load balancing:

  • one server crashes
  • high latency
  • no scalability

With load balancing:

✔ scalable system

✔ fault tolerant

✔ high availability

Types of Load Balancing

🟦 1. Server-side load balancing

👉 Load balancer sits between client and servers

Client → LB → Server1 / Server2 / Server3

✔ most common

✔ centralized control

🟩 2. Client-side load balancing

👉 Client chooses which server to call

Client → Server1 / Server2 / Server3

✔ no central LB

✔ used in gRPC + microservices

🟨 3. DNS load balancing

👉 DNS returns different IPs for same domain

example.com → IP1 / IP2 / IP3

✔ simple

✔ global distribution

🟪 4. Global load balancing (CDN-based)

👉 Routes user to nearest region

✔ used by big companies

✔ latency optimization

🧠 3. LOAD BALANCING IMPLEMENTATIONS

🟦 1. Hardware Load Balancer

  • physical devices
  • expensive
  • high performance

🟩 2. Software Load Balancer

  • Nginx
  • HAProxy
  • Node.js proxy

✔ flexible

✔ widely used

🟨 3. Cloud Load Balancer

  • AWS ELB
  • GCP Load Balancer
  • Azure LB

✔ auto scaling

✔ managed service

🟪 4. API Gateway (advanced form)

  • authentication
  • routing
  • rate limiting
  • logging

👉 acts as smart L7 load balancer

🟥 5. Client-side LB

  • gRPC client
  • service discovery (Consul, Kubernetes)
Load balancing Algorithms

🟦 Round Robin

👉 distribute sequentially

🟩 Least Connections

👉 send to least busy server

🟨 IP Hash

👉 same user → same server

🟪 Weighted Round Robin

👉 powerful servers get more traffic

🟥 Random

👉 simple but unstable

Load Balancers

🧠 LOAD BALANCER TYPES — DEEP DIVE

🟦 1. Hardware Load Balancer

🧠 What it is

👉 A physical device (appliance) built only for traffic distribution.

It sits between internet and servers:

Internet → Hardware LB → Server 1 / Server 2 / Server 3

⚙️ How it works internally

  • ASIC chips (special hardware processors)
  • handles TCP/IP directly
  • does routing at wire speed
  • no general-purpose CPU overhead

🧠 Features

  • L4 + L7 routing
  • SSL termination
  • DDoS protection
  • health checks

🧠 Examples

  • F5 BIG-IP
  • Citrix NetScaler
  • Cisco ACE

✔ Pros

  • extremely fast (hardware acceleration)
  • very stable
  • handles millions of requests/sec
  • low latency

❌ Cons

  • very expensive 💰
  • hard to scale (buy new device)
  • vendor lock-in
  • less flexible than software

🧠 Use cases

  • banks
  • telecom companies
  • government systems
  • legacy enterprise systems

🟩 2. Software Load Balancer

🧠 What it is

👉 Load balancer implemented in software running on servers.

⚙️ How it works

Runs as a process:

Client → Nginx / HAProxy / Node.js → backend servers

🧠 Examples

  • Nginx
  • HAProxy
  • Node.js proxy servers

🧠 Features

  • HTTP routing
  • reverse proxy
  • SSL termination
  • caching
  • compression

✔ Pros

  • flexible
  • cheap (runs on normal servers)
  • easy to configure
  • widely used in startups + big tech

❌ Cons

  • slower than hardware LB
  • requires server resources
  • scaling depends on infrastructure

🧠 Use cases

  • APIs
  • microservices
  • web apps
  • WebSocket routing

🟨 3. Cloud Load Balancer

🧠 What it is

👉 Fully managed load balancing service by cloud providers.

⚙️ Architecture

User → Cloud LB → Auto-scaled servers

🧠 Examples

  • AWS Elastic Load Balancer (ELB)
  • Google Cloud Load Balancer
  • Azure Load Balancer

🧠 Features

  • auto scaling integration
  • health checks
  • multi-region routing
  • SSL offloading
  • DDoS protection

✔ Pros

  • no maintenance
  • auto scaling support
  • global distribution
  • highly reliable

❌ Cons

  • expensive at scale
  • less control
  • vendor dependency

🧠 Use cases

  • SaaS applications
  • large APIs
  • global systems (Netflix-style apps)

🟪 4. API Gateway (Smart Load Balancer)

🧠 What it is

👉 A smart L7 load balancer + control layer for microservices

⚙️ Architecture

Client → API Gateway → microservices

🧠 What it does (VERY IMPORTANT)

Not just routing:

✔ authentication

✔ rate limiting

✔ logging

✔ request transformation

✔ caching

✔ load balancing

🧠 Examples

  • Kong
  • Amazon API Gateway
  • Apigee
  • Nginx (can act as gateway)

✔ Pros

  • central control point
  • security layer
  • microservices-friendly
  • observability built-in

❌ Cons

  • single bottleneck if not scaled
  • added latency
  • complex configuration

🧠 Use cases

  • microservices architecture
  • fintech apps
  • large backend systems

🟥 5. Client-Side Load Balancing

🧠 What it is

👉 Client decides which server to call using service discovery.

⚙️ Architecture

Client → Server A / Server B / Server C
(no central LB)

🧠 How client knows servers?

Via:

  • Consul
  • etcd
  • Kubernetes DNS
  • service registry

🧠 Examples

  • gRPC load balancing
  • Kubernetes internal services
  • Netflix Eureka (old architecture)

✔ Pros

  • no central bottleneck
  • faster routing (no hop)
  • scalable in distributed systems

❌ Cons

  • complex client logic
  • requires service discovery
  • harder debugging
  • inconsistent behavior across clients

🧠 Use cases

  • microservices (gRPC)
  • Kubernetes internal networking
  • distributed systems

🧠 FINAL COMPARISON (VERY IMPORTANT)

Regionalization and Latency
Overal REGIONALIZATION

Regionalization and Latency is one of the most important concepts in modern distributed systems design. It directly affects how fast your app feels, how scalable it is globally, and even how much it costs to run.

Let’s go step by step: what it is, where it’s used, why it matters, 50 interview-level questions, and a real project idea.

1. What is Regionalization?

Regionalization means designing a system to operate across multiple geographic regions (e.g., US-East, Europe, Asia).

Instead of serving all users from one server location, you:

  • Deploy servers in multiple regions
  • Route users to the closest region
  • Replicate data across regions

👉 Example:

  • User in Uzbekistan → served from Europe or Middle East region
  • User in USA → served from US-East region
Overal Latency

Latency is the time delay between a user action and system response.

Example:

  • You click a button → server responds in 200ms → latency = 200ms

Latency is affected by:

  • Distance (major factor)
  • Network quality
  • Server load
  • Routing efficiency
Why Regionalization + Latency matters

Without it:

  • Users far from server experience slow apps
  • High bounce rate
  • Poor UX
  • Timeout errors in APIs

With it:

  • Faster response time
  • Better UX globally
  • Higher scalability
  • Fault tolerance (region failure doesn’t break system)
Where is it used?

1. Social Media

  • Instagram, TikTok, Facebook → edge servers globally

2. Streaming

  • Netflix, YouTube → CDN + regional caches

3. E-commerce

  • Amazon → nearest warehouse + regional APIs

4. Gaming

  • PUBG, Fortnite → region-based game servers

5. Finance

  • Trading systems → ultra-low latency regions

6. SaaS apps

  • Google Docs, Figma → global collaboration with sync regions
Key Concepts
  • CDN (Content Delivery Network)
  • Edge computing
  • GeoDNS routing
  • Data replication (eventual vs strong consistency)
  • Active-active vs active-passive regions
  • Failover strategies
  • Load balancing per region
QA

🟢 Beginner Level (1–15)

1. What is latency?

Latency is the time delay between a user request and the system’s response.

2. What causes latency?

  • Physical distance between client and server
  • Network congestion
  • Server processing time
  • Database queries
  • Routing inefficiencies

3. What is regionalization in system design?

Regionalization means deploying your system in multiple geographic regions to serve users from the closest location.

4. Why is regionalization important?

It reduces latency, improves availability, and provides better user experience globally.

5. What is RTT (Round Trip Time)?

RTT is the total time for a request to go from client → server → client.

6. What is propagation delay?

Time taken for data to physically travel through the network.

7. What is a data center?

A physical facility that hosts servers, storage, and networking infrastructure.

8. What is a region in cloud computing?

A geographic area containing multiple data centers (e.g., US-East, Europe-West).

9. What is a CDN?

A Content Delivery Network caches content closer to users to reduce latency.

10. How does distance affect latency?

Greater distance increases travel time for data packets, increasing latency.

11. What is edge location?

A small data center closer to users used for caching and fast responses.

12. What is caching?

Storing frequently used data temporarily for faster access.

13. What is DNS?

DNS translates domain names into IP addresses.

14. What is request routing?

The process of directing user requests to a specific server or region.

15. What is geographic load balancing?

Routing traffic based on user location to the nearest server.

🟡 Intermediate Level (16–35)

16. How does a CDN reduce latency?

It serves content from edge servers closest to users instead of the origin server.

17. What is GeoDNS?

A DNS system that routes users to servers based on geographic location.

18. What is active-active architecture?

Multiple regions serve traffic simultaneously.

19. What is active-passive architecture?

One region is active, others are standby for failover.

20. What is data replication?

Copying data across multiple regions or databases.

21. What is eventual consistency?

Data updates propagate over time; not all regions are instantly synchronized.

22. What is strong consistency?

All users see the same data immediately after update.

23. Why is write latency harder than read latency?

Writes must be replicated across regions, increasing coordination time.

24. What is cross-region replication?

Synchronizing data between geographically separate regions.

25. What is a failover system?

Automatically switching to a backup region when the primary fails.

26. What is edge computing?

Processing data closer to the user instead of central servers.

27. What is cache invalidation?

Removing or updating outdated cached data.

28. What is a hot region?

A region actively serving traffic.

29. What is a cold region?

A backup region with no or minimal traffic.

30. What is split-brain problem?

When two regions think they are the primary, causing data inconsistency.

31. What is load balancing?

Distributing traffic across multiple servers.

32. What is latency-based routing?

Routing requests to the lowest-latency region.

33. What is multi-region architecture?

System deployed across multiple geographic regions.

34. What is a session problem in multi-region systems?

User session data may not sync across regions.

35. What is data locality?

Keeping data close to where it is used most frequently.

🔴 Advanced Level (36–50)

36. How does AWS Route 53 reduce latency?

It uses latency-based routing to send users to the fastest region.

37. What is multi-master replication?

Multiple regions can write data simultaneously.

38. What is quorum in distributed systems?

A majority agreement mechanism for consistency in distributed data.

39. Explain CAP theorem in multi-region systems.

You can only guarantee 2 of 3:

  • Consistency
  • Availability
  • Partition tolerance

40. How do global systems handle authentication?

Using centralized identity providers or token-based systems (JWT, OAuth).

41. What is consistency lag?

Delay between data update in one region and its replication to others.

42. What is request fan-out?

A single request is split into multiple requests across regions/services.

43. How do companies reduce global latency?

  • CDNs
  • Edge servers
  • Geo routing
  • Caching
  • Data replication

44. What is disaster recovery (DR) region?

A backup region used when primary region fails.

45. How do you handle user sessions globally?

  • Store sessions in distributed cache (Redis cluster)
  • Or use stateless JWT tokens

46. What is dynamic content caching problem?

Dynamic data changes frequently so caching must be carefully invalidated.

47. How does Netflix reduce latency globally?

  • CDNs for video streaming
  • Regional caching
  • Edge servers close to ISPs

48. What is cross-region database consistency problem?

Keeping data synchronized without conflicts or delays.

49. How do you reduce write latency in global systems?

  • Local writes + async replication
  • Event-driven architecture
  • Multi-master databases

50. Design a global low-latency chat system (answer idea)

  • WebSocket servers in each region
  • GeoDNS routing
  • Redis per region
  • Async message replication
  • CDN for static assets
  • Failover routing
WebSocket (practice)
Overview

👉 WebSockets are a persistent, two-way communication protocol between client and server.

Unlike HTTP:

HTTP: request → response → close

WebSocket:

connection opens → stays open → both sides can send data anytime

⚡ Key idea

👉 Both client and server can talk freely anytime:

  • Client → Server ✅
  • Server → Client ✅

🍽️ Simple analogy

  • HTTP = ordering food 🍔
  • SSE = radio 📻 (server talks only)
  • WebSocket = phone call 📞 (both talk freely)

⚡ 2. WebSocket lifecycle

  1. Client sends HTTP request (handshake)
  1. Server upgrades to WebSocket protocol
  1. Connection becomes persistent
  1. Both sides send messages anytime
  1. Connection closes when one side disconnects
USAGE

How WebSockets Work in Phone Calls

  1. Signaling (Setup): WebSockets act as a persistent, full-duplex communication channel between the phone app and the server. When you dial, the browser or app sends a "call invitation" (often using SIP—Session Initiation Protocol) over a Secure WebSocket (WSS) connection to the VoIP server.
  1. Bridging to Telephony: The server receives this WebSocket message and bridges it to traditional telephony networks (PSTN) or other VoIP clients.
  1. Real-Time Data: Once the connection is made, the audio itself is usually streamed via WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication) for low-latency, peer-to-peer audio transfer.
  1. AI Processing: In specialized use cases, live call audio can be streamed directly to an AI assistant or transcription engine via a WebSocket for real-time analysis.

    Yeastar +4

Full WebSocket Use Cases

WebSockets are designed for low-latency, bidirectional, real-time communication. Key use cases include:

  • Live Chat and Messaging: Instant messaging platforms (like WhatsApp Web, Facebook Messenger, Slack) use WebSockets for real-time message delivery and typing indicators.
  • Real-time Collaborative Editing: Tools like Google Docs or Figma use WebSockets to sync changes between multiple users editing the same document simultaneously.
  • Online Multiplayer Gaming: Gaming clients use WebSockets to send player actions and receive game state updates in real-time, requiring low-latency synchronization.
  • Financial Trading Dashboards: Stock or crypto platforms (like TradingView) use WebSockets to push live price updates, order book changes, and ticker updates, where delays of even a second are unacceptable.
  • Live Location Tracking: Ride-sharing apps (like Uber) use WebSockets to send live GPS coordinates from the driver's phone to the passenger's app.
  • Live Dashboards/Alerts: Real-time monitoring systems (e.g., IoT data, system alerts) push notifications to a dashboard the moment an event occurs.

    Ably Realtime +4

const { WebSocketServer } = require("ws");

const wss = new WebSocketServer({ port: 5050 });

console.log("WebSocket server running on ws://localhost:5050");

wss.on("connection", (ws, req) => {
  console.log("\n=== NEW CLIENT CONNECTED ===");

  // 🧠 1. Incoming HTTP upgrade request headers
  console.log("📥 Request headers:");
  console.log(req.headers);

  console.log("\n📥 Client IP:", req.socket.remoteAddress);

  // 🟢 Send initial message
  const welcomeMsg = "Welcome! You are connected to WebSocket server";
  ws.send(welcomeMsg);

  console.log("📤 Sent to client:", welcomeMsg);

  // 🧠 2. Incoming messages
  ws.on("message", (message, isBinary) => {
    const msg = message.toString();

    console.log("\n📩 Received from client:");
    console.log("Raw:", message);
    console.log("String:", msg);
    console.log("Is Binary:", isBinary);

    // response
    const response = `Server echo: ${msg}`;

    ws.send(response);

    console.log("📤 Sent to client:", response);
  });

  // 🧠 3. Connection close
  ws.on("close", () => {
    console.log("\n❌ Client disconnected");
  });

  // 🧠 4. Errors
  ws.on("error", (err) => {
    console.log("\n⚠️ WebSocket error:", err);
  });
});

  <input id="msg" placeholder="Type message" />
  <button onclick="sendMsg()">Send</button>

  <div id="chat"></div>

  <script>
    const socket = new WebSocket("ws://localhost:5050");

    socket.onopen = () => {
      addMessage("Connected to server");
    };

    socket.onmessage = (event) => {
      addMessage("Server: " + event.data);
    };

    function sendMsg() {
      const input = document.getElementById("msg");
      const message = input.value;

      socket.send(message);
      addMessage("You: " + message);

      input.value = "";
    }

    function addMessage(msg) {
      const div = document.getElementById("chat");
      const p = document.createElement("p");
      p.textContent = msg;
      div.appendChild(p);
    }
  </script>
</body>

NETWORKING ESSENTIALS
RIR

👉 RIR (Regional Internet Registry) is an organization that manages and distributes IP addresses in a specific region of the world.

  • It gives IP addresses to ISPs and organizations
  • Each RIR is responsible for a geographic area
  • Example: RIPE (Europe), APNIC (Asia), ARIN (North America)
UDP: Fast but Unreliable

User Datagram Protocol (UDP) is the machinegun of protocols. It offers few features on top of IP but is very fast. Spray and pray is the right way to think about this. It provides a simpler, connectionless service with no guarantees of delivery, ordering, or duplicate protection.

If you write an application that receives UDP datagrams, you'll be able to see where they came from (i.e. the source IP address and port) and where they're going (i.e. the destination IP address and port). But that's it! The rest is a binary blob.

Key characteristics of UDP include:

  1. Connectionless: No handshake or connection setup
  1. No guarantee of delivery: Packets may be lost without notification
  1. No ordering: Packets may arrive in a different order than sent
  1. Lower latency: Less overhead means faster transmission

No setup sounds great but 2 and 3 kinda suck, so why would you want to use UDP?

UDP is perfect for applications where speed is more important than reliability, such as live video streaming, online gaming, VoIP, and DNS lookups. In these cases the application or client is equipped to handle the occasional packet loss or out of order packet. For VOIP as an example, the client might just drop the occasional packet leading to a hiccup in the audio but overall the conversation is still intelligible. This is vastly preferable to retransmitting those lost packets and clogging up the network with ACKs.

Browsers don't have widespread support for UDP yet outside of WebRTC (we'll get into it). If you're thinking about a design which could use UDP (like the spamming of hearts and reactions in Facebook Live Comments), think about what you'll do for your browser-based users. It might be that your app-based users get a real-time UDP stream of reactions while browser-based users a slower, batched HTTP stream which you spread out over time in the UI.

TCP: Reliable but with Overhead

TCP: Reliable but with Overhead

Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is the workhorse of the internet. It provides reliable, ordered, and error-checked delivery of data. It establishes a connection through a three-way handshake (we saw this illustrated above with the HTTP example) and maintains that connection throughout the communication session.

This connection is called a "stream" and is a stateful connection between the client and server — it also gives us a basis to talk about ordering: two messages sent in the same stream/connection will arrive in the same order. TCP will ensure that recipients of messages acknowledge their receipt and, if they don't, will retransmit the message until it is acknowledged.

Key Characteristics of TCP

  1. Connection-oriented: Establishes a dedicated connection before data transfer
  1. Reliable delivery: Guarantees that data arrives in order and without errors
  1. Flow control: Prevents overwhelming receivers with too much data
  1. Congestion control: Adapts to network congestion to prevent collapse

TCP is ideal for applications where data integrity is critical — that is, basically everything where UDP is not a good fit.

When to Choose Each Protocol

In system design interviews, most interviewers will expect you're using TCP by default — it often doesn't need to be directly mentioned. That's good because that's also our recommendation!

But you'll be able to earn extra points if you can make the case for a UDP application and not bungle the details. So the question you should be asking yourself is whether UDP is a better fit for your use-case.

You might choose UDP when:

  • Low latency is critical (real-time applications, gaming)
  • Some data loss is acceptable (media streaming)
  • You're handling high-volume telemetry or logs where occasional loss is acceptable
  • You don't need to support web browsers (or you have an alternative for that client)

Modern applications often use both protocols. For example, a web-based video conferencing app might use TCP/HTTP for signaling and authentication but UDP/WebRTC for the actual audio/video streams.

TCP vs UDP Comparison

FeatureUDPTCP
ConnectionConnectionlessConnection-oriented
ReliabilityBest-effort deliveryGuaranteed delivery
OrderingNo ordering guaranteesMaintains order
Flow ControlNoYes
Congestion ControlNoYes
Header Size8 bytes20-60 bytes
SpeedFasterSlower due to overhead
Use CasesStreaming, gaming, VoIPEverything Else
Application Layer Protocols
HTTP/HTTPS: The Web's Foundation

Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is the de-facto standard for data communication on the web. It's a request-response protocol where clients send requests to servers, and servers respond with the requested data.

HTTP is a stateless protocol, meaning that each request is independent and the server doesn't need to maintain any information about previous requests. This is generally a good thing. In system design you'll want to minimize the surface area of your system that needs to be stateful where possible. Most simple HTTP servers can be described as a function of the request parameters — they're stateless!

Here's a simple HTTP request/response. You can actually open up a TCP connection and send an HTTP request/response by hand with netcat (nc on the command line) if you'd like!

Simple HTTP Request/Response

You'll see a few key concepts:

  1. Request methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.
  1. Status codes: 200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error, etc.
  1. Headers: Metadata about the request or response
  1. Body: The actual content being transferred

The HTTP request methods and status codes are well-defined and standardized (think of them like enums). It's good to know some of the common ones, but most interviewers aren't going to get into this level of detail except if you're using a RESTful API.

Common Request Methods

  • GET: Request data from the server. GET requests should be idempotent and don't have a body.
  • POST: Send data to the server.
  • PUT: Update data on the server.
  • PATCH: Update a resource partially.
  • DELETE: Delete data from the server. DELETE requests should be idempotent.

Common Status Codes

  • Success (2xx)
    • 200 OK: The request was successful
    • 201 Created: The request was successful and a new resource was created
  • Moved (3xx)
    • 302 Found: The requested resource has been moved temporarily
    • 301 Moved Permanently: The requested resource has been moved permanently
  • Client Error (4xx)
    • 404 Not Found: The requested resource was not found
    • 401 Unauthorized: The request requires authentication
    • 403 Forbidden: The server understood the request but refuses to authorize it
    • 429 Too Many Requests: The client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time
  • Server Error (5xx)
    • 500 Server Error: The server encountered an error
    • 502 Bad Gateway: The server received an invalid response from the upstream server

The headers are much more flexible (think of them like key/value pairs). This flexibility demonstrates the pragmatic design philosophy that underlies much of the HTTP spec.

HTTP headers are a great example of how to design an interface that is flexible to unknown future use-cases and provides a good lesson for API design. Content negotiation is a perfect case study.

The HTTP Accepts-Encoding header as an example provides clients a way to indicate they can handle different types of content encoding. This allows servers to provide (e.g.) gzip or br (brotli) encoded responses if they're available. Servers can then respond with the most efficient encoding for that client with Content-Encoding: X providing both backward compatibility and graceful degradation.

HTTPS adds a security layer (TLS/SSL) to encrypt communications, protecting against eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks. If you're building a public website you're going to be using HTTPS without exception. Generally speaking this means that the contents of your HTTP requests and responses are encrypted and safe in transit.

While the contents of your HTTPS requests and responses are encrypted, they aren't guaranteed to be generated by your client! Your API should never trust the contents of the request body without validating it. A common mistake is to include the user's ID in the request body and use it to make a database call. If an attacker can change the request body, they can change the user ID and read arbitrary user data. Ouch!

This doesn't mean you can't include user IDs in your requests. It just means you need to be able to validate them on the server and your API shouldn't ask for anything you can't trust.

That's HTTP in a nutshell! Now let's talk about how to use it to build APIs.

REST: Simple and Flexible

REST: Simple and Flexible

While HTTP can be used directly to build websites, oftentimes system designs are concerned with the communication between services via APIs. For creating these APIs, we have three main paradigms: REST, GraphQL, and gRPC.

REST is the most common API paradigm you'll use in system design interviews. It's a simple and flexible way to create APIs that are easy to understand and use. The core principle behind REST is that clients are often performing simple operations against resources (think of them like database tables or files on a server).

In RESTful API design, the primary challenge is to model your resources and the operations you can perform on them. RESTful API's take advantage of the HTTP methods or verbs together with some opinionated conventions about the paths and the body of the request. They often use JSON to represent the resources in both the request and response bodies — although it's not strictly required.

If you've followed our Delivery Framework, your Core Entities will oftentimes map directly to the resources in your API. Bonus!

A simple RESTful API might look like this (where User is a JSON object representing a user):

GET /users/{id} -> User

Here we're using the HTTP method "GET" to indicate that we're requesting a resource. The {id} is a placeholder for the resource ID, in this case the user ID of the user we want to retrieve.

When we want to update that user, we can use the HTTP method "PUT" to indicate that we're updating a pre-existing resource.

PUT /users/{id} -> User
{
"username": "john.doe",
"email": "john.doe@example.com"
}

We can also create new resources by using the HTTP method "POST". We'll include the body the content of the resource we want to create. Note that I'm not specifying an ID here because the server will assign one.

POST /users -> User
{
"username": "stefan.mai",
"email": "stefan@hellointerview.com"
}

Finally, resources can be nested to represent relationships between resources. For example, a user might have many posts, so we can represent that relationship by nesting the posts under the user resource.

GET /users/{id}/posts -> [Post]

Many engineers often think in terms of methods like updateUser or startGame. These are operations, not resources, so they're not RESTful.

In REST, we want to think in terms of resources and the operations you can perform on them. So our updateUser might be PUT /users/{id} and our startGame might be PATCH /games with { "status": "started" }.

Where to Use It

Overall REST is very flexible for a wide variety of use-cases and applications. ElasticSearch uses it to manage documents, configure indexes, and more. Check out that deep dive if you want to see a great example of a RESTful API.

REST is not going to be the most performant solution for very high throughput services, and generally speaking JSON is a pretty inefficient format for serializing and deserializing data.

That said, most applications aren't going to be bottlenecked by request serialization. Like TCP, REST is where we'd suggest you default for your interviews. It's well-understood and a good baseline for building scalable systems. You should reach for GraphQL, gRPC, SSE, or WebSockets if you have specific needs that REST can't meet. For practical REST API design patterns, see our API Design guide.

REST VS RESTFUL

Follows all core constraints:

  • stateless
  • proper HTTP methods
  • resource-based URLs
  • uniform interface

🔥 Key Differences

FeatureRESTRESTful
TypeConcept / architectureImplementation
NatureTheoretical rulesReal API
UsageDesign guidelineWorking system
Example“Use GET for fetching”GET /users API

🧠 What is Consistent Hashing?

Consistent Hashing is a technique used in distributed systems to distribute data across nodes (servers) in a way that minimizes data movement when nodes are added or removed.

👉 Traditional hashing:

hash(key) % N   // N = number of servers

Problem:

  • If N changes → ALL keys remap ❌

👉 Consistent hashing:

  • Maps keys and servers onto a circular space (hash ring)
  • Only small subset of keys move when topology changes ✅

🔁 Core Idea

  • Hash both:
    • Servers
    • Keys
  • Place them on a ring (0 → 2^32 or 2^64)

📍 Rule:

A key belongs to the first server clockwise

🔵 Visual Representation (Hash Ring)

0 ─────────────────────────── 2^32
│                             │
│      (Server A)             │
│          ●                  │
│                             │
│   ● (Key1)                  │
│                             │
│                 ● (Server B)│
│                             │
│      ● (Key2)               │
│                             │
│            ● (Server C)     │
│                             │
└─────────────────────────────┘

👉 Key is assigned to next server clockwise

⚙️ How It Works (Step-by-Step)

1. Hash servers

hash("Server A") → position on ring

2. Hash keys

hash("user:123") → position

3. Assign key

  • Move clockwise
  • First server encountered = owner

🔥 Why Not Modulo Hashing?

FeatureModulo HashingConsistent Hashing
Node change❌ massive rehash✅ minimal movement
Scalability❌ poor✅ excellent
Distributed systems❌ weak✅ ideal

🧩 Problem It Solves

Without Consistent Hashing

Adding 1 server:

Before: hash(key) % 3
After:  hash(key) % 4

💥 Almost all keys remapped

With Consistent Hashing

Adding 1 server:

  • Only keys between neighboring nodes move

✅ ~1/N data moves

🧱 Virtual Nodes (VNodes)

Problem:

  • Uneven distribution

Solution:

  • Each server has multiple positions
Server A → A1, A2, A3
Server B → B1, B2, B3

✅ Benefits:

  • Better load balancing
  • Fault tolerance

⚡ Advantages

  • Minimal data movement
  • Horizontal scalability
  • Load balancing (with vnodes)
  • Fault tolerance
  • Used in real-world distributed systems

❌ Disadvantages

  • Slightly complex implementation
  • Requires good hash function
  • Needs virtual nodes for balance
Usage

🌍 Real-World Use Cases

1. Distributed Caching

  • Redis
  • Memcached

👉 Avoid cache invalidation on scaling

2. NoSQL Databases

  • Apache Cassandra
  • DynamoDB

👉 Data partitioning across nodes

3. Load Balancers

  • Sticky sessions
  • Request routing

4. CDN (Content Delivery Networks)

  • Cloudflare
  • Akamai

👉 Route users to closest/consistent node

5. Distributed Storage Systems

  • Hadoop HDFS

🧪 Example (Simple)

Servers:

A → 10
B → 50
C → 90

Key:

K1 → 60 → goes to C
K2 → 20 → goes to B

🧠 Practice Problems

🟢 Easy

  1. Why does modulo hashing fail in scaling?
  1. What is a hash ring?
  1. What happens when a node is removed?

🟡 Medium

  1. Explain virtual nodes
  1. How does consistent hashing reduce rebalancing?
  1. Implement consistent hashing

🔴 Hard

  1. Design distributed cache using consistent hashing
  1. Handle hot keys problem
  1. Combine consistent hashing with replication
Implementation

import hashlib
import bisect

class ConsistentHash:
def init(self, nodes=None, replicas=3):
self.replicas = replicas
self.ring = []
self.nodes = {}

    if nodes:
        for node in nodes:
            self.add_node(node)

def hash(self, key):
    return int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)

def add_node(self, node):
    for i in range(self.replicas):
        key = self.hash(f"{node}-{i}")
        self.ring.append(key)
        self.nodes[key] = node
    self.ring.sort()

def get_node(self, key):
    h = self.hash(key)
    idx = bisect.bisect(self.ring, h) % len(self.ring)
    return self.nodes[self.ring[idx]]
🎯 50 Interview Questions

🟢 Basics (1–15)

1. What is consistent hashing?

A technique to distribute keys across nodes such that minimal keys are remapped when nodes change.

2. Why is it used?

To ensure scalability and stability in distributed systems when nodes are added/removed.

3. Difference from modulo hashing?

  • Modulo: hash(key) % N → all keys remap if N changes
  • Consistent hashing → only ~1/N keys move

4. What is a hash ring?

A circular space where both nodes and keys are mapped using a hash function.

5. How are keys mapped?

Each key is assigned to the first node clockwise on the ring.

6. What happens when a node is added?

Only keys in the range between the new node and its predecessor are reassigned.

7. What happens when a node is removed?

Its keys are reassigned to the next node clockwise.

8. Why clockwise traversal?

It ensures a deterministic and simple lookup rule.

9. What is a hash collision?

When two different inputs produce the same hash value.

10. What hash functions are used?

Common ones:

  • MD5
  • SHA-1
  • MurmurHash (fast & widely used)

11. What is uniform distribution?

Keys are evenly spread across nodes to avoid overload.

12. Why do we hash servers?

To place them in the same keyspace as data, enabling consistent mapping.

13. What is scalability?

Ability to add/remove nodes without major disruption.

14. What is partitioning?

Splitting data across multiple nodes.

15. What is rebalancing?

Redistributing keys when nodes change.

🟡 Intermediate (16–35)

16. What are virtual nodes (vnodes)?

Each physical node is represented by multiple positions on the ring.

17. Why are vnodes needed?

To improve load balancing and reduce uneven distribution.

18. How many virtual nodes per server?

Typically 100–300+, depending on system size and load.

19. Tradeoffs of vnodes?

  • ✅ Better balance
  • ❌ More memory & complexity

20. How to handle skew?

Use:

  • More virtual nodes
  • Better hash functions
  • Load monitoring

21. What is load imbalance?

Some nodes receive more keys than others.

22. What is replication factor?

Number of copies of each key stored across nodes.

23. How does Apache Cassandra use consistent hashing?

  • Uses a ring with tokens
  • Each node owns a range of data
  • Supports replication across nodes

24. How does DynamoDB use it?

  • Uses partitioning based on hashed keys
  • Internally inspired by consistent hashing (from Amazon Dynamo paper)

25. What is token range?

A segment of the hash ring that a node is responsible for.

26. What is ring size?

Range of hash values (e.g., 0 → 2^32).

27. What happens on node failure?

  • Keys are redirected to replica nodes or next node
  • System continues functioning

28. How to rebalance data?

  • Add/remove nodes
  • Automatically redistribute affected key ranges

29. What is hot key problem?

Certain keys receive disproportionately high traffic.

30. Solutions to hot keys?

  • Replication
  • Caching
  • Key sharding (split one key into many)

31. What is data locality?

Keeping related data close together for efficiency.

32. What is sharding?

Splitting data into smaller parts across nodes.

33. Compare with rendezvous hashing

  • Rendezvous hashing:
    • No ring
    • Simpler lookup
  • Consistent hashing:
    • Ring-based
    • Easier to visualize

34. What is sticky session?

User requests are always routed to the same server.

35. What is distributed cache invalidation?

Ensuring all nodes update/remove stale cached data.

🔴 Advanced (36–50)

36. Design a distributed cache system

  • Use consistent hashing to assign keys
  • Use replication for fault tolerance
  • Example: Redis cluster

37. Design URL shortener using consistent hashing

  • Hash short URL → assign to node
  • Store mapping in distributed storage
  • Ensures scalability

38. How to scale to millions of nodes?

  • Use hierarchical hashing
  • Partition rings
  • Use metadata services

39. How to monitor imbalance?

  • Track load per node
  • Use metrics dashboards
  • Auto-adjust vnode count

40. CAP theorem relation?

Consistent hashing helps in partition tolerance, but tradeoffs exist between:

  • Consistency
  • Availability

41. Consistency vs availability tradeoff?

  • Strong consistency → slower
  • High availability → eventual consistency

42. How to handle replication?

Store data on:

  • Primary node
  • Next N nodes clockwise

43. Multi-region deployment?

  • Use multiple rings or geo-aware routing
  • Combine with CDNs like Cloudflare

44. Failure recovery strategies?

  • Replication
  • Automatic failover
  • Data repair mechanisms

45. Gossip protocol relation?

Used (e.g., in Cassandra) to share node state across cluster.

46. Compare with range-based partitioning

  • Range partitioning:
    • Good for ordered queries
    • Poor scalability
  • Consistent hashing:
    • Better distribution
    • Less predictable ranges

47. When NOT to use consistent hashing?

  • When you need:
    • Range queries
    • Strong ordering
    • Simple small systems

48. Implement with weighted nodes

Assign more virtual nodes to stronger servers.

49. Optimize lookup time

  • Use binary search on sorted ring
  • Use balanced trees or skip lists

50. How does Kubernetes use hashing (conceptually)?

Kubernetes uses hashing for:

  • Service routing
  • Load balancing (not pure consistent hashing, but similar ideas)

🌍 Content Delivery Network (CDN) — Deep Dive

📘 1. What is a CDN?

A Content Delivery Network (CDN) is a distributed network of servers that delivers content (images, videos, APIs, static files) from the closest location to the user.

🧠 Simple idea:

Instead of loading from one far server → load from a nearby server

📦 Example:

  • User in Tashkent requests image
  • Instead of loading from USA server ❌
  • CDN serves from nearby region ✅

⚙️ 2. How CDN Works

4

🔁 Request Flow:

User → DNS → CDN Edge Server → (cache hit?)
   → YES → return content
   → NO → fetch from origin → cache → return

server.js

const express = require("express");
const fs = require("fs");

const app = express();

function loadCache() {
  return JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("./cache.json"));
}

function saveCache(cache) {
  fs.writeFileSync("./cache.json", JSON.stringify(cache, null, 2));
}

// SIMULATED ORIGIN
function fetchFromOrigin(key) {
  return `Data for ${key} from origin`;
}

// CDN ENDPOINT
app.get("/cdn/:key", (req, res) => {
  const key = req.params.key;
  const cache = loadCache();

  if (cache[key]) {
    return res.json({ source: "CACHE", data: cache[key] });
  }

  const data = fetchFromOrigin(key);
  cache[key] = data;
  saveCache(cache);

  res.json({ source: "ORIGIN", data });
});

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("CDN simulation running");
});
