50+ CDN Interview Q&A (3+ lines each)

🟢 Basics (1–15)

1. What is a CDN?

A CDN is a network of distributed servers that deliver content closer to users.

It reduces latency and improves performance.

It is widely used in modern web applications.

2. Why use CDN?

To improve speed and reduce load on origin server.

It provides faster content delivery.

It also improves reliability.

3. What is edge server?

An edge server is a CDN server located near users.

It caches content for faster access.

It reduces latency significantly.

4. What is origin server?

The origin server is the main source of content.

CDN fetches data from it when needed.

It is the backend server.

5. What is cache hit?

When requested content is found in CDN cache.

It results in fast response.

No need to contact origin.

6. What is cache miss?

When content is not in cache.

CDN fetches from origin.

Slower than cache hit.

7. What is latency?

Time taken to deliver content.

CDN reduces latency.

Important for user experience.

8. What is TTL?

Time To Live defines cache duration.

After expiry, content is refreshed.

Used in caching strategy.

9. What is DNS routing?

DNS directs user to nearest CDN server.

It improves speed.

Used in CDN systems.

10. What is static content?

Content that does not change often.

Example: images, CSS, JS.

Ideal for CDN.

Example: user dashboard.

Harder to cache.

12. What is caching?

Storing data for faster access.

CDN uses caching heavily.

Improves performance.

13. What is edge computing?

Running logic at edge servers.

Reduces latency further.

Used in modern CDNs.

14. What is DDoS protection?

CDN absorbs malicious traffic.

Protects origin server.

Improves security.

15. What is geo-routing?

🟡 Intermediate (16–35)

16. How CDN reduces latency?

19. What is CDN caching strategy?

Includes TTL and invalidation.

Balances performance and freshness.

20. What is origin shield?

Intermediate cache between CDN and origin.

Reduces origin load further.

Improves efficiency.

21. What is CDN failover?

Switching to another server if one fails.

Improves availability.

Used in distributed systems.

22. What is CDN compression?

Reducing file size for faster transfer.

Example: gzip, brotli.

Improves performance.

23. What is cache hierarchy?

Multiple levels of caching.

Edge → regional → origin.

Improves efficiency.

24. What is CDN purge?

Directing request to best server.

Based on location or load.

34. What is hot cache?

Frequently accessed cached data.

Fast responses.

Improves performance.

35. What is CDN cost optimization?

Reducing origin traffic and bandwidth.

CDN helps save costs.

🔴 Advanced (36–55)

36. How CDN handles large traffic?

By distributing load across edge servers.

37. What is edge logic?

38. What is CDN consistency issue?

How CDN knows which server to route the request?

✅ How DNS chooses one server among many (CDN)

🔁 Exact Flow

1. User → asks DNS: "example.com?"
2. DNS sees the request coming from a resolver IP (ISP / Google DNS)
3. CDN DNS checks its INTERNAL DATABASE:
     - list of all edge servers (pre-configured)
     - their regions (Tashkent, Frankfurt, etc.)
     - health + load
4. DNS maps resolver IP → approximate region (GeoIP)
5. DNS selects nearest/healthy server IP from its list
6. DNS returns THAT IP to user

🧠 Key Answers to Your Questions

❓ “Does DNS have server list?”

👉 YES

  • CDN provider maintains full list of edge servers internally
  • This is pre-configured + constantly updated

❓ “How does DNS know closest server?”

👉 It does NOT use hop count directly

It uses:

  • IP → region mapping (GeoIP database)
  • sometimes latency measurements
  • server health/load

👉 So:

“Closest” = best guess based on IP location, not exact distance

❓ “Does DNS calculate network path?”

👉 ❌ NO

DNS does NOT run routing algorithms

👉 That is handled later by the network (BGP / Anycast)

⚡ Important Separation (THIS IS THE CONFUSION)

🟢 DNS does:

  • choose which IP to return

🔵 Network (BGP) does:

  • route request to actual closest server

🔥 Final One-Line Truth

DNS chooses a server using a pre-known list + IP-based location guess; it does NOT calculate actual network distance — routing is handled later by the network.
replication

🧠 What is Replication?

Replication is the process of storing copies of the same data on multiple nodes to improve:

  • Availability
  • Fault tolerance
  • Read performance

👉 Instead of one server holding data, multiple servers hold the same data.

🎯 Why Replication?

Without replication:

  • Single server failure = 💥 data unavailable

With replication:

  • Failure → another node serves data ✅
types of replication

🔁 Types of Replication

1. Synchronous Replication

6

  • Data is written to all replicas before success
  • ✅ Strong consistency
  • ❌ Higher latency

2. Asynchronous Replication

  • Primary writes first, replicas updated later
  • ✅ Fast writes
  • ❌ Risk of data loss

3. Semi-Synchronous

  • Hybrid approach
  • Wait for at least one replica before success
replication models

Primary–Replica (Leader–Follower)

  • One leader handles writes
  • Replicas handle reads

Multi-Leader

  • Multiple nodes accept writes
  • Conflict resolution required

Leaderless (Dynamo-style)

  • Any node can accept writes
  • Uses quorum (R/W)

Used in:

  • Apache Cassandra
  • DynamoDB

⚡ Key Concepts

  • Replication factor (RF) → number of copies
  • Quorum (R/W) → minimum nodes for read/write
  • Eventual consistency
  • Strong consistency
  • Replication lag
usage in real world

Databases

  • MySQL (read replicas)
  • PostgreSQL

Distributed Systems

  • Apache Kafka (partition replication)

Caching Systems

  • Redis cluster replication

Cloud Storage

  • Amazon Web Services S3 replication

app.js

const fs = require("fs");
const path = require("path");

const PRIMARY = "./primary/data";
const REPLICAS = ["./replica1/data", "./replica2/data"];

// Ensure directories exist
[PRIMARY, ...REPLICAS].forEach(dir => {
  if (!fs.existsSync(dir)) fs.mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true });
});

// Write file to primary and replicate
function writeFile(filename, content) {
  const filePath = path.join(PRIMARY, filename);
  fs.writeFileSync(filePath, content);
  console.log(`Primary write: ${filename}`);

  replicate(filename, content);
}

// Replication (async simulation)
function replicate(filename, content) {
  REPLICAS.forEach(replica => {
    const filePath = path.join(replica, filename);

    setTimeout(() => {
      fs.writeFileSync(filePath, content);
      console.log(`Replicated to ${replica}`);
    }, Math.random() * 1000); // simulate lag
  });
}

// Read from any replica
function readFile(filename) {
  for (let replica of REPLICAS) {
    const filePath = path.join(replica, filename);
    if (fs.existsSync(filePath)) {
      return fs.readFileSync(filePath, "utf-8");
    }
  }
  return "Not found";
}

// Demo
writeFile("test.txt", "Hello replication!");
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("Read:", readFile("test.txt"));
}, 1500);
Q&A

1. What is replication?

Copying data across multiple nodes for availability and fault tolerance.

2. Why is replication used?

  • High availability
  • Fault tolerance
  • Read scalability

3. What is a replica?

A copy of data stored on another node.

4. What is a primary node?

Node that handles writes.

5. What is a replica node?

Node that handles reads (usually).

6. What is synchronous replication?

Write completes only after all replicas confirm.

7. What is asynchronous replication?

Write completes before replicas are updated.

8. What is eventual consistency?

Data becomes consistent after some time.

9. What is strong consistency?

All nodes see the same data immediately.

10. What is replication lag?

Delay between primary and replica updates.

11. What is failover?

Switching to replica when primary fails.

12. What is redundancy?

Having multiple copies of data.

13. What is data durability?

Guarantee that data is not lost.

14. What is read scaling?

Using replicas to handle more read requests.

15. What is write amplification?

One write → multiple replica writes.

🟡 Intermediate (16–35)

16. What is primary-replica model?

Single write node, multiple read nodes.

17. What is multi-primary replication?

Multiple nodes accept writes.

18. What is leaderless replication?

No primary node; all nodes equal.

19. What is quorum?

Minimum number of nodes required for read/write.

20. What is read quorum?

Number of replicas needed to return a read.

21. What is write quorum?

Number of replicas needed to confirm a write.

22. What is split brain?

Two nodes think they are primary.

23. What causes replication lag?

  • Network delay
  • Heavy load
  • Slow replicas

24. How to reduce lag?

  • Faster network
  • Better hardware
  • Optimize writes

25. What is conflict resolution?

Handling conflicting writes in multi-primary.

26. Conflict resolution strategies?

  • Last write wins
  • Vector clocks
  • CRDTs

27. What is vector clock?

Tracks version history across nodes.

28. What is idempotent write?

Write that produces same result if repeated.

29. What is anti-entropy?

Process to sync replicas over time.

30. What is hinted handoff?

Store writes temporarily if node is down.

31. What is read repair?

Fix stale replicas during read.

32. What is write-through replication?

Write immediately propagated.

33. What is write-behind replication?

Delayed replication.

34. What is snapshot replication?

Copy full dataset periodically.

35. What is log-based replication?

Replicate changes via logs (e.g., WAL).

🔴 Advanced (36–55)

36. What is CAP theorem?

Tradeoff between Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance.

37. How does replication relate to CAP?

Replication helps availability but may sacrifice consistency.

38. What is consistency level?

Guarantee of how fresh data is.

39. What is monotonic read?

Reads never go backwards in time.

40. What is read-after-write consistency?

You see your own writes immediately.

41. What is geo-replication?

Replication across regions.

42. What is eventual vs strong consistency tradeoff?

Speed vs correctness.

43. What is leader election?

Choosing a primary node dynamically.

44. What is Raft algorithm?

Consensus algorithm for leader election.

45. What is Paxos?

Another consensus algorithm.

46. How does Apache Cassandra replicate data?

Uses leaderless model with quorum.

47. How does MySQL replicate?

Uses binlog (log-based replication).

48. What is WAL (Write Ahead Log)?

Logs changes before applying them.

49. What is durability vs availability?

  • Durability: data safe
  • Availability: system accessible

50. What happens if replication fails?

  • Retry
  • Failover
  • Data inconsistency risk

51. What is backpressure?

Slowing writes when replicas lag.

52. What is replication topology?

Structure of nodes (tree, ring, mesh).

53. What is cascading replication?

Replica replicates to another replica.

54. When NOT to use replication?

  • Small systems
  • Low availability requirements

55. Biggest challenge in replication?

Balancing:

  • Consistency
  • Availability
  • Latency

🧠 Final Interview Summary

👉 Best answer:

“Replication is used to improve availability and fault tolerance by maintaining multiple copies of data. It can be synchronous or asynchronous, with tradeoffs between consistency and performance. Systems like Cassandra use leaderless replication with quorum, while MySQL uses primary-replica with log-based replication.”
CUSTOM QA
  1. How is replication implemented in database level?
The replica knows new data is written because the primary database writes every change into a sequential log (WAL / binlog / oplog), and the replica continuously reads that log using a replication offset (pointer).

⚙️ EXACT MECHANISM

1. Every write gets logged

When you do:

UPDATE usersSET balance=100WHERE id=5;

The primary DB immediately writes this into a log:

LSN 1001: UPDATE users SET balance=100 WHERE id=5
LSN 1002: INSERT ...
LSN 1003: DELETE ...

2. Replica remembers “where it stopped”

Replica stores:

Last applied position = LSN 1001

This is called:

  • offset
  • replication cursor
  • log sequence number (LSN)

3. Replica continuously checks for new logs

Replica → asks primary:
"Give me everything after LSN 1001"

Primary responds:

LSN 1002
LSN 1003
LSN 1004

4. Replica applies them

Apply LSN 1002 → update DB
Apply LSN 1003 → update DB
Update offset → 1003

🧠 KEY IDEA

The replica does NOT “detect new data”

It tracks a position in a log and pulls everything after it

🔁 TWO MODES

🟢 PULL MODEL (most common)

Replica asks:

“What’s new since my last position?”

🟡 PUSH MODEL

Primary sends:

“Here are new changes”

⚙️ REAL DATABASE TERMS

ConceptMeaning
WAL / Binlogchange log
LSN / Offsetposition in log
Replication streamdata pipeline
Apply processreplay changes

🌍 SIMPLE ANALOGY

Think of a YouTube video:

  • Primary = live stream recording
  • Log = timeline
  • Replica = viewer
  • Offset = current timestamp

Replica says:

“Give me everything after 10:32:15”

🔥 FINAL ONE-LINE ANSWER

The replica knows new data exists by tracking a log position (offset/LSN) and continuously reading new entries from the primary’s write-ahead log or binlog after that position.

Regional Partitioning

🧠 What is Regional Partitioning?

Regional Partitioning is a data distribution strategy where data is stored based on geographical regions.

👉 Instead of splitting by hash or ID:

  • You split by location (region)
US users  → US servers
EU users  → EU servers
Asia users → Asia servers

🎯 Core Idea

“Keep data close to where it is used”

⚙️ How It Works

  1. Identify user region (IP / profile / request)
  1. Route request to nearest region
  1. Store & process data in that region

🌍 Example Architecture

8

🧩 Partitioning Strategies

1. Geographic Partitioning

  • By country or continent

2. Latency-based Routing

  • Route to closest server

3. Data Residency Partitioning

  • Based on legal requirements

🔥 Why Use Regional Partitioning?

✅ Benefits

  • Lower latency (faster response)
  • Better user experience
  • Compliance (GDPR, etc.)
  • Reduced cross-region traffic
  • Fault isolation

❌ Challenges

  • Data consistency across regions
  • Complex routing
  • Cross-region queries are hard
  • Replication complexity

🌍 Real-World Systems

  • Netflix → global content delivery
  • Amazon → regional marketplaces
  • Google → multi-region infrastructure
  • Cloudflare → edge-based routing

🔁 Regional Partitioning + Replication

👉 Common setup:

Region = primary data owner
Other regions = replicas

Example:

  • US → primary
  • EU → replica
  • Asia → replica

🧠 Key Concepts

  • Geo-routing
  • Data sovereignty
  • Multi-region replication
  • Failover across regions
Projects
geo-system/
 ├── server.js
 ├── regions/
 │    ├── us/
 │    ├── eu/
 │    └── asia/
const fs = require("fs");
const path = require("path");

const regions = {
  us: path.join(__dirname, "regions/us"),
  eu: path.join(__dirname, "regions/eu"),
  asia: path.join(__dirname, "regions/asia"),
};

// ensure folders exist
Object.values(regions).forEach(dir => {
  if (!fs.existsSync(dir)) fs.mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true });
});

// region routing logic
function getRegion(user) {
  if (user.country === "USA") return "us";
  if (user.country === "Germany") return "eu";
  return "asia";
}

// replication mapping
const replicationMap = {
  us: "eu",
  eu: "asia",
  asia: "us",
};

function saveFile(user, filename, content) {
  const region = getRegion(user);
  const primaryPath = path.join(regions[region], filename);

  fs.writeFileSync(primaryPath, content);
  console.log(`Saved in PRIMARY region: ${region}`);

  replicate(region, filename, content);
}

function replicate(region, filename, content) {
  const backupRegion = replicationMap[region];
  const backupPath = path.join(regions[backupRegion], filename);

  setTimeout(() => {
    fs.writeFileSync(backupPath, content);
    console.log(`Replicated to BACKUP region: ${backupRegion}`);
  }, 1000);
}

// test
saveFile({ country: "USA" }, "file1.txt", "Hello from US");
saveFile({ country: "Germany" }, "file2.txt", "Hello from EU");

Q&A

🎯 50+ Regional Partitioning Q&A

🟢 Basics (1–15)

1. What is regional partitioning?

Splitting data based on geographic regions.

2. Why use it?

To reduce latency and improve user experience.

3. What is geo-routing?

Routing users to nearest region.

4. What is data locality?

Keeping data close to user.

5. What is latency?

Time taken for request-response.

6. What is region?

A physical geographic deployment area.

7. What is availability zone?

Subset of region (cloud concept).

8. What is data sovereignty?

Data must stay within specific country.

9. What is multi-region system?

System deployed across multiple regions.

10. What is failover?

Switching to another region on failure.

11. What is primary region?

Main region storing data.

12. What is secondary region?

Backup region.

13. What is cold region?

Region used only during failure.

14. What is hot region?

Actively serving traffic.

15. What is global load balancing?

Routing traffic across regions.

🟡 Intermediate (16–35)

16. How to route users to region?

  • IP-based routing
  • DNS routing
  • Geo-location services

17. What is latency-based routing?

Send request to fastest region.

18. What is geo-DNS?

DNS resolves to region-specific IP.

19. What is replication across regions?

Copying data between regions.

20. What is cross-region consistency?

Keeping data same across regions.

21. What is eventual consistency in geo systems?

Data sync happens after delay.

22. What is strong consistency challenge?

High latency across regions.

23. What is read locality?

Reads served from nearest region.

24. What is write locality?

Writes handled in local region.

25. What is global database?

Database spanning multiple regions.

26. What is conflict resolution in regions?

Handling conflicting updates across regions.

27. What is active-active setup?

All regions handle traffic.

28. What is active-passive setup?

One region active, others standby.

29. What is replication lag across regions?

Delay between region sync.

30. What is traffic steering?

Directing traffic intelligently.

31. What is edge computing?

Processing near user location.

32. What is CDN role?

Deliver content from nearest server.

33. What is regional isolation?

Failure in one region doesn’t affect others.

34. What is global consistency tradeoff?

Latency vs correctness.

35. What is partition tolerance?

System continues despite network issues.

🔴 Advanced (36–55)

36. How does Netflix use regional partitioning?

Content served from nearest region using CDN + regional services.

37. How does Amazon use it?

Separate marketplaces and data per region.

38. What is CAP theorem impact?

Geo systems favor availability + partition tolerance.

39. What is global failover strategy?

Switch DNS or load balancer to another region.

40. What is data replication strategy?

Primary region + replicas globally.

41. What is quorum in geo systems?

Majority nodes must agree.

42. What is latency vs consistency tradeoff?

Closer data = faster, but less consistent globally.

43. What is multi-region transaction challenge?

High latency + complexity.

44. What is eventual convergence?

All regions become consistent over time.

45. What is split-brain across regions?

Multiple regions act as primary.

46. How to prevent split-brain?

Leader election + consensus (Raft).

47. What is global index problem?

Indexing data across regions is hard.

48. What is write forwarding?

Forward write to primary region.

49. What is local write + async replication?

Write locally, sync later globally.

50. When NOT to use regional partitioning?

  • Small apps
  • Low traffic
  • No global users

51. Biggest challenge?

Maintaining consistency globally.

52. Best practice?

Combine with:

  • Replication
  • Caching
  • CDN

53. What is hybrid approach?

Regional + consistent hashing.

54. What is global ID strategy?

Use UUID to avoid conflicts.

55. Final interview answer?

“Regional partitioning distributes data geographically to reduce latency and improve availability. It’s commonly combined with replication and geo-routing, but introduces challenges like consistency and cross-region coordination.”
Handling Failures and Fault Mode
definition

⚠️ Handling Failures & Fault Modes

REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC

🧠 What is a Failure Mode?

A failure mode is the way a system can fail.

👉 Examples:

  • Network timeout
  • Server crash
  • Partial response
  • Data inconsistency
🔥 Types of Failures (Common Across All)

🔥 Types of Failures (Common Across All)

Failure TypeDescription
TimeoutRequest takes too long
Network failurePacket loss / disconnect
Server crashService goes down
Partial failureSome services fail, others work
Data inconsistencyReplicas differ
OverloadToo many requests
⚙️ REST Failure Handling

📌 Characteristics

  • Stateless
  • HTTP-based
  • Simple error model

🚨 Common Failure Modes in REST

  1. Timeout (slow API)
  1. 5xx errors (server failure)
  1. 4xx errors (client issues)
  1. Partial failure (microservices)
  1. Retry storms

🛠️ Handling Failures in REST

1. HTTP Status Codes

200 OK
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error
503 Service Unavailable

2. Retry Mechanism

  • Retry on:
    • 500
    • 503
  • Use exponential backoff

3. Circuit Breaker Pattern

  • Stops calling failing service

👉 Example:

  • Hystrix (Netflix)

4. Timeouts

fetch(url, { timeout:3000 })

5. Idempotency

  • Safe retries (PUT, GET)

6. Load Balancing

  • Avoid overloaded nodes
⚙️ GraphQL Failure Handling

📌 Characteristics

  • Single endpoint (/graphql)
  • Field-level execution
  • Partial success possible

🚨 Failure Modes in GraphQL

  1. Resolver failure
  1. Partial data return
  1. N+1 query explosion
  1. Timeout in nested queries

🔥 Key Difference

👉 GraphQL can return:

{
  "data": { "user":null },
  "errors": [{ "message":"User not found" }]
}

✅ Partial success

❌ Not full failure like REST

🛠️ Handling Failures in GraphQL

1. Error + Data Together

  • Allows graceful degradation

2. Resolver-Level Handling

resolve:async () => {
try {
returnawaitservice();
  }catch {
returnnull;
  }
}

3. DataLoader (fix N+1)

  • Batch requests

👉 Popular tool:

  • DataLoader

4. Query Complexity Limiting

  • Prevent heavy queries

5. Timeout per Resolver

6. Schema Design

  • Nullable vs non-null fields
gRPC Failure handling

📌 Characteristics

  • Uses HTTP/2
  • Binary protocol (fast)
  • Strong typing

🚨 Failure Modes in gRPC

  1. Connection drop
  1. Deadline exceeded
  1. Stream interruption
  1. Backpressure issues

🛠️ Handling Failures in gRPC

1. Status Codes (gRPC-specific)

OK
UNAVAILABLE
DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
INTERNAL

2. Deadlines (Timeouts)

client.call(request, { deadline:Date.now()+3000 })

3. Retries (Built-in support)

  • Automatic retry policies

4. Streaming Recovery

  • Resume streams

5. Load Balancing

  • Built-in support

6. Backpressure Handling

  • Control flow in streams
REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC

⚔️ REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC (Failures)

FeatureRESTGraphQLgRPC
Error handlingHTTP codesdata + errorsstatus codes
Partial success❌✅❌
Timeout controlBasicPer resolverStrong (deadlines)
Retry supportManualManualBuilt-in
PerformanceMediumMediumHigh
Streaming❌❌✅
Insight

🧠 Key Interview Insights

🔥 1. Partial Failure

  • REST → full failure
  • GraphQL → partial success
  • gRPC → call fails

🔥 2. Timeout Handling

  • REST → client-side
  • GraphQL → resolver-level
  • gRPC → deadlines (best)

🔥 3. Retry Strategy

  • REST → manual
  • GraphQL → tricky (depends on resolvers)
  • gRPC → built-in retry policies

code
REST Retry Example
async function fetchWithRetry(url, retries = 3) {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(url);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Fail");
    return res.json();
  } catch (err) {
    if (retries > 0) {
      return fetchWithRetry(url, retries - 1);
    }
    throw err;
  }
}
GraphQL Resolver Handling
const resolvers = {
  Query: {
    user: async () => {
      try {
        return await getUser();
      } catch {
        return null;
      }
    }
  }
};
gRPC Deadline Example
client.getUser(request, { deadline: Date.now() + 2000 }, (err, res) => {
  if (err) console.error(err);
});
🎯 50+ Interview Q&A (with Answers)

🟢 Basics (1–15)

1. What is a failure mode?

A way in which a system can fail.

2. What is timeout?

When request exceeds allowed time.

3. What is retry?

Re-attempting failed request.

4. What is circuit breaker?

Stops calls to failing service.

5. What is partial failure?

Some components fail, others succeed.

6. What is idempotency?

Repeated requests give same result.

7. What is 5xx error?

Server-side failure.

8. What is 4xx error?

Client-side error.

9. What is overload?

Too many requests.

10. What is backpressure?

Controlling request flow.

11. What is failover?

Switch to backup system.

12. What is graceful degradation?

Reduce features instead of failing.

13. What is cascading failure?

One failure triggers others.

14. What is SLA?

Service level agreement.

15. What is latency?

Time taken to respond.

🟡 Intermediate (16–35)

16. How REST handles failures?

HTTP codes + retries.

17. How GraphQL handles failures?

Returns partial data + errors.

18. How gRPC handles failures?

Status codes + deadlines.

19. What is DEADLINE_EXCEEDED?

gRPC timeout error.

20. What is UNAVAILABLE?

Service not reachable.

21. What is N+1 problem?

Too many DB calls in GraphQL.

22. Solution to N+1?

Batching (DataLoader).

23. What is retry storm?

Too many retries overload system.

24. How to avoid retry storm?

Backoff + jitter.

25. What is exponential backoff?

Increasing retry delay.

26. What is jitter?

Random delay to avoid spikes.

27. What is rate limiting?

Control request frequency.

28. What is bulkhead pattern?

Isolate failures.

29. What is timeout propagation?

Passing timeout across services.

30. What is health check?

Check if service is alive.

31. What is liveness probe?

Check if app running.

32. What is readiness probe?

Check if app ready.

33. What is fallback?

Alternative response.

34. What is cache fallback?

Return cached data.

35. What is partial response?

Incomplete data returned.

🔴 Advanced (36–55)

36. Which is best for failure handling?

gRPC (strongest control).

37. Why GraphQL allows partial success?

Field-level execution.

38. Why REST fails completely?

Endpoint-based design.

39. How to design resilient API?

Retries + timeouts + circuit breakers.

40. What is distributed tracing?

Track request across services.

41. Tool for tracing?

Jaeger

42. What is observability?

Logs + metrics + tracing.

43. What is chaos engineering?

Test failures intentionally.

44. Tool for chaos?

Chaos Monkey

45. What is fault injection?

Simulate failures.

46. What is resilience?

Ability to recover from failure.

47. What is SLA violation?

Failure to meet guarantees.

48. What is circuit open state?

Stop requests.

49. What is half-open state?

Test recovery.

50. What is fallback data?

Default response.

51. What is eventual recovery?

System heals over time.

Handles retries, timeouts automatically.

Istio

54. What is retry budget?

Limit retries.

55. Final interview answer?

“Handling failures differs across REST, GraphQL, and gRPC. REST uses HTTP status codes and retries, GraphQL supports partial responses with error fields, and gRPC provides strong built-in mechanisms like deadlines, retries, and streaming control. gRPC offers the most robust failure handling, while GraphQL provides the best flexibility for partial failures.”
Rate Limiting and Throttling
docs

Rate limiting is a technique used to control how many requests a client can make to a server in a given time window.

👉 Goal:

Prevent abuse, overload, and ensure fair usage.

🧠 Simple idea:

“You can only call this API 100 times per minute.”

⚙️ 2. Why Rate Limiting is Needed

Without it:

  • ❌ DDOS attacks can crash systems
  • ❌ One user can consume all resources
  • ❌ API becomes unstable
  • ❌ Cost increases massively

🧱 Used in:

  • Google APIs (Maps, Cloud)
  • OpenAI API usage limits
  • Stripe payment APIs
  • Social media APIs

⚙️ 3. Where Rate Limiting Happens

7

Layers:

  1. Client (frontend throttling)
  1. API Gateway (main control)
  1. Backend service middleware
  1. Database/Redis (tracking requests)

🧠 4. Core Concepts

⏱️ Time Window

Example:

100 requests per 60 seconds

👤 Per User / IP / API Key

Rate limit can be based on:

  • IP address
  • User ID
  • API Key
  • Device

⚔️ 5. Rate Limiting Algorithms

This is VERY important for interviews.

🟢 1. Fixed Window Counter

7

Idea:

  • Count requests in a fixed time window
0–60 sec → 100 requests allowed
reset every minute

❌ Problem:

Burst traffic at boundary

🟡 2. Sliding Window

Idea:

  • Smooth over time

👉 More accurate than fixed window

🔵 3. Token Bucket (MOST USED)

7

Idea:

  • Bucket fills with tokens
  • Each request consumes 1 token
Capacity = 100 tokens
Refill = 1 token/sec

✅ Pros:

  • Handles bursts
  • Smooth traffic

🔴 4. Leaky Bucket

Idea:

  • Requests processed at constant rate

👉 Like water dripping from bucket

⚖️ Comparison Table

AlgorithmBurst HandlingComplexityUsage
Fixed Window❌ BadEasyBasic APIs
Sliding Window⚠️ MediumMediumModerate systems
Token Bucket✅ BestMediumReal systems
Leaky Bucket⚠️ ControlledMediumQueues

💻 6. Implementation (Node.js Rate Limiter)

We’ll build Token Bucket style (simple version).

📦 Basic Express Rate Limiter

constexpress=require("express");
constapp=express();

constrequests= {};
constLIMIT=5;// max requests
constWINDOW=60*1000;// 1 minute

app.use((req,res,next) => {
constip=req.ip;

if (!requests[ip]) {
requests[ip]= [];
  }

constnow=Date.now();

// remove old requests
requests[ip]=requests[ip].filter(
timestamp =>now-timestamp<WINDOW
  );

if (requests[ip].length>=LIMIT) {
returnres.status(429).send("Too many requests");
  }

requests[ip].push(now);
next();
});

app.get("/", (req,res) => {
res.send("Hello with rate limiting");
});

app.listen(3000);

🚀 7. Production Version (Redis-based)

Real systems use Redis:

  • Fast
  • Distributed
  • Shared across servers

Example idea:

key = user_id
value = request count
expire = 60s

🧪 8. Real System Flow

Client → API Gateway → Rate Limiter → Service → DB

⚠️ 9. Common Problems

  • ❌ Shared state in distributed systems
  • ❌ Clock sync issues
  • ❌ IP spoofing
  • ❌ Bursty traffic at boundaries
  • ❌ Race conditions

🧠 10. Best Practices

  • Use Redis for distributed rate limiting
  • Prefer token bucket algorithm
  • Apply limits per:
    • user
    • IP
    • API key
  • Return proper HTTP code:
    • 429 Too Many Requests
  • Add retry headers:
Retry-After: 60

🧠 11. Mental Model

Rate Limiting = Traffic Controller 🚦

It decides:

  • Who can enter
  • How fast
  • When to stop
50+ Interview Q&A

🟢 Basics (1–15)

1. What is rate limiting?

Rate limiting is a technique used to control how many requests a user or client can send to a server within a specific time window.

It ensures that system resources are not overused by a single user or malicious actor.

It helps maintain stability, performance, and fair usage across all clients.

2. Why is rate limiting needed?

Rate limiting is needed to prevent abuse, such as bots or attackers sending too many requests.

Without it, servers can become overloaded and crash under heavy traffic.

It also ensures fair distribution of resources among all users.

3. What problem does rate limiting solve?

It solves the problem of excessive traffic that can degrade or crash backend systems.

It prevents denial-of-service situations where servers are overwhelmed.

It also helps control API costs and maintain predictable performance.

4. What is a rate limit window?

A rate limit window is the time interval during which requests are counted.

For example, 100 requests per 60 seconds is a fixed window.

After the window resets, the counter starts again from zero.

5. What is HTTP 429 status code?

HTTP 429 means “Too Many Requests” from the client.

It is returned when a user exceeds the allowed request limit.

It often includes a retry-after header telling when to try again.

6. What is API throttling?

API throttling is a controlled delay or restriction of requests when traffic is high.

Instead of rejecting requests immediately, the system may slow them down.

It ensures smooth performance under heavy load.

7. What is quota in rate limiting?

A quota is the total number of requests allowed for a user in a given period.

For example, 10,000 requests per day is a quota.

Once exceeded, access is restricted until reset.

8. What is burst traffic?

Burst traffic refers to a sudden spike in requests within a very short time.

It often happens during promotions, events, or bot attacks.

Rate limiting systems must handle bursts without crashing.

9. What is fairness in rate limiting?

Fairness means every user gets equal access to system resources.

No single user should dominate or overload the system.

It ensures stable and predictable service for all clients.

10. What is per-user rate limiting?

Per-user rate limiting applies limits based on user identity.

Each authenticated user gets their own request quota.

This prevents one user from affecting others in the system.

11. What is IP-based rate limiting?

IP-based rate limiting tracks requests from a specific IP address.

It is commonly used for public APIs without authentication.

However, it can be bypassed using proxies or VPNs.

12. What is API key rate limiting?

API key rate limiting tracks usage based on a unique API key.

Each application or client gets a separate usage quota.

It is commonly used in third-party API services.

13. What is middleware in rate limiting?

Middleware is a layer that checks requests before they reach the backend.

It can count requests and enforce limits in real time.

It is commonly used in frameworks like Express or Spring Boot.

14. What is a gateway in rate limiting?

An API gateway is a centralized entry point for all client requests.

It handles authentication, routing, and rate limiting.

It prevents overload before requests reach backend services.

15. What is request throttling vs rate limiting?

Rate limiting blocks requests after a limit is reached.

Throttling slows down requests instead of rejecting them immediately.

Both are used to control traffic but behave differently under load.

🟡 Intermediate (16–35)

16. What is fixed window rate limiting?

Fixed window counts requests in a strict time interval like 1 minute.

Once the limit is reached, further requests are blocked until reset.

It is simple but can cause traffic spikes at window boundaries.

17. What is sliding window rate limiting?

Sliding window tracks requests over a rolling time period.

It smooths out traffic instead of resetting abruptly like fixed windows.

It provides more accurate and fair limiting.

18. What is token bucket algorithm?

Token bucket allows requests based on available tokens in a bucket.

Tokens are added at a fixed rate and consumed per request.

It allows short bursts but maintains long-term limits.

19. What is leaky bucket algorithm?

Leaky bucket processes requests at a constant rate like water dripping.

Incoming requests are queued and processed slowly.

It ensures smooth traffic flow without spikes.

20. Why is token bucket widely used?

Token bucket is flexible and allows controlled bursts of traffic.

It balances performance and fairness effectively.

It is widely used in real-world distributed systems.

21. What is distributed rate limiting?

Distributed rate limiting works across multiple servers.

It ensures all servers share the same request limit state.

Tools like Redis are commonly used for synchronization.

22. Why is Redis used in rate limiting?

Redis provides fast in-memory storage for counters.

It allows multiple servers to share rate limit data.

It is highly efficient for distributed environments.

23. What is atomic increment?

Atomic increment ensures safe updates in concurrent environments.

It prevents race conditions when multiple requests update counters.

Redis provides atomic operations like INCR for this purpose.

24. What is TTL in rate limiting?

TTL (Time To Live) defines when stored data expires automatically.

It is used to reset rate limit counters after a time window.

This removes the need for manual cleanup.

25. What is burst capacity?

Burst capacity allows temporary exceeding of normal limits.

It is useful when traffic spikes suddenly.

Token bucket algorithm typically supports burst capacity.

26. What is backpressure?

Backpressure is a mechanism to slow down incoming traffic.

It prevents system overload by rejecting or delaying requests.

It helps maintain system stability under stress.

27. What is retry-after header?

Retry-after tells the client when to retry after being rate-limited.

It is returned along with HTTP 429 response.

It improves client-side handling of rate limits.

28. What is concurrency limit?

Concurrency limit restricts how many requests are processed simultaneously.

It is different from request-per-second limits.

It protects backend threads and resources from overload.

29. What is API gateway rate limiting?

It is rate limiting applied at the API gateway layer.

It acts as a central control point before traffic reaches services.

It is widely used in microservice architectures.

30. What is request fingerprinting?

Request fingerprinting identifies unique clients using multiple parameters.

It may combine IP, user-agent, and API key.

It helps prevent bypassing rate limits.

31. What is dynamic rate limiting?

Dynamic rate limiting adjusts limits based on system load.

It increases or decreases allowed requests in real time.

It helps maintain system stability under varying traffic.

32. What is global rate limiting?

Global rate limiting applies limits across the entire system.

It ensures total system traffic does not exceed capacity.

It is often used in cloud-based APIs.

33. What is endpoint-based rate limiting?

It applies different limits to different API endpoints.

For example, login may have stricter limits than data fetching.

It improves security and resource allocation.

34. What is request queue in rate limiting?

A request queue stores incoming requests when limits are exceeded.

These requests are processed later when capacity is available.

It helps avoid immediate rejection of traffic.

35. What is fairness algorithm?

Fairness algorithm ensures equal distribution of resources.

It prevents one client from dominating system capacity.

It is critical in multi-tenant systems.

🔴 Advanced (36–55)

36. Why is token bucket preferred in production?

Token bucket allows controlled bursts while maintaining long-term limits.

It is flexible and adapts to real-world traffic patterns.

This makes it ideal for production systems.

37. What is race condition in rate limiting?

Race condition happens when multiple requests update counters simultaneously.

It can lead to incorrect rate calculations.

Distributed systems use atomic operations to prevent this.

38. What is distributed inconsistency?

It happens when different servers have different rate limit states.

This can lead to unfair or incorrect limiting.

Redis or centralized stores solve this issue.

39. What is API abuse?

API abuse refers to excessive or malicious usage of an API.

It includes scraping, spamming, or automated attacks.

Rate limiting is a key defense mechanism.

40. What is edge rate limiting?

Edge rate limiting is applied at CDN or edge servers.

It blocks bad traffic before reaching the main backend.

It improves performance and reduces backend load.

41. What is adaptive rate limiting?

Adaptive rate limiting changes limits based on system health.

If system load is high, limits are reduced automatically.

It helps maintain stability in real-time systems.

42. What is retry policy?

Retry policy defines how clients should retry failed requests.

It often includes exponential backoff strategy.

It prevents repeated overload on the server.

43. What is overload protection?

Overload protection prevents system failure during extreme traffic.

It uses rate limiting, queuing, and request rejection.

It ensures graceful degradation instead of crashing.

44. What is priority-based rate limiting?

It assigns higher priority to important requests.

Critical operations are processed before low-priority ones.

It is used in financial and real-time systems.

45. What is sliding log algorithm?

It stores timestamps of each request in a log.

It calculates requests within a rolling time window.

It is accurate but memory expensive.

46. What is idempotency in rate limiting?

Idempotency ensures repeated requests produce the same result.

It helps safely retry requests without duplication.

It is important in payment and transaction systems.

47. What is microservice rate limiting?

It applies rate limits at individual service level.

Each microservice can have its own limits.

It ensures isolated and scalable control.

48. What is global system capacity?

It is the maximum total load a system can handle.

Rate limiting ensures traffic does not exceed this capacity.

It prevents system-wide failures.

49. What is request prioritization?

It ranks requests based on importance or type.

High priority requests are processed first.

It improves user experience under heavy load.

50. What is final concept of rate limiting?

Rate limiting is a traffic control mechanism for APIs and systems.

It ensures stability, fairness, and protection from abuse.

It is a fundamental part of scalable system design.

🚀 FINAL SUMMARY

Rate limiting is not just a feature — it is a system survival mechanism.

👉 Without it → system crashes

👉 With it → controlled, scalable architecture

project
const express = require("express");
const app = express();

app.use(express.json());

/*
  Store structure:
  {
    "ip_address": [timestamp1, timestamp2, ...]
  }
*/
const requests = {};

// CONFIG
const LIMIT = 5; // max requests
const WINDOW = 10 * 1000; // 10 seconds

// ============================
// RATE LIMITING MIDDLEWARE
// ============================
function rateLimiter(req, res, next) {
  const ip = req.ip;

  if (!requests[ip]) {
    requests[ip] = [];
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  // remove old requests outside window
  requests[ip] = requests[ip].filter(
    (timestamp) => now - timestamp < WINDOW
  );

  // check limit
  if (requests[ip].length >= LIMIT) {
    const retryAfter = Math.ceil(WINDOW / 1000);

    return res.status(429).json({
      message: "Too many requests",
      retryAfter: `${retryAfter} seconds`
    });
  }

  // add current request
  requests[ip].push(now);

  next();
}

// ============================
// APPLY MIDDLEWARE
// ============================
app.use(rateLimiter);

// ============================
// TEST ROUTE
// ============================
app.get("/api/data", (req, res) => {
  res.json({
    message: "Success ✅",
    time: new Date().toISOString()
  });
});

// ============================
app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Server running on http://localhost:3000");
});
RATE LIMITING VS THROTLING

✅ Correct version

🟢 Rate limiting = the rule

Defines how many requests are allowed in a time window

Example:

  • 5 requests per 10 seconds

🔴 Throttling = the enforcement action

What the system does when the limit is exceeded

Example actions:

  • reject request (HTTP 429)
  • delay request
  • queue request
  • slow down responses

📘 1. What is Authentication vs Authorization?

🧠 Authentication (AuthN)

👉 “Who are you?”

  • Verifies user identity
  • Happens at login

Example:

  • username + password
  • token login
  • OAuth login

🧠 Authorization (AuthZ)

👉 “What are you allowed to do?”

  • Checks permissions after login

Example:

  • admin → can delete users
  • user → can only read data

⚔️ Difference

FeatureAuthenticationAuthorization
PurposeIdentity checkPermission check
QuestionWho are you?What can you do?
HappensLoginAfter login
Depends onCredentialsRoles/permissions

⚙️ 2. How Authentication Works (Flow)

5

Step-by-step:

  1. User logs in
  1. Server validates credentials
  1. Server generates token (JWT)
  1. Client stores token
  1. Client sends token with every request
  1. Server verifies token

🔐 3. Types of Authentication

1. Session-based

  • Server stores session
  • Cookie used

2. Token-based (JWT)

👉 Most modern systems use this

  • Stateless
  • Scalable
  • Secure

Used in:

  • Node.js APIs
  • Mobile apps

3. OAuth (Google login)

  • Login via third-party

4. Basic Auth (old)

  • username:password in headers

🛡️ 4. Authorization Models

🟢 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

7

Example roles:

  • admin
  • user
  • editor

🟡 Permission-Based

  • read_users
  • delete_users
  • update_users

🔵 Attribute-Based (ABAC)

  • based on conditions (age, location, time)

🚀 6. Node.js Auth System (FULL PROJECT)
📦 Install
npm init -y
npm install express jsonwebtoken fs
📁 server.js
const express = require("express");
const fs = require("fs");
const jwt = require("jsonwebtoken");

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const SECRET = "mysecretkey";

// Load users
function getUsers() {
  return JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("./users.json"));
}

---

# 🔐 LOGIN (Authentication)

app.post("/login", (req, res) => {
  const { username, password } = req.body;

  const users = getUsers();
  const user = users.find(
    u => u.username === username && u.password === password
  );

  if (!user) {
    return res.status(401).json({ message: "Invalid credentials" });
  }

  const token = jwt.sign(
    { id: user.id, role: user.role },
    SECRET,
    { expiresIn: "1h" }
  );

  res.json({ token });
});

---

# 🛡️ MIDDLEWARE (Authorization check)

function authMiddleware(req, res, next) {
  const token = req.headers.authorization;

  if (!token) return res.status(401).send("No token");

  try {
    const decoded = jwt.verify(token.split(" ")[1], SECRET);
    req.user = decoded;
    next();
  } catch (err) {
    return res.status(403).send("Invalid token");
  }
}

---

# 🔐 ROLE CHECK

function roleMiddleware(role) {
  return (req, res, next) => {
    if (req.user.role !== role) {
      return res.status(403).send("Forbidden");
    }
    next();
  };
}

---

# 🔥 PROTECTED ROUTES

// user route
app.get("/profile", authMiddleware, (req, res) => {
  res.json({ message: "User profile", user: req.user });
});

// admin route
app.delete(
  "/users",
  authMiddleware,
  roleMiddleware("admin"),
  (req, res) => {
    res.json({ message: "User deleted (admin only)" });
  }
);

---

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Server running on 3000");
});
🧪 7. How to Test

Pagination
docs

📄 Pagination — Complete Guide

🧠 What is Pagination?

Pagination is the process of splitting large datasets into smaller chunks (pages).

👉 Instead of returning 1M records:

Page 1 → 10 items
Page 2 → next 10 items

🎯 Why Pagination?

  • Improve performance ⚡
  • Reduce memory usage 🧠
  • Better UX 📱
  • Lower network cost 🌐

📦 Types of Pagination

1️⃣ Offset-Based Pagination (Classic)

8

📌 Idea

LIMIT10 OFFSET20

👉 Skip first 20 rows, return next 10

✅ Pros

  • Simple
  • Easy to implement
  • Works with page numbers

❌ Cons

  • Slow for large offsets
  • Can return inconsistent data (if data changes)

2️⃣ Cursor-Based Pagination (Recommended)

8

📌 Idea

Use last item as reference:

WHERE id> last_id
LIMIT10

✅ Pros

  • Fast for large datasets
  • Consistent results
  • Ideal for infinite scroll

❌ Cons

  • No direct page jumping
  • Slightly more complex

3️⃣ Keyset Pagination (Optimized Cursor)

👉 Uses indexed fields (like created_at, id)

WHERE created_at< last_seen
ORDERBY created_atDESC
LIMIT10

4️⃣ Seek Pagination

👉 Similar to keyset, but optimized for sorted queries

⚔️ Comparison

TypeSpeedConsistencyJump to Page
Offset❌ slow❌ inconsistent✅
Cursor✅ fast✅ consistent❌
Keyset✅ fastest✅ consistent❌
Implementation

🟢 1. Offset Pagination (Node.js + SQL)

asyncfunctiongetUsers(page=1,limit=10) {
constoffset= (page-1)*limit;

constusers=awaitdb.query(
"SELECT * FROM users LIMIT ? OFFSET ?",
    [limit,offset]
  );

returnusers;
}

🟡 2. Cursor Pagination (Node.js)

asyncfunctiongetUsers(lastId,limit=10) {
letquery="SELECT * FROM users";
letparams= [];

if (lastId) {
query+=" WHERE id > ?";
params.push(lastId);
  }

query+=" ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT ?";
params.push(limit);

returnawaitdb.query(query,params);
}

🔴 3. GraphQL Cursor Example

{
  users(first: 10, after: "cursor123") {
    edges {
      node {
        id
        name
      }
      cursor
    }
  }
}

🚀 Real Systems

  • Instagram → infinite scroll (cursor)
  • Twitter → timeline pagination
  • YouTube → page-based + cursor mix

⚠️ Common Problems

1. Duplicate Data

  • Happens with offset when data changes

2. Missing Data

  • Insert/delete during pagination

3. Large Offset Slow Query

OFFSET1000000-- very slow

4. Sorting Issues

  • Must use consistent ordering

🧠 Best Practices

  • Use cursor pagination for large systems
  • Always sort by indexed column
  • Use stable ordering (id or timestamp)
  • Limit page size (e.g., max 100)
  • Return next_cursor

Buffer in protocols (HTTP,TCP,UDP,QUIC,SMTP…)

🧠 What is a Buffer (in networking)?

A buffer is temporary memory used to:

  • Hold data before sending 📤
  • Hold data after receiving 📥
  • Smooth out speed differences between systems

🌐 Protocol-by-Protocol Breakdown

🌍 HTTP (Application Layer)

6

👉 Does HTTP have a buffer?

✅ Yes (but indirectly)

How:

  • HTTP runs on top of TCP
  • Buffering happens in:
    • Browser (client buffer)
    • Server (response buffer)
    • Proxies (e.g., NGINX buffering)

Example:

  • Server generates large response → sends in chunks → buffered before full send

🔗 TCP (Transport Layer)

👉 Does TCP have buffers?

✅ YES (very important)

Built-in buffers:

  • Send buffer
  • Receive buffer

Why:

  • Flow control
  • Congestion control
  • Reliability (retransmissions)

Key concept:

App → TCP Send Buffer → Network → TCP Receive Buffer → App

⚡ UDP (Transport Layer)

👉 Does UDP have buffers?

✅ Yes (but minimal)

Characteristics:

  • No reliability
  • No retransmission
  • No ordering

Buffers:

  • OS-level send/receive buffers only

👉 If buffer overflows → packets dropped ❌

🚀 QUIC (Modern Transport Protocol)

👉 Does QUIC have buffers?

✅ YES (advanced buffering)

4

Runs on:

  • UDP (but adds its own logic)

Buffers include:

  • Stream-level buffers
  • Connection-level buffers

Why:

  • Multiplex streams
  • Avoid head-of-line blocking
  • Handle retransmissions

👉 Used in:

  • HTTP/3

📧 SMTP (Email Protocol)

👉 Does SMTP have buffers?

✅ Yes (application-level + server queues)

6

Key concept:

  • Store-and-forward

Buffers:

  • Mail server queues (disk-based buffer)
  • Retry queues if delivery fails

Example:

  • Email not delivered → stored → retried later

⚔️ Summary Table

ProtocolBuffer TypeWhere
HTTPIndirectApp + TCP + proxies
TCPStrongBuilt-in (send/receive)
UDPMinimalOS buffers only
QUICAdvancedStreams + connection
SMTPPersistentMail queues (disk)

🔥 Key Interview Insight

👉 If they ask:

“Do protocols have buffers?”

Best answer:

“Buffering is mostly handled by the transport layer and OS rather than the protocol definition itself. TCP has built-in send and receive buffers, UDP relies on OS buffers, and higher-level protocols like HTTP and SMTP use application-level buffering or queues.”

⚠️ Important Concept (Very Asked)

Buffer vs Queue

  • Buffer → short-term memory (RAM)
  • Queue → can be long-term (disk, retries)

👉 Example:

  • TCP → buffer
  • SMTP → queue

🧠 Real-World Scenario

Slow client problem:

  • Server sends data fast
  • Client reads slow

👉 Solution:

  • Buffer stores extra data temporarily
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
docs

📘 1. What is RBAC?

RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) is an authorization model where:

Permissions are assigned to roles, and roles are assigned to users.

🧠 Simple idea:

Instead of:

  • giving permissions to each user ❌

You do:

  • user → role → permissions ✅

🧩 Example:

UserRole
Aliadmin
Bobeditor
Johnviewer

⚙️ 2. How RBAC works

6

🔁 Flow:

  1. User logs in
  1. System identifies role
  1. Role maps to permissions
  1. Middleware checks permission
  1. Allow or deny request

🧱 3. Core Components of RBAC

👤 User

A person or system using the application.

🎭 Role

A category like:

  • admin
  • editor
  • user

🔑 Permission

Specific action:

  • read_users
  • delete_users
  • update_posts

🔗 Role-Permission mapping

Example:

admin → all permissions
editor → edit + read
user → read only

💻 4. Database Model (Real System Design)

🧾 users table

id| username| role_id

🧾 roles table

id| name
1| admin
2| editor
3|user

🧾 permissions table

id| name
1| read_users
2| delete_users
3| update_users

🧾 role_permissions table (many-to-many)

role_id| permission_id
1|1
1|2
1|3
2|1
2|3
3|1

⚙️ 5. How RBAC works in API (Flow)

Request → Auth → Get Role → Check Permissions → Allow/Deny
project
const express = require("express");
const fs = require("fs");

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const roles = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("./roles.json"));
const users = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("./users.json"));

---

# 🔐 AUTH MIDDLEWARE (mock login)
function auth(req, res, next) {
  const username = req.headers["username"];

  const user = users.find(u => u.username === username);

  if (!user) return res.status(401).send("User not found");

  req.user = user;
  next();
}

---

# 🛡️ RBAC MIDDLEWARE
function permit(action) {
  return (req, res, next) => {
    const role = req.user.role;
    const permissions = roles[role];

    if (!permissions.includes(action)) {
      return res.status(403).send("Forbidden");
    }

    next();
  };
}

---

# 🔥 ROUTES

// public login check
app.get("/me", auth, (req, res) => {
  res.json(req.user);
});

// read users
app.get("/users", auth, permit("read_users"), (req, res) => {
  res.json(users);
});

// delete user
app.delete("/users", auth, permit("delete_users"), (req, res) => {
  res.send("User deleted");
});

// update user
app.put("/users", auth, permit("update_users"), (req, res) => {
  res.send("User updated");
});

---

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("RBAC server running");
});

Cursor-based Pagination
docs

📍 Cursor-Based Pagination (Deep Dive)

🧠 What is Cursor-Based Pagination?

Cursor pagination is a method where instead of using page numbers, you use a pointer (cursor) to the last item you fetched.

👉 Think:

“Give me the next items after THIS record”

🔁 Basic Idea

Instead of:

page=3&limit=10

You use:

after_id=50&limit=10

Or:

cursor=eyJpZCI6NTA=

⚙️ How It Works

Step 1: First request

SELECT*FROM users
ORDERBY id
LIMIT10;

Response includes:

{
  "data": [...],
  "nextCursor":10
}

Step 2: Next request

SELECT*FROM users
WHERE id>10
ORDERBY id
LIMIT10;

🧠 Visual Model

7

🔑 Key Concept

Cursor = “last seen item pointer”

It can be:

  • ID
  • Timestamp
  • Encoded token

🧩 Types of Cursor Pagination

1. ID-Based Cursor

WHERE id> last_id

✔ Simple

✔ Fast

❌ Requires ordered IDs

2. Timestamp-Based Cursor

WHERE created_at< last_seen_time
ORDERBY created_atDESC

✔ Good for feeds

✔ Time-based ordering

❌ Requires careful indexing

3. Compound Cursor

WHERE (created_at, id)< (last_time, last_id)

✔ Prevents duplicates

✔ Handles same timestamps

4. Encoded Cursor (Base64)

eyJpZCI6NTAsInRpbWUiOiIyMDI2LTAxLTAxIn0=

✔ Hides internal structure

✔ Safer for APIs

⚔️ Cursor vs Offset Pagination

FeatureOffsetCursor
Speed❌ slow for large data✅ fast
Consistency❌ unstable✅ stable
Page jumping✅ yes❌ no
Infinite scroll❌ bad✅ perfect
Scaling❌ poor✅ excellent

🚀 Why Big Systems Use Cursor Pagination

Used by:

  • Instagram → feed scroll
  • Twitter → timeline
  • LinkedIn → activity feed
Implementation

💻 Implementation (Node.js + SQL)

🔹 First request

asyncfunctiongetUsers(limit=10) {
constusers=awaitdb.query(`
    SELECT * FROM users
    ORDER BY id ASC
    LIMIT ?
  `, [limit]);

constlastId=users[users.length-1]?.id;

return {
    data:users,
    nextCursor:lastId
  };
}

🔹 Next request

asyncfunctiongetUsersAfter(cursor,limit=10) {
constusers=awaitdb.query(`
    SELECT * FROM users
    WHERE id > ?
    ORDER BY id ASC
    LIMIT ?
  `, [cursor,limit]);

constlastId=users[users.length-1]?.id;

return {
    data:users,
    nextCursor:lastId
  };
}

🔥 Real Problem Cursor Solves

❌ Offset problem:

  • Page shifts when new data inserted
  • Slow at high offset

✅ Cursor solves:

  • Stable pagination
  • No skipping rows
  • Uses index directly

🧠 Important Internal Detail

Cursor pagination works well because:

👉 It uses INDEX SCANS instead of OFFSET scans

So database does:

Jump directly to last_id in index → continue scanning

⚠️ Limitations

  • ❌ Cannot jump to page 10 directly
  • ❌ More complex API
  • ❌ Needs stable ordering field

🧪 Best Practices

  • Always use ORDER BY
  • Use indexed columns (id, timestamp)
  • Never rely on unstable fields
  • Return nextCursor always
  • Encode cursor if exposed externally

🧠 Interview-Ready Answer

“Cursor-based pagination uses a pointer to the last fetched item instead of page numbers. It avoids the performance issues of OFFSET by leveraging indexed lookups, making it efficient and consistent for large datasets and real-time feeds.”

🔥 Bonus Insight (Senior Level)

Cursor pagination is basically:

“State is moved from server → client”

Instead of:

  • Server remembering page

You:

  • Send state (cursor) with every request
API Keys vs JWT Tokens
docs

🔐 API Keys vs JWT Tokens (Deep Dive)

📘 1. What are they?

🔑 API Key

An API key is a simple secret string used to identify an application or client.

Example:

x-api-key: 8f3a91d2-xyz-123

👉 Think:

“Who is calling my API?” (app-level identity)

🎟️ JWT Token

A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed token that contains user identity + metadata + claims.

Example:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...

👉 Think:

“Who is this user and what can they do?”

⚙️ 2. How they work

🔑 API Key Flow

5

Steps:

  1. Client sends API key
  1. Server checks key
  1. If valid → allow request

🎟️ JWT Flow

6

Steps:

  1. User logs in
  1. Server generates JWT
  1. Client stores token
  1. Sends token in every request
  1. Server verifies signature

Protocol Buffers and Type Safety

📦 Protocol Buffers & Type Safety

🧠 What are Protocol Buffers?

Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) is a language-neutral, platform-neutral binary serialization format created by Google.

👉 Think:

“Define your data once → generate strongly-typed code → serialize/deserialize efficiently”

⚡ Why Protobuf?

  • Smaller payloads than JSON (binary)
  • Faster serialization/deserialization
  • Strong typing across services
  • Backward/forward compatible

🧩 Core Pieces

1) .proto Schema

syntax = "proto3";

message User {
  int32 id = 1;
  string name = 2;
  string email = 3;
}

2) Code Generation

Use protoc to generate typed classes in:

  • JS/TS, Go, Java, Python, etc.

3) Serialization

constbytes=User.encode(user).finish();
constdecoded=User.decode(bytes);

🔐 What is Type Safety?

Type safety ensures:

  • Data matches expected structure & types
  • Errors are caught early (compile-time or validation-time)
  • Contracts between services are reliable

🔥 Protobuf & Type Safety

FeatureJSONProtobuf
Schema❌ optional✅ required
Typesweakstrong
Validationruntimecompile-time + runtime
Performanceslowerfaster

⚙️ Key Protobuf Concepts

🟢 Field Numbers

int32 id = 1;
  • Used in binary encoding
  • Never change existing numbers

🟡 Optional / Repeated

string name = 1;       // optional (proto3 default)
repeated string tags = 2;

🔴 Enums

enum Role {
  USER = 0;
  ADMIN = 1;
}

🟣 Nested Messages

message Post {
  string title = 1;
}

message User {
  repeated Post posts = 2;
}

🔄 Backward / Forward Compatibility

Rules:

  • ✅ Add new fields → safe
  • ❌ Remove fields → risky
  • ❌ Change field numbers → breaking
  • ✅ Mark deprecated fields

🚀 Where Protobuf is Used

  • gRPC
  • Microservices communication
  • Internal APIs at scale
  • High-performance systems
💻 Mini Project — Protobuf in Node.js
🎯 Goal
Define schema
Serialize data
Deserialize data
Show type safety benefits
📁 Setup
npm init -y
npm install protobufjs
📄 user.proto
syntax = "proto3";

message User {
  int32 id = 1;
  string name = 2;
  string email = 3;
}
📄 index.js
const protobuf = require("protobufjs");

async function run() {
  const root = await protobuf.load("user.proto");
  const User = root.lookupType("User");

  // Create payload
  const payload = { id: 1, name: "Ali", email: "ali@mail.com" };

  // Validate (type safety at runtime)
  const err = User.verify(payload);
  if (err) throw Error(err);

  // Encode
  const message = User.create(payload);
  const buffer = User.encode(message).finish();

  console.log("Serialized:", buffer);

  // Decode
  const decoded = User.decode(buffer);
  console.log("Decoded:", decoded);
}

run();

🎯 50+ Interview Q&A (with Answers)

🟢 Basics (1–15)

1. What is Protobuf?

Binary serialization format by Google.

2. Why use Protobuf?

Efficiency + type safety.

3. What is a .proto file?

Schema definition file.

4. What is serialization?

Convert object → bytes.

5. What is deserialization?

Bytes → object.

6. What is type safety?

Ensuring correct data types.

7. What is schema?

Structure definition of data.

8. What is field number?

Unique identifier for each field.

9. What is proto3?

Latest version of Protobuf syntax.

10. What is repeated field?

Array-like field.

11. What is enum?

Predefined constant values.

12. What is optional field?

Field that may or may not exist.

13. What is binary format?

Compact machine-readable format.

14. What is strongly typed system?

Strict type enforcement.

15. What is weak typing?

Flexible but error-prone typing.

🟡 Intermediate (16–35)

16. How does Protobuf ensure type safety?

Schema + validation + generated code.

17. What happens if type mismatches?

Validation fails or decoding error.

18. What is backward compatibility?

New version works with old data.

19. What is forward compatibility?

Old system can read new data.

20. How to maintain compatibility?

Never change field numbers.

21. What is default value behavior?

Missing fields use defaults.

22. What is packed encoding?

Efficient encoding for repeated fields.

23. What is oneof?

Mutually exclusive fields.

oneof contact {
  string email = 1;
  string phone = 2;
}

24. What is message nesting?

Message inside another message.

25. What is schema evolution?

Changing schema safely over time.

26. What is reflection?

Inspect schema at runtime.

27. What is protoc?

Protobuf compiler.

28. What is code generation?

Generating typed classes from schema.

29. What is wire format?

Binary encoding format.

30. What is field tag?

Combination of field number + type.

31. What is unknown field handling?

Ignored safely in proto3.

32. What is deterministic serialization?

Same input → same binary output.

33. What is validation in Protobuf?

Checking data against schema.

34. What is schema registry?

Store and manage schemas.

35. What is versioning strategy?

Add fields, don’t modify existing ones.

🔴 Advanced (36–55)

36. How does gRPC use Protobuf?

Defines services + messages.

37. What is RPC definition in Protobuf?

service UserService {
  rpc GetUser(UserRequest) returns (User);
}

38. What is streaming in gRPC?

Sending multiple messages over one connection.

39. What is performance advantage?

Binary + compact → faster network usage.

40. What is schema enforcement benefit?

Prevents runtime errors.

41. What is JSON mapping in Protobuf?

Convert Protobuf ↔ JSON.

42. What is cross-language support?

Works across multiple languages.

43. What is compression advantage?

Binary compresses better than JSON.

44. What is Protobuf limitation?

Less human-readable.

45. What is debugging challenge?

Binary data harder to inspect.

46. When NOT to use Protobuf?

  • Public APIs needing readability
  • Simple apps

47. What is API contract?

Agreement between services.

48. What is schema-first design?

Define schema before implementation.

49. What is code-first approach?

Generate schema from code.

50. What is strict schema validation?

Reject invalid data.

51. What is evolution risk?

Breaking compatibility.

52. What is message size optimization?

Use smaller field types.

53. What is field reservation?

Reserve removed field numbers.

54. What is compatibility testing?

Test schema changes.

55. Final interview answer?

“Protocol Buffers provide a strongly typed, schema-based way to serialize data efficiently. They ensure type safety through defined schemas and generated code, making them ideal for high-performance systems like gRPC where backward compatibility and compact data transfer are critical.”
Rate Limiting and Throttling (implementations)
Fixed Window Counter

Idea

You allow, for example, 5 requests per 10 seconds.

You keep:

  • current window start
  • request count in that window

When the window changes, reset the counter.

class FixedWindowRateLimiter {
  constructor(limit, windowSizeMs) {
    this.limit = limit;
    this.windowSizeMs = windowSizeMs;
    this.store = new Map();
  }

  isAllowed(userId) {
    const now = Date.now();
    const windowStart = Math.floor(now / this.windowSizeMs) * this.windowSizeMs;

    if (!this.store.has(userId)) {
      this.store.set(userId, {
        windowStart,
        count: 1,
      });
      return true;
    }

    const userData = this.store.get(userId);

    // New window -> reset counter
    if (userData.windowStart !== windowStart) {
      userData.windowStart = windowStart;
      userData.count = 1;
      return true;
    }

    // Same window
    if (userData.count < this.limit) {
      userData.count++;
      return true;
    }

    return false;
  }
}

// Example
const limiter = new FixedWindowRateLimiter(5, 10000);

for (let i = 1; i <= 7; i++) {
  console.log(`Request ${i}:`, limiter.isAllowed("user1"));
  
}

Pros

  • very simple
  • fast
  • easy to store in memory or Redis

Cons

  • burst problem at window boundary

Example burst problem

If limit is 5 per 10 sec:

  • user sends 5 requests at 09.999s
  • then 5 requests at 10.001s

That becomes 10 requests almost instantly.

Sliding Window Log

Idea

Store the timestamp of every request.

On each new request:

  • remove old timestamps outside the time window
  • count the remaining timestamps
  • if count < limit, allow and add new timestamp

This is more accurate than fixed window.

class SlidingWindowLogRateLimiter {
  constructor(limit, windowSizeMs) {
    this.limit = limit;
    this.windowSizeMs = windowSizeMs;
    this.store = new Map();
  }

  isAllowed(userId) {
    const now = Date.now();

    if (!this.store.has(userId)) {
      this.store.set(userId, []);
    }

    const timestamps = this.store.get(userId);

    // Remove timestamps older than the window
    while (timestamps.length > 0 && timestamps[0] <= now - this.windowSizeMs) {
      timestamps.shift();
    }

    if (timestamps.length < this.limit) {
      timestamps.push(now);
      return true;
    }

    return false;
  }
}

// Example
const limiter = new SlidingWindowLogRateLimiter(5, 10000);

for (let i = 1; i <= 7; i++) {
  console.log(`Request ${i}:`, limiter.isAllowed("user1"));
}

Pros

  • accurate
  • no hard window boundary issue like fixed window

Cons

  • memory heavy
  • storing every request timestamp can be expensive
  • shift() on arrays is not ideal for huge scale

Sliding Window Counter

This is an optimized version of sliding window.

Instead of storing every request timestamp, you keep:

  • current window count
  • previous window count

Then estimate how much of the previous window still overlaps.

class SlidingWindowCounterRateLimiter {
  constructor(limit, windowSizeMs) {
    this.limit = limit;
    this.windowSizeMs = windowSizeMs;
    this.store = new Map();
  }

  isAllowed(userId) {
    const now = Date.now();
    const currentWindowStart = Math.floor(now / this.windowSizeMs) * this.windowSizeMs;
    const elapsed = now - currentWindowStart;
    const weight = elapsed / this.windowSizeMs;

    if (!this.store.has(userId)) {
      this.store.set(userId, {
        currentWindowStart,
        currentCount: 0,
        previousCount: 0,
      });
    }

    const data = this.store.get(userId);

    // Move windows if needed
    if (data.currentWindowStart !== currentWindowStart) {
      const windowsPassed =
        (currentWindowStart - data.currentWindowStart) / this.windowSizeMs;

      if (windowsPassed === 1) {
        data.previousCount = data.currentCount;
      } else {
        data.previousCount = 0;
      }

      data.currentCount = 0;
      data.currentWindowStart = currentWindowStart;
    }

    const estimatedCount =
      data.currentCount + data.previousCount * (1 - weight);

    if (estimatedCount < this.limit) {
      data.currentCount++;
      return true;
    }

    return false;
  }
}

// Example
const limiter = new SlidingWindowCounterRateLimiter(5, 10000);

for (let i = 1; i <= 7; i++) {
  console.log(`Request ${i}:`, limiter.isAllowed("user1"));
}
Token Bucket

Idea

Each user has a bucket of tokens.

  • bucket has max capacity
  • tokens refill over time
  • every request consumes 1 token
  • if no token is available, reject

This is one of the most common real-world strategies.

class TokenBucketRateLimiter {
  constructor(capacity, refillRatePerSecond) {
    this.capacity = capacity;
    this.refillRatePerSecond = refillRatePerSecond;
    this.store = new Map();
  }

  isAllowed(userId) {
    const now = Date.now();

    if (!this.store.has(userId)) {
      this.store.set(userId, {
        tokens: this.capacity,
        lastRefillTime: now,
      });
    }

    const bucket = this.store.get(userId);

    const timePassed = (now - bucket.lastRefillTime) / 1000;
    const refillAmount = timePassed * this.refillRatePerSecond;

    bucket.tokens = Math.min(this.capacity, bucket.tokens + refillAmount);
    bucket.lastRefillTime = now;

    if (bucket.tokens >= 1) {
      bucket.tokens -= 1;
      return true;
    }

    return false;
  }
}

// Example
const limiter = new TokenBucketRateLimiter(5, 1); // 5 tokens max, refill 1/sec

for (let i = 1; i <= 7; i++) {
  console.log(`Request ${i}:`, limiter.isAllowed("user1"));
}

Pros

  • supports bursts
  • smooth refill behavior
  • very practical for APIs

Cons

  • slightly more complex than fixed window

Why people like token bucket

Suppose:

  • capacity = 10
  • refill = 2 tokens/sec

If a user was idle, they can burst up to 10 requests instantly.

After that, they are limited by refill rate.

That makes it flexible.

Leaky Bucket

Idea

Requests enter a queue.

They leave the queue at a fixed speed.

This smooths traffic.

So token bucket controls whether a request can happen based on tokens.

Leaky bucket controls outgoing flow at a constant rate.

JavaScript implementation

class LeakyBucketRateLimiter {
  constructor(capacity, leakRatePerSecond) {
    this.capacity = capacity;
    this.leakRatePerSecond = leakRatePerSecond;
    this.store = new Map();
  }

  isAllowed(userId) {
    const now = Date.now();

    if (!this.store.has(userId)) {
      this.store.set(userId, {
        water: 0,
        lastLeakTime: now,
      });
    }

    const bucket = this.store.get(userId);

    const timePassed = (now - bucket.lastLeakTime) / 1000;
    const leaked = timePassed * this.leakRatePerSecond;

    bucket.water = Math.max(0, bucket.water - leaked);
    bucket.lastLeakTime = now;

    if (bucket.water < this.capacity) {
      bucket.water += 1;
      return true;
    }

    return false;
  }
}

// Example
const limiter = new LeakyBucketRateLimiter(5, 1);

for (let i = 1; i <= 7; i++) {
  console.log(`Request ${i}:`, limiter.isAllowed("user1"));
}

Pros

  • smoother outgoing traffic
  • good for protecting downstream systems

Cons

  • can reject bursty users more aggressively
  • conceptually less natural for some API quotas
rate limiting in technologies

🧠 1. NestJS (what it actually uses)

In NestJS, the official package is:

👉 @nestjs/throttler

⚙️ Under the hood

Default behavior is basically:

✅ Fixed Window Counter

Example

import {ThrottlerModule }from'@nestjs/throttler';

@Module({
  imports: [
ThrottlerModule.forRoot({
      ttl:60,// window (seconds)
      limit:10,// max requests
    }),
  ],
})
exportclassAppModule {}

🧠 What this means

  • ttl = 60 → window = 60 seconds
  • limit = 10 → max 10 requests
  • After 60 sec → reset

👉 That is Fixed Window

⚠️ Important

By default:

  • uses in-memory store ❌ (not scalable)

For production:

  • use Redis store (shared state)

API Versioning Strategies
docs

📘 1. What is API Versioning?

API versioning is the strategy of managing changes in an API without breaking existing clients.

👉 Goal:

Let old and new clients work at the same time safely.

⚠️ Why Versioning is Needed

APIs change over time:

  • Fields added/removed
  • Response structure changes
  • Business logic updates
  • Deprecations

Without versioning:

❌ Old apps break

❌ Clients fail silently

❌ Backward compatibility is lost

⚙️ 2. Main Versioning Strategies

🟢 1. URI Versioning (Most Common)

7

📌 Example:

GET /api/v1/users
GET /api/v2/users

✅ Pros:

  • Very simple
  • Easy to debug
  • Cache-friendly
  • Widely used

❌ Cons:

  • URL duplication
  • Hard to maintain many versions

🧠 Used by:

  • Twitter
  • GitHub

🟡 2. Query Parameter Versioning

📌 Example:

GET /users?version=1
GET /users?version=2

✅ Pros:

  • Flexible
  • No URL duplication

❌ Cons:

  • Not REST-clean
  • Harder caching
  • Can be ignored by proxies

🔵 3. Header Versioning (Most Clean)

8

📌 Example:

GET /users
Headers:
  Accept-Version: v2

or

X-API-Version: 2

✅ Pros:

  • Clean URLs
  • REST compliant
  • Flexible routing

❌ Cons:

  • Harder to debug manually
  • Requires gateway support

🟣 4. Content Negotiation (Advanced REST)

📌 Example:

Accept: application/vnd.company.v2+json

✅ Pros:

  • Very REST-compliant
  • Fine-grained control

❌ Cons:

  • Complex
  • Rarely used in simple systems

🟠 5. Subdomain Versioning

📌 Example:

v1.api.example.com
v2.api.example.com

✅ Pros:

  • Strong separation
  • Good for large systems

❌ Cons:

  • DNS complexity
  • Harder infra management

⚔️ Comparison Table

StrategySimplicityScalabilityCache FriendlyUsage
URI (/v1)⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Most common
Query param⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Rare
Headers⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Modern APIs
Content negotiation⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Advanced systems
Subdomain⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Large infra
Implementation

💻 3. Implementation (Node.js Example)

🟢 URI Versioning

app.get("/api/v1/users", (req,res) => {
res.json({ version:1, users: ["A","B"] });
});

app.get("/api/v2/users", (req,res) => {
res.json({ version:2, users: [{ name:"A" }, { name:"B" }] });
});

🔵 Header Versioning

app.get("/users", (req,res) => {
constversion=req.headers["x-api-version"];

if (version==="2") {
returnres.json({ users: [{ name:"A" }] });
  }

res.json({ users: ["A"] });
});

  1. What is rolling deprecation? → gradual shutdown
  1. What is canary versioning? → partial traffic v2
  1. What is A/B API versioning? → testing versions
  1. What is backward-compatible API? → old clients work
  1. What is forward compatibility? → future-proof design
  1. What is API lifecycle? → create → maintain → deprecate
  1. What is version explosion problem? → too many versions
  1. What is API governance? → managing API rules
  1. What is contract testing? → validate API consistency
  1. What is schema registry? → versioned schema storage
  1. What is microservice versioning? → service-level versions
  1. What is API gateway version routing? → central routing
  1. What is feature flag alternative? → runtime control
  1. What is multi-client versioning? → different apps use different APIs
  1. What is global API versioning? → consistent across systems
  1. What is schema compatibility rule? → safe evolution rules
  1. Final answer? → versioning ensures safe API evolution without breaking clients
URI vs URL
URI

🔹 URI (Uniform Resource Identifier)

  • General concept
  • Identifies a resource (by name, location, or both)
  • Includes:
    • URL
    • URN

👉 Example:

  • https://example.com/page (URL → also a URI)
  • urn:isbn:123456789 (URN → also a URI)
URL

🔹 URL (Uniform Resource Locator)

  • Specific type of URI
  • Tells where the resource is and how to access it
  • Includes:
    • protocol (https, ftp, etc.)
    • domain
    • path

👉 Example:

  • https://example.com/page
    • https → protocol
    • example.com → location
    • /page → resource path
COMPARISON
TypeMeaningExample
URIIdentifier (general)urn:isbn:123
URLLocation + accesshttps://example.com
URNName onlyurn:isbn:0451450523
URN

🔹 URN (Uniform Resource Name)

📌 Definition

A URN is a type of URI that identifies a resource by name, not by location

🔹 Key idea

  • ❌ No info about where the resource is
  • ❌ No info about how to access it
  • ✅ Only a unique identifier (name)

🔹 Example

urn:isbn:0451450523
  • urn → scheme
  • isbn:0451450523 → unique book identifier

👉 This identifies a book, but:

  • you don’t know where it is
  • you can’t directly fetch it
GPT VERSION

🔥 Key Difference

  • URI = identifier (bigger category)
  • URL = locator (subset of URI)

👉 All URLs are URIs

👉 Not all URIs are URLs

🧠 Simple analogy

  • URI = person's identity (name or address)
  • URL = person's home address (exact location)
