Difference Between URL and URI

Last Updated : 12 Jul, 2025

In Web browsers and Internet connections, it is important to understand the difference between a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) and a Uniform Resource Location (URL). Both URIs and URLs are pointers to things like web pages, images, documents, or other online content. However, they have distinctive characteristics and functions that set them apart from one another.

What is URL (Uniform Resource Locator)?

URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is often defined as a string of characters that is directed to an address. It provides a way to retrieve the presentation of the physical location by describing its network location or primary access mechanism.

To locate a resource on the internet, use a Uniform Resource Locator or URL. It serves as both a resource reference and an access point. A unique resource—which could be an image, an HTML page, a CSS document, or anything else—is always displayed by a URL.

URL

The protocol is described within the URL which is employed to retrieve the resource and resource name. The URL contains http/https at the start of the resource may be a web-type resource. Similarly, it begins with ftp FTPf the resource may be a file and mailto if the resource is an email address. The syntax of a URL is shown below where the primary part is employed for protocol and the remainder of the part is employed for the resource which consists of a website name or program name.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/minimum-cost-graph/

Here, the domain name describes the server (web service) and program name (path to the directory and file on the server).

Syntax of URL

Every HTTP URL adheres to its generic URI's syntax. As a result, the syntax of the URL and the URI are comparable. It is provided below:

  • Scheme: A scheme is the initial part of a URL; it is a protocol that a browser must employ in order to seek a resource. HTTP and HTTPS are the protocols that are most often used for websites.
  • Authority: The domain name and port, two sub-components of the authority, are separated by a colon. The resource's registered name, such as javatpoint.com, can be used as the domain name, and the port on a web server serves as the technical entry point to the resource. For HTTP, port 80 is used, and for HTTPS, port 443.
  • Path: The path on the web server shows the full route to the resource. A possible format is /software/htp/index.html.
  • Query String: The string containing the name and value pair is known as the query string. When it appears in a URL, the information is provided by following the path component. "?key1=value1&key2=value2" is one example.
  • Fragment: It is an optional element that comes before the hash(#) symbol. It is made up of a fragment identification that points the way to a backup resource.
  • For Ex: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/computer-networks/difference-between-url-and-uri/

What is URI (Uniform Resource Identifier)?

Similar to URL, URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) is also a string of characters that identifies a resource on the web either by using location, name or both. It allows uniform identification of the resources. A URI is additionally grouped as a locator, a name or both which suggests it can describe a URL, URN or both. The term identifier within the URI refers to the prominence of the resources, despite the technique used.

The former category in URI is URL, during which a protocol is employed to specify the accessing method of the resource and resource name is additionally laid out in the URL. A URL may be a non-persistent sort of the URI. A URN is required to exist globally unique and features a global scope.A string identifier that points to an online resource is called a URI, or uniform resource identifier. Any resource on the internet can be identified by this string of characters by either its name, its location, or both. Scheme, authority, path, query, and fragment are all contained in a URI. The most widely used URI systems include ftp, Idap, telnet, HTTPs, HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), etc.

Syntax of URI

  • Scheme: A scheme is the initial part of a Uniform Resource Locator (URI). It consists of a string of characters, which can be any combination of a letter, number, plus sign, or hyphen (_), and is followed by a colon (:). The most widely used protocols are irc, file, ftp, data, and http. It is necessary to register the schemes with IANA.
  • Authority: Two slashes (//) come before the optional authority component. There are three smaller parts to it:
    • user details: It might have a colon (:) between the username and an optional password.
    • host: It has an IP address or a registered name on it. The IP address has to be put in square brackets [] around it.
    • Path: Optional
  • Port: A series of path segments divided by a slash(/) make up this path. It is always supplied by the URI; however, the path may be null or empty.
  • Query: It is an optional element that comes before the question mark (?). It has a non-hierarchical query string with data in it.
  • Fragment: It is an optional element that comes before the hash(#) symbol. It is made up of a fragment identification that points the way to a backup resource. 

Difference Between URL and URI

URLURI
URL is used to describe the identity of an item.URI provides a technique for defining the identity of an item.
URL links a web page, a component of a web page or a program on a web page with the help of accessing methods like protocols.URI is used to distinguish one resource from other regardless of the method used.
URL provides the details about what type of protocol is to be used.URI doesn’t contains the protocol specification.
URL is a type of URI.URI is the superset of URL.
It comprises of protocol, domain, path, hash, and so on.It comprises of scheme, authority, path, query and many more.
Ex-https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/Ex- urn:isbn:0-294-56559-3

What is a URN?

A Uniform Resource Name (URN) is a kind of Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) this is used to uniquely perceive resources at the net in a chronic and region-unbiased way. Unlike Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), which specify the location of a useful resource and how to get right of entry to it, URNs are meant to function continual, globally specific identifiers for sources irrespective of their contemporary region.

The primary reason of URNs is to provide a strong and lengthy-lasting identifier for resources, even supposing their place or access strategies trade over time. URNs are normally used for naming sources which includes documents, articles, books, and other types of virtual content.

Comparison Between URL vs URI vs URN

  • Purpose: URIs are used to perceive sources at the net, at the same time as URLs specify the area and get admission to method for getting access to sources, and URNs provide persistent, place-impartial identifiers.
  • Structure: URLs include the network location and access protocol, whilst URNs consist of a scheme and unique identifier for the resource. URIs encompass both of these systems.
  • Usage: URLs are normally used to get admission to web pages and resources without delay, whilst URNs are less normally used however provide stability and patience for useful resource identity. URIs function the overarching term that consists of each URLs and URNs.
CACHING METHODS

🧠 Caching — System Design (Notion Notes)

📌 1. Why Caching?

🔹 Problem

  • Database becomes bottleneck
  • High latency (20–50 ms per query)
  • High read traffic

🔹 Solution

Store frequently accessed data in fast memory (cache)
  • DB read → ~50 ms
  • Cache read → ~1 ms
    👉 ~50x faster

🔹 Benefits

  • ✅ lower latency
  • ✅ reduced DB load
  • ✅ better scalability

📌 2. Where to Cache

🔹 1. External Cache (Most Important)

Examples:

  • Redis
  • Memcached

👉 Between app and DB

App → Cache → DB

✔ shared across servers

✔ supports TTL, eviction

🔹 2. CDN (Content Delivery Network)

👉 Cache near users globally

Flow:

User → CDN → Origin Server

✔ reduces latency (300ms → 20ms)

✔ best for static content

🔹 3. Client-Side Cache

  • Browser cache
  • Mobile app storage

✔ no network call

❌ hard to control

🔹 4. In-Process Cache

👉 Inside application memory

Examples:

  • config
  • feature flags
  • hot keys

✔ fastest

❌ not shared across instances

📌 3. Cache Patterns

🔹 1. Cache-Aside (Most Important)

Flow:

1. Check cache
2. If miss → fetch DB
3. Store in cache
4. Return

✔ most common

✔ flexible

🔹 2. Write-Through

App → Cache → DB

✔ strong consistency

❌ slower writes

🔹 3. Write-Behind (Write-Back)

App → Cache → (async) DB

✔ fast writes

❌ risk of data loss

🔹 4. Read-Through

App → Cache → DB (if miss)

✔ centralized logic

❌ complex

📌 4. Eviction Policies

🔹 LRU (Default)

  • remove least recently used

🔹 LFU

  • remove least frequently used

🔹 FIFO

  • remove oldest

🔹 TTL (Important)

  • expire data after time

📌 5. Common Problems

🔥 1. Cache Stampede

  • many requests hit DB when cache expires

✔ Solution:

  • request coalescing
  • cache warming

🔥 2. Cache Consistency

  • cache ≠ DB data

✔ Solution:

  • invalidate on write
  • TTL
  • eventual consistency

🔥 3. Hot Keys

  • one key gets massive traffic

✔ Solution:

  • replicate key
  • in-process cache
  • rate limiting

📌 6. When to Use Caching

Use when:

  • read-heavy workload
  • expensive queries
  • high DB CPU
  • strict latency requirements

📌 7. How to Design Caching (Interview Flow)

1. Identify bottleneck

“DB queries are slow (30–50 ms)”

2. Decide what to cache

  • frequently read
  • rarely updated

3. Choose pattern

  • usually cache-aside

4. Set eviction

  • LRU + TTL

5. Handle problems

  • invalidation
  • failures
  • stampede

📌 8. Key Insight

Caching = trading consistency for performance

📌 9. Final Summary

  • Cache reduces latency drastically
  • Redis is default external cache
  • Cache-aside is most common pattern
  • TTL + LRU is standard setup
  • Always handle invalidation & failures

🧠 Interview One-Liners

  • “Cache reduces DB load and improves latency”
  • “Cache-aside is the most common pattern”
  • “We use TTL + LRU for eviction”
  • “Cache introduces consistency challenges”
handling regional partitioning
Geographic routing with spillover

When to use it

Use this when users should normally go to the nearest region, but you want a fallback when that region gets overloaded.

Global load balancers commonly support failover / active-passive and also active-active multi-region serving. Google Cloud documents both patterns in its load balancing and failover docs.

Core components

  • Global DNS or global load balancer
  • Health checks
  • Regional capacity metrics
  • Spillover policy
  • Session/data affinity policy

How to implement it

Step 1: Define a home region

Map users to a preferred region.

Example:

Uzbekistan -> eu-central
India -> asia-south
Germany -> europe-west

Step 2: Add a spillover table

Keep a fallback map:

constspilloverMap= {
"asia-central": ["europe-west","middle-east"],
"europe-west": ["europe-north","us-east"],
};

Step 3: Route based on health + capacity

Pseudo-logic:

functionchooseRegion(userGeo,requestType) {
constprimary=geoToPrimaryRegion(userGeo);
constcandidates= [primary, ...(spilloverMap[primary]|| [])];

for (constregionofcandidates) {
consthealth=getRegionHealth(region);
constload=getRegionLoad(region);

if (health==="healthy"&&load<0.75) {
returnregion;
    }
  }

returnprimary;
}

Step 4: Protect writes

Reads are easy to spill.

Writes are harder.

If traffic spills from region A to region B, then either:

  • region B proxies writes back to A, or
  • the user temporarily writes in B and you replicate later, or
  • only read-only endpoints spill

A safe first version is:

  • spill reads
  • keep writes pinned to home region

What breaks

  • latency increases for overflow users
  • session stickiness gets messy
  • region-local caches miss more often
  • write ownership can become inconsistent if spillover is too permissive

Strong production pattern

Use:

  • read spillover
  • write pinning
  • sticky sessions for a short TTL
  • circuit breaker so traffic does not flap between regions
service level sharding

That is service-level sharding / application-level sharding.

🔹 Idea

Instead of only sharding databases, you also shard the services/servers:

Users in shard A → Service A → DB A
Users in shard B → Service B → DB B

So the app server itself knows:

  • which users it owns
  • which DB it talks to

🔹 Why do this

  • more control
  • custom routing logic
  • easier optimization per shard
  • can isolate hot shards better
  • service and DB can scale together

🔹 This is common

Large systems often shard at:

  • routing layer
  • service layer
  • database layer

Not only DB layer.

🔹 Benefit over only DB sharding

If only DB is sharded:

  • app still needs shared logic
  • traffic may still hit same service cluster

If service is also sharded:

  • compute load is split too
  • cache is split too
  • queue/workers can be split too

🔹 Tradeoff

  • more complexity
  • deployment becomes harder
  • cross-shard operations become harder
  • rebalancing is harder
Consistent hashing with rebalancing

When to use it

Use this when traffic or data should be distributed by key, not only by geography.

Core components

  • hash ring
  • shard ownership map
  • routing library
  • rebalancer
  • migration worker

How to implement it

Step 1: Hash keys to partitions

Example:

functionhashKey(key) {
// simplified
leth=0;
for (constchofkey)h= (h*31+ch.charCodeAt(0))>>>0;
returnh;
}

functionpartitionForKey(key,partitionCount) {
returnhashKey(key)%partitionCount;
}

Step 2: Map partitions to regions

constpartitionOwners= {
0:"asia-central",
1:"asia-central",
2:"europe-west",
3:"us-east",
};

Step 3: Route by partition owner

functionrouteRequest(key) {
constpartition=partitionForKey(key,1024);
returnpartitionOwners[partition];
}

Step 4: Rebalance hot partitions

If partition 17 is hot:

  • choose a colder region
  • copy data
  • warm cache
  • switch ownership
  • drain old owner

Migration state machine:

IDLE
-> COPYING
-> DUAL_READ_OPTIONAL
-> DUAL_WRITE_OPTIONAL
-> CUTOVER
-> DRAIN_OLD
-> DONE

Step 5: Add versioned metadata

Every router should read a versioned partition map.

{
version:42,
owners: {
17:"europe-west"
  }
}

If routers use stale maps, requests go to the wrong region.

What breaks

  • cache churn after movement
  • stale routing maps
  • partial migration during failures
  • cross-region copy cost

Best practice

Do not move raw user keys directly. Move logical partitions, not individual records.

virtual shards

Virtual shards / virtual partitions

This is usually the best practical design.

When to use it

Use this when you want much finer balancing than “one region owns one big chunk.”

Core components

  • many logical partitions, for example 1,000 or 10,000
  • ownership table
  • partition load metrics
  • movement controller

Spanner’s docs explicitly discuss hash-based logical sharding and load-based splitting across key space.

How to implement it

Step 1: Create many virtual partitions

constVIRTUAL_PARTITION_COUNT=4096;

functionvirtualPartition(key) {
returnhashKey(key)%VIRTUAL_PARTITION_COUNT;
}

Step 2: Assign them unevenly if needed

constregionAssignments= {
"asia-central": [0,1,2,3,4,5],
"europe-west": [6,7,8,9],
"us-east": [10,11,12],
};

In practice, store the reverse mapping: vp -> region.

Step 3: Track per-partition heat

For each virtual partition:

  • QPS
  • read/write split
  • p95 latency
  • CPU
  • storage
  • queue lag

Step 4: Move a few partitions at a time

If region A is hot:

  • choose the hottest 5 virtual partitions
  • migrate only those
  • observe
  • repeat

Step 5: Automate placement

Simple heuristic:

if (region.cpu>75&&partition.qps>threshold) {
movePartition(partitionId,coldestRegion());
}

What breaks

  • metadata service becomes critical
  • too many tiny partitions adds overhead
  • partition movement may split related data too aggressively

Best practice

Keep virtual partitions small enough to move, but large enough not to create routing chaos.

Replicate reads, centralize writes

Replicate reads, centralize writes

When to use it

Use this when reads are huge and writes are modest.

Core components

  • one write leader
  • read replicas in multiple regions
  • replication stream
  • read routing policy
  • staleness policy

How to implement it

Step 1: Pick a write owner

All writes go to one region or one leader DB.

Step 2: Replicate outward

Use:

  • database replication
  • CDC stream
  • event log
  • snapshot + tailing updates

Step 3: Route reads locally

functionchooseReadRegion(userGeo) {
returnnearestHealthyReplica(userGeo);
}

Step 4: Add read consistency modes

For example:

  • eventual
  • read-after-write
  • strong

If user just updated profile, read from leader for 10 seconds.

functionreadProfile(userId,options) {
if (options.requireFresh) {
returnreadFromLeader(userId);
  }
returnreadFromNearestReplica(userId);
}

What breaks

  • replication lag
  • stale reads
  • user confusion after writes
  • replica lag spikes during incidents

Best practice

Make freshness explicit in the API.

Example:

  • product catalog: eventual is fine
  • balance/payment: eventual is dangerous
Active-active multi-region writes

Use this only when you really need local writes in multiple regions.

Redis Active-Active docs describe a CRDT-based model where each copy accepts reads and writes and then converges under eventual consistency.

Core components

  • conflict strategy
  • replication channel
  • convergence model
  • idempotent writes
  • per-record versioning

How to implement it

There are three broad models:

Model A: Last-write-wins

Easy, but risky.

{
userId:"123",
value:"new name",
updatedAt:1710000000
}

Conflict rule:

winner=recordwithmax(updatedAt)

Good for:

  • preferences
  • low-risk profile fields

Bad for:

  • counters
  • money
  • inventory

Model B: CRDT-like data types

Use mergeable structures:

  • counters
  • sets
  • maps
  • append-only logs

Example grow-only counter:

{
regionCounters: {
"asia-central":4,
"europe-west":3
  }
}

Final count = sum of region counters.

Model C: Region ownership by entity

A safer business approach:

  • each entity has a home-write region
  • other regions proxy writes or queue transfer

This is often easier than full arbitrary active-active.

What breaks

  • duplicate operations
  • clock skew
  • merge bugs
  • user-visible anomalies

Best practice

If you need active-active, first classify fields:

  • mergeable
  • overwrite-safe
  • must stay single-writer

Do not treat all data the same.

hot key splitting

When to use it

Use this when one object, tenant, or key gets far more traffic than the rest.

AWS DynamoDB docs warn that a single partition can throttle even when the table overall has capacity, and adaptive capacity can help but hot partitions still matter. Google Spanner docs also discuss hotspots and load-based splitting.

Core components

  • hotspot detector
  • key split strategy
  • fanout reader
  • merge logic

How to implement it

Strategy A: Add random/hash suffixes

Instead of:

post:123:likes

Use:

post:123:likes:0
post:123:likes:1
post:123:likes:2
post:123:likes:3

Write path:

functionbucketForWrite(userId,shardCount) {
returnhashKey(userId)%shardCount;
}

Read path:

asyncfunctiontotalLikes(postId,shardCount) {
lettotal=0;
for (leti=0;i<shardCount;i++) {
total+=awaitget(`post:${postId}:likes:${i}`);
  }
returntotal;
}

Strategy B: Cache the hot object globally

If the hot key is read-heavy, cache it at edge/CDN/app cache and avoid the DB path.

Strategy C: Isolate the hot tenant

Move the noisy customer to its own shard or region.

What breaks

  • read fanout cost
  • aggregation complexity
  • uneven bucket distribution
  • application code gets more complex

Best practice

Use hot-key splitting mainly for:

  • counters
  • feed fanout
  • viral objects
  • large tenants
Load shedding

When to use it

Use this when a region is already overloaded and you need to protect the core path.

Core components

  • overload detector
  • priority classes
  • queue depth / latency thresholds
  • rejection policy

How to implement it

Step 1: Classify traffic

Example:

  • P0: login, checkout, payments
  • P1: search
  • P2: recommendations
  • P3: analytics

Step 2: Reject by class when overloaded

functionshouldShed(request,metrics) {
if (metrics.cpu<85&&metrics.queueLag<1000)returnfalse;

if (request.priority==="P3")returntrue;
if (request.priority==="P2"&&metrics.cpu>90)returntrue;

returnfalse;
}

Step 3: Return degraded responses

Instead of total failure:

  • empty recommendations
  • stale cache
  • delayed writes
  • reduced result size

Step 4: Add concurrency caps

classSemaphore {
  constructor(limit) {
this.limit=limit;
this.current=0;
  }
  tryAcquire() {
if (this.current>=this.limit)returnfalse;
this.current++;
returntrue;
  }
  release() {
this.current--;
  }
}

What breaks

  • unfair rejection
  • clients retry too aggressively
  • accidental shedding of critical traffic

Best practice

Always combine load shedding with:

  • retry budgets
  • exponential backoff
  • idempotency keys
queue based smoothing

When to use it

Use this when work does not need to finish synchronously.

Kafka’s model is useful here because topics are partitioned, and within a consumer group each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer at a time; the partition count controls maximum parallelism.

Core components

  • durable queue/topic
  • producer in hot region
  • workers in colder regions
  • partitioning scheme
  • retry / DLQ

How to implement it

Step 1: Put expensive work onto a queue

Examples:

  • emails
  • thumbnails
  • analytics
  • webhooks
  • notifications
awaitqueue.publish("send-email", {
  userId,
  templateId,
  regionHint:"asia-central"
});

Step 2: Consume from colder regions

Workers in multiple regions pull jobs.

Step 3: Partition intelligently

Partition by:

  • tenant
  • user
  • object id
  • workload type

Do not create a single giant partition for all jobs.

Step 4: Add backpressure

If queue lag exceeds threshold:

  • slow producers
  • drop low-priority jobs
  • scale workers

What breaks

  • queue lag becomes invisible until too late
  • one bad partition becomes hot
  • poison messages block progress

Best practice

Track:

  • queue depth
  • oldest message age
  • retry counts
  • DLQ size
  • per-partition skew
in pagination what if new data is added in the previously paginated list
ACID
docs

🧱 ACID in SQL Databases (Deep Dive)

📘 1. What is ACID?

ACID is a set of guarantees that ensure database reliability and correctness.

It stands for:

  • A → Atomicity
  • C → Consistency
  • I → Isolation
  • D → Durability

🧠 Simple idea:

ACID ensures your database behaves correctly even when things go wrong (crash, failure, concurrency).

⚙️ 2. ACID Overview

7

🧨 3. A = Atomicity (ALL or NOTHING)

📘 Meaning

A transaction is treated as a single unit.

Either ALL operations succeed OR NONE happen.

💻 Example:

BEGIN;

UPDATE accountsSET balance= balance-100WHERE id=1;
UPDATE accountsSET balance= balance+100WHERE id=2;

COMMIT;

❌ If crash happens halfway:

  • First update done
  • Second fails

👉 DB will ROLLBACK everything

⚙️ How DB implements Atomicity:

  • Uses Transaction Log (Undo Log)
  • Before changes → old state saved
  • If failure → rollback using log

🧩 4. C = Consistency

📘 Meaning

Database must always move from valid state → valid state

Rules must never break.

💻 Example:

balance>=0

If a transaction violates this → it is rejected.

⚙️ How DB ensures it:

  • Constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY)
  • Triggers
  • Check constraints
  • Schema rules

🧠 Key idea:

Consistency is not about speed — it is about correctness rules.

🔄 5. I = Isolation (VERY IMPORTANT)

📘 Meaning

Transactions should not interfere with each other.

Even if running at the same time → result should look like they ran one by one.

💥 Problem without isolation:

Two users withdraw money at same time → double spend bug.

⚙️ Isolation Levels:

5

1. Read Uncommitted

  • Dirty reads allowed ❌
  • Fast but unsafe

2. Read Committed (default in many DBs)

  • No dirty reads
  • Still allows non-repeatable reads

3. Repeatable Read

  • Same query → same result
  • Prevents update anomalies

4. Serializable

  • Strongest isolation
  • Transactions behave like sequential execution

⚙️ How DB implements Isolation:

1. Locking (Pessimistic)

  • Row locks
  • Table locks

2. MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)

  • Multiple versions of data
  • Readers don’t block writers

Used in:

  • PostgreSQL
  • MySQL

💾 6. D = Durability (CRASH SAFE)

📘 Meaning

Once a transaction is committed → it must never be lost.

Even if server crashes immediately after commit.

⚙️ How DB ensures durability:

1. WAL (Write Ahead Logging)

Before writing to disk:

  • log is written first

If crash happens:

  • DB replays log

2. Disk Flush (fsync)

  • Data is forced to disk
  • Not just memory

🧠 Key idea:

“If commit happened → data must survive reboot”

🔥 7. Full Transaction Lifecycle

START TRANSACTION
   ↓
Write to WAL log
   ↓
Apply changes in memory
   ↓
Commit
   ↓
Flush to disk

BEGIN;

UPDATE accountsSET balance= balance-500WHERE id=1;
UPDATE accountsSET balance= balance+500WHERE id=2;

COMMIT;

If crash happens:

StepResult
Before commitrollback

⚠️ 11. Common Interview Traps

  • ACID ≠ speed (it sacrifices performance for safety)
  • Isolation ≠ locking only (MVCC also used)
  • Consistency ≠ replication consistency (different concept)
  • Durability ≠ backup (it is transaction guarantee)
. 50+ ACID Interview Q&A (3+ lines each)

1. What is ACID?

ACID is a set of properties that guarantee reliable transaction processing in databases.

It ensures that data remains correct even in case of crashes or concurrent operations.

It is essential for systems like banking and financial applications.

2. What is Atomicity?

Atomicity means a transaction is treated as a single unit of work.

Either all operations inside it succeed or none of them are applied.

If failure occurs, the database rolls back to the previous state.

3. What is Consistency?

Consistency ensures that a database always moves from one valid state to another valid state.

It enforces rules like constraints, foreign keys, and checks.

If a rule is violated, the transaction is rejected.

4. What is Isolation?

Isolation ensures that concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other.

Each transaction behaves as if it is running alone in the system.

It prevents issues like dirty reads and race conditions.

5. What is Durability?

Durability ensures that once a transaction is committed, it will not be lost.

Even if the system crashes immediately after commit, data remains safe.

It is achieved using logs and disk persistence.

6. What is a transaction?

A transaction is a group of database operations executed as a single unit.

It ensures ACID properties are applied to multiple operations together.

It is used in critical systems like payments and transfers.

7. What is rollback?

Rollback is the process of undoing a transaction when an error occurs.

It restores the database to its previous stable state.

It is used to maintain atomicity.

8. What is commit?

Commit finalizes a transaction and saves changes permanently.

Once committed, changes cannot be undone easily.

It triggers durability mechanisms like logging.

9. What is a transaction log?

A transaction log records all changes before they are applied to the database.

It helps in recovery after crashes.

It is essential for atomicity and durability.

10. What is isolation level?

Isolation level defines how visible one transaction is to others.

It controls concurrency behavior and consistency trade-offs.

Examples include Read Committed and Serializable.

11. What is dirty read?

A dirty read happens when a transaction reads uncommitted data.

If the other transaction rolls back, the data becomes invalid.

It is prevented in higher isolation levels.

12. What is non-repeatable read?

It happens when the same query returns different results within a transaction.

This occurs when another transaction modifies data in between reads.

It is solved using repeatable read isolation.

13. What is phantom read?

A phantom read occurs when new rows appear in repeated queries.

It happens when another transaction inserts new data.

Serializable isolation prevents this issue.

14. What is MVCC?

MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) allows multiple versions of data.

Readers do not block writers and vice versa.

It improves concurrency performance.

15. What is WAL?

WAL (Write Ahead Logging) ensures changes are logged before being written.

If a crash occurs, the database uses logs to recover data.

It guarantees durability.

🟡 Intermediate (16–35)

16. Why is ACID important?

ACID ensures data correctness, reliability, and crash safety.

It is essential for financial and critical systems.

Without ACID, data corruption can occur easily.

17. What is atomic commit?

Atomic commit ensures all changes in a transaction are applied together.

If one operation fails, the entire transaction is rolled back.

It prevents partial updates.

18. What is consistency rule enforcement?

It ensures database rules like constraints are always followed.

Violations automatically cause transaction failure.

It keeps data valid at all times.

19. What is isolation problem?

Without isolation, transactions can interfere with each other.

This leads to incorrect or inconsistent results.

Isolation solves concurrency issues.

20. What is serializable isolation?

Serializable is the strongest isolation level.

It ensures transactions execute as if sequentially.

It prevents all concurrency anomalies.

21. What is locking in DB?

Locking prevents other transactions from modifying data.

It ensures safe concurrent access.

It is used in pessimistic concurrency control.

22. What is deadlock?

Deadlock happens when two transactions wait on each other forever.

Neither can proceed causing system blockage.

Databases detect and resolve deadlocks automatically.

23. What is write skew?

Write skew occurs in concurrent transactions modifying related data.

It leads to inconsistent final states.

Serializable isolation prevents it.

24. What is checkpoint in DB?

A checkpoint is a saved state of database memory to disk.

It helps reduce recovery time after crashes.

It is part of durability strategy.

25. What is crash recovery?

Crash recovery restores database state after failure.

It uses logs to replay or undo transactions.

It ensures ACID guarantees are maintained.

26. What is commit protocol?

Commit protocol defines how transactions are finalized safely.

Two-phase commit is a common example.

It ensures distributed consistency.

27. What is two-phase commit?

It is a distributed transaction protocol with prepare and commit phases.

All nodes must agree before committing.

It ensures consistency across systems.

28. What is pessimistic locking?

It locks data before access to prevent conflicts.

It assumes conflicts are likely.

It is safe but slower.

29. What is optimistic locking?

It assumes conflicts are rare and checks before commit.

If conflict is found, transaction is retried.

It improves performance in low contention systems.

30. What is dirty write?

Dirty write happens when one transaction overwrites uncommitted data.

It leads to data corruption.

ACID prevents it through isolation.

31. What is snapshot isolation?

Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a consistent snapshot of data.

It avoids locking and improves concurrency.

It is based on MVCC.

32. What is consistency in distributed systems?

It refers to all nodes having the same data at the same time.

It is different from ACID consistency.

It relates to CAP theorem.

33. What is durability guarantee?

It ensures committed data is permanently stored.

Even hardware failure cannot erase it.

It is achieved using logs and disk writes.

34. What is transaction boundary?

It defines the start and end of a transaction.

Operations inside are treated as one unit.

It is controlled using BEGIN and COMMIT.

35. What is rollback segment?

It stores old versions of data for undo operations.

It is used during rollback or crash recovery.

It supports atomicity.

🔴 Advanced (36–55)

36. How does DB ensure atomicity internally?

It uses undo logs to store previous state before changes.

If a failure happens, logs are used to revert changes.

This guarantees all-or-nothing behavior.

37. How does consistency differ from replication consistency?

ACID consistency refers to data rules within a database.

Replication consistency refers to sync between multiple nodes.

They are completely different concepts.

38. How does isolation improve concurrency?

It prevents transactions from interfering with each other.

Each transaction behaves independently.

This reduces race conditions.

39. Why is isolation expensive?

Higher isolation levels require locks or version tracking.

This increases CPU and memory usage.

It reduces performance but increases safety.

40. How does MVCC improve performance?

It allows multiple versions of data instead of locking.

Readers don’t block writers.

This improves concurrency significantly.

41. What is log-based recovery?

It uses transaction logs to rebuild database state.

It replays committed transactions after crash.

It ensures durability.

42. What is shadow paging?

It keeps original data unchanged and writes changes to new pages.

After commit, new pages replace old ones.

It is an alternative to logging.

43. What is strict 2PL?

Strict Two Phase Locking holds locks until transaction completes.

It prevents dirty reads and ensures serializability.

It is used in many relational databases.

44. What is write-ahead logging rule?

Changes must be written to log before actual data is modified.

This ensures recovery is always possible.

It is fundamental for durability.

45. What is redo log?

Redo log is used to reapply committed transactions after crash.

It ensures durability of committed data.

It works with undo logs.

46. What is undo log?

Undo log stores previous state of data before modification.

It is used for rollback operations.

It ensures atomicity.

47. What is consistency checkpoint?

It is a point where database state is fully stable.

It reduces recovery time.

It improves crash recovery efficiency.

48. What is isolation anomaly?

It is incorrect behavior caused by weak isolation levels.

Examples include dirty reads and phantom reads.

Stronger isolation levels eliminate them.

49. What is ACID tradeoff?

ACID improves safety but reduces performance.

It adds overhead due to logging and locking.

Systems choose balance based on use case.

50. What is final ACID concept?

ACID ensures safe, correct, and reliable transaction processing.

It guarantees atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability.

It is the foundation of relational databases.

📘 1. What is a Graph Database?

A graph database stores data as:

  • 🟢 Nodes (entities)
  • 🔗 Edges (relationships)
  • 🧠 Properties (data on nodes/edges)

🧠 Simple idea:

Instead of asking “what is the data?”

(Ali) ──FRIEND──> (Bob)
(Ali) ──LIKES───> (Pizza)
(Bob) ──WORKS_AT→ (Google)

⚙️ 2. How Graph Databases Work

6

🔁 Core structure:

  • Node → entity (user, product, city)
  • Edge → relationship (friend, bought, likes)
  • Property → data (age, price)

🧠 3. Why Graph Databases Exist

Relational DBs struggle with:

  • deep joins
  • complex relationships
  • multi-hop queries

Example:

“Friends of friends who like same movies”

SQL becomes slow and complex.

Graph DB solves it naturally.

🧩 4. Real-world Example

Ali → friend → Bob → friend → John
Ali → likes → Football
John → likes → Football

👉 Query: “People like Ali who like football”

Graph DB solves in milliseconds.

WHERE a.name = "Ali"

WHERE a.name = "Ali"
RETURN b

👉 “Friends of friends”

💻 10. Simple Project (Node.js Graph Simulation)

We simulate graph DB using JSON.

📁 graph.json
{
  "Ali": {
    "friends": ["Bob", "John"],
    "likes": ["Football"]
  },
  "Bob": {
    "friends": ["Ali"],
    "worksAt": "Google"
  },
  "John": {
    "friends": ["Ali"],
    "likes": ["Football"]
  }
}
🚀 server.js
const express = require("express");
const fs = require("fs");

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

function loadGraph() {
  return JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("./graph.json"));
}

// GET NODE
app.get("/node/:name", (req, res) => {
  const graph = loadGraph();
  const node = graph[req.params.name];

  if (!node) {
    return res.status(404).json({ message: "Node not found" });
  }

  res.json(node);
});

// GET FRIENDS
app.get("/friends/:name", (req, res) => {
  const graph = loadGraph();
  const node = graph[req.params.name];

  if (!node) return res.status(404).json({ message: "Not found" });

  res.json(node.friends || []);
});

// FRIEND OF FRIENDS (GRAPH TRAVERSAL)
app.get("/fof/:name", (req, res) => {
  const graph = loadGraph();
  const node = graph[req.params.name];

  if (!node) return res.status(404).json({ message: "Not found" });

  let result = new Set();

  (node.friends || []).forEach(friend => {
    (graph[friend]?.friends || []).forEach(f => {
      if (f !== req.params.name) result.add(f);
    });
  });

  res.json([...result]);
});

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Graph DB running");
});
🧪 11. Testing
Get node:
GET /node/Ali
Friends:
GET /friends/Ali
Friends of friends:
GET /fof/Ali

🟢 Basics (1–15)

1. What is a graph database?

A graph database stores data as nodes and relationships.

A node represents an entity like a user or product.

It stores properties like name or age.

3. What is an edge?

An edge represents a relationship between nodes.

It defines how two nodes are connected.

Example: friend, likes, works_at.

4. What is a property?

A property is key-value data stored in nodes or edges.

It adds details to entities.

Example: age, name, weight.

They efficiently handle complex relationships.

Neo4j is a popular graph database.

🧱 Wide Column Databases — Deep Dive

📘 1. What is a Wide Column Database?

A wide column database stores data in rows and dynamic columns, where each row can have a different set of columns.

👉 Unlike SQL (fixed schema)

👉 Unlike key-value (single value)

👉 It groups columns into column families

🧠 Simple idea:

“Each row is flexible, and columns can be huge and dynamic.”

📦 Example:

Row: user_1
  name → Ali
  age → 22
  city → Tashkent
  hobby → coding

Row: user_2
  name → Bob
  email → bob@mail.com
  country → Uzbekistan

👉 Notice: columns differ per row

⚙️ 2. How Wide Column DB Works

9

🔁 Structure:

  • Keyspace (Database)
    • Column Families (Tables)
      • Rows (Partition Key)
        • Columns (Dynamic)

🧠 3. Core Concept

Instead of storing:

❌ SQL style:

Fixed columns for all rows

✅ Wide column style:

Each row can have different columns

🧩 4. Column Family Concept

A column family is like a table, but flexible.

Example:

Column Family: Users

Each row:

user_1 → { name, age, city }
user_2 → { name, email }

⚙️ 5. Real-World Database

Used by:

  • Apache Cassandra
  • HBase
  • Facebook (messages, inbox systems)

🧠 6. Why Wide Column DB Exists

Relational DBs struggle with:

  • huge data scale
  • unpredictable schema
  • time-series data
  • distributed writes

💥 7. Use Cases

🟢 1. Messaging systems

user_1 → messages: [msg1, msg2, msg3]

🟡 2. IoT data

sensor_1 → temperature, humidity, pressure

🔵 3. Logs

server_1 → log entries over time

🔴 4. Analytics

Huge time-series datasets

⚙️ 8. Architecture

🔁 Flow:

Client → Partition Key → Node → Column Family → Data

🧠 Key idea:

Data is distributed using partition key (hashing)

project

data.json

{
  "user_1": {
    "name": "Ali",
    "age": 22,
    "city": "Tashkent"
  },
  "user_2": {
    "name": "Bob",
    "email": "bob@mail.com",
    "country": "UZ"
  }
}

server.js

const express = require("express");
const fs = require("fs");

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

function loadDB() {
  return JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("./data.json"));
}

function saveDB(db) {
  fs.writeFileSync("./data.json", JSON.stringify(db, null, 2));
}

// GET ROW
app.get("/row/:key", (req, res) => {
  const db = loadDB();
  const key = req.params.key;

  if (!db[key]) {
    return res.status(404).json({ message: "Row not found" });
  }

  res.json(db[key]);
});

// ADD COLUMN TO ROW
app.post("/row/:key/column", (req, res) => {
  const { column, value } = req.body;
  const db = loadDB();
  const key = req.params.key;

  if (!db[key]) {
    db[key] = {};
  }

  db[key][column] = value;

  saveDB(db);

  res.json({ message: "Column added" });
});

// DELETE COLUMN
app.delete("/row/:key/column/:column", (req, res) => {
  const db = loadDB();
  const key = req.params.key;
  const column = req.params.column;

  if (db[key]) {
    delete db[key][column];
  }

  saveDB(db);

  res.json({ message: "Column deleted" });
});

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Wide Column DB running");
});
internals

Used to distribute data across nodes.

🟡 Clustering columns

Used for sorting inside a partition.

Merging multiple SSTables for efficiency.

🟢 Basics (1–15)

7. What is Cassandra?

It is used for big data systems.

8. What is HBase?

It supports large-scale distributed storage.

It is used in big data processing.

9. What is schema flexibility?

10. What is sparse data?

Used in distributed systems.

13. What is write optimization?

System is optimized for fast writes.

It is ideal for logs and time-series data.

Reads may be slower.

14. What is distributed storage?

Data is stored across multiple machines.

It improves reliability and scaling.

Used in Cassandra.

15. What is column-oriented storage?

Data is stored by columns instead of rows.

It improves analytics performance.

Used in wide column systems.

🟡 Intermediate (16–35)

16. Why wide column DB is scalable?

Because data is distributed using partition keys.

Each node handles part of dataset.

It allows horizontal scaling.

17. What is SSTable?

Immutable storage file used in Cassandra.

It stores sorted data.

Used for efficient reads.

18. What is compaction?

Process of merging SSTables.

It improves read performance.

It removes duplicates.

19. What is memtable?

In-memory structure before writing to disk.

It stores recent writes.

It improves write performance.

20. What is write path?

Process of writing data in DB.

Includes memtable and log writing.

Optimized for speed.

21. What is read path?

Process of retrieving data.

Checks memtable and SSTables.

Uses indexes.

22. What is replication factor?

Number of copies of data stored.

It improves fault tolerance.

Used in Cassandra.

23. What is consistency level?

Defines how many nodes must respond.

Higher level = more consistency.

Lower level = faster reads.

24. What is quorum?

Majority of nodes must respond.

Used for balance between speed and safety.

Common in distributed DBs.

25. What is tunable consistency?

You can choose consistency level per query.

It gives flexibility.

Used in Cassandra.

26. What is data locality?

Data stored close to access patterns.

It improves performance.

Important in distributed systems.

27. What is time-series data?

Data indexed by time.

Wide column DB is perfect for it.

Used in monitoring systems.

28. What is log-structured storage?

Data is written sequentially.

It improves write performance.

Used in Cassandra.

29. What is distributed query?

Query executed across multiple nodes.

Results are merged.

Used in large systems.

30. What is anti-pattern?

Bad design that reduces performance.

Example: wrong partition key.

Causes hotspot issues.

31. What is hot partition?

One partition receives too much traffic.

It slows system.

Needs better key design.

32. What is data modeling in Cassandra?

Designing based on queries not relations.

Denormalization is common.

Performance-focused.

33. What is write amplification?

One write causes multiple internal writes.

Happens in compaction.

Impacts performance.

34. What is read amplification?

One read requires multiple disk reads.

Happens when data is fragmented.

Optimized using indexes.

35. What is distributed consistency?

Ensuring all nodes agree on data.

Hard in distributed systems.

Tradeoff with availability.

🔴 Advanced (36–55)

36. Why Cassandra avoids joins?

Joins are expensive in distributed systems.

It prefers denormalized data.

Improves performance.

37. What is data partitioning strategy?

Deciding how data is split across nodes.

Uses hashing of partition key.

Affects performance.

38. What is gossip protocol?

Nodes communicate state with each other.

Used in Cassandra.

Ensures cluster awareness.

39. What is hinted handoff?

Temporary storage for failed writes.

Delivered when node recovers.

Improves reliability.

40. What is anti-entropy repair?

Process of syncing inconsistent data.

Ensures all replicas match.

Used in Cassandra.

41. What is eventual repair?

Fixing inconsistencies over time.

Not immediate.

Used in distributed DBs.

42. What is bloom filter?

Probabilistic structure for checking existence.

Reduces disk reads.

Used in SSTables.

43. What is read optimization?

Techniques to improve read performance.

Includes caching and indexing.

Important in Cassandra.

44. What is write durability?

Ensuring writes are not lost.

Uses commit logs.

Ensures recovery.

45. What is cluster topology?

Arrangement of nodes in system.

Affects routing and performance.

Important in distributed DB.

46. What is token ring?

Used in Cassandra for data distribution.

Each node gets a range of tokens.

Ensures balanced load.

47. What is load balancing?

Distributing requests evenly across nodes.

Prevents overload.

Improves performance.

48. What is data replication strategy?

Defines how copies of data are stored.

Improves fault tolerance.

Used in Cassandra.

49. What is eventual read consistency?

Reads may return stale data temporarily.

Eventually becomes correct.

Tradeoff for performance.

50. What is final concept?

Wide column databases store flexible, distributed, high-scale data using rows and dynamic columns.

They are optimized for writes, scalability, and big data workloads.

They power systems like Cassandra and large distributed platforms.

Key-Value Stores
docs

🔑 Key-Value Stores (NoSQL) — Deep Dive

📘 1. What is a Key-Value Database?

A key-value store is a database where data is stored as a simple pair:

🔑 Key → unique identifier

📦 Value → data (string, JSON, blob, etc.)

🧠 Simple idea:

“Give me the key → I give you the value.”

📦 Example:

user:1 → {"name":"Ali", "age":22}
session:abc123 → {"userId":1, "expires":...}
cart:42 → ["item1", "item2"]

⚙️ 2. How Key-Value Stores Work

7

🔁 Core mechanism:

  1. Hash key
  1. Find location
  1. Return value instantly

⚡ Data structure used:

👉 Hash Table (like Map in programming)

🧠 3. Key Characteristics

🟢 1. Extremely fast lookup

Because it uses hash-based access:

O(1) average time complexity

🟡 2. Simple structure

No joins

No schema

No relations

🔵 3. Highly scalable

Can be distributed across many servers easily.

🔴 4. Limited querying

You cannot do complex queries like SQL.

⚙️ 4. Real-world Key-Value Database

Used by:

  • Redis
  • Amazon DynamoDB
  • Amazon internal caching systems

💻 5. Where Key-Value Stores Are Used

🧾 1. Caching system

user:1 → cached profile

🔐 2. Session storage

session_id → user data

🛒 3. Shopping cart

cart:user123 → items

📊 4. Real-time analytics

page_views:home → 12345

⚙️ 6. Internal Architecture

🧠 Main components:

  • Hash function
  • Memory store / disk store
  • Replication layer
  • Sharding system

🔁 Flow:

Key → Hash Function → Node → Value Retrieved
project
{
  "user:1": { "name": "Ali", "age": 22 },
  "user:2": { "name": "Bob", "age": 25 }
}

server.js

const express = require("express");
const fs = require("fs");

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

function loadDB() {
  return JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("./data.json"));
}

function saveDB(db) {
  fs.writeFileSync("./data.json", JSON.stringify(db, null, 2));
}

// GET VALUE BY KEY
app.get("/get/:key", (req, res) => {
  const db = loadDB();
  const key = req.params.key;

  if (!db[key]) {
    return res.status(404).json({ message: "Key not found" });
  }

  res.json(db[key]);
});

// SET VALUE
app.post("/set", (req, res) => {
  const { key, value } = req.body;

  const db = loadDB();
  db[key] = value;

  saveDB(db);

  res.json({ message: "Saved successfully" });
});

// DELETE KEY
app.delete("/delete/:key", (req, res) => {
  const db = loadDB();
  const key = req.params.key;

  delete db[key];

  saveDB(db);

  res.json({ message: "Deleted" });
});

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Key-Value DB running on 3000");
});

req:

POST /set
{
  "key": "user:3",
  "value": { "name": "John", "age": 30 }
}
PRO_VS_CONS

🧠 10. Advantages

  • Extremely fast
  • Simple design
  • Scales horizontally
  • Perfect for caching

❌ 11. Limitations

  • No complex queries
  • No joins
  • No filtering on values
  • Limited analytics support
🔥 12. Internal Concepts (Advanced)

🟢 Hashing

Key is converted to hash → stored in memory.

🟡 Consistent Hashing

Used for distributed systems to balance load.

🔵 Replication

Data copied across multiple nodes for reliability.

🔴 Eviction policies

When memory is full:

  • LRU (Least Recently Used)
  • LFU (Least Frequently Used)

🧠 13. When to use Key-Value DB

✔ Best for:

  • caching
  • sessions
  • leaderboards
  • counters
  • real-time data

❌ Not good for:

  • joins
  • complex queries
  • relational data
50+ Interview Q&A (3+ lines each)

🟢 Basics (1–15)

1. What is a key-value database?

A key-value database stores data as pairs of keys and values.

Each key is unique and maps directly to a value.

It is one of the simplest types of NoSQL databases.

2. What is a key?

A key is a unique identifier used to retrieve a value.

It acts like an address for stored data.

No two values can share the same key.

3. What is a value?

A value is the actual data stored in the database.

It can be string, JSON, or even binary data.

It is retrieved using its corresponding key.

4. Why use key-value stores?

They are extremely fast and simple to use.

They provide constant-time lookup for data.

They are ideal for caching and session storage.

5. What is Redis?

Redis is an in-memory key-value database.

It is used for caching and real-time systems.

It supports advanced data structures like lists and sets.

6. What is hashing in key-value stores?

Hashing converts a key into a fixed location in memory.

It allows fast retrieval of values.

It is the core of key-value performance.

7. What is a hash table?

A hash table is a data structure used internally in key-value stores.

It maps keys to memory locations using a hash function.

It provides O(1) average lookup time.

8. What is in-memory database?

It stores data in RAM instead of disk.

This makes it extremely fast.

Redis is a popular example.

9. What is persistence?

Persistence means storing data permanently on disk.

Even if system restarts, data is not lost.

Some key-value stores support optional persistence.

10. What is caching?

Caching stores frequently used data in fast storage.

It reduces database load and improves performance.

Key-value stores are commonly used for caching.

11. What is a session store?

It stores user session data temporarily.

Each session is identified by a key.

It is commonly used in web applications.

12. What is TTL?

TTL (Time To Live) defines how long a key exists.

After expiration, the key is automatically removed.

It is useful for temporary data.

13. What is eviction policy?

It defines which data is removed when memory is full.

Common policies include LRU and LFU.

It prevents memory overflow.

14. What is O(1) lookup?

It means constant time access regardless of data size.

Key-value stores achieve this using hashing.

It makes them extremely fast.

15. What is distributed key-value store?

It is a key-value system running across multiple servers.

It improves scalability and fault tolerance.

DynamoDB is an example.

🟡 Intermediate (16–35)

16. Why is Redis fast?

Redis stores everything in memory instead of disk.

It uses optimized data structures.

It avoids expensive disk I/O.

17. What is consistent hashing?

It is a technique to distribute keys across servers.

It minimizes rebalancing when nodes are added.

It is used in distributed systems.

18. What is replication?

Replication copies data across multiple nodes.

It improves reliability and availability.

If one node fails, others still serve data.

19. What is sharding?

Sharding splits data across multiple machines.

Each shard stores part of the dataset.

It improves scalability.

20. What is hot key problem?

A single key receives too many requests.

It overloads one server.

It requires load balancing strategies.

21. What is read-heavy system?

A system where reads are more than writes.

Key-value stores are ideal for this.

Caching improves performance.

22. What is write-heavy system?

A system with frequent updates.

Key-value stores can handle it with proper design.

But persistence may become bottleneck.

23. What is data eviction?

Removing old or unused data from memory.

It frees space for new data.

It is essential in in-memory databases.

24. What is LRU?

Least Recently Used policy removes old unused data.

It keeps frequently used data in memory.

It is commonly used in caching systems.

25. What is LFU?

Least Frequently Used removes rarely accessed data.

It tracks usage frequency.

It is more complex than LRU.

26. What is eventual consistency?

Data becomes consistent over time across nodes.

It is common in distributed key-value systems.

It improves availability.

27. What is partition tolerance?

System continues working even if network splits occur.

It is part of CAP theorem.

Key-value stores often prioritize it.

28. What is CAP theorem?

It defines tradeoff between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.

Key-value stores often choose availability.

It guides system design.

29. What is cache miss?

When requested data is not in cache.

It requires fetching from slower storage.

It reduces performance temporarily.

30. What is cache hit?

When data is found in cache.

It provides fast response.

It improves system efficiency.

31. What is write-through cache?

Data is written to cache and database simultaneously.

It ensures consistency.

But it may be slower.

32. What is write-back cache?

Data is written to cache first and database later.

It is faster but riskier.

It improves performance.

33. What is key collision?

Two keys map to same hash location.

It can reduce performance.

Handled using chaining or probing.

34. What is cluster mode?

Database runs across multiple nodes.

It improves scalability.

Used in Redis clusters.

35. What is memory fragmentation?

Unused memory spaces inside RAM.

It reduces efficiency.

Managed by memory allocators.

🔴 Advanced (36–55)

36. Why key-value DB is used in caching?

Because it provides extremely fast O(1) lookup.

It reduces load on primary database.

It improves system performance.

37. What is distributed caching?

Caching across multiple servers.

It improves availability and scalability.

Redis clusters are used.

38. What is cache invalidation?

Removing outdated data from cache.

It ensures correctness.

It is one of the hardest problems.

39. What is cache stampede?

Multiple requests try to fetch missing cache at same time.

It causes overload on database.

Solutions include locking and throttling.

40. What is lazy loading cache?

Data is loaded into cache only when requested.

It improves efficiency.

But first request is slow.

41. What is preloading cache?

Data is loaded into cache before request.

It improves performance.

Used in predictive systems.

42. What is distributed lock?

A lock across multiple systems.

It ensures only one process modifies data.

Redis can implement it.

43. What is atomic operation?

An operation that completes fully or not at all.

Redis supports atomic commands.

It prevents race conditions.

44. What is throughput?

Number of operations processed per second.

Key-value stores have high throughput.

It is critical for performance systems.

45. What is latency?

Time taken to complete a request.

Key-value stores have low latency.

Because of in-memory design.

46. What is fan-out problem?

One request triggers many sub-requests.

It can overload system.

Caching reduces impact.

47. What is data durability?

Ensuring data is not lost permanently.

Some key-value stores support persistence.

Others prioritize speed.

48. What is hybrid storage?

Combination of memory and disk storage.

Balances speed and persistence.

Used in modern databases.

49. What is real-world use case?

Used in caching, sessions, leaderboards, and counters.

It is widely used in web systems.

It supports high-scale applications.

50. What is final concept?

Key-value stores are the fastest and simplest NoSQL databases.

They map keys directly to values using hashing.

They are essential for modern scalable systems.

Document Databases
docs

A document database is a type of NoSQL database that stores data in flexible, JSON-like documents instead of rows and columns.

👉 Each record = a document (JSON/BSON)

👉 Each document can have a different structure

🧠 Simple idea:

Instead of tables → you store JSON objects.

📦 Example Document

{
  "id":1,
  "name":"Ali",
  "age":22,
  "skills": ["node","react"],
  "address": {
    "city":"Tashkent",
    "zip":100000
  }
}

⚙️ 2. How Document Databases Work

7

🔁 Structure:

  • Database → contains collections
  • Collections → contain documents
  • Documents → JSON objects

Example:

Database: SchoolDB
  └── Collection: Students
        └── Document: { student data }

🧠 3. Key Characteristics

🟢 Schema-less

No fixed structure required.

{ "name":"Ali" }
{ "name":"Bob", "age":20 }

👉 Both are valid in same collection.

🟡 Nested data support

{
  "user": {
    "name":"Ali",
    "contact": {
      "email":"a@mail.com"
    }
  }
}

🔵 Horizontal scaling

Data can be distributed across multiple servers easily.

⚔️ 4. Document DB vs SQL

FeatureSQLDocument DB
StructureFixed tablesFlexible JSON
SchemaStrictDynamic
JoinsStrongWeak
ScalingVerticalHorizontal
SpeedMediumHigh (reads)

🧩 5. Why Document Databases Exist

Relational databases struggle when:

  • Data is unstructured
  • Schema changes frequently
  • High scalability needed
  • Nested objects exist

Used in:

  • Social media feeds
  • Product catalogs
  • User profiles
  • Event logs

🧠 6. How Queries Work

Example query:

db.users.find({ age:22 })

More advanced:

db.users.find({
"address.city":"Tashkent"
})

Aggregation:

db.users.aggregate([
  { $match: { age: { $gt:18 } } },
  { $group: { _id:"$city", count: { $sum:1 } } }
])
Sample DBs
  • MongoDB → most popular document DB
  • Firebase → Firestore
  • Amazon → DynamoDB (document-like)

server.js

const express = require("express");
const fs = require("fs");

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

function getUsers() {
  return JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("./users.json"));
}

// GET ALL USERS
app.get("/users", (req, res) => {
  res.json(getUsers());
});

// FILTER USERS (LIKE DOCUMENT QUERY)
app.get("/users/search", (req, res) => {
  const { city } = req.query;

  const users = getUsers().filter(u => u.city === city);

  res.json(users);
});

// FIND BY FIELD (nested-like query simulation)
app.get("/users/age/:age", (req, res) => {
  const age = parseInt(req.params.age);

  const users = getUsers().filter(u => u.age === age);

  res.json(users);
});

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Document DB server running");
});

50+ Interview Q&A (3+ lines each)

🟢 Basics (1–15)
1. What is a document database?
A document database stores data in JSON-like documents instead of rows and columns.

Each document can have a different structure and fields.

It is part of NoSQL databases designed for flexibility and scalability.
2. What is a document?
A document is a JSON or BSON object that represents a single record.

It can contain nested structures and arrays.

Each document is self-contained and independent.
3. What is a collection?
A collection is a group of documents in a document database.

It is similar to a table in SQL databases.

However, it does not enforce a fixed schema.
4. What is schema-less database?
A schema-less database does not require predefined structure.

Each document can have different fields and formats.

This allows flexibility in storing evolving data.
5. Why use document databases?
They are used because they handle unstructured and semi-structured data well.

They allow fast development without strict schema design.

They also scale easily in distributed systems.
6. What is BSON?
BSON is Binary JSON used internally in some document databases.

It is more efficient for storage and processing than plain JSON.

It supports additional data types like dates and binary data.
7. What is embedding in document DB?
Embedding means storing related data inside a document.

For example, address inside user document.

It reduces the need for joins.
8. What is referencing?
Referencing means storing relationships using IDs between documents.

It is similar to foreign keys in SQL.

It is used when data is large or shared.
9. What is MongoDB?
MongoDB is a popular document-oriented NoSQL database.

It stores data in BSON documents.

It is widely used in modern web applications.
10. What is a query in document DB?
A query is used to search or filter documents.

It works on fields inside JSON objects.

It is flexible and supports nested queries.
11. What is aggregation?
Aggregation is a way to process and transform data in document DB.

It performs operations like grouping, filtering, and sorting.

It is similar to SQL GROUP BY.
12. What is horizontal scaling?
Horizontal scaling means adding more machines instead of upgrading one.

Document databases are designed for this.

It improves performance and availability.
13. What is vertical scaling?
Vertical scaling means increasing resources of a single machine.

SQL databases typically use this model.

It has physical hardware limits.
14. What is a NoSQL database?
NoSQL databases are non-relational databases.

They include document, key-value, graph, and column stores.

They are designed for scalability and flexibility.
15. What is schema evolution?
Schema evolution means changing data structure over time.

Document databases support this easily.

No migration is required.
🟡 Intermediate (16–35)
16. Why document DB is faster?
Because data is stored as a single object.

No joins are needed in most cases.

This reduces query complexity.
17. What is nested document?
A document inside another document.

It represents hierarchical data structure.

It avoids multiple tables.
18. What is indexing?
Indexing improves query performance.

It creates fast lookup structures for fields.

It is similar to SQL indexes.
19. What is replica set?
A replica set is a group of database copies.

It provides high availability and fault tolerance.

Used in MongoDB systems.
20. What is sharding?
Sharding splits data across multiple servers.

It improves scalability for large datasets.

Each shard holds part of the data.
21. What is CAP theorem?
It defines tradeoff between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.

Document databases often choose availability and partition tolerance.

Consistency is eventually achieved.
22. What is eventual consistency?
Data becomes consistent over time across nodes.

Immediate consistency is not guaranteed.

It is common in distributed systems.
23. What is query flexibility?
It means ability to query dynamic fields.

No fixed schema is required.

Queries can target nested fields.
24. What is denormalization?
Storing duplicated data to improve performance.

It avoids joins.

Common in document databases.
25. What is ACID vs BASE?
ACID ensures strict consistency.

BASE allows eventual consistency for scalability.

Document DB often follows BASE.
26. What is read scalability?
Ability to handle many read operations efficiently.

Document DBs are optimized for this.

Replication improves read performance.
27. What is write scalability?
Ability to handle many write operations.

Sharding helps distribute writes.

Important for large systems.
28. What is data locality?
Related data is stored together.

It improves performance.

Common in document databases.
29. What is schema flexibility?
Ability to change structure without migrations.

Each document can differ.

It speeds up development.
30. What is query planner?
It decides the best way to execute queries.

It uses indexes and statistics.

It improves performance.
31. What is TTL index?
It automatically deletes documents after time expires.

Used for session storage.

Helps in temporary data management.
32. What is read preference?
It defines which replica node handles read requests.

It improves load distribution.

Common in replica sets.
33. What is write concern?
It defines how many nodes must confirm write.

Higher write concern means more safety.

It affects performance.
34. What is data modeling?
Designing how data is stored in documents.

It depends on access patterns.

Important for performance.
35. What is anti-pattern in document DB?
Poor design that hurts performance.

Example: overusing references or joins.

It leads to slow queries.
🔴 Advanced (36–55)
36. Why document DB avoids joins?
Joins are expensive in distributed systems.

Document DB prefers embedding instead.

It improves read performance.
37. What is embedding vs referencing?
Embedding stores data inside document.

Referencing links separate documents.

Choice depends on use case.
38. What is distributed document storage?
Data is stored across multiple nodes.

It improves scalability.

Requires synchronization mechanisms.
39. What is data duplication?
Same data stored in multiple places.

It improves read speed but increases storage.

Common in document DB.
40. What is consistency model?
Defines how data is synchronized across nodes.

Document DB often uses eventual consistency.

It affects reliability.
41. What is read/write split?
Reads and writes are handled separately.

Reads often go to replicas.

Writes go to primary node.
42. What is hot shard?
A shard receiving too much traffic.

It causes performance imbalance.

Needs rebalancing.
43. What is data partitioning?
Splitting dataset into smaller parts.

It improves scalability.

Used in sharding.
44. What is schema design strategy?
Designing documents based on queries.

Not normalization like SQL.

Focus is on performance.
45. What is indexing cost?
Indexes improve reads but slow writes.

They consume storage space.

Tradeoff must be balanced.
46. What is consistency lag?
Delay between replicas updating data.

It causes temporary inconsistency.

Common in distributed DBs.
47. What is document versioning?
Storing multiple versions of same document.

Used for audit and history tracking.

Helps in recovery.
48. What is real-world use case?
Used in social media, catalogs, and logs.

Handles flexible and nested data.

Scales well for large systems.
49. What is tradeoff in document DB?
Flexibility vs strict consistency.

Performance vs normalization.

Scaling vs joins.
50. What is final concept?
Document databases store flexible JSON data at scale.

They avoid joins and support horizontal scaling.

They are ideal for modern web applications.
🚀 FINAL TAKEAWAY
👉 Document DB = flexible + scalable + JSON-based storage

👉 Best for modern apps with evolving data structures

Circuit break,
