RABBITMQ

🐰 RabbitMQ Deep Dive — Notion Ready (Interview Complete Guide)

🧠 What is RabbitMQ?

👉 RabbitMQ is a message broker that allows services to communicate asynchronously using queues.

Producer → Exchange → Queue → Consumer

📐 Architecture

6

🔤 Core Components

1️⃣ Producer

👉 Sends message

Service A → sends message

2️⃣ Exchange

👉 Router of messages

  • Receives message from producer
  • Decides which queue to send to

3️⃣ Queue

👉 Stores messages until consumed

4️⃣ Consumer

👉 Receives and processes messages

5️⃣ Binding

👉 Rule connecting exchange → queue

🔥 Exchange Types (VERY IMPORTANT)

1. Direct Exchange

Exact match routing
routing key = "order.created"

👉 Goes only to matching queue

2. Fanout Exchange

Broadcast

👉 Sends message to ALL queues

3. Topic Exchange

Pattern-based routing
order.*
order.created

👉 Wildcards:

  • → one word
  • # → many words

4. Headers Exchange

👉 Routing based on headers (rare)

🧠 Message Flow

Producer → Exchange → Queue → Consumer

Steps:

  1. Producer sends message
  1. Exchange receives
  1. Exchange routes based on rules
  1. Queue stores
  1. Consumer pulls

⚙️ Important Features

✅ Acknowledgment (ACK)

👉 Consumer confirms message processed

ACK → remove message
NACK → requeue or drop

❌ What if no ACK?

👉 Message stays → can be redelivered

🔁 Message Retry

  • NACK + requeue
  • Dead Letter Exchange (DLX)

💀 Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)

👉 Failed messages go here

Use when:

  • Message fails multiple times
  • TTL expired

⚡ Message Durability

Durable Queue

Survives broker restart

Persistent Message

Stored on disk

👉 BOTH required for full durability

🧠 Prefetch (IMPORTANT)

limit how many messages a consumer can handle

Example:

prefetch = 1

👉 Consumer gets 1 message at a time

⚔️ Competing Consumers

Multiple consumers → same queue

👉 Load balancing

📦 Work Queue Pattern

Queue → multiple workers

👉 Used for:

  • background jobs
  • email sending
  • processing tasks

📢 Pub/Sub Pattern

Using fanout exchange

1 message → many consumers

🧠 Ordering

👉 RabbitMQ:

Order is guaranteed per queue
NOT across multiple consumers

⚠️ Message Loss Cases

  • No persistence
  • No ACK
  • Broker crash

🔐 At-Least-Once Delivery

RabbitMQ guarantees:

At least once

👉 May cause duplicates → must handle idempotency

🧠 Idempotency (IMPORTANT)

👉 Same message processed multiple times → no issue

Example:

Use unique ID
Check if already processed

⚡ Scaling RabbitMQ

Vertical Scaling

  • More CPU/RAM

Horizontal Scaling

  • Clustering
  • Federation
  • Sharding queues

🧠 Clustering vs Federation

Clustering

👉 Nodes share state

Federation

👉 Loose connection between brokers

⚡ High Availability

  • Mirrored queues
  • Quorum queues (modern approach)

🧠 Quorum Queue

👉 Based on Raft consensus

Better than classic mirrored queues

⚠️ Backpressure

👉 When consumers are slow:

  • Queue grows
  • Memory pressure

Solutions:

  • Prefetch
  • Rate limiting
  • More consumers

🔄 RabbitMQ vs Kafka

FeatureRabbitMQKafka
ModelQueueLog
Orderingper queuepartition
Use casetask queueevent streaming
Replay❌ limited✅ yes

🎯 Most Asked Interview Questions

❓ What is RabbitMQ?

👉 Message broker for async communication

❓ What is exchange?

👉 Router of messages

❓ Types of exchange?

👉 direct, fanout, topic, headers

❓ What is ACK?

👉 Confirmation from consumer

❓ What is DLQ?

👉 Failed messages queue

❓ What is prefetch?

👉 Limits unprocessed messages per consumer

❓ What is durability?

👉 Survive restart (queue + message)

❓ What is at-least-once?

👉 Message may be delivered more than once

❓ How to avoid duplicates?

👉 Idempotency

❓ How to scale?

👉 Consumers, clustering, quorum queues

🧾 Final Summary

  • RabbitMQ = async communication
  • Exchange = routing
  • Queue = storage
  • Consumer = processing
  • Supports:
    • durability
    • retry
    • DLQ
    • scaling

🧠 Perfect Interview Answer

👉 RabbitMQ is a message broker that enables asynchronous communication between services using exchanges, queues, and routing keys. It supports multiple exchange types, acknowledgments, retries, and high availability mechanisms like quorum queues, making it suitable for task queues and event-driven architectures.

RabbitMQ and Kafka
Overal

🧠 0. Big Picture (start here)

Both Kafka and RabbitMQ are message brokers

👉 They let services communicate asynchronously

Service A → Broker → Service B

⚡ Why they exist

Without them:

Service A → directly calls Service B ❌

Problems:

  • tight coupling
  • failures cascade
  • slow systems

🔥 With broker

Producer → Broker → Consumer

✔ decoupled

✔ scalable

✔ fault-tolerant

Rabbit MQ
Overal

🟣 RabbitMQ (Queue-based)

🧠 Core idea

Messages go to queues and are consumed then removed

🔧 Flow

Producer → Exchange → Queue → Consumer

🧩 Components

1. Producer

Sends message

2. Exchange

Routes messages

Types:

  • direct
  • fanout
  • topic

3. Queue

Stores messages

4. Consumer

Reads messages

🔥 Important behavior

Message → consumed → deleted

📦 Use cases

  • task queues
  • background jobs
  • request-response
🧠 What is an Exchange (RabbitMQ)
🧠 Types of Exchange (VERY IMPORTANT)

1. Direct

Exact match routing key
key: order → queue: order_queue

2. Fanout

Send to ALL queues
broadcast

3. Topic

Pattern matching
order.* → order_queue

4. Headers (rare)

Based on message headers

🔥 Simple analogy

Exchange = router
Queue = destination

🧠 Final answer (interview)

“An exchange in RabbitMQ is responsible for routing messages from producers to one or more queues based on routing rules.”
Kafka
Overal

🟢 Kafka (Log-based / streaming)

🧠 Core idea

Messages are stored in logs (topics) and NOT deleted after consumption

🔧 Flow

Producer → Topic (partitioned log) → Consumer

🧩 Components

1. Topic

Like category

2. Partition

Splits data

Topic → partition1, partition2

3. Offset

Position of message

4. Consumer Group

Multiple consumers sharing load

🔥 Important behavior

Message → stays in Kafka
Consumer tracks offset

📦 Use cases

  • event streaming
  • analytics
  • logging
  • big data pipelines
VS

⚔️ Kafka vs RabbitMQ (CORE DIFFERENCE)

FeatureRabbitMQKafka
ModelQueueLog
Messageremoved after consumestays
Speedmoderatevery high
Replaynoyes
Scalinglimitedmassive
Use casetasksstreaming
🧠 Simple analogy

🧠 Simple analogy

RabbitMQ

Mailbox 📬
Take letter → gone

Kafka

Log file 📜
Read → still exists

🔥 Interview questions you WILL get

1. Difference?

RabbitMQ deletes messages after consumption, Kafka keeps them and uses offsets for tracking.

2. When to use RabbitMQ?

For task queues and background jobs where messages should be processed once.

3. When to use Kafka?

For high-throughput streaming and event-driven architectures where replay is needed.

4. What is partition?

Kafka splits topic into partitions to enable parallel processing and scalability.

5. What is consumer group?

Group of consumers sharing load, each partition goes to one consumer.

6. What is offset?

Position of message in partition log.

7. What is exchange (RabbitMQ)?

Component that routes messages to queues based on rules.

8. Delivery guarantee?

  • RabbitMQ → at least once
  • Kafka → at least once / exactly once (config)

🔥 SUPER IMPORTANT (say this in interview)

“RabbitMQ is better for task-based messaging, while Kafka is designed for high-throughput event streaming with durable logs.”

⚡ Real-world mapping

RabbitMQ

Send email queue
Order processing
Background jobs

Kafka

User activity tracking
Logs pipeline
Real-time analytics

🧠 10-sec summary

RabbitMQ → queue → delete message
Kafka → log → keep message

🚀 If you have 5 more minutes

Memorize this:

RabbitMQ:
- exchange
- queue
- routing
- message removed

Kafka:
- topic
- partition
- offset
- message retained
Rabbit MQ vs Kafka Recap vs backpressure
Rabbit MQ

🔥 1. RabbitMQ Internal Mental Model

At a high level you see:

Producer → Exchange → Queue → Consumer

But internally RabbitMQ is doing MUCH more:

Connection → Channel → Exchange → Binding → Queue → Message Store → Consumer → ACK

We break each piece.

🔌 2. Connection vs Channel (VERY IMPORTANT)

Connection

  • TCP connection between your app and RabbitMQ
  • Expensive to create
One app → few connections

Channel

  • Lightweight virtual connection inside TCP connection
One connection → many channels

👉 Why?

Opening TCP is expensive → channels are cheap

So production rule:

Use 1 connection, multiple channels

🧠 3. What Happens When Producer Sends Message

Step-by-step:

Step 1 — Producer publishes

channel.publish(exchange, routing_key, message)

Step 2 — Exchange receives message

Exchange does NOT store messages.

It only:

1. Looks at routing key
2. Checks bindings
3. Decides destination queues

Step 3 — Routing via Bindings

Binding = rule:

Exchange → Queue (with condition)

Example:

Exchange: order_exchange
Queue: email_queue
Binding key: order.created

So:

routing_key = "order.created"
→ goes to email_queue

Step 4 — Message enters Queue

Now queue decides:

Store in RAM OR disk

💾 4. Queue Internals (CRITICAL)

RabbitMQ queues are NOT just simple arrays.

They are complex structures with:

1. In-memory buffer

Fast access

2. Disk storage

Durability

⚡ Behavior

If:

Queue small → mostly RAM
Queue large → spill to disk

Lazy Queue Mode

Store directly on disk

Used when:

Millions of messages expected

🔄 5. Message Lifecycle

Let’s follow ONE message:

Step 1

Producer sends message

Step 2

Exchange routes message

Step 3

Queue stores message

Step 4

RabbitMQ PUSHES message to consumer

Important:

RabbitMQ is PUSH-based (not pull like Kafka)

Step 5

Message becomes:

"Unacknowledged"

Step 6 — Consumer processes

Example:

Send email

Step 7 — ACK

Consumer → ACK → RabbitMQ

Then:

Message removed from queue

⚠️ 6. What If Consumer Crashes?

This is where RabbitMQ shines.

Scenario:

Message delivered
Consumer crashes before ACK

RabbitMQ:

Requeues message
Sends to another consumer

👉 That is at-least-once delivery

🔥 7. Prefetch (Backpressure Control)

Without control:

RabbitMQ pushes 1000 messages → one consumer

Consumer dies.

With prefetch:

channel.prefetch(1)

Means:

1 message at a time

Flow:

Receive → process → ACK → next message

Why this matters

Prevents overload
Ensures fair distribution

🔁 8. Retry + DLQ (REAL PRODUCTION FLOW)

This is where most devs fail interviews.

Basic Problem

Message fails → retry immediately → fails → infinite loop

Bad.

Real Solution (Pattern)

main.queue
↓ fail
retry.queue (TTL = 10s)
↓ expires
main.queue again
↓ fails many times
dlq.queue

Internally

Uses:

  • TTL
  • DLX (Dead Letter Exchange)

Flow

main.queue
↓ failure
dead-letter-exchange
↓
retry.queue (wait)
↓ TTL expired
back to main.queue
↓ still fails
→ dlq.queue

💣 9. Ordering Guarantees

RabbitMQ guarantees:

Order inside ONE queue

BUT:

Multiple consumers → order may break

Example:

Message 1 → Consumer A
Message 2 → Consumer B

Execution order may differ.

🔒 10. Durability (Real Mechanics)

To make message safe:

Step 1 — Durable Queue

Queue metadata saved

Step 2 — Persistent Message

Message written to disk

Step 3 — fsync

Ensure OS writes to disk

Tradeoff:

Durability ↑ → Performance ↓

⚡ 11. Throughput Limitations

RabbitMQ slower than Kafka because:

- Complex routing (exchange logic)
- Per-message ACK tracking
- Queue locking

🔥 12. Clustering (Short but deep)

RabbitMQ cluster:

Multiple nodes

BUT queues live on one node (by default).

Problem:

Node dies → queue lost

Solution:

Mirrored queues / quorum queues

Quorum Queues (Modern)

Based on Raft algorithm.

Leader + followers

Guarantee:

Majority must agree before message is accepted

🧠 FINAL INTERNAL MODEL

Producer
→ Channel
→ Exchange (routing)
→ Binding (rules)
→ Queue (RAM + disk)
→ Consumer (push)
→ ACK/NACK
→ Retry / DLQ

⚡ Interview Killer Summary

RabbitMQ =
Push-based system
Routing via exchange
Queue stores messages
ACK ensures reliability
Prefetch controls load
DLQ handles failure
Kafka

🔥 1. Kafka Core Mental Model

Forget queue thinking.

Kafka is:

Distributed append-only log

Meaning:

Messages are NOT removed after consumption
They are appended like a file

Visual

Offset:   0        1        2        3
        [msg1]  [msg2]  [msg3]  [msg4]

Kafka only does:

Append → Read → Never modify

🔥 2. Full Internal Architecture

Producer → Broker → Topic → Partition → Log → Consumer Group → Offset

Let’s break each.

🔌 3. Broker (Kafka Server)

A broker is a Kafka server.

Cluster:

Broker1, Broker2, Broker3

Kafka is always:

Distributed system

🧠 4. Topic

Topic = logical stream of data.

Example:

orders
payments
logs

Important:

Topic is NOT where data is stored physically

⚡ 5. Partition (MOST IMPORTANT)

Topic is split into partitions.

Example:

Topic: orders

Partition 0 → [msg1, msg4, msg7]
Partition 1 → [msg2, msg5, msg8]
Partition 2 → [msg3, msg6, msg9]

Why partitions exist

Parallelism + scalability

Key rule

Ordering is guaranteed ONLY inside a partition

🔑 6. Partition Selection (CRITICAL)

When producer sends message:

partition = hash(key) % number_of_partitions

Example

key = userId = 42
hash(42) % 3 = partition 1

So:

Same key → always same partition
→ order preserved for that key

💾 7. Log Storage (REAL INTERNALS)

Each partition is a log file on disk.

Inside:

segment files:
000000000.log
000001000.log
000002000.log

Behavior

Append-only writes (VERY FAST)
Sequential disk I/O (not random)

That’s why Kafka is fast.

📌 8. Offset (CRITICAL)

Offset = position in log.

Example:

msg1 → offset 0
msg2 → offset 1
msg3 → offset 2

Important difference vs RabbitMQ

RabbitMQ:

Broker tracks message consumption

Kafka:

Consumer tracks offset

🔄 9. Consumer Groups

Consumers work in groups.

Example:

Topic: orders (3 partitions)

Consumer Group A:
Consumer1 → Partition 0
Consumer2 → Partition 1
Consumer3 → Partition 2

Rule

1 partition → 1 consumer (per group)

Why?

Parallel processing + load balancing

⚠️ 10. Rebalancing (INTERVIEW FAVORITE)

When:

Consumer joins/leaves group

Kafka:

Reassigns partitions

Example:

Consumer2 crashes
→ its partition assigned to Consumer1

Problem

Temporary pause in processing

🔁 11. Message Lifecycle

Step 1 — Producer sends

Producer → broker

Step 2 — Broker appends

Message added to partition log

Step 3 — Replication

Leader → Followers

Step 4 — Consumer reads

Reads from offset

Step 5 — Offset commit

Consumer stores last read offset

🔥 12. Replication (VERY IMPORTANT)

Each partition has replicas.

Example:

Partition 0:
Leader → Broker1
Follower → Broker2, Broker3

Flow

Producer → Leader
Leader → Followers

Acknowledgment modes

1. acks=0

No confirmation (fast but unsafe)

2. acks=1

Leader confirms only

3. acks=all (important)

All replicas must confirm

Safe but slower.

⚡ 13. Why Kafka Is So Fast

1. Sequential Writes

Append-only → no random disk access

2. Zero Copy (OS optimization)

Kafka uses:

sendfile()

Data goes:

Disk → Network (without copying to user space)

3. Batching

Messages sent in batches

4. No per-message ACK tracking

Unlike RabbitMQ:

Kafka doesn’t track each message individually

🔥 14. Retention (BIG DIFFERENCE)

Kafka does NOT delete messages after consumption.

Instead:

Keep messages for:
- time (e.g., 7 days)
- size (e.g., 1GB)

Example

Retention = 7 days

Even if consumed:

Message still exists

🔁 15. Replay (Killer Feature)

Consumer can:

Reset offset → read old messages again

Example

Bug in analytics service
→ reset offset
→ reprocess data

RabbitMQ cannot do this.

⚠️ 16. Backpressure

Kafka handles differently.

RabbitMQ:

Push → must limit (prefetch)

Kafka:

Pull → consumer controls speed

So:

Slow consumer ≠ broker overload

🔒 17. Ordering

Kafka guarantees:

Order inside partition only

Problem

Multiple partitions:

Global ordering is NOT guaranteed

⚡ 18. Exactly Once (Reality)

Kafka supports:

Idempotent producer + transactions

BUT:

"Exactly once" = very complex

In reality:

Most systems use at-least-once

🧠 FINAL INTERNAL MODEL

Producer
→ Partition selection (hash key)
→ Broker leader
→ Append to log
→ Replicate to followers
→ Consumer group reads
→ Offset tracked by consumer

⚔️ FINAL COMPARISON (REAL THINKING)

ConceptKafkaRabbitMQ
ModelLogQueue
DeliveryPullPush
Replay✅❌
RoutingSimpleComplex (exchange)
ThroughputVery highMedium
Use caseEvent streamingTask processing

🔥 Interview Killer Line

RabbitMQ = Task distribution system
Kafka     = Distributed event storage system
Backpressure

1. What is Backpressure?

Backpressure means:

Producer is sending faster than consumer can process.

Example:

Producer sends 10,000 messages/sec
Consumer processes 1,000 messages/sec

Problem:

9,000 messages/sec become backlog

So backpressure asks:

How does the system slow down, buffer, or protect itself?

2. Why Backpressure Happens

Usually because:

Consumer is slow
Database is slow
External API is slow
Message processing is heavy
Traffic spike happens

Example:

Email service can send only 100 emails/sec
Order service produces 1000 email jobs/sec

Without backpressure:

Queue grows
RAM grows
Disk grows
Latency grows
System crashes

3. RabbitMQ Backpressure

RabbitMQ is push-based.

RabbitMQ → pushes messages → consumer

So if RabbitMQ pushes too many messages, consumer can overload.

That is why RabbitMQ uses:

prefetch

Prefetch

channel.prefetch(1)

Means:

Send only 1 unacked message to this consumer at a time.

Flow:

Consumer receives message
Processes it
ACKs it
RabbitMQ sends next one

So RabbitMQ backpressure is mainly:

Limit unacknowledged messages

Example

Without prefetch:

Consumer receives 1000 messages
Consumer can process only 10
Memory overload

With prefetch 10:

Consumer receives max 10 messages
After ACK, gets more

4. Kafka Backpressure

Kafka is pull-based.

Consumer → pulls messages → Kafka

So consumer controls how fast it reads.

If consumer is slow:

It simply polls less often

Kafka does not force messages into consumer memory.

Backpressure in Kafka is mainly:

Consumer lag

Consumer Lag

Consumer lag means:

Producer writes faster than consumer reads

Example:

Latest offset = 10,000
Consumer offset = 6,000
Lag = 4,000 messages

Kafka does not crash immediately.

It stores the backlog in partitions.

5. Main Difference

RabbitMQ backpressure = protect consumer from pushed messages
Kafka backpressure = monitor lag because consumer controls pulling

6. What Happens If Backpressure Is Ignored?

In RabbitMQ:

Queue grows
Memory alarm triggers
RabbitMQ blocks publishers
Consumers overload
Latency increases

In Kafka:

Consumer lag grows
Old messages may expire by retention
Processing becomes delayed

Important Kafka risk:

If lag is too high and retention is 7 days,
consumer may lose unread messages after 7 days.

7. How to Fix Backpressure

RabbitMQ

Use:

prefetch
more consumers
faster processing
DLQ
retry with delay
separate queues by priority

Kafka

Use:

more partitions
more consumers in same group
batch processing
increase processing speed
monitor consumer lag
adjust retention

8. Interview-Level Answer

Backpressure is when producers generate messages faster than consumers can process them.

In RabbitMQ, because it is push-based, we control it using prefetch, ACKs, queue limits, and sometimes publisher blocking.

In Kafka, because it is pull-based, the consumer controls read speed, so backpressure appears as consumer lag. We solve it by scaling consumers, increasing partitions, batching, optimizing processing, and monitoring lag.

RabbitMQ = push control
Kafka = lag control
Unit Testing

1. What is unit testing?

Unit testing means testing the smallest meaningful part of your application in isolation.

Usually a “unit” is:

function
classmethod
service method
utility helper
controller logic
React component behavior
NestJS service

Example:

functionadd(a,b) {
returna+b;
}

Unit test:

test("adds two numbers", () => {
expect(add(2,3)).toBe(5);
});

The goal is simple:

“Does this small piece of logic work correctly by itself?”

2. What things are tested in unit testing?

Functions

functioncalculateDiscount(price,percent) {
returnprice- (price*percent)/100;
}

Test:

expect(calculateDiscount(100,10)).toBe(90);

You test:

input → output
edge cases
invalid inputs
business rules

Services

Example in backend:

classUserService {
  constructor(userRepo) {
this.userRepo=userRepo;
  }

async getUserName(id) {
constuser=awaitthis.userRepo.findById(id);
returnuser.name;
  }
}

In unit testing, you do not use real database.

You mock it:

constfakeRepo= {
  findById:jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id:1, name:"Ali" })
};

Then test only service logic.

Validation logic

functionisValidEmail(email) {
returnemail.includes("@");
}

Test:

expect(isValidEmail("test@gmail.com")).toBe(true);
expect(isValidEmail("wrongemail")).toBe(false);

Error handling

functiondivide(a,b) {
if (b===0)thrownewError("Cannot divide by zero");
returna/b;
}

Test:

expect(() =>divide(10,0)).toThrow("Cannot divide by zero");

Edge cases

Example:

findMax([1,2,3])// 3
findMax([])// what should happen?
findMax([-5,-1])// -1

Unit tests should cover normal and dangerous cases.

3. What should NOT usually be tested in unit tests?

In unit tests, you usually do not test:

real database connection
real API requests
real file upload
real browser behavior
real payment gateway
real email sending
full user flow

Because those are integration or E2E tests.

Instead, in unit tests you use:

mock database
mock API
mock email service
mock repository
mock cache
mock queue

4. Unit testing vs Integration testing vs E2E testing

Unit testing

Tests one small part.

Does this function/service work?

Example:

calculateTotal(cart)

Integration testing

Tests multiple parts together.

Does service + database work together?

Example:

POST /users creates user in test database

E2E testing

Tests full real user flow.

Can user open website, login, click button, and see result?

Example:

Open browser → login → create order → check dashboard

5. Jest, Cypress, Playwright — difference

Jest

Best for:

unit testing
integration testing
backend testing
React component testing
utility function testing
NestJS service testing

Jest runs in Node.js environment.

Example:

test("should return total price", () => {
expect(calculateTotal([10,20])).toBe(30);
});

Use Jest when you want to test logic.

Cypress

Best for:

E2E testing
browser testing
UI flow testing
clicking buttons
forms
login flow
frontend behavior

Example:

cy.visit("/login");
cy.get("#email").type("test@gmail.com");
cy.get("#password").type("123456");
cy.get("button").click();
cy.contains("Dashboard");

Cypress is more browser/user-flow focused.

Playwright

Best for:

E2E testing
cross-browser testing
Chrome, Firefox, Safari
modern frontend testing
parallel browser tests

Example:

test("login works",async ({ page }) => {
awaitpage.goto("/login");
awaitpage.fill("#email","test@gmail.com");
awaitpage.fill("#password","123456");
awaitpage.click("button");
awaitexpect(page.getByText("Dashboard")).toBeVisible();
});

Playwright is similar to Cypress but stronger for multi-browser testing.

6. Simple comparison

ToolBest forRuns where?
JestUnit + integration testsNode.js
CypressE2E frontend testsBrowser
PlaywrightE2E cross-browser testsBrowser
VitestFast unit tests, Vite appsNode/browser-like
Testing LibraryReact component behaviorwith Jest/Vitest

7. What should you use?

For your stack:

Backend Node.js / NestJS / Express → Jest
Frontend React components → Jest/Vitest + React Testing Library
Full browser flows → Playwright or Cypress

My recommendation:

Unit tests: Jest
Integration tests: Jest + Supertest
E2E tests: Playwright

For interview, say:

“For unit testing I usually use Jest because it is great for testing functions, services, controllers, and mocking dependencies. For E2E testing I would use Cypress or Playwright because they run real browser flows. Playwright is especially good when we need cross-browser testing.”

8. What is mocking?

Mocking means replacing real dependency with fake one.

Example: instead of real database:

constmockUserRepo= {
  findById:jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({
    id:1,
    name:"Ali"
  })
};

Why?

Because unit test should test only your logic, not database.

9. Good unit test structure

Most unit tests follow:

Arrange → prepare data
Act → run function
Assert → check result

Example:

test("returns discounted price", () => {
// Arrange
constprice=100;
constdiscount=20;

// Act
constresult=calculateDiscount(price,discount);

// Assert
expect(result).toBe(80);
});

10. What makes a good unit test?

Good unit test should be:

fast
isolated
repeatable
easy to understand
focused on one behavior
not dependent on real database/API

Bad unit test:

depends on internet
depends on real DB data
tests too many things at once
hard to understand
breaks randomly

11. Interview-ready answer

You can say:

Unit testing is testing the smallest part of the application in isolation, like a function, class method, service, or component logic. In unit tests, we usually test business rules, return values, edge cases, validation, and error handling. We avoid real databases, real APIs, and real external services by using mocks. For JavaScript and Node.js, Jest is commonly used for unit testing. Cypress and Playwright are more suitable for E2E testing because they test real browser behavior and user flows. In a real project, I would use Jest for backend unit/integration tests, Supertest for API integration tests, and Playwright or Cypress for full user flow testing.
Integration Testing

Integration testing

Integration testing checks whether multiple parts of the app work together correctly.

Not just one function.

It tests things like:

controller + service
service + repository
API route + database
auth middleware + protected route
backend + external service mock

Main question:

“Do these modules work correctly together?”

Unit vs Integration

Unit test

Test one service method alone.
Database is mocked.

Integration test

Call real API endpoint.
Use real test database.
Check real response.

Example:

POST /users
↓
Controller receives request
↓
Service validates data
↓
Repository saves to test DB
↓
Response returns created user

That is integration testing.

What do we test?

In backend projects, integration tests usually test:

API endpoints
database operations
authentication
authorization
middleware
validation pipes
service + repository connection
error responses

Example cases:

POST /users creates user
GET /users returns users from DB
POST /login returns token
GET /profile fails without token
GET /profile works with token

Tools

For Node.js / Express / NestJS:

Jest
Supertest
Test database
Docker test DB
Prisma/TypeORM/Sequelize test config

For frontend + backend:

Playwright
Cypress

But for backend integration testing, the most common is:

Jest + Supertest

Example with Express

App:

importexpressfrom"express";

constapp=express();
app.use(express.json());

constusers= [];

app.post("/users", (req,res) => {
const { name }=req.body;

if (!name) {
returnres.status(400).json({ message:"Name is required" });
  }

constuser= { id:users.length+1, name };
users.push(user);

res.status(201).json(user);
});

exportdefaultapp;

Integration test:

importrequestfrom"supertest";
importappfrom"./app.js";

describe("POST /users", () => {
it("should create a user",async () => {
constresponse=awaitrequest(app)
.post("/users")
.send({ name:"Ali" });

expect(response.status).toBe(201);
expect(response.body).toEqual({
      id:1,
      name:"Ali"
    });
  });

it("should return 400 if name is missing",async () => {
constresponse=awaitrequest(app)
.post("/users")
.send({});

expect(response.status).toBe(400);
expect(response.body.message).toBe("Name is required");
  });
});

Here we are testing:

Express route
JSON body parser
Validation logic
Response status
Response body

So this is integration testing.

With real database

Real integration test usually uses a separate test database:

app_test_db

Before each test:

clean database
insert test data
run request
check response
check database

Example idea:

beforeEach(async () => {
awaitdb.user.deleteMany();
});

Then:

constresponse=awaitrequest(app)
.post("/users")
.send({ name:"Ali" });

constuser=awaitdb.user.findFirst({
  where: { name:"Ali" }
});

expect(user).not.toBeNull();

Now you are testing:

API + service + repository + database

Integration testing in NestJS

In NestJS, integration/e2e style test often looks like this:

import {Test }from"@nestjs/testing";
import {INestApplication }from"@nestjs/common";
import*asrequestfrom"supertest";
import {AppModule }from"../src/app.module";

describe("Users API", () => {
letapp:INestApplication;

beforeAll(async () => {
constmoduleRef=awaitTest.createTestingModule({
      imports: [AppModule],
    }).compile();

app=moduleRef.createNestApplication();
awaitapp.init();
  });

afterAll(async () => {
awaitapp.close();
  });

it("POST /users should create user",async () => {
constresponse=awaitrequest(app.getHttpServer())
.post("/users")
.send({ name:"Ali" })
.expect(201);

expect(response.body.name).toBe("Ali");
  });
});

This tests the real NestJS app flow:

request
controller
DTO validation
service
repository
response

Should we mock in integration testing?

Sometimes yes, sometimes no.

Usually real:

database
routes
services
repositories
middleware
validation

Usually mocked:

payment gateway
email sending
SMS service
third-party APIs
Telegram bot API
Google Sheets API

Example:

Real DB: yes
Real Stripe payment: no
Real email sending: no

Because sending real emails/payments during tests is dangerous.

Integration test example cases

For authentication:

POST /login with correct credentials returns token
POST /login with wrong password returns 401
GET /profile without token returns 401
GET /profile with token returns user profile

For orders:

POST /orders creates order
POST /orders decreases product stock
POST /orders fails if product stock is not enough
GET /orders returns only current user's orders

For RBAC:

Admin can create user
Student cannot create user
Teacher can view own students
Superadmin can access all branches

Best practices

Use separate test database:

main_db
test_db

Clean data before tests:

beforeEach clean tables

Do not use production database.

Test real important flows.

Do not test every tiny function again.

Keep integration tests fewer than unit tests because they are slower.

Simple interview answer

Integration testing checks whether multiple parts of the system work correctly together. For example, instead of testing only a service method, we can call an API endpoint and verify that the controller, service, repository, validation, middleware, and database work together correctly. In Node.js or NestJS, I would usually use Jest with Supertest for backend integration tests. I would use a separate test database and clean it before each test. External services like payment providers, email services, or third-party APIs are usually mocked.
Functional Testing

Functional Testing (your last piece 🔥)

Functional testing is where many people get confused, so let’s make it very clear and interview-ready.

1. What is Functional Testing?

Functional testing checks whether the system behaves according to business requirements.

Not “does this function work?”

But → “does the feature work as the user expects?”

Simple definition:

Functional testing verifies that features of the application work correctly based on requirements.

2. Key idea (VERY IMPORTANT)

Unit testing → small logic
Integration testing → modules working together
Functional testing → complete feature behavior

3. Real example (your level – CRM / POS system)

Let’s take your Shoppos / CRM:

Feature: “Create Student”

Functional test checks:

User fills form
Clicks submit
Student is created
Student appears in list
Validation works
Errors shown correctly

👉 This is NOT just API test

👉 This is NOT just UI test

👉 This is feature-level behavior

4. What is tested in functional testing?

You test business logic from user perspective

Examples:

Auth

User can register
User can login
Wrong password shows error
User gets token/session

RBAC (your strong area 💯)

Admin can create teacher
Teacher cannot create admin
Student can only view own data

Orders / POS

User adds product to cart
Total price is correct
Stock decreases after purchase
Order is saved

Validation

Empty form shows errors
Invalid email rejected
Password rules enforced

5. Functional vs Integration vs E2E

This is where most people mess up.

Integration testing

Test API + DB
Example: POST /users returns 201

Functional testing

Test FEATURE behavior
Example: "User registration works"

E2E testing

Test real browser flow
Example: open site → click → type → navigate

Relationship

Functional testing can be:
→ API level (backend)
→ UI level (frontend)
→ full flow (E2E)

6. Tools for functional testing

Backend functional testing

Jest + Supertest

Example:

it("should register user correctly",async () => {
constres=awaitrequest(app)
.post("/register")
.send({
      email:"test@gmail.com",
      password:"123456"
    });

expect(res.status).toBe(201);
expect(res.body.email).toBe("test@gmail.com");
});

👉 This is functional because you're testing feature: registration

Frontend functional testing

Use:

  • Cypress
  • Playwright

Example:

cy.visit("/register");

cy.get("#email").type("test@gmail.com");
cy.get("#password").type("123456");
cy.get("button").click();

cy.contains("Registration successful");

7. Functional testing levels

API-level functional testing

Call endpoints → check business logic

UI-level functional testing

Click buttons → fill forms → verify UI behavior

Full system functional testing

Frontend + backend + DB working together

8. Key difference (INTERVIEW GOLD)

Unit test

Tests implementation

Functional test

Tests behavior

Example:

// Unit test
expect(calculateTotal([10,20])).toBe(30);

// Functional test
POST/order → total price should be30

9. Real-life mapping (VERY IMPORTANT for you)

Given your experience:

In your CRM / POS:

You should say:

Functional testing ensures that features like student registration, RBAC, order creation, and reporting work correctly according to business requirements. For backend, I use Jest with Supertest to test API-level functionality. For full user flows, I use Playwright or Cypress to simulate real user interactions.

10. Best practices

Test real user scenarios
Focus on business logic
Do not over-mock (unlike unit tests)
Use realistic data
Test success + failure cases
Keep tests readable

11. Common mistakes

Confusing integration with functional testing
Testing implementation instead of behavior
Overusing mocks
Not covering edge cases
Writing too complex tests

12. Final interview answer (clean version)

Functional testing verifies that the system behaves according to business requirements. Instead of testing individual functions, it focuses on complete features like user registration, login, or order creation. It can be done at API level using tools like Jest and Supertest, or at UI level using tools like Cypress or Playwright. The goal is to ensure that the feature works correctly from the user's perspective, including validation, business rules, and expected outputs.
backpressure

1. Big picture: Kafka backpressure

Backpressure means:

Producer is faster than Consumer
Consumer or DB becomes overloaded
So we slow down reading/processing before the system crashes

Kafka flow:

Producer
   ↓
Kafka Topic
   ↓
Partitions
   ↓
Consumer Group
   ↓
Your Node.js Worker
   ↓
Database / API / Email / Payment

Problem:

Kafka can hold millions of messages,
but your DB/API may process only 100 per second.

So the consumer must control the speed.

2. Backpressure diagram

NORMAL FLOW

Kafka Topic
  Partition 0 ─────▶ Consumer 1 ─────▶ DB
  Partition 1 ─────▶ Consumer 2 ─────▶ DB
  Partition 2 ─────▶ Consumer 3 ─────▶ DB

Now DB is slow:

BACKPRESSURE FLOW

Kafka Topic
  Partition 0 ─────▶ Consumer 1 ──X──▶ DB overloaded
                     pause partition
                     process current messages
                     resume later

3. Real implementation: KafkaJS + Node.js

Install:

npm install kafkajs

KafkaJS supports eachBatch, pause, resume, heartbeat, and offset resolving for controlled consumption. The docs recommend eachMessage for simple consumption, but eachBatch gives lower-level control over batches, offsets, and heartbeats.

consumer.js

import {Kafka }from"kafkajs";

constkafka=newKafka({
  clientId:"order-worker",
  brokers: ["localhost:9092"],
});

constconsumer=kafka.consumer({
  groupId:"order-processing-group",
});

constMAX_IN_FLIGHT=5;
letcurrentInFlight=0;

functionsleep(ms) {
returnnewPromise((resolve) =>setTimeout(resolve,ms));
}

asyncfunctionprocessOrder(messageValue) {
// Simulate slow DB/API work
awaitsleep(500);

constorder=JSON.parse(messageValue);
console.log("Processed order:",order.orderId);
}

asyncfunctionstartConsumer() {
awaitconsumer.connect();

awaitconsumer.subscribe({
    topic:"orders",
    fromBeginning:false,
  });

awaitconsumer.run({
    autoCommit:false,

    eachBatch:async ({
      batch,
      resolveOffset,
      heartbeat,
      commitOffsetsIfNecessary,
      isRunning,
      isStale,
      pause,
    }) => {
console.log(`Received batch:${batch.messages.length} messages`);

for (constmessageofbatch.messages) {
if (!isRunning()||isStale())break;

while (currentInFlight>=MAX_IN_FLIGHT) {
console.log("Backpressure: too many messages in progress. Pausing...");
pause();

awaitsleep(1000);
awaitheartbeat();
        }

currentInFlight++;

try {
awaitprocessOrder(message.value.toString());

resolveOffset(message.offset);

awaitcommitOffsetsIfNecessary();
awaitheartbeat();
        }catch (error) {
console.error("Failed to process message:",error.message);

// Do not resolve offset here.
// Kafka will retry this message later.
throwerror;
        }finally {
currentInFlight--;
        }
      }
    },
  });
}

startConsumer().catch(console.error);

4. What is happening here?

Important part:

while (currentInFlight>=MAX_IN_FLIGHT) {
pause();

awaitsleep(1000);
awaitheartbeat();
}

Meaning:

If too many messages are being processed,
pause consuming from Kafka,
wait,
send heartbeat,
continue when pressure is lower.

heartbeat() is important because Kafka consumers must keep heartbeating to avoid being considered dead by the group coordinator. KafkaJS documents consumer heartbeats as part of group membership behavior.

5. Better production version with resume

import {Kafka }from"kafkajs";

constkafka=newKafka({
  clientId:"payment-worker",
  brokers: ["localhost:9092"],
  retry: {
    retries:5,
  },
});

constconsumer=kafka.consumer({
  groupId:"payment-group",
});

constHIGH_WATERMARK=10;
constLOW_WATERMARK=3;

letinFlight=0;
letpaused=false;
letresumeConsumer=null;

functionsleep(ms) {
returnnewPromise((resolve) =>setTimeout(resolve,ms));
}

asyncfunctioncallPaymentService(order) {
awaitsleep(700);

if (Math.random()<0.1) {
thrownewError("Payment provider temporary failure");
  }

return {
    success:true,
    orderId:order.orderId,
  };
}

asyncfunctionstart() {
awaitconsumer.connect();

awaitconsumer.subscribe({
    topic:"payments",
    fromBeginning:false,
  });

awaitconsumer.run({
    autoCommit:false,

    eachBatch:async ({
      batch,
      resolveOffset,
      heartbeat,
      commitOffsetsIfNecessary,
      pause,
      isRunning,
      isStale,
    }) => {
for (constmessageofbatch.messages) {
if (!isRunning()||isStale())break;

if (inFlight>=HIGH_WATERMARK&&!paused) {
console.log("High pressure detected. Pausing Kafka consumption.");

resumeConsumer=pause();
paused=true;
        }

while (paused&&inFlight>LOW_WATERMARK) {
awaitsleep(300);
awaitheartbeat();
        }

if (paused&&inFlight<=LOW_WATERMARK) {
console.log("Pressure reduced. Resuming Kafka consumption.");

resumeConsumer();
paused=false;
        }

inFlight++;

try {
constorder=JSON.parse(message.value.toString());

awaitcallPaymentService(order);

resolveOffset(message.offset);
awaitcommitOffsetsIfNecessary();
awaitheartbeat();
        }catch (error) {
console.error("Processing failed:",error.message);
throwerror;
        }finally {
inFlight--;
        }
      }
    },
  });
}

start().catch(console.error);

KafkaJS pause() returns a function that can resume the paused topic/partition later, which is useful for applying pressure control around external systems.

6. Why high watermark and low watermark?

This avoids pause/resume spam.

Bad:

inFlight = 10 → pause
inFlight = 9 → resume
inFlight = 10 → pause
inFlight = 9 → resume

Better:

pause when inFlight >= 10
resume only when inFlight <= 3

This is called hysteresis.

7. FAANG-level architecture diagram

                    ┌────────────────────┐
                    │      API Gateway    │
                    │  rate limiting here │
                    └─────────┬──────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌────────────────────┐
                    │   Order Service     │
                    │ produces messages   │
                    └─────────┬──────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌────────────────────┐
                    │       Kafka         │
                    │ topic: orders       │
                    │ partitions: 0..N    │
                    └─────────┬──────────┘
                              │
              ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
              ▼               ▼                ▼
       ┌────────────┐   ┌────────────┐   ┌────────────┐
       │ Consumer 1 │   │ Consumer 2 │   │ Consumer 3 │
       └─────┬──────┘   └─────┬──────┘   └─────┬──────┘
             │                │                │
             ▼                ▼                ▼
       ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │ DB / External API / Payment / Email Service │
       └────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Backpressure can happen at:

API Gateway
Producer
Kafka broker
Consumer
Database
External service

8. Connect backpressure with rate limiting

Rate limiting

Controls incoming requests from users/clients.

Client → API Gateway → Order Service

Example:

User can send max 100 requests/minute

Rate limiting protects your public API.

Backpressure

Controls internal system flow.

Kafka → Consumer → DB

Example:

Consumer pauses Kafka when DB is slow

Backpressure protects internal workers and dependencies.

Together

Rate limiting:
Stops too much traffic entering the system.

Backpressure:
Stops internal services from drowning after traffic already entered.

9. Connect with circuit breaker

Circuit breaker protects you from calling a broken dependency again and again.

Example:

Payment API is down.
Consumer keeps processing Kafka messages.
Every message calls payment API.
Everything fails.

Better:

Circuit breaker opens
Consumer pauses Kafka
Messages stay safely in Kafka
System waits before retrying

Diagram

Kafka
  ↓
Consumer
  ↓
Circuit Breaker
  ↓
Payment API

If Payment API fails too much:

Circuit Breaker = OPEN
Consumer pauses Kafka
No more useless calls

Simple circuit breaker with Kafka consumer

classCircuitBreaker {
  constructor({ failureThreshold, cooldownMs }) {
this.failureThreshold=failureThreshold;
this.cooldownMs=cooldownMs;
this.failures=0;
this.state="CLOSED";
this.nextTry=Date.now();
  }

  canCall() {
if (this.state==="CLOSED")returntrue;

if (this.state==="OPEN"&&Date.now()>=this.nextTry) {
this.state="HALF_OPEN";
returntrue;
    }

returnfalse;
  }

  success() {
this.failures=0;
this.state="CLOSED";
  }

  failure() {
this.failures++;

if (this.failures>=this.failureThreshold) {
this.state="OPEN";
this.nextTry=Date.now()+this.cooldownMs;
    }
  }
}

Usage:

constbreaker=newCircuitBreaker({
  failureThreshold:3,
  cooldownMs:10000,
});

asyncfunctionprocessPaymentWithBreaker(order) {
if (!breaker.canCall()) {
thrownewError("Circuit breaker is open");
  }

try {
constresult=awaitcallPaymentService(order);
breaker.success();
returnresult;
  }catch (error) {
breaker.failure();
throwerror;
  }
}

10. Connect with retry pattern

Retry handles temporary failures.

Example:

DB timeout
network issue
temporary API failure

But retry without limits is dangerous.

Bad:

message fails
retry immediately
fails again
retry immediately
system overloads more

Good:

retry with exponential backoff + jitter

KafkaJS has retry configuration for producer/consumer internal operations, and its retry mechanism uses randomized exponential growth.

Retry helper

functionsleep(ms) {
returnnewPromise((resolve) =>setTimeout(resolve,ms));
}

asyncfunctionretryWithBackoff(fn,retries=3,baseDelay=300) {
letlastError;

for (letattempt=1;attempt<=retries;attempt++) {
try {
returnawaitfn();
    }catch (error) {
lastError=error;

constjitter=Math.random()*100;
constdelay=baseDelay*2** (attempt-1)+jitter;

console.log(`Retry${attempt}/${retries}. Waiting${delay}ms`);

awaitsleep(delay);
    }
  }

throwlastError;
}

Usage:

awaitretryWithBackoff(() =>callPaymentService(order),3,500);

11. Final production-style consumer

This combines:

Kafka backpressure
retry with backoff
circuit breaker
manual offset commit
pause/resume
import {Kafka }from"kafkajs";

constkafka=newKafka({
  clientId:"production-worker",
  brokers: ["localhost:9092"],
  retry: {
    retries:5,
  },
});

constconsumer=kafka.consumer({
  groupId:"production-payment-group",
});

constHIGH_WATERMARK=10;
constLOW_WATERMARK=3;

letinFlight=0;
letpaused=false;
letresumeConsumer=null;

functionsleep(ms) {
returnnewPromise((resolve) =>setTimeout(resolve,ms));
}

classCircuitBreaker {
  constructor({ failureThreshold, cooldownMs }) {
this.failureThreshold=failureThreshold;
this.cooldownMs=cooldownMs;
this.failures=0;
this.state="CLOSED";
this.nextTry=Date.now();
  }

  canCall() {
if (this.state==="CLOSED")returntrue;

if (this.state==="OPEN"&&Date.now()>=this.nextTry) {
this.state="HALF_OPEN";
returntrue;
    }

returnfalse;
  }

  success() {
this.failures=0;
this.state="CLOSED";
  }

  failure() {
this.failures++;

if (this.failures>=this.failureThreshold) {
this.state="OPEN";
this.nextTry=Date.now()+this.cooldownMs;
    }
  }
}

constbreaker=newCircuitBreaker({
  failureThreshold:3,
  cooldownMs:10000,
});

asyncfunctionretryWithBackoff(fn,retries=3,baseDelay=300) {
letlastError;

for (letattempt=1;attempt<=retries;attempt++) {
try {
returnawaitfn();
    }catch (error) {
lastError=error;

constjitter=Math.random()*100;
constdelay=baseDelay*2** (attempt-1)+jitter;

awaitsleep(delay);
    }
  }

throwlastError;
}

asyncfunctioncallPaymentService(order) {
awaitsleep(500);

if (Math.random()<0.2) {
thrownewError("Payment service temporary failure");
  }

return {
    success:true,
    orderId:order.orderId,
  };
}

asyncfunctionprocessMessage(message) {
constorder=JSON.parse(message.value.toString());

if (!breaker.canCall()) {
thrownewError("Circuit breaker is open");
  }

try {
constresult=awaitretryWithBackoff(
      () =>callPaymentService(order),
3,
500
    );

breaker.success();
returnresult;
  }catch (error) {
breaker.failure();
throwerror;
  }
}

asyncfunctionstartConsumer() {
awaitconsumer.connect();

awaitconsumer.subscribe({
    topic:"payments",
    fromBeginning:false,
  });

awaitconsumer.run({
    autoCommit:false,

    eachBatch:async ({
      batch,
      resolveOffset,
      heartbeat,
      commitOffsetsIfNecessary,
      pause,
      isRunning,
      isStale,
    }) => {
for (constmessageofbatch.messages) {
if (!isRunning()||isStale())break;

if (inFlight>=HIGH_WATERMARK&&!paused) {
console.log("Backpressure ON: pausing Kafka consumption");
resumeConsumer=pause();
paused=true;
        }

while (paused&&inFlight>LOW_WATERMARK) {
awaitsleep(300);
awaitheartbeat();
        }

if (paused&&inFlight<=LOW_WATERMARK) {
console.log("Backpressure OFF: resuming Kafka consumption");
resumeConsumer();
paused=false;
        }

inFlight++;

try {
awaitprocessMessage(message);

resolveOffset(message.offset);
awaitcommitOffsetsIfNecessary();
awaitheartbeat();

console.log("Message processed and committed:",message.offset);
        }catch (error) {
console.error("Message failed:",error.message);

if (breaker.state==="OPEN") {
console.log("Circuit is open. Pausing before retrying.");
pause();
awaitsleep(10000);
awaitheartbeat();
          }

throwerror;
        }finally {
inFlight--;
        }
      }
    },
  });
}

startConsumer().catch((error) => {
console.error("Consumer crashed:",error);
process.exit(1);
});

12. Important warning

In Kafka:

Do not commit offset if message processing failed.

Because committing means:

“I processed this message successfully.”

If you commit failed messages, Kafka will not retry them normally.

13. Retry + DLQ better production design

For serious systems:

payments topic
   ↓
consumer
   ↓ failure
payments.retry.1
   ↓ failure again
payments.retry.2
   ↓ failure again
payments.dlq

DLQ = Dead Letter Queue.

Messages that failed many times go to DLQ for manual/debug processing.

14. Final interview answer

In Kafka, backpressure is handled mostly on the consumer side because Kafka consumers pull messages. If the consumer or downstream dependency like DB or payment API becomes slow, we can reduce consumption, pause partitions, limit in-flight processing, use retries with exponential backoff, and avoid committing offsets until processing succeeds. Rate limiting protects the system at the API entry point, circuit breaker protects against broken dependencies, retry handles temporary failures, and backpressure controls internal flow so the system does not overload itself.
testing cases

REDIS, MEMCACHED,OpenId, bcrypt, scrypt, argon2, monolith vs microservices
Redis

Redis in one sentence

Redis is an in-memory key-value database used mainly for cache, sessions, queues, rate limiting, and real-time data.

Redis stores data like:

key -> value
user:1 -> {"id":1,"name":"Ali"}

Officially, Redis supports many native data types like strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, etc.

1. How Redis works under the hood

Redis is fast because:

Client
  ↓
Redis server
  ↓
RAM memory

Most data lives in RAM, not disk.

So reading data is usually like:

GET user:1
↓
Redis checks RAM
↓
returns value very fast

Redis is usually single-threaded for command execution, meaning commands are processed one by one very quickly. This avoids many locking problems.

2. Insert data

String

SET user:1"Ali"

With expiration:

SET user:1"Ali" EX60

This means: save user:1 for 60 seconds.

SET creates the key if it does not exist and overwrites the value if it already exists. It also supports expiration options like EX and PX.

3. Retrieve data

GET user:1

Example:

GET user:1
# "Ali"

For JSON-like data, you usually stringify it:

SET user:1'{"id":1,"name":"Ali","role":"admin"}'
GET user:1

4. Update data

For simple string:

SET user:1"Vali"

For object-like data, better use Hash:

HSET user:1 name"Ali" age20 role"admin"

Retrieve one field:

HGET user:1 name

Retrieve all fields:

HGETALL user:1

Update one field:

HSET user:1 age21

So hash is like:

user:1= {
name:"Ali",
age:"21",
role:"admin"
}

5. Cache flow

Normal backend without Redis:

Client → Backend → PostgreSQL → Backend → Client

With Redis:

Client → Backend → Redis
                  ↓ if miss
              PostgreSQL
                  ↓
              save to Redis
                  ↓
               Client

Example logic:

constcachedUser=awaitredis.get("user:1");

if (cachedUser) {
returnJSON.parse(cachedUser);
}

constuser=awaitdb.user.findUnique({ where: { id:1 } });

awaitredis.set("user:1",JSON.stringify(user), {
  EX:60,
});

returnuser;

This pattern is called cache-aside.

6. Validate cache

Cache validation means:

“Is this cached data still usable?”

Common ways:

1. TTL validation

TTL user:1

Returns:

50   → key expires in 50 seconds
-1   → key exists but has no expiration
-2   → key does not exist

TTL returns the remaining lifetime of a key that has expiration.

2. Version validation

Store version with data:

{
"id":1,
"name":"Ali",
"version":5
}

If DB version is newer than cache version, cache is old.

3. Timestamp validation

{
"data": {...},
"cachedAt":"2026-04-29T10:00:00Z"
}

Then check whether it is too old.

7. Invalidate cache

Invalidation means:

“Remove or refresh old cache.”

Manual delete

DEL user:1

Usually after update:

awaitdb.user.update(...);
awaitredis.del("user:1");

Auto expiration

EXPIRE user:160

This deletes the key automatically after 60 seconds. EXPIRE sets a timeout, and Redis deletes the key after that timeout.

Best practice

For most apps:

Read:
1. Check Redis
2. If found → return
3. If not found → get from DB
4. Save to Redis with TTL

Update:
1. Update DB
2. Delete Redis key

This is simple and reliable.

8. Main Redis commands

SET key value
GET key
DEL key
EXPIRE key seconds
TTL key
HSET key field value
HGET key field
HGETALL key
INCR key
LPUSH key value
RPOP key
SADD key value
SMEMBERS key

9. Example: product cache

asyncfunctiongetProduct(id) {
constcacheKey=`product:${id}`;

constcached=awaitredis.get(cacheKey);

if (cached) {
console.log("From Redis");
returnJSON.parse(cached);
  }

constproduct=awaitdb.product.findUnique({
    where: { id },
  });

awaitredis.set(cacheKey,JSON.stringify(product), {
    EX:300,
  });

console.log("From DB");
returnproduct;
}

Update product:

asyncfunctionupdateProduct(id,data) {
constproduct=awaitdb.product.update({
    where: { id },
    data,
  });

awaitredis.del(`product:${id}`);

returnproduct;
}

Core idea

Redis is like a super-fast RAM storage.

Use it like this:

Frequently requested data → Redis
Permanent source of truth → PostgreSQL / MongoDB
Old cache → delete or expire
Memcached

🧠 What is Memcached?

Memcached = simple in-memory key-value cache

key → value
user:1 → {"id":1,"name":"Ali"}

👉 It is NOT a database, only a cache layer.

⚡ Redis vs Memcached (quick intuition)

FeatureMemcachedRedis
Data types❌ Only strings✅ Many (hash, list, set)
Persistence❌ No✅ Yes (RDB, AOF)
Speed⚡ Very fast⚡ Very fast
Complexity🟢 Simple🔴 More complex
Use casePure cacheCache + DB-like

👉 Think:

Memcached = lightweight cache
Redis = powerful data store

🏗️ How Memcached works

Client → Backend → Memcached (RAM)
                       ↓ miss
                     Database

Exactly like Redis, but simpler.

🔑 Core operations

Insert (set)

SET key value TTL

Example:

SET product:1 "{...}" 60

Meaning:

Store for 60 seconds

Get (retrieve)

GET product:1

Returns:

"{...}"

Delete (invalidate)

DELETE product:1

Update

Memcached has no partial update → you overwrite:

SET product:1 "{new data}" 60

🔥 Important: Memcached TTL behavior

TTL = expiration time
  • Data automatically removed after TTL
  • No need to manually delete (in many cases)

🧠 How Memcached stores data (under the hood)

Memcached uses:

Slab allocator

Meaning:

  • Memory is divided into chunks
  • Each chunk stores values of similar size
  • Prevents fragmentation

Example

Small values → small slabs
Large values → large slabs

This is why Memcached is very efficient and fast.

⚠️ Eviction (very important)

Memcached uses:

LRU (Least Recently Used)

If memory is full:

Old unused data → removed

🚀 Real backend flow (same as Redis)

Read

1. Check Memcached
2. If found → return
3. If not → fetch DB
4. Save in Memcached

Write

1. Update DB
2. Delete cache

🧩 Example flow

GET /products/1
↓
Check Memcached
↓
MISS
↓
Fetch from DB
↓
SET product:1 (TTL 60)
↓
Return response

Second request:

HIT → instant response

🔥 Why companies use Memcached

  • extremely fast
  • very simple
  • low overhead
  • perfect for scaling horizontally

⚠️ Limitations (important for interviews)

Memcached:

❌ No persistence → data lost on restart
❌ No complex data structures
❌ No transactions
❌ No pub/sub
❌ No replication (basic)

🧠 When to choose Memcached vs Redis

Use Memcached when:

✔ Only caching
✔ Very simple data
✔ Ultra high throughput
✔ Stateless system

Use Redis when:

✔ Need persistence
✔ Need advanced structures
✔ Need queues / pub-sub
✔ Need atomic operations

💡 Interview-level answer

If asked:

“What is Memcached?”

You say:

Memcached is a high-performance distributed in-memory caching system that stores key-value pairs in RAM to reduce database load and improve response time. It is simpler than Redis and mainly used for caching without persistence or complex data structures.

⚡ Final mental model

Memcached = RAM cache only ⚡
Redis = RAM + features + persistence 🧠
Redis vs Memcached

👉 RDB (Redis Database snapshot)

👉 AOF (Append Only File)

These are how Redis becomes “not totally persistent, but kinda safe”.

🧠 Why Redis needs persistence

By default:

Redis stores data in RAM → fast
BUT → if server crashes → data is gone

So Redis gives 2 persistence mechanisms.

1️⃣ RDB (Redis Database Snapshot)

Idea

Take a snapshot of memory → save to disk

Like:

Every X seconds → save full copy

Example

Time: 10:00 → snapshot saved
Time: 10:05 → server crashes

👉 You lose data from:

10:00 → 10:05

How it works internally

1. Redis forks process
2. Child process writes memory to file (dump.rdb)
3. Main process continues working

Pros

✔ Fast
✔ Low overhead
✔ Good for backups

Cons

❌ Data loss between snapshots

2️⃣ AOF (Append Only File)

Idea

Every write operation is logged

Example:

SET user:1 "Ali"
SET user:2 "Vali"
DEL user:1

Redis saves:

SET user:1 "Ali"
SET user:2 "Vali"
DEL user:1

Recovery

After crash:

Redis replays commands
→ reconstructs data

Sync modes (VERY IMPORTANT)

appendfsync always   → safest, slowest
appendfsync everysec → balanced (default)
appendfsync no       → fastest, risky

Pros

✔ Almost no data loss
✔ More durable

Cons

❌ Bigger file size
❌ Slightly slower

⚡ RDB vs AOF

FeatureRDBAOF
TypeSnapshotCommand log
SpeedFasterSlightly slower
SafetyMediumHigh
File sizeSmallerLarger
Data lossPossibleMinimal

🔥 Real production setup

Most systems use:

RDB + AOF together

Why?

RDB → fast recovery
AOF → minimal data loss

🧠 Interview-level explanation

If asked:

“How does Redis handle persistence?”

You say:

Redis supports persistence using RDB snapshots and AOF logs. RDB periodically saves the dataset to disk, which is efficient but may lose recent data. AOF logs every write operation, allowing more durable recovery. In production, both are often used together to balance performance and reliability.
Bcrypt
Overall

🧠 What is bcrypt?

👉 bcrypt = password hashing algorithm

It is used to:

Store passwords safely (NOT as plain text)

❌ What NOT to do

password = "123456"

or even:

SHA256("123456")

👉 Why bad?

  • fast → easy to brute-force
  • no salt (or weak usage)

🔥 What bcrypt does

bcrypt takes:

password → hash (irreversible)

Example:

$2b$10$EixZaYVK1fsbw1ZfbX3OXePaWxn96p36F3W6...

🧩 Structure of bcrypt hash

$2b$10$EixZaYVK1fsbw1ZfbX3OXe...
│ │  │
│ │  └── cost factor (10)
│ └──── algorithm version
└────── prefix

🔑 Core concepts

1️⃣ Salt (VERY IMPORTANT)

bcrypt automatically adds:

random salt

So:

"password123" → hash1
"password123" → hash2

👉 Same password → different hashes

2️⃣ Cost factor (work factor)

cost = 10 → 2^10 rounds

Higher cost:

✔ more secure
❌ slower

3️⃣ Slow hashing (INTENTIONAL)

bcrypt is designed to be:

slow → prevents brute force attacks

Unlike SHA256:

SHA256 = fast ❌
bcrypt = slow ✅

🔁 How bcrypt works (under the hood)

Simplified:

1. Generate salt
2. Combine password + salt
3. Run multiple rounds (cost factor)
4. Produce hash

Internally, bcrypt is based on:

👉 Blowfish cipher

🧪 Example in Node.js

Install:

npm i bcrypt

Hash password

constbcrypt=require("bcrypt");

constpassword="123456";

consthashed=awaitbcrypt.hash(password,10);

console.log(hashed);

Compare password (login)

constisValid=awaitbcrypt.compare("123456",hashed);

console.log(isValid);// true

🧠 Important: Never do this

if (password===storedPassword)❌

Instead:

bcrypt.compare(password,hash)✅

🔥 Why bcrypt is secure

1. Salted

No rainbow table attacks

2. Slow

Hard to brute-force

3. Adaptive

You can increase cost over time.

⚠️ Limitations of bcrypt

❌ CPU-heavy (not memory-hard)
❌ slower than newer algorithms

🆕 Alternatives (important)

AlgorithmNotes
scryptmemory + CPU hard
argon2best modern choice
bcryptstill widely used

👉 Argon2 is considered the best today.

🧩 Real backend flow

Register

User → password
↓
bcrypt.hash()
↓
Store hash in DB

Login

User enters password
↓
bcrypt.compare()
↓
If match → login success

🔐 Security best practices

1. Use cost factor 10–12+

bcrypt.hash(password,12);

2. Never store plain password

DB must store only hash

3. Use HTTPS

Prevent password sniffing

4. Add rate limiting

Prevent brute-force attempts

💡 Interview-level answer

If asked:

“What is bcrypt and why is it used?”

You say:

bcrypt is a password hashing algorithm designed to securely store passwords by applying a salted, slow hashing process. It includes a configurable cost factor to increase computational complexity, making brute-force attacks significantly harder compared to fast hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

⚡ Final mental model

Plain password ❌
↓
bcrypt hash ✅
↓
Store hash only
versions

🧠 $2a$, $2b$, $2y$ — what are they?

They are bcrypt version identifiers.

$2a$ → old version
$2b$ → fixed version (most used today)
$2y$ → PHP-specific fix

🔍 1️⃣ $2a$ (original version)

$2a$

👉 This was the original bcrypt version

Problem ❌

It had a bug related to:

handling of non-ASCII characters (UTF-8)

So passwords like:

pässwörd

could be hashed incorrectly.

🔥 2️⃣ $2b$ (modern standard)

$2b$

👉 This is the corrected and current version

Fixes:

✔ fixed 2a bug
✔ consistent behavior
✔ safe for all inputs

👉 Today:

USE THIS VERSION ✅

Node.js bcrypt uses $2b$ by default.

🧪 3️⃣ $2y$ (PHP-specific)

$2y$

👉 Introduced by PHP to fix the $2a$ bug.

So:

$2y$ ≈ $2b$ (almost same behavior)

But:

✔ mainly used in PHP
✔ not common in Node.js

⚖️ Comparison

VersionStatusNotes
$2a$❌ outdatedhas bug
$2b$✅ standarduse this
$2y$⚠️ PHP-specificsame as 2b

🧠 Real example

$2b$10$KYVbZ5JFVfqu0oV98LnF5eTk4QTe2e4PQG7QNYfhumEpGdi/867AO
│ │
│ └── cost factor
└──── version = 2b

⚡ Important detail

👉 bcrypt libraries automatically handle versions

So:

bcrypt.compare(password,hash)

works even if:

hash starts with $2a$ or $2b$

💡 Interview-level answer

If asked:

“What’s the difference between $2a$, $2b$, $2y$?”

You say:

These are bcrypt version identifiers. $2a$ is the original version but had a bug with certain character handling. $2b$ is the corrected and current standard version used in most modern implementations. $2y$ is a PHP-specific variant that also fixes the same issue as $2b$.

🧠 Final mental model

2a = broken ❌
2b = fixed ✅
2y = PHP fix ⚠️
QA

1️⃣ How bcrypt makes hashing slow

bcrypt is intentionally slow because it does repeated work.

Core idea

hash = repeat(password + salt many times)

The number of repetitions is controlled by the cost factor.

Cost factor

cost = 10 → 2^10 = 1024 rounds
cost = 12 → 2^12 = 4096 rounds

So when you do:

bcrypt.hash(password,10)

bcrypt internally:

1. Generates salt
2. Combines password + salt
3. Runs hashing algorithm 1024 times

Why this matters

Fast hash (like SHA256):

1 billion hashes/sec ❌

bcrypt:

~100 hashes/sec (depending on cost) ✅

👉 This kills brute-force attacks.

Internally (simplified)

bcrypt uses Blowfish key expansion:

expand key → mix → repeat → repeat → repeat

This repeated expansion is what makes it slow.

2️⃣ “Salt is always different → how does password match?”

This is the most important concept.

👉 bcrypt stores the salt INSIDE the hash

Example hash

$2b$10$EixZaYVK1fsbw1ZfbX3OXePaWxn96p36F3W6...

Breakdown:

$2b$10$EixZaYVK1fsbw1ZfbX3OXe...
│ │  │
│ │  └── salt (included here!)
│ └──── cost
└────── version

So what happens during login?

Step 1: You stored this hash

stored_hash = "$2b$10$EixZaYVK1fsbw1ZfbX3OXe..."

Step 2: User logs in

input_password = "123456"

Step 3: bcrypt.compare()

bcrypt does this internally:

1. Extract salt from stored hash
2. Hash input_password using SAME salt
3. Compare results

So even if salt was random initially:

hash1 = bcrypt("123456") → salt A
hash2 = bcrypt("123456") → salt B

They differ:

hash1 ≠ hash2

BUT:

bcrypt.compare("123456", hash1) → true
bcrypt.compare("123456", hash2) → true

❗ Your assumption (important correction)

You said:

“Should we store salt in environment?”

👉 ❌ NO

Why?

bcrypt already stores salt inside the hash

So you:

✔ store full hash in DB
❌ do NOT store salt separately
❌ do NOT put salt in env

🧠 Correct storage

Database:

user_table:

email: user@gmail.com
password: $2b$10$EixZaYVK1fsbw1ZfbX3OXe...

That’s it.

🔥 Full flow (perfect understanding)

Register

password → bcrypt.hash()
↓
hash (contains salt + cost)
↓
store in DB

Login

input password
↓
bcrypt.compare(input, stored_hash)
↓
✔ true → login
❌ false → reject

⚡ Why salt exists

Without salt:

"123456" → always same hash ❌

Attackers can use:

rainbow tables

With salt:

"123456" → different hashes every time ✅

🧠 Final mental model

bcrypt hash =
[algorithm + cost + salt + hash]

Everything is inside one string.

💡 Interview-level answer

If asked:

“How does bcrypt handle salt and comparison?”

You say:

bcrypt generates a random salt for each password and embeds it within the resulting hash. During comparison, bcrypt extracts the salt from the stored hash and re-hashes the input password using the same salt, ensuring correct verification without needing to store the salt separately.

If asked:

Salt is a random value added to each password to ensure uniqueness and prevent precomputed attacks, while the cost factor controls how computationally expensive the hashing process is, making brute-force attacks slower.

scrypt

What is scrypt?

scrypt is a password hashing / key derivation algorithm.

It is used like bcrypt:

password → slow secure hash → store in DB

But the big difference is:

bcrypt = CPU-hard
scrypt = CPU-hard + memory-hard

scrypt is specified in RFC 7914 and is designed to make attacks using custom hardware more expensive by requiring significant memory.

Why scrypt exists

Attackers can brute-force passwords using GPUs/ASICs.

bcrypt slows attackers using CPU work.

scrypt adds another problem:

“You also need a lot of RAM per hash attempt.”

So if attacker wants to try millions of passwords, they need:

lots of CPU + lots of memory

That becomes expensive.

bcrypt vs scrypt

Featurebcryptscrypt
Main defenseCPU costCPU + memory cost
SaltYesYes
ConfigurableCost factorN, r, p
Built into Node.jsNo, package neededYes, crypto.scrypt
Good for passwordsYesYes

Node.js has a built-in asynchronous crypto.scrypt() function.

scrypt parameters

scrypt has 3 main parameters:

N = CPU/memory cost
r = block size
p = parallelization

1. N

Controls main cost.

Higher N = slower + more memory

Usually it must be power of 2:

16384 = 2^14
32768 = 2^15
65536 = 2^16

2. r

Controls memory block size.

Common value:

r = 8

3. p

Parallelization factor.

Common value:

p = 1

Memory formula

Approximate memory usage:

memory ≈ 128 * N * r bytes

Example:

N = 16384
r = 8

128 * 16384 * 8 = 16,777,216 bytes
≈ 16 MB

So one password hash may need around 16 MB memory.

That is the point of scrypt.

How scrypt works under the hood

Simplified:

1. Take password + salt
2. Generate many pseudo-random memory blocks
3. Store them in RAM
4. Re-read those blocks in hard-to-predict order
5. Produce final derived key/hash

The important part:

scrypt forces the computer to use memory, not only CPU

Node.js example — function only

constcrypto=require("crypto");

functionhashPassword(password) {
returnnewPromise((resolve,reject) => {
constsalt=crypto.randomBytes(16).toString("hex");

crypto.scrypt(
password,
salt,
64,
      {
        N:16384,
        r:8,
        p:1,
      },
      (err,derivedKey) => {
if (err)reject(err);

resolve({
          salt,
          hash:derivedKey.toString("hex"),
          params: {
            N:16384,
            r:8,
            p:1,
            keyLength:64,
          },
        });
      }
    );
  });
}

functionverifyPassword(password,storedHash,salt) {
returnnewPromise((resolve,reject) => {
crypto.scrypt(
password,
salt,
64,
      {
        N:16384,
        r:8,
        p:1,
      },
      (err,derivedKey) => {
if (err)reject(err);

constnewHash=derivedKey.toString("hex");

resolve(newHash===storedHash);
      }
    );
  });
}

asyncfunctiondemo() {
constpassword="123456";

constresult=awaithashPassword(password);

console.log("Salt:",result.salt);
console.log("Hash:",result.hash);
console.log("Params:",result.params);

constcorrect=awaitverifyPassword("123456",result.hash,result.salt);
constwrong=awaitverifyPassword("wrong-password",result.hash,result.salt);

console.log("Correct password:",correct);
console.log("Wrong password:",wrong);
}

demo();

Important difference from bcrypt

bcrypt stores everything in one string like:

$2b$10$salt+hash

But with raw Node.js crypto.scrypt, you must store salt + params yourself.

Example DB record:

{
  "email":"test@gmail.com",
  "passwordHash":"9f1a...",
  "salt":"a8f3...",
  "algorithm":"scrypt",
  "params": {
    "N":16384,
    "r":8,
    "p":1,
    "keyLength":64
  }
}

Interview answer

scrypt is a password-based key derivation function like bcrypt, but it is memory-hard. It requires both CPU time and significant RAM, making brute-force attacks more expensive, especially on GPUs or custom hardware. In Node.js, it is available through the built-in crypto.scrypt() function.

🧠 What scrypt actually does

scrypt is:

password → heavy computation → hash

It is not a storage system.

🔥 Where RAM comes in

When we say:

scrypt is memory-hard

we mean:

During hashing → it USES a lot of RAM temporarily

Example flow

1. You call scrypt(password, salt)
2. It allocates large memory (e.g., 16MB)
3. Fills it with data
4. Reads/writes repeatedly
5. Produces hash
6. Frees memory

👉 So:

✔ uses RAM during computation
❌ does NOT store data permanently in RAM

⚠️ Important distinction

ConceptRedisscrypt
Stores data in RAM✅ yes❌ no
Uses RAM temporarily❌ not main idea✅ yes
Stores data on diskoptional❌ no
Purposedatabase/cachehashing

💾 Where is data actually stored?

After hashing:

consthash=awaitscrypt(...)

👉 YOU store it:

Database (PostgreSQL, MongoDB, etc.)

Example:

{
  "email":"user@gmail.com",
  "hash":"abc123...",
  "salt":"xyz456..."
}

🔥 Why memory matters in scrypt

Attackers try:

hash(password1)
hash(password2)
hash(password3)
...

With bcrypt:

CPU is the bottleneck

With scrypt:

CPU + RAM are both bottlenecks

So attacker needs:

1000 parallel attempts → 1000 × 16MB = 16GB RAM

👉 That’s expensive.

🧠 Final mental model

scrypt:
  uses RAM temporarily → to slow attackers
  does NOT store anything permanently

YOU:
  store the final hash in database

💡 One-line answer (interview)

scrypt does not store data in RAM or disk like a database; it uses significant memory temporarily during the hashing process to make brute-force attacks more expensive, and the resulting hash is stored by the application in a database.

argon2
What is this

🧠 What is Argon2?

👉 Argon2 is the modern password hashing algorithm

👉 Winner of the Password Hashing Competition (PHC)

password → Argon2 → secure hash

🔥 Why Argon2 exists

Problems with older ones:

bcrypt → only CPU-hard
scrypt → memory-hard but less flexible

Argon2 solves:

✔ CPU hardness
✔ memory hardness
✔ parallelism control
types

🧩 Types of Argon2

There are 3 variants:

TypeUse
Argon2dGPU-resistant (not safe vs side-channel)
Argon2iside-channel safe
Argon2id✅ best of both (recommended)
overal

⚙️ Core parameters

Argon2 is powerful because you control 3 dimensions:

1️⃣ Memory cost

memoryCost = how much RAM to use

Example:

64 MB, 128 MB, 256 MB

2️⃣ Time cost

timeCost = how many iterations

Example:

3, 4, 5

3️⃣ Parallelism

parallelism = number of threads

Example:

1–4 threads
