The V8 vs libuv boundary is where JavaScript execution ends and system-level asynchronous scheduling begins: V8 runs code and microtasks, while libuv handles event loop phases, OS interaction, and thread pool execution.
Event loop “tick order” precision

Great — this is where things become real senior-level Node.js understanding.

We’ll define the exact execution order of one event loop iteration (“tick”) across:

  • V8 (JS + microtasks)
  • libuv (event loop + macrotasks)

🧠 1. What is an “event loop tick”?

A tick = one full cycle of:

executing JS → draining microtasks → running one libuv phase → repeating

⚙️ 2. FULL TICK ORDER (MOST IMPORTANT DIAGRAM)

1. Execute synchronous JS (call stack)
2. Drain Microtasks (V8)
3. Enter libuv event loop phase
4. Execute ONE macrotask batch
5. Drain Microtasks again (V8)
6. Move to next libuv phase
7. Repeat

🔥 3. REAL libuv phase order (macrotasks)

Inside one tick, libuv runs phases in this order:

timers
pending callbacks
idle / prepare
poll
check
close callbacks

BUT ⚠️ only ONE phase (or part of it) runs per tick depending on scheduling.

🧠 4. The CRITICAL RULE (INTERVIEW GOLD)

Microtasks ALWAYS run between EVERY transition.

Meaning:

After JS
→ microtasks
After timers
→ microtasks
After I/O
→ microtasks
After check phase
→ microtasks

⚡ 5. STEP-BY-STEP EXECUTION MODEL

Let’s formalize one tick:

🟢 STEP 1: Run synchronous code (V8)

console.log("A")

Call stack executes fully.

🔵 STEP 2: Drain microtasks (V8)

Promise.then callbacks
queueMicrotask

👉 MUST fully empty before moving on.

🟡 STEP 3: libuv phase starts

Example: timers phase

setTimeout callbacks

Only eligible callbacks execute

🔵 STEP 4: Microtasks again (V8)

After timers:

Promise callbacks run again

🟠 STEP 5: Next libuv phase

Could be:

  • I/O callbacks
  • poll
  • check (setImmediate)

🔵 STEP 6: Microtasks again

Always drained after each phase.

🔥 6. FULL REAL EXAMPLE (VERY IMPORTANT)

console.log("A");

setTimeout(() =>console.log("B"),0);

Promise.resolve().then(() =>console.log("C"));

setImmediate(() =>console.log("D"));

console.log("E");

Step-by-step tick execution:

🟢 1. Sync (V8)

A
E

🔵 2. Microtasks (V8)

C

🟡 3. Timers phase (libuv)

B

🔵 4. Microtasks again

(no new ones)

🟠 5. Check phase (libuv)

D

✅ Final output:

A
E
C
B
D

🧠 7. Key Insight (VERY IMPORTANT)

A tick is NOT “one function execution”.

It is:

a microtask-drained + phase-executed + microtask-drained loop

⚙️ 8. Priority hierarchy (CRITICAL)

HIGHEST
↓
Call Stack (sync JS)
Microtasks (Promises)
Timers (setTimeout)
I/O callbacks
setImmediate (check phase)
Close callbacks
LOWEST

🚨 9. Common misconception

❌ Wrong:

Event loop runs one callback per tick

❌ Correct:

Event loop runs phases, and each phase may execute multiple callbacks, with microtasks draining between them

🧠 10. Mental model (senior view)

Think like this:

V8 = CPU executing instructions
Microtasks = urgent queue inside CPU
libuv = scheduler deciding which system work runs next
OS = actual execution layer

🔥 11. ONE-LINE SENIOR SUMMARY

A Node.js event loop tick consists of synchronous JS execution, a full microtask drain in V8, execution of a libuv phase (timers/I/O/etc.), and another microtask drain before continuing to the next phase.
Thread pool saturation behavior (advanced missing depth)

Great — this is one of the most important “real-world Node.js scalability failure points” and it’s often missing even in advanced explanations.

We’ll go deep into:

  • libuv thread pool internals
  • saturation behavior
  • queueing effects
  • performance collapse patterns
  • real production implications

🧠 1. What is “thread pool saturation”?

libuv has a fixed thread pool:

default size = 4

So only 4 blocking tasks can execute at once.

When saturation happens:

All 4 threads are busy
+ new tasks arrive
= queue builds up

👉 This is called thread pool saturation

⚙️ 2. Where saturation applies

Thread pool is used for:

  • file system (fs.*)
  • crypto (pbkdf2, bcrypt)
  • DNS (dns.lookup)
  • compression (zlib)

🔥 3. What actually happens internally

libuv model:

           incoming tasks
                  ↓
        ┌──────────────────┐
        │ FIFO task queue  │
        └──────────────────┘
           ↓   ↓   ↓   ↓
      [T1][T2][T3][T4]   ← worker threads

When full:

new tasks → WAIT in queue

🧠 4. Key behavior (VERY IMPORTANT)

✔ Threads do NOT scale automatically

Unlike OS thread systems, libuv:

  • does NOT spawn new threads dynamically
  • uses fixed-size pool

✔ Queue is unbounded (important detail)

👉 This is critical:

  • queue can grow indefinitely
  • no backpressure at libuv level

⚡ 5. What happens during saturation (step-by-step)

Assume:

4 threads
100 fs.readFile requests

🧵 Phase 1: Fill workers

T1 → task 1
T2 → task 2
T3 → task 3
T4 → task 4

🧵 Phase 2: Queue buildup

Queue:
task 5
task 6
task 7
...
task 100

🧵 Phase 3: Execution delay grows

Each task must wait:

wait time ≈ (queue position × avg task duration)

So latency increases linearly.

🔥 6. Hidden danger: “global shared pool”

Important:

The thread pool is shared across the entire process.

So this happens:

fs.readFile (app A)
bcrypt hash (auth system)
dns lookup (API calls)
image compression (upload service)

ALL compete for SAME 4 threads.

⚠️ 7. Real production failure pattern

Symptoms:

  • API latency spikes
  • random timeouts
  • CPU looks normal (misleading!)
  • fs operations “slow randomly”

Root cause:

thread pool = saturated
→ queue grows
→ callbacks delayed
→ event loop looks fine but work is stuck

🧠 8. Why CPU usage may NOT increase

This confuses many developers.

Even under saturation:

  • CPU might be low
  • system still slow

Why?

Because:

threads are waiting on blocking I/O (disk, crypto, syscall)

So CPU is idle while queue is huge.

⚙️ 9. Starvation effect (VERY IMPORTANT)

❌ Problem:

Some tasks get delayed so long that:

  • request timeout happens
  • upstream systems retry
  • load increases even more

👉 cascading failure

🔁 10. Event loop impact

Even though event loop is fine:

event loop = waiting for thread completion callbacks

So it looks like:

  • “Node is slow”
  • but actually: thread pool is stuck

🔥 11. Increasing thread pool size

You can tune:

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8

or:

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16

BUT important tradeoff:

IncreaseEffect
more threadsmore parallelism
too manycontext switching overhead
too highCPU thrashing

🧠 12. Optimal sizing rule (senior insight)

Best practice:

thread pool size ≈ number of CPU cores OR slightly above

But depends on workload:

  • heavy crypto → increase slightly
  • fs-heavy → moderate increase
  • mixed workloads → careful tuning

⚡ 13. Why saturation is NOT visible in event loop

Because:

event loop only sees “completed tasks”

It does NOT see:

  • waiting queue
  • blocked thread pool
  • internal backlog

🧭 14. Mental model (VERY IMPORTANT)

JS → requests work
libuv → queues work
thread pool → executes work (limited workers)
queue → hidden bottleneck
event loop → only sees finished results

🔥 15. Real analogy

Think:

JS = customers
libuv = receptionist
thread pool = 4 workers in kitchen
queue = waiting line outside kitchen

Even if customers are many:

  • only 4 chefs cook
  • line grows
  • service slows

🚨 16. Key interview-level insight

Thread pool saturation is NOT a CPU problem — it is a concurrency bottleneck in libuv’s fixed worker pool causing unbounded queue delay.

🔥 FINAL SUMMARY

Thread pool saturation in libuv occurs when all worker threads are busy, causing incoming blocking operations to queue indefinitely. This leads to increasing latency, hidden backlog buildup, and performance degradation even when CPU usage appears normal, because the bottleneck is concurrency—not computation.
Q&A
So does event loop run inside of LIBUV library

Yes — event loop runs inside libuv.

But the important senior-level clarification is:

libuv is not “just the event loop” — the event loop is only one core component inside libuv.

🧠 Clean Answer

✅ YES:

The event loop is implemented inside libuv as:

  • uv_run()
  • uv_loop_t state machine
  • internal phases (uv__io_poll, timers, etc.)

So when Node.js runs async code → it eventually enters libuv’s event loop.

🔁 Where exactly it lives

Inside libuv, the event loop is:

uv_loop_t (main structure)
   ↓
uv_run() (entry function)
   ↓
internal loop phases
   ↓
OS polling + callbacks execution

So the event loop is literally:

a function + state machine running on top of uv_loop_t

⚙️ How it is executed

When Node.js starts:

JS Code
  ↓
Node API layer
  ↓
libuv
  ↓
uv_run(loop, UV_RUN_DEFAULT)
  ↓
EVENT LOOP STARTS RUNNING

🔥 Key Insight (Very Important)

❌ Wrong thinking:

“Event loop is separate from libuv”

✅ Correct thinking:

libuv = event-driven runtime system

event loop = its central scheduler

🧠 Even deeper truth

libuv has two main execution modes:

1. EVENT LOOP MODE (default)

  • runs continuously
  • waits for I/O
  • executes callbacks
uv_run(loop,UV_RUN_DEFAULT);

2. ONE-SHOT MODE

  • runs once
  • exits after tasks finish
uv_run(loop,UV_RUN_ONCE);

3. NO-WAIT MODE

  • checks events
  • doesn’t block
uv_run(loop,UV_RUN_NOWAIT);

🔥 Final Mental Model

Think like this:

libuv = engine
event loop = engine's main control system
OS = hardware signals provider

So:

  • libuv owns the loop
  • loop drives execution
  • OS feeds events
  • callbacks execute JS

🧭 One-line senior summary

The event loop is not outside libuv — it is the core scheduling mechanism implemented inside libuv’s uv_run() over uv_loop_t.
How is asyncronous handled

We’ll break it step-by-step so you understand how asynchronous work is actually handled inside libuv and how it connects to Node.js.

🧠 1. First principle: JavaScript is NOT async

JavaScript itself is:

  • single-threaded
  • synchronous execution model

So this is NOT handled by JS:

fs.readFile("a.txt",cb);

JS only says:

“Hey system, do this later and call me back”

⚙️ 2. Who actually handles async?

👉 libuv handles all asynchronous behavior.

It does it using 3 main mechanisms:

1. Event Loop
2. OS async APIs (epoll / IOCP / kqueue)
3. Thread Pool

🔁 3. BIG PICTURE FLOW (VERY IMPORTANT)

JavaScript
   ↓
Node.js API layer
   ↓
libuv
   ↓
[ OS OR Thread Pool ]
   ↓
Callback queued
   ↓
Event loop executes callback

🧵 4. TWO TYPES OF ASYNC WORK

This is the most important distinction.

🔵 TYPE 1: OS-NATIVE ASYNC (FAST PATH)

Used for:

  • network requests (TCP/HTTP)
  • socket I/O

How it works:

JS request
   ↓
libuv registers socket with OS
   ↓
OS monitors socket (epoll/kqueue/IOCP)
   ↓
OS says: "data ready"
   ↓
libuv gets event
   ↓
callback scheduled in event loop

💡 Key idea:

No threads are used here.

👉 The OS itself does async monitoring.

🔴 TYPE 2: THREAD POOL ASYNC (SLOW PATH)

Used for:

  • file system (fs.readFile)
  • crypto
  • DNS lookup

Why thread pool?

Because:

these operations are BLOCKING in OS

So libuv does this:

JS request
   ↓
libuv sends job to thread pool
   ↓
worker thread executes blocking syscall
   ↓
result returned
   ↓
callback queued in event loop

🔁 5. EVENT LOOP ROLE (ORCHESTRATOR)

The event loop inside libuv does NOT execute async work.

It only:

- waits for events
- picks completed tasks
- runs callbacks

Event loop cycle:

1. check timers
2. check OS events
3. run pending callbacks
4. run thread pool results
5. repeat

🧠 6. REAL EXAMPLE

Example: fs.readFile

fs.readFile("file.txt",cb);

Step-by-step:

1. JS calls fs.readFile
2. Node calls libuv (uv_fs_read)
3. libuv sends task to thread pool
4. thread reads file (blocking syscall)
5. thread finishes
6. result pushed to event loop queue
7. event loop executes callback(cb)

Example: HTTP request

http.get(url,cb);
1. socket created
2. OS registers socket
3. epoll watches it
4. data arrives
5. OS notifies libuv
6. callback scheduled
7. event loop runs callback

🔥 7. IMPORTANT INSIGHT (SENIOR LEVEL)

libuv does NOT “make async”

It coordinates async behavior from 3 sources:

SourceType
OS kerneltrue async I/O
Thread poolsimulated async
Event loopcallback scheduler

⚙️ 8. WHAT EVENT LOOP REALLY DOES

Inside libuv, the event loop is basically:

while (alive) {

run_timers();// setTimeout
run_io_events();// sockets (OS)
run_thread_results();// fs, crypto
run_immediates();// setImmediate

}

🧠 9. ONE SIMPLE MENTAL MODEL

Think like this:

JS = requester
libuv = dispatcher
OS = fast hardware async engine
thread pool = backup workers
event loop = traffic controller

🚨 10. COMMON MISUNDERSTANDING

❌ Wrong:

async means parallel execution in JS

✅ Correct:

async means "defer execution + resume later via event loop"

🔥 FINAL SUMMARY

Asynchronous behavior in Node.js is handled by libuv using a combination of OS-level async APIs, a thread pool for blocking tasks, and an event loop that schedules callbacks when operations complete.
What is thread pool

📌 Definition

A thread pool is a fixed group of worker threads used to execute blocking or CPU-heavy tasks asynchronously.

👉 Instead of creating a new thread every time (expensive), libuv reuses a small set of threads.

🧠 2. Why does libuv need a thread pool?

Because the OS has a problem:

❌ Some operations are BLOCKING:

  • File system (readFile)
  • DNS lookup
  • Compression / crypto
  • Some native APIs

If JS waited for them → everything would freeze.

So libuv solves it:

“I will move blocking work to background threads”

⚙️ 3. Default Thread Pool Size

By default:

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE = 4

Meaning:

  • 4 worker threads exist
  • 4 tasks can run in parallel
  • others wait in queue

You can increase it:

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8node app.js

🔁 4. Thread Pool Architecture

                libuv main thread
                        ↓
                Task queue (FIFO)
                        ↓
        ┌────────┬────────┬────────┬────────┐
        │Thread 1│Thread 2│Thread 3│Thread 4│
        └────────┴────────┴────────┴────────┘
                        ↓
                 completion queue
                        ↓
                Event loop callback

🧵 5. How a Task Enters Thread Pool

Example:

fs.readFile("file.txt",cb);

Step-by-step:

1. JS calls fs.readFile
2. Node API sends request to libuv
3. libuv creates a uv_work_t job
4. job goes into thread pool queue
5. worker thread picks it
6. OS syscall happens (blocking)
7. result stored
8. completion pushed to event loop
9. callback executed in JS

⚙️ 6. Internal Structure (Simplified)

Inside libuv:

structuv__work {
void (*work_cb)(void*);// actual task
void (*done_cb)(void*);// callback after finish
};

Thread behavior:

Each thread does:

while (true) {
task=get_task_from_queue();
execute(task.work_cb);
push_to_completion_queue(task.done_cb);
}

🔥 7. Important Concept: FIFO Queue

Tasks are processed:

First In → First Out

So if you queue 100 tasks:

  • first 4 run immediately
  • remaining wait

🧠 8. What goes into Thread Pool?

YES (uses thread pool):

  • fs operations
  • crypto (bcrypt, pbkdf2)
  • DNS lookup
  • zlib compression

NO (does NOT use thread pool):

  • HTTP requests
  • TCP sockets
  • timers (setTimeout)
  • UI events

Those use OS async (epoll/kqueue/IOCP)

⚡ 9. Thread Pool vs Event Loop

ComponentRole
Thread poolexecutes blocking work
Event loopschedules callbacks
OS kernelhandles real async I/O

🔁 10. Full Execution Model

Example:

crypto.pbkdf2(password,salt,cb);

Flow:

JS thread
  ↓
libuv API
  ↓
Thread pool queue
  ↓
Worker thread executes hashing
  ↓
Result ready
  ↓
Event loop picks callback
  ↓
JS callback runs

🧠 11. Key Insight (VERY IMPORTANT)

Thread pool does NOT make Node.js multi-threaded

Instead:

  • JS still runs on single thread
  • only background work is parallel

⚠️ 12. Thread Pool Limitation (REAL WORLD ISSUE)

If all threads are busy:

Thread 1 → busy
Thread 2 → busy
Thread 3 → busy
Thread 4 → busy

👉 New tasks WAIT in queue

This causes:

  • latency spikes
  • slow fs/crypto operations

🔥 13. Advanced Insight (Senior Level)

Thread pool is shared globally

Meaning:

  • fs + crypto + dns ALL use same pool
  • one heavy task can block others

Example problem:

crypto.pbkdf2 (heavy CPU)
fs.readFile (waiting)
dns lookup (waiting)

👉 all compete for same 4 threads

🧭 14. Mental Model

Think like this:

JS = boss
libuv = manager
thread pool = workers
OS = factory machine
event loop = coordinator

🔥 FINAL SUMMARY

The thread pool in libuv is a fixed group of background worker threads that execute blocking operations (like file system and crypto tasks) asynchronously so that the main JavaScript thread never gets blocked.
How does the os know which task is CPU heavy

Good question — and the key idea is this:

❗ The OS does NOT decide whether a task is “CPU-heavy” or “async vs blocking”.

That decision is made by the application / runtime (like Node.js and libuv) — not the operating system.

🧠 1. First correction (VERY important)

❌ Wrong assumption:

“OS knows which task is CPU-heavy”

✅ Correct:

The OS only:

  • runs threads
  • schedules CPU time
  • executes system calls

It does NOT classify workloads.

⚙️ 2. So who decides what is CPU-heavy?

👉 libuv + Node.js API layer decides

When you call something like:

crypto.pbkdf2()
fs.readFile()

Node already knows:

“this is blocking / expensive → send to thread pool”

🧵 3. How the decision is actually made

Inside libuv, every API is explicitly designed.

Example:

FunctionClassification
fs.readFilethread pool task
crypto.pbkdf2thread pool task
http requestOS async
setTimeouttimer queue

👉 This mapping is HARD-CODED in the runtime.

🔥 4. Why OS cannot decide this

The OS only sees:

- threads
- system calls
- memory usage

It has NO semantic understanding like:

  • “this is encryption”
  • “this is file reading”
  • “this is CPU heavy”

⚙️ 5. What OS actually does

The OS only does:

🧠 1. CPU Scheduling

Decides:

  • which thread runs now
  • how long it runs

🧠 2. I/O Handling

  • disk operations
  • network sockets

🧠 3. Interrupts

  • signals from hardware

🧵 6. So how does async really work?

Let’s break it properly:

🔴 Case 1: CPU-heavy task (thread pool)

crypto.pbkdf2()

Flow:

JS → libuv recognizes “blocking task”
   → send to thread pool
   → worker thread runs CPU work
   → OS just schedules that thread normally

👉 OS does NOT classify it — it just runs threads.

🔵 Case 2: Network I/O (no thread pool)

http.request()

Flow:

JS → libuv
   → register socket with OS
   → OS monitors socket (epoll/kqueue)
   → OS notifies when ready

👉 Again: OS does NOT decide heavy/light

🧠 7. Real truth (senior-level insight)

“CPU-heavy” is NOT a runtime detection — it is a design-time decision inside the library

⚡ 8. What actually makes something “heavy”?

It depends on:

1. Blocking nature

  • Does it wait for disk/CPU?

2. Duration

  • long computation = heavy

3. System call type

  • synchronous disk I/O → heavy
  • socket polling → not heavy (handled by kernel async APIs)

🔥 9. Key mental model

OS = executor (runs threads)
libuv = scheduler (decides where task goes)
Node.js = classifier (knows task type)

🚨 10. Critical misunderstanding to avoid

❌ “OS detects heavy tasks”

❌ “OS chooses thread pool usage”

❌ “OS makes async decisions”

None of these are true.

🧭 FINAL SUMMARY

The OS does NOT know or classify CPU-heavy tasks. Instead, the runtime (libuv + Node.js) explicitly decides which operations are CPU-bound and sends them to a thread pool, while the OS only schedules threads and handles low-level execution.
So there is some kinda table defining the tasks

Yes — there is effectively a mapping system (like a table) inside libuv and Node.js

BUT it is NOT a dynamic OS-level table.

It is:

❗ A hardcoded dispatch system in the Node.js + libuv source code, not something the OS manages.

⚙️ 1. What you are imagining

You’re imagining something like:

Task Type Table (hypothetical)

fs.readFile → thread pool
crypto → thread pool
http → OS async
setTimeout → timer system

👉 This idea is correct in concept.

But the implementation is NOT a database or OS table.

🔥 2. What it REALLY is

It is a set of API bindings + internal dispatch functions

Each Node.js API directly calls a specific libuv function.

🧵 3. Real architecture (IMPORTANT)

JavaScript API
   ↓
Node.js binding layer (C++)
   ↓
libuv function (C)
   ↓
Thread pool OR OS backend OR timer system

📦 4. Example mappings (REAL behavior)

🔴 File system

fs.readFile()

Internally maps to:

uv_fs_read()

👉 goes to THREAD POOL

🔴 Crypto

crypto.pbkdf2()

Maps to:

uv_crypto_pbkdf2()

👉 goes to THREAD POOL

🔵 Network

http.request()

Maps to:

uv_tcp_connect()
uv_poll_start()

👉 goes to OS (epoll/kqueue/IOCP)

🟡 Timers

setTimeout()

Maps to:

uv_timer_start()

👉 goes to timer heap (min-heap)

🧠 5. So is it a “table”?

Yes — BUT more accurately:

It is a dispatch mapping inside source code, not a runtime lookup table.

Think of it like:

if (operation==FS)→thread_pool
if (operation==TCP)→OS_event_loop
if (operation==TIMER)→timer_heap

BUT implemented as:

  • separate modules
  • function calls
  • bindings

NOT a single centralized table.

⚙️ 6. Why it is designed like this

Because libuv must be:

✔ Fast

No lookup overhead

✔ Predictable

Each API has fixed behavior

✔ OS-independent

Same API works on Linux, Windows, macOS

🔥 7. Key insight (VERY IMPORTANT)

The “classification of tasks” happens at the API design level, NOT at runtime by OS.

So:

  • Node.js decides what type of work it is
  • libuv decides how to execute it
  • OS just executes threads/events

🧵 8. Mental model (correct version)

Developer code
   ↓
Node.js API (knows task type)
   ↓
libuv (routes task)
   ↓
[ thread pool | OS async | timer system ]
   ↓
event loop
   ↓
callback execution

🚨 9. Critical correction

❌ Wrong:

“OS has a table of task types”

❌ Wrong:

“libuv asks OS what kind of task this is”

✅ Correct:

The runtime already knows the task type and routes it explicitly.

🧠 FINAL SUMMARY

Yes, there is a “mapping system”, but it is implemented as hardcoded API-to-backend routing inside Node.js and libuv source code, not as a dynamic table in the OS.
what does the uv stand for in phases

Good question — this is a naming confusion a lot of people have.

In libuv:

“uv” does NOT stand for “phases” or anything specific in the event loop.

It is simply part of the project name: libuv.

🧠 1. What does “uv” actually mean?

📌 Short answer:

  • “uv” has no official expanded meaning
  • It is just a name chosen for the library

🧾 2. Origin of the name

libuv originally came from the Node.js ecosystem when developers needed a cross-platform async I/O library.

They combined:

  • “lib” = library
  • “uv” = internal project name (not an acronym)

So:

libuv = “library + uv (name fragment)”

⚙️ 3. Why do you see “uv_” everywhere?

Because inside the codebase:

  • all functions are prefixed with uv_
  • all structures are uv_*

Example:

uv_loop_t
uv_timer_t
uv_run()
uv__io_poll()

🧠 4. Does “uv” relate to event loop phases?

❌ No.

Event loop phases like:

  • timers
  • poll
  • check
  • pending callbacks

are NOT called uv phases

They are just internal steps inside:

uv_run() → event loop execution function

🔁 5. Where “uv” actually appears in phases

You might see things like:

uv__run_timers()
uv__io_poll()
uv__run_pending()

Here:

👉 “uv__” just means:

“this function belongs to libuv internal implementation”

NOT a phase name.

🔥 6. Correct mental model

Think like this:

libuv = system
uv_* = internal components of that system
event loop phases = execution stages inside uv_run()

So:

  • “uv” = namespace prefix
  • “phases” = logical steps inside event loop
  • no direct relationship between “uv” and “phases meaning”

🧠 FINAL SUMMARY

“uv” in libuv does NOT stand for anything related to event loop phases — it is simply a naming prefix used for all internal structures and functions in the library.

DEVELOPER CONSOLE

🧑‍💻 Developer Console (Browser DevTools)

▶️ Why Developer Console exists

📖 Notes

  • Code often contains errors (bugs) — very common in development
  • Browsers hide errors from normal users
  • Without tools, debugging is impossible
  • So browsers provide Developer Tools (DevTools)
  • DevTools allow you to:
    • View errors
    • Inspect code execution
    • Run JavaScript manually
    • Debug scripts
  • Most developers prefer:
    • Google Chrome
    • Mozilla Firefox
      because they have the best DevTools

▶️ How to open Developer Tools

📖 Notes

💻 Google Chrome

  • Open DevTools:
    • Windows/Linux: F12
    • Mac: Cmd + Opt + J
  • Opens directly in Console tab
  • Shows:
    • Errors (red)
    • Warnings
    • Logs
  • Console also has a command line (>):
    • Run JavaScript directly
    • Press Enter to execute

🌐 Other browsers

  • Firefox / Edge:
    • Usually F12
  • Interface is similar across browsers

🍏 Safari (Mac only)

  • Must first enable:
    • Settings → Advanced → “Show Develop menu”
  • Then:
    • Cmd + Opt + C opens console
  • Adds a Develop menu in top bar

▶️ Console usage

📖 Notes

  • Used to:
    • View runtime errors
    • Debug JavaScript
    • Test code snippets
    • Inspect variables
  • Errors show:
    • Message
    • File name
    • Line number (clickable link)
  • Example:
    • bug.html:12 → error location

▶️ Multi-line code in console

📖 Notes

  • Pressing Enter → runs code immediately
  • To write multiple lines:
    • Use Shift + Enter
  • Useful for:
    • Functions
    • Loops
    • Large code blocks

▶️ Why DevTools are important

📖 Notes

  • Without DevTools:
    • Errors are invisible
    • Debugging is impossible
  • With DevTools:
    • You can see real-time issues
    • Test code instantly
    • Understand execution flow

use String

⚡ Modern JavaScript Mode: "use strict"

▶️ Why "use strict" exists

📖 Notes

  • JavaScript evolved without breaking old code
  • New features were added while keeping old behavior
  • Problem:
    • ❌ Old mistakes and bad decisions stayed forever
  • Solution introduced in ECMAScript 5 (ES5) in 2009:
    • Added strict mode
    • Requires explicit activation using "use strict"

▶️ What is "use strict"?

📖 Notes

  • It is a directive (string):
    "use strict";
  • Enables modern JavaScript behavior
  • When placed at top of script:
    • Entire script runs in strict mode
  • Can also be used inside functions:
    • Only that function becomes strict

▶️ How to use strict mode

📖 Notes

✔️ Correct usage

"use strict";

// modern behavior enabled

❌ Incorrect usage

alert("code");

// "use strict" ignored (not at top)

"use strict";
  • Only comments are allowed above it
  • Must be the first statement

▶️ Strict mode in functions

📖 Notes

  • Can be applied to a single function:
functiontest() {
"use strict";
}
  • Affects only that function
  • Mostly used at global script level

▶️ No way to disable strict mode

📖 Notes

  • Once enabled:
    • ❌ Cannot turn off strict mode
  • There is:
    • ❌ no "no use strict"

▶️ Strict mode in browser console

📖 Notes

  • Console does NOT use strict mode by default
  • This can cause confusing results

✔️ How to enable it in console:

  1. Multi-line mode:
    • Shift + Enter
    • Then write:
      "use strict";
  1. Alternative safe method:
(function() {
"use strict";

// your code here
})();

▶️ Do we still need "use strict" today?

📖 Notes

  • Modern JS already enables strict mode automatically in:
    • Classes
    • Modules
  • So in modern projects:
    • Often not required manually
  • But still useful in:
    • Simple scripts
    • Learning phase
    • Older environments

▶️ Why strict mode is good

📖 Notes

  • Helps catch errors early
  • Prevents unsafe behavior
  • Makes code more predictable
  • Improves performance in some engines
  • Forces cleaner coding practices

🧠 Questions (25)

<summary>Click to expand</summary>

  1. What year did ES5 introduce strict mode? → 2009
  1. What enables strict mode? → "use strict"
  1. Is it a keyword or string? → String directive
  1. Where should it be placed? → At top of script
  1. What happens if not at top? → It is ignored
  1. Can comments be above it? → Yes
  1. Can strict mode be used in functions? → Yes
  1. What is scope in function strict mode? → Only that function
  1. Can strict mode be disabled later? → No
  1. Is there "no use strict"? → No
  1. Does console use strict mode by default? → No
  1. How to enable in console? → Shift+Enter multi-line
  1. Alternative safe console method? → IIFE wrapper
  1. What is IIFE? → Immediately invoked function
  1. Do modern modules use strict mode? → Yes automatically
  1. Do classes use strict mode? → Yes automatically
  1. Do we always need "use strict" today? → Not always
  1. Why still use it? → Better error detection
  1. What problem does strict mode fix? → Silent JS errors
  1. Is JS backward compatible? → Yes
  1. What was issue before strict mode? → Bad decisions stayed forever
  1. Does strict mode improve performance? → Sometimes
  1. Is strict mode reversible? → No
  1. Default tutorial assumption? → Strict mode

variable

📦 Variables in JavaScript

▶️ Why variables are needed

📖 Notes

  • JavaScript programs handle information
  • Examples:
    • Online shop → products, cart
    • Chat app → users, messages
  • Variables are used to store data in memory

▶️ What is a variable?

📖 Notes

  • A variable = named storage for data
  • Created using let
letmessage;
  • Assign value using =
message="Hello";
  • Access value by name:
alert(message);
  • Can also declare + assign in one line:
letmessage="Hello";

▶️ Multiple variables

📖 Notes

  • Multiple declarations possible:
letuser="John",age=25,message="Hi";
  • ❌ Not recommended (bad readability)
  • Better style:
letuser="John";
letage=25;
letmessage="Hi";

▶️ var vs let

📖 Notes

  • var = old way
  • let = modern standard
  • Differences exist but not important yet
  • let should be used in modern code

▶️ How variables behave (real-life analogy)

📖 Notes

  • Variable = box with label
  • Value is stored inside box
  • Value can be changed
letmessage="Hello";
message="World";
  • Old value is replaced

▶️ Copying variables

📖 Notes

lethello="Hello";
letmessage=hello;
  • Both variables now contain same value

▶️ Re-declaration error

📖 Notes

  • Variable can be declared only once
letmessage="Hi";
letmessage="Bye";// ❌ Error

▶️ Variable naming rules

📖 Notes

  • Allowed:
    • letters
    • digits
    • $ and _
  • ❌ Cannot start with number

✔️ Valid:

letuserName;
let$;
let_;

❌ Invalid:

let1a;// error
letmy-name;// error
  • Naming style: camelCase
    • userName, shoppingCart
  • Case matters:
    • apple ≠ APPLE

▶️ Reserved names

📖 Notes

  • Cannot use JS keywords:
    • let, return, class, function

▶️ Constants

📖 Notes

  • Use const for unchangeable values
constmyBirthday="18.04.1982";
  • ❌ Cannot reassign:
myBirthday="01.01.2000";// error

▶️ Uppercase constants

📖 Notes

  • Used for fixed known values
  • Style: ALL CAPS
constCOLOR_RED="#F00";
  • Used as aliases for hard-coded values
  • Improves readability and prevents mistakes

▶️ Naming best practices

📖 Notes

  • Use meaningful names:
    • userName, shoppingCart
  • Avoid:
    • a, b, data, value
  • Be consistent with team naming
  • Good naming = better code understanding

▶️ Reusing variables (bad practice)

📖 Notes

  • Reusing variables causes confusion
  • Makes debugging harder
  • Better to create new variables
  • Modern engines optimize extra variables anyway

▶️ Summary

📖 Notes

  • let → modern variable
  • var → old style
  • const → unchangeable variable
  • Variables store data in memory
  • Good naming is extremely important

Data types

Here is your Notion-ready structured notes (Notes first → Questions after) 👇

📊 Data Types in JavaScript

▶️ Introduction to Data Types

📖 Notes

  • Every value in JavaScript has a type
  • Example types:
    • string
    • number
  • JavaScript has 8 basic data types
  • Variables are dynamically typed:
    • A variable can change type at runtime
letmessage="hello";
message=123456;// valid

🔢 Number Type

📖 Notes

  • Represents:
    • integers
    • floating-point numbers
letn=123;
letm=12.345;
  • Supports operations:
    • +, , , /

▶️ Special numeric values

📖 Notes

  • Infinity → mathematical infinity
  • Infinity → negative infinity
  • NaN → Not a Number (error result)
alert(1/0);// Infinity
alert("abc"/2);// NaN

▶️ NaN behavior

📖 Notes

  • NaN is sticky
  • Any operation with NaN → NaN
NaN+1;// NaN
  • Exception:
    • NaN ** 0 = 1

▶️ Safety of math operations

📖 Notes

  • JS does NOT crash on bad math
  • Instead returns:
    • NaN
    • Infinity

🧠 BigInt

📖 Notes

  • Number type cannot safely handle very large integers
  • Safe range:
    • ±(2^53 − 1)
  • BigInt allows arbitrary large integers
constbig=1234567890123456789012345678901234567890n;
  • Created by adding n at the end

📝 String Type

📖 Notes

  • Strings are written in quotes:
leta="Hello";
letb='Hello';
letc=`Hello`;

▶️ 3 types of quotes

  • " " → double quotes
  • ' ' → single quotes
  • → backticks

▶️ Backticks (Template Strings)

📖 Notes

  • Allow embedding expressions:
letname="John";
console.log(`Hello${name}`);
console.log(`Result:${1+2}`);
  • Only backticks support ${...}

🔤 No Character Type

📖 Notes

  • JS does NOT have char
  • Only:
    • string
  • Even single characters are strings

🔘 Boolean Type

📖 Notes

  • Only two values:
    • true
    • false
letisChecked=true;
  • Used for:
    • yes/no
    • conditions
  • Result of comparisons:
4>1;// true

🚫 null

📖 Notes

  • Special value meaning:
    • “empty”
    • “unknown”
  • Not object reference
letage=null;

❓ undefined

📖 Notes

  • Means:
    • value not assigned
letage;
console.log(age);// undefined
  • Can be manually assigned (not recommended)

🧱 Objects & Symbols

📖 Notes

  • Primitive types → single values
  • Object → complex data structure (collections)
  • Symbol:
    • creates unique identifiers
    • advanced topic (later)

🔍 typeof operator

📖 Notes

  • Used to check type of value
typeof123;// "number"
typeof"hi";// "string"

▶️ Special cases

  • typeof null → "object" ❌ (bug)
  • typeof alert → "function"
  • Functions are treated specially

▶️ Syntax forms

typeofx
typeof(x)
  • Both are same
  • typeof is an operator, not a function

Alert, Promt, Confirm

💬 Interaction in JavaScript (alert, prompt, confirm)

▶️ Introduction

📖 Notes

  • JavaScript provides browser interaction functions
  • Used to communicate with users
  • These functions are modal
    • Block page interaction until closed
  • Main 3 functions:
    • alert
    • prompt
    • confirm

🚨 alert()

📖 Notes

  • Shows a simple message box
  • Waits until user clicks OK
  • Blocks page interaction
alert("Hello");
  • Called a modal window
    • User cannot interact with page until closed

✍️ prompt()

📖 Notes

  • Used to get input from user
  • Syntax:
result=prompt(title, [default]);

Parameters:

  • title → message shown to user
  • default → initial input value (optional)

▶️ Behavior

  • User types input → returns text
  • User clicks Cancel / Esc → returns null
letage=prompt("How old are you?",100);
alert(`You are${age} years old`);

⚠️ Important note (IE)

  • If default is missing → IE shows "undefined"
  • Always provide empty string for safety:
prompt("Test","");

✅ confirm()

📖 Notes

  • Shows OK / Cancel dialog
  • Used for yes/no decisions
letisBoss=confirm("Are you the boss?");

Returns:

  • true → OK clicked
  • false → Cancel clicked

📦 Summary of all 3 functions

📖 Notes

alert()

  • Shows message
  • No input
  • Blocks page

prompt()

  • Gets user input
  • Returns:
    • string or null

confirm()

  • Yes/No question
  • Returns:
    • true or false

⚠️ Common limitations

📖 Notes

  • All are modal
    • stop script execution
  • Browser controls:
    • Position (usually center)
    • Style (cannot be changed)
  • Not customizable UI

Type Conversions in JavaScript

▶️ Introduction

📖 Notes

  • JavaScript automatically converts values between types
  • Happens in operations like math, output, and conditions
  • Sometimes we need explicit conversion

🧵 String Conversion

📖 Notes

  • Converts any value → string
  • Happens automatically in alert()
  • Can be done manually:
String(value);
  • Examples:
    • true → "true"
    • null → "null"

🧠 Questions (3-line answers)

<details>
<summary>Click to expand</summary>

1. What is string conversion?

String conversion changes any value into text form.

It happens automatically in functions like alert().

We can also use String(value) manually.

2. When does string conversion happen?

It happens when JavaScript needs to display values.

For example, in alert or console output.

Also when we explicitly call String().

3. What happens to true and false?

true becomes "true" as a string.

false becomes "false" as a string.

All values are converted into readable text.

</details>

🔢 Numeric Conversion

📖 Notes

  • Converts values → numbers
  • Happens automatically in math operations
"6"/"2"// 3
  • Manual conversion:
Number("123");

▶️ Rules

  • undefined → NaN
  • null → 0
  • true → 1
  • false → 0
  • invalid string → NaN

🧠 Questions (3-line answers)

<details>
<summary>Click to expand</summary>

1. What is numeric conversion?

Numeric conversion turns values into numbers.

It happens automatically in mathematical operations.

We can also force it using Number().

2. What happens if string is invalid?

If a string cannot be converted, result is NaN.

NaN means Not a Number error state.

It shows conversion failure in JavaScript.

3. What does null become?

null becomes 0 in numeric conversion.

It represents an empty or missing value.

So JS treats it as zero.

4. What does undefined become?

undefined becomes NaN in numeric conversion.

It means value was never assigned.

So JS cannot convert it to number.

</details>

🔘 Boolean Conversion

📖 Notes

  • Converts values → true / false
  • Used in conditions and logic
Boolean(value);

▶️ Rules

  • Falsy:
    • 0
    • ""
    • null
    • undefined
    • NaN
  • Everything else → true

🧠 Questions (3-line answers)

<details>
<summary>Click to expand</summary>

1. What is boolean conversion?

Boolean conversion changes values into true or false.

It is used in conditions like if statements.

It can also be done using Boolean().

2. What values are false?

0, empty string, null, undefined, and NaN are false.

These are called falsy values in JavaScript.

They represent absence or emptiness.

3. What values are true?

All values except falsy ones are true.

Even "0" and " " (space) are true.

Because they are non-empty strings.

4. Is "0" true or false?

"0" is true in JavaScript.

Because it is a non-empty string.

Only empty string "" is false.

</details>

📌 Summary

📖 Notes

  • 3 main conversions:
    • String → display
    • Number → math
    • Boolean → logic
  • Key rules:
    • "0" → true (boolean)
    • null → 0
    • undefined → NaN

🧠 Final Questions (3-line answers)

<details>
<summary>Click to expand</summary>

1. What are the 3 type conversions?

There are string, number, and boolean conversions.

They happen automatically in JavaScript operations.

We can also do them manually using functions.

2. When does string conversion happen?

It happens when values are shown to user.

For example in alert or console.log.

Also when using String() function.

3. When does numeric conversion happen?

It happens during math operations like + or /.

Also when using Number() function explicitly.

Used when working with numeric input.

4. When does boolean conversion happen?

It happens in conditions and logical checks.

Also when using Boolean() function.

Used for decision making in code.

</details>

Object.keys / values / entries (Deep Dive)

1. What they are (core idea)

These methods convert an object → iterable array representation:

Object.keys(obj)// ["key1", "key2"]
Object.values(obj)// [value1, value2]
Object.entries(obj)// [["key1", value1], ["key2", value2]]

👉 They let you treat objects like arrays → unlock map, filter, etc.

2. Internal behavior (important)

When you call:

Object.keys(obj)

JavaScript engine:

  1. Iterates over all enumerable own properties
  1. Skips:
    • prototype properties
    • non-enumerable properties
    • symbol keys

👉 This is similar to for...in but safer (no prototype chain)

3. Time Complexity (VERY IMPORTANT)

Let n = number of properties

🔹 Object.keys(obj)

Object.keys(obj)

Complexity

Time:  O(n)
Space: O(n)

Why?

  • Iterates over all keys → O(n)
  • Creates new array → O(n)

🔹 Object.values(obj)

Object.values(obj)

Complexity

Time:  O(n)
Space: O(n)

Same reasoning:

  • iterate all properties
  • store values in array

🔹 Object.entries(obj)

Object.entries(obj)

Complexity

Time:  O(n)
Space: O(n)

But slightly heavier:

  • creates nested arrays [key, value]

⚠️ Important Insight

These are NOT constant time operations

Object.keys(bigObject)

👉 If bigObject has 100k keys → you just did O(n) work

4. Iteration Cost vs Direct Access

Direct access

obj.name

👉 O(1)

Using Object.keys

Object.keys(obj).includes("name")

👉 O(n)

🔥 Big difference in real systems.

5. Real-world Performance Insight

In backend systems (like your CRM):

❌ Bad:

Object.keys(users).forEach(...)

on every request for large object

👉 costly

✅ Better:

  • use Map
  • use indexed structure
  • avoid repeated full scans

6. Map vs Object (deep difference)

FeatureObjectMap
keys typestring/symbolany
iterationObject.keysmap.keys()
return typearrayiterator
performanceslower for large dynamic databetter

👉 Important:

map.keys()→ iterator (lazy)
Object.keys()→ full array (eager)

⚡ Performance implication

for (letkeyofmap.keys()) {}

👉 memory efficient

for (letkeyofObject.keys(obj)) {}

👉 creates full array first

7. Transforming Objects (Deep Explanation)

This pattern is VERY important:

Object.fromEntries(
Object.entries(obj).map(...)
)

Step-by-step complexity

1. Object.entries(obj)

→ O(n)

2. .map(...)

→ O(n)

3. Object.fromEntries(...)

→ O(n)

Final Complexity

Time:  O(n)
Space: O(n)

👉 but 3 passes over data

⚠️ Performance insight

For large data:

Object.entries→ map → fromEntries

👉 creates multiple intermediate arrays

🔥 Optimized version (single pass)

functiondoublePrices(obj) {
constresult= {};

for (letkeyinobj) {
result[key]=obj[key]*2;
  }

returnresult;
}

👉 Still O(n), but:

  • no intermediate arrays
  • lower memory usage

8. Hidden Costs (Senior-level insight)

❗ Garbage Collection pressure

Object.entries(obj).map(...)

creates:

  • entries array
  • mapped array
  • new object

👉 more GC work

❗ Memory overhead

For large objects:

  • entries array = big
  • intermediate arrays = big

👉 In high-performance systems → avoid chaining

9. Symbol Keys Behavior

constsym=Symbol("id");

constobj= {
  name:"Ali",
  [sym]:123
};

Object.keys(obj)// ["name"]
Object.values(obj)// ["Ali"]
Object.entries(obj)// [["name", "Ali"]]

👉 Symbols are ignored

To include symbols:

Reflect.ownKeys(obj)

👉 returns:

["name",Symbol(id)]

10. Order of Keys (important)

JS objects maintain order:

  1. integer-like keys (sorted)
  1. string keys (in insertion order)
  1. symbol keys

Example:

constobj= {
2:"b",
1:"a",
  name:"Ali"
};

Object.keys(obj)
// ["1", "2", "name"]

11. Real Use Cases

🔹 Sum values

functionsumSalaries(salaries) {
letsum=0;

for (letvalueofObject.values(salaries)) {
sum+=value;
  }

returnsum;
}

Complexity:

Time: O(n)
Space: O(n) (values array)

🔹 Optimized version (no extra array)

functionsumSalaries(salaries) {
letsum=0;

for (letkeyinsalaries) {
sum+=salaries[key];
  }

returnsum;
}

Complexity:

Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)

👉 Better for large data

12. When to use what

Use Object.keys / values / entries when:

  • working with small-medium objects
  • using array methods (map/filter)
  • readability is priority

Avoid them when:

  • object is very large
  • performance critical path
  • inside loops
  • high-frequency backend logic

13. Advanced Insight (VERY IMPORTANT)

❗ Anti-pattern

for (leti=0;i<1000;i++) {
Object.keys(obj)
}

👉 complexity becomes:

O(n * 1000)

Better

constkeys=Object.keys(obj);

for (leti=0;i<1000;i++) {
// reuse keys
}

14. Summary (Senior-level)

Object.keys/values/entries = O(n)

They:

  • iterate entire object
  • allocate memory
  • create arrays

Key takeaways:

  • not free operations
  • avoid repeated calls
  • prefer single-pass loops in critical code
  • Map is better for dynamic data
  • chaining = readable but less efficient

🚀 Final Insight

👉 For interviews / real systems:

Use Object.entries for clarity
Use for..in for performance
Use Map for scalability
REST PARAMETER

📘 JavaScript – Rest Parameters & Spread Syntax

🔽 What problem are we solving?

  • JS functions can receive any number of arguments
  • But by default, only declared parameters are used
  • We need:
    • A way to collect unlimited arguments
    • A way to expand arrays into arguments

🔹 Rest Parameters (...)

▶️ Definition

  • Used in function parameters to collect remaining arguments into an array
function sumAll(...args) {
  let sum = 0;
  for (let arg of args) sum += arg;
  return sum;
}

▶️ Key Behavior

  • ...args gathers all remaining values into an array
  • Works with any number of inputs
sumAll(1) → 1
sumAll(1,2) → 3
sumAll(1,2,3) → 6

▶️ Mixing with normal parameters

function showName(firstName, lastName, ...titles) {
  // firstName → "Julius"
  // lastName → "Caesar"
  // titles → ["Consul", "Imperator"]
}

⚠️ Important Rule

  • Rest parameter must be last
❌ function f(a, ...rest, b) // ERROR
✅ function f(a, b, ...rest)

🔹 arguments Object (Old Way)

▶️ What is it?

  • Special array-like object containing all arguments
function showName() {
  console.log(arguments[0]);
}

▶️ Problems

  • Not a real array ❌
  • No .map(), .filter() ❌
  • Cannot partially capture arguments ❌

▶️ Important Note

  • Arrow functions ❌ do NOT have arguments
function f() {
  let arrow = () => console.log(arguments[0]);
}

✅ Conclusion

  • Prefer rest parameters over arguments

🔹 Spread Syntax (...)

▶️ Definition

  • Used to expand iterable (array/string) into individual values

▶️ Example (Math.max problem)

let arr = [3,5,1];

Math.max(arr) ❌ → NaN
Math.max(...arr) ✅ → 5

▶️ Combine multiple arrays

Math.max(...arr1, ...arr2)

▶️ Mix with values

Math.max(1, ...arr1, 2, ...arr2, 25)

🔹 Array Merging

let merged = [0, ...arr1, 2, ...arr2];

Result:

[0, ...arr1, 2, ...arr2]

🔹 Spread with Strings

let str = "Hello";
[...str] → ["H","e","l","l","o"]

▶️ Why it works?

  • Spread uses iterators internally
  • Same behavior as for...of

🔹 Spread vs Array.from

▶️ Similar

[...str]
Array.from(str)

▶️ Difference

FeatureSpreadArray.from
Works with iterable✅✅
Works with array-like❌✅

🔹 Copying Arrays

let arrCopy = [...arr];

▶️ Behavior

  • Creates new reference
  • Does NOT affect original
arr === arrCopy → false

🔹 Copying Objects

let objCopy = { ...obj };

▶️ Important Concept

  • This is a shallow copy
  • Nested objects are still shared

🔥 Key Differences (INTERVIEW GOLD)

▶️ Rest vs Spread

FeatureRest (...)Spread (...)
UsageFunction paramsFunction calls / arrays
PurposeCollect valuesExpand values
OutputArrayIndividual elements

▶️ Mental Model

Rest  → "collect"
Spread → "expand"

🚀 Real-World Use Cases

▶️ Flexible APIs

function log(...messages)

▶️ Merging data

const full = [...arr1, ...arr2]

▶️ Cloning state (React)

setState({ ...prevState, newValue })

🧠 Interview Traps

⚠️ 1. Rest must be last

⚠️ 2. Spread only works with iterable

⚠️ 3. arguments is not an array

⚠️ 4. Spread = shallow copy

⚠️ 5. Arrow functions don’t have arguments

✅ Final Summary

  • ... has two meanings
    • Rest → collect into array
    • Spread → expand into values
  • Prefer rest over arguments
  • Use spread for:
    • Function calls
    • Copying
    • Merging
  • Core concept:
    • 👉 Rest = input handling
    • 👉 Spread = output expansion
